He was asked how long he stayed, and said "a day or part of a day." He was told: "Rather, you remained a hundred years." Look at your food and drink, which has not changed, and at your donkey, which is bones.
Then Allah put flesh on the bones of the donkey before his eyes. The man said: "I know that Allah is over all things competent."
l: Resurrection is a sign the Qur’an returns to again and again.
Time is under Allah’s control: food stayed fresh while the donkey decayed.
The questions of believers are answered by showing, not scolding.

stories.title: Arabia before the Prophet ﷺ
p: To understand the Prophet’s ﷺ mission, you need to see the world he was born into: a tribal Arabia between two empires, with Makkah as a trading and religious centre, the Kaaba filled with idols, and a society known as the age of ignorance (jahiliyyah).
It was not without virtues, such as generosity, hospitality and bravery, but it was also a land of feuds, fortune-telling, interest, and the burying of daughters.
l: The Qur’an did not come into an empty world: it answered real problems.
Pure monotheism, the religion of Ibrahim, had survived among a few seekers (hanifs).
Every society has good it can build on and wrongs it must leave.
stories.src: Sira of Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Hisham; Qur’an 106, 81:8–9

stories.title: The slander (al-Ifk)
p: On the return from the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq, ‘A’ishah went to look for a lost necklace, and when she returned the caravan had left, thinking she was in her howdah. She waited, and a Companion, Safwan ibn al-Mu’attal, found her and brought her to Madinah on his camel without a word.

The hypocrites, led by ‘Abdullah ibn Ubayy, spread a lie about her. For about a month the Prophet ﷺ and his household were in pain, until Allah revealed ten verses of Surah al-Nur declaring her innocent.
l: Do not pass on what you cannot verify. Allah says: "When you heard it, why did not the believers think good of themselves?"
A slander can hurt a whole household and a community.
Allah’s answer to patience and trust was a public revelation.
stories.src: Qur’an 24:11–20; Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (‘A’ishah)

stories.title: The Year of Delegations
p: After the conquest of Makkah and Tabuk, deputations arrived from across Arabia to meet the Prophet ﷺ and accept Islam, so many that the ninth year was named the Year of Delegations. Surah al-Nasr describes it: "you see people entering the religion of Allah in multitudes."

He received them in the courtyard of the mosque, honoured them and taught them. He also sent men to teach and judge among them: Mu’adh ibn Jabal and Abu Musa to Yemen, ‘Ali, Khalid and others to different regions.
l: When the Prophet ﷺ gave the first call he was alone; within twenty years the Peninsula was Muslim.
The sending of Mu’adh shows how the faith was taught gradually: first tawhid, then prayer, then zakah.
The year of victory was a year of humility.
stories.src: Qur’an 110; Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim; Sira

stories.title: The Prophet at home
p: Those who knew him best, his family and his servants, are our best witnesses. ‘A’ishah said he used to be "in the service of his family", sewing his own clothes and mending his shoes, and when the prayer was called, he would go out.

He was gentle with children, spent time with his wives, joked, listened, and raced. And in his own words: "The best of you are the best to their families, and I am the best of you to my family." (Sunan al-Tirmidhi)
l: Real character shows at home.
He did not think household work beneath a leader.
He loved and expressed it: he told people when he loved them.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, Sunan al-Tirmidhi, Sunan Abi Dawud

stories.title: A day in his life
p: He slept early, woke in the last third of the night and prayed until his feet were swollen. When ‘A’ishah asked why, since his past and future sins had been forgiven, he said: "Should I not be a grateful servant?"
His days were full of prayer, teaching, visiting the sick, resolving disputes, and time with his family. He ate simply, smiled often and never criticised food.
l: The greatest man in history stayed the most grateful.
He lived simply by choice.
The Companions described him as always smiling.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, Sunan al-Tirmidhi (Shama’il)

stories.title: Mercy to animals and the earth
p: The Prophet ﷺ taught that kindness to animals can earn forgiveness, and cruelty can earn punishment. A man forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog; a woman punished for locking up a cat.
He told people not to overload their camels, to sharpen the knife before slaughtering, and not to burn an ants’ nest.
l: Mercy extends beyond people to all creatures.
Whatever has a moist liver has a reward in kindness.
Trees and water are a trust, not only a resource.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, Sunan Abi Dawud

stories.title: Hamzah, the lion of Allah
p: Hamzah was the Prophet’s ﷺ uncle and foster brother, and one of the strongest men in Makkah. He accepted Islam after hearing that Abu Jahl had insulted the Prophet ﷺ, and went to the Kaaba and struck Abu Jahl on the head with his bow.
He fought at Badr and was killed at Uhud by Wahshi. The Prophet ﷺ called him the master of the martyrs.
l: His Islam began in defence of someone dear and grew into conviction.
The Prophet ﷺ wept for him, and was never as sad as on that day.
Wahshi’s later repentance showed that Islam forgave even this.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari; Sira

stories.title: Khalid ibn al-Walid, the sword of Allah
p: Khalid was the great cavalry commander of Quraysh and the one who turned the tide at Uhud. He became Muslim after Hudaybiyyah and fought at Mu’tah, where the Prophet ﷺ called him "a sword among the swords of Allah."
Under Abu Bakr and ‘Umar he led the Muslim armies in Iraq and Syria and was never defeated in battle.
l: A man who was an enemy became a defender once the truth reached him.
Talent used for the cause finds its place.
He asked for martyrdom and died in his bed. He said it was a test of sincerity.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari; Sira

stories.title: Abu Dharr al-Ghifari
p: Abu Dharr lived among the tribe of Ghifar, who were highway robbers. Hearing of a man in Makkah claiming to be a prophet, he sent his brother to investigate and then went himself, stayed in the Sacred Mosque for days, and lived on Zamzam water until he met the Prophet ﷺ.
He accepted Islam, declared it in the mosque and was beaten by Quraysh. He is remembered for plain living, truthfulness and for always speaking the truth to those in power.
l: The search for the truth is worth a long journey.
Zamzam was his food for a month. He said he grew fat and felt no hunger.
The Prophet ﷺ told him to love the poor and speak the truth, even if bitter.
stories.src: Sahih Muslim; Sahih al-Bukhari

stories.title: Abu Hurayrah and the memory of the hadith
p: Abu Hurayrah came from the tribe of Daws in Yemen and accepted Islam in 7 AH at Khaybar. He stayed in the Prophet’s ﷺ mosque as one of the people of the Suffah, living on whatever people shared, and learned by sitting with him.
He prayed for his memory, and it did not fail him. He narrated more hadith than any other Companion.
l: Hunger and poverty did not stop him from learning.
His kindness to his mother is also a lesson.
The Prophet ﷺ gave him a name from a small cat he carried.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (his own accounts)

stories.title: Asma’ bint Abi Bakr, she of the two belts
p: Asma’ was the elder daughter of Abu Bakr and the sister of ‘A’ishah. On the night of the Hijrah, she brought food for the Prophet ﷺ and her father in the cave of Thawr, and tore her waist-belt in two to tie the bag and the water skin. The Prophet ﷺ called her "the one with the two belts."
She emigrated while pregnant and gave birth in Quba to ‘Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, the first Muslim baby born in Madinah.
l: Courage in a woman or a girl can carry a whole mission.
She stood up to Abu Jahl when he asked about her father.
She stayed steady as her son was killed: "Faith is not shaken."
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Hijrah account, Asma’ narrates)

stories.title: Fatimah, the daughter of the Prophet ﷺ
p: Fatimah was the youngest daughter of the Prophet ﷺ and Khadijah, wife of ‘Ali and mother of al-Hasan and al-Husayn. She was in Makkah in the worst years and cleaned the Prophet’s ﷺ back when Quraysh threw camel entrails on him.
In Madinah she lived in poverty. When her hands hurt from grinding grain, she asked her father for a servant and he taught her instead a dhikr, tasbih of Fatimah.
l: A great person’s daughter lived in hardship by choice.
The dhikr he gave her is better than a servant.
He called her "a part of me."
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim

stories.title: Zayd ibn Harithah, the beloved
p: Zayd was captured as a boy in a raid, sold as a slave in Makkah and ended up in the service of Khadijah, who gave him to the Prophet ﷺ. When his father and uncle came to pay a ransom and take him home, the Prophet ﷺ let Zayd choose. Zayd said: "I will not prefer anyone to you."
The Prophet ﷺ freed him and announced that he was his son. Zayd is the only Companion named in the Qur’an.
l: Love and good treatment can make a person choose servitude with the right master over freedom among his own.
Islam raised a former slave to be a general.
The Prophet ﷺ loved him and his son Usamah.
stories.src: Sira; Sahih al-Bukhari; Qur’an 33:37

stories.title: Abu ‘Ubaydah, the trustworthy one of the ummah
p: Abu ‘Ubaydah ‘Amir ibn ‘Abdullah ibn al-Jarrah was among the first to accept Islam through Abu Bakr and one of the ten promised Paradise. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Every nation has a trustworthy one, and the trustworthy one of this nation is Abu ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah."
At Uhud, he pulled out the rings of the Prophet’s ﷺ helmet with his teeth, losing his front teeth, and was called the best of men for it.
l: Trustworthiness can be a title.
He was a leader who was modest. Told to command, he refused to take credit.
He chose to stay with his men in the plague, and died with them.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim

stories.title: Mu’adh ibn Jabal, the scholar of halal and haram
p: Mu’adh accepted Islam as a young man in Madinah, at the second pledge of ‘Aqabah. He became one of the greatest scholars among the Companions. The Prophet ﷺ said: "The most knowledgeable of my nation in halal and haram is Mu’adh ibn Jabal."
When he was sent to Yemen as a teacher and judge, the Prophet ﷺ walked with him to give him advice, and told him: "O Mu’adh, perhaps you will not see me after this year."
l: The Prophet ﷺ told him: "By Allah I love you," and then gave him a dua to say after every prayer.
Judgement requires first knowing the Qur’an, then the Sunnah, then reasoning.
He taught people to recite and to remember Allah.
stories.src: Sunan al-Tirmidhi, Sunan Abi Dawud, Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim

stories.title: Suhayb al-Rumi, the profitable trade
p: Suhayb was a Byzantine-born man raised among Arabs, who became rich in Makkah. When he decided to emigrate to Madinah, Quraysh stopped him and said that he had come with nothing and would not leave with wealth. He gave them all his possessions in return for being allowed to go.
The Prophet ﷺ, when he heard, is reported to have said: "Profitable trade, Abu Yahya!" and verse 2:207 is said to have been revealed about him.
l: Faith is worth everything a person owns.
He was the narrator of the story of the trench and the boy, which shows a man with faith remembered what faith costs.
‘Umar chose him to lead the prayer at his funeral.
stories.src: Sira; al-Hakim; Sahih Muslim (Suhayb narrates the boy and the king)

stories.title: Thumamah, tied to the pillar
p: The Prophet ﷺ’s horsemen captured a man and brought him to the mosque, tying him to a pillar. It was Thumamah ibn Uthal, chief of Banu Hanifah, who had been an enemy. The Prophet ﷺ asked: "What do you have, Thumamah?" He said: "Good, O Muhammad. If you kill me, you kill a man of blood; if you pardon, you pardon one who is thankful; if you want wealth, ask and you will get it."

For three days, the Prophet ﷺ asked and he gave the same answer. Then he said: "Release Thumamah." He went to a palm grove, washed and returned, and said: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His Messenger."
l: The Prophet ﷺ treated a prisoner with dignity in his own mosque.
Kindness changed Thumamah from the person he hated most to the person he loved most.
Thumamah protected Muslims later by refusing Makkah grain.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (Abu Hurayrah)

stories.title: Hatim’s daughter and her brother ‘Adi
p: After a raid on the tribe of Tayy, the Muslims captured the daughter of Hatim al-Ta’i, who was famed for generosity. She stood before the Prophet ﷺ and said: "My father has died and the one who looked after me is absent. Do me a favour, and Allah will favour you." The Prophet ﷺ freed her, gave her clothes and travel money, and sent her to her people.
She found her brother ‘Adi, a Christian chieftain who had fled to Syria, and told him what she had seen. He went to meet the Prophet ﷺ and became a Muslim.
l: Good treatment of a woman prisoner opened a chieftain’s heart.
The Prophet ﷺ honoured her as the daughter of a generous man.
‘Adi’s conversion shows how stories of the Prophet’s ﷺ conduct spread.
stories.src: Sira of Ibn Ishaq; Sunan al-Tirmidhi (‘Adi on 9:31); Sahih al-Bukhari (‘Adi’s words on the Hajj and the lady of Hira)

stories.title: The three trapped in the cave
p: The Prophet ﷺ told of three men who took shelter in a cave when a huge rock rolled down and sealed the entrance. They could not move it, and they agreed that the only way out was to call upon Allah by mentioning a good deed each had done purely for His sake.

One had served his elderly parents before anyone else. One had resisted a wrong he could easily have committed out of fear of Allah. One had kept and increased the wages of a worker who forgot them, and returned the whole of it. After each prayer the rock shifted a little, until it opened and they walked out.
l: A deed done in secret, only for Allah, can become a way out in the hardest moment.
Kindness to parents, restraint from sin and honesty with money are three ways of showing taqwa.
Calling on Allah by a good deed (tawassul by righteous deeds) is a form of dua the Prophet ﷺ taught through this story.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 2272 and 3465, Sahih Muslim 2743 (narrated by Ibn ‘Umar)

stories.title: The man who killed ninety-nine
p: A man from the people before had killed ninety-nine people. He asked who was the most knowledgeable person on earth and was directed to a monk. He asked the monk if there was repentance for him. The monk said no, and the man killed him too, making one hundred.

He asked again and was sent to a scholar, who told him that nothing stands between him and repentance, and that he should leave his land of evil and go to a land of worshippers of Allah. On the way he died, and the angels of mercy and the angels of punishment disputed over him. Allah ordered the distance to be measured, and he was found closer to the land of the righteous, so the angels of mercy took him.
l: No sin is greater than Allah’s mercy for the one who sincerely turns back.
Real repentance includes leaving the place and company that lead you to the sin.
A knowledgeable adviser gives hope without making sin light, while a hasty one can push someone to despair.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 3470, Sahih Muslim 2766 (narrated by Abu Sa’id al-Khudri)

stories.title: The leper, the bald man and the blind man
p: The Prophet ﷺ told of three men of Bani Isra’il, a leper, a bald man and a blind man, whom Allah wished to test. He sent an angel to each in turn. Each was asked what he wished for most, and each was healed and given wealth: camels, cows and sheep.

The angel then returned to each, disguised as a poor traveller, asking for a little help. The first two denied it and claimed the wealth was inherited, and they lost it all. The blind man replied that Allah had restored his sight and that he could take whatever he wished, for he would never hold back anything taken for Allah’s sake. The angel told him that he was pleased with him, and displeased with the other two.
l: Blessings are a test of gratitude as much as hardship is a test of patience.
Admitting that everything is from Allah makes generosity easy.
Forgetting where wealth came from, and who helped us when we had nothing, is a danger that comes with rising up.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 3464, Sahih Muslim 2964 (narrated by Abu Hurayrah)

stories.title: Jurayj, the monk who was patient
p: Jurayj was a devoted worshipper among Bani Isra’il who had built a small hermitage to pray in. While he was praying one day, his mother called him. He said: "My Lord, my mother and my prayer," and carried on praying. She called a second and third time, and each time he continued, so she said: "O Allah, do not let him die until he sees the faces of prostitutes."

Afterwards a woman accused him falsely, saying that he was the father of her baby. When people came to tear down his hermitage, he prayed, touched the baby and asked who his father was. The baby spoke and named a shepherd. The people offered to rebuild the hermitage in gold, but he asked only for clay as it had been.
l: A parent’s call is serious enough that it can outweigh a voluntary prayer.
Allah protects His sincere servants and can clear them in ways nobody expects.
Do not be quick to judge a righteous person on a rumour.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 1206, 3436, Sahih Muslim 2550 (narrated by Abu Hurayrah)

stories.title: The loan sent across the sea
p: The Prophet ﷺ told of a man from Bani Isra’il who asked another for a loan of a thousand dinars. The lender asked for witnesses; the borrower said: "Allah is sufficient as a witness." The lender asked for a guarantor; the borrower said: "Allah is sufficient as a guarantor." The lender said: "You have spoken the truth," and gave him the money for a fixed time.

The borrower crossed the sea, but could not find a ship to return on the day the debt was due. He cut a piece of wood, hollowed it, put the thousand dinars and a letter inside, sealed it, and threw it into the sea, asking Allah to deliver it. The lender, waiting at the shore for a ship, found the piece of wood and took it home as firewood, and found the money and the letter inside.
l: Trust in Allah and a sincere effort to keep your word go together.
Honesty with a debt is an act of worship, and Allah helps the one who keeps it.
The story shows the borrower doing everything he could, then leaving the rest to Allah.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 2291 and 1498 (narrated by Abu Hurayrah)

stories.title: The woman and the thirsty dog
p: The Prophet ﷺ told of a prostitute from Bani Isra’il who was walking by a well and saw a dog circling it, panting, close to dying of thirst. She took off her leather sock, tied it to her head covering, and drew up water for the dog. Allah forgave her for that.

When the Companions asked whether there is reward in serving animals, he said: "There is a reward in every living creature." In another narration, he also warned of a woman who was punished because of a cat she had tied up and neither fed nor released.
l: A small kindness, done sincerely, can bring forgiveness that a long life of other deeds did not.
Mercy to animals is a part of faith; the Prophet ﷺ made it a ground for reward and for punishment.
We never know which of our deeds Allah will accept, so never belittle a good deed.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 3321, 3467, Sahih Muslim 2245 (narrated by Abu Hurayrah)

stories.title: The merchant who forgave debts
p: The Prophet ﷺ said that there was a man who used to lend to people, and when he saw someone struggling to repay, he told his boys: "Forgive him; perhaps Allah will forgive us." When he met Allah, Allah forgave him.

Another narration adds that Allah said to the angels: "We are more entitled to that than he is. Overlook his faults." The story is told alongside the Prophet’s own teaching that whoever gives time to a debtor in difficulty or forgives him will be in the shade of Allah on the Day of Resurrection.
l: Forgiving others a debt can bring forgiveness for ourselves.
Generosity does not require being rich; a lender can be generous with time and with what he is owed.
Allah treats us the way we treat His servants.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 2078 and 3480, Sahih Muslim 1562 (narrated by Abu Hurayrah and Hudhayfah)

stories.title: The land and the buried gold
p: The Prophet ﷺ told of a man who bought a piece of land from another and found in it a jar of gold. He told the seller: "Take your gold from me; I bought the land from you, not the gold." The seller replied: "I sold you the land and everything in it." Neither would accept the gold.

They took the dispute to a third man, who asked whether they had children. One had a boy and the other a girl. The judge told them to marry the two, to spend on themselves from the gold, and to give charity from it.
l: Honesty can make people compete in giving up what is not theirs.
Sound judgment sometimes finds a settlement better than either side’s demands.
A wealth that comes without being sought can be a trial; handling it well is a mark of faith.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 3472, Sahih Muslim 1721 (narrated by Abu Hurayrah)

stories.title: The prophet and the ant
p: The Prophet ﷺ told of a prophet from the earlier prophets who was resting under a tree when an ant bit him. He had the ant’s whole colony burned. Allah revealed to him: "Because one ant bit you, you burned a whole nation that glorifies Me?"
In one narration, the revelation said: "Why not just one ant?" The story is short, but the Prophet ﷺ kept it among the stories he told.
l: Justice includes proportion: punishing the one who harmed us, not the whole group.
Even the smallest creatures glorify Allah (17:44), and deserve care.
Allah corrects His prophets gently, and the correction was recorded as a lesson for everyone.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 3019, 3319, Sahih Muslim 2241 (narrated by Abu Hurayrah)

stories.title: Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh
p: Asiya lived in the house of the most arrogant ruler of her time, yet believed in the Lord of Musa. The Qur’an holds her up as an example for all believers, men and women: "Allah presents an example of those who believed: the wife of Pharaoh, when she said, My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds, and save me from the wrongdoing people."

She is also the woman who found the baby Musa floating in the river and asked her husband to let him live: "[He will be] a comfort of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him; perhaps he may benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son."
l: Faith does not depend on your surroundings; a believer can stand out in the most hostile home.
Her dua asks for two things: nearness to Allah, and deliverance from a person and his deeds.
Allah used a believing woman in Pharaoh’s palace to protect the prophet who would humble him.
stories.src: Qur’an 66:11, 28:8–9; Sahih al-Bukhari 3411 and Sahih Muslim 2431

stories.title: The mother of Musa
p: Allah inspired the mother of Musa to nurse him, and when she feared for his life, to place him in a chest and cast it into the river, with the promise: "Do not fear and do not grieve. Indeed, We will return him to you and will make him [one] of the messengers."

Her heart became "empty" of everything but Musa, and she would have given away her secret had Allah not strengthened her heart. She sent her daughter to follow him, and Allah returned him to her to nurse: "So We restored him to his mother that her eye might be comforted and not grieve and that she would know that the promise of Allah is true."
l: Trusting Allah may mean doing what looks most dangerous, when He has promised.
Her heart was strengthened because she believed, and a heart bound by faith can bear what seems unbearable.
Allah’s promise is always true, though it may arrive by a route we did not expect.

stories.title: The mother of Maryam
p: The wife of ‘Imran vowed that the child in her womb would be dedicated to Allah. When she gave birth to a girl, she said: "My Lord, I have delivered a female", for she had hoped for a boy to serve in the temple. But Allah knew better what she had delivered: "And the male is not like the female."

She named her Maryam and sought Allah’s protection for her and her descendants from Satan. Allah accepted Maryam "with good acceptance" and made her grow "a good plant". The Prophet ﷺ said that Satan touches every child at birth, except Maryam and her son.
l: A vow made for Allah’s sake shapes a child’s whole life.
The best of plans can look different from what we hoped; Allah’s choice was better than her wish.
Praying for your children, before they are even born, is a long tradition of righteous parents.
stories.src: Qur’an 3:33–37; Sahih al-Bukhari 3431 and Sahih Muslim 2366

stories.title: Umm Salamah, the wise counsellor
p: Hind bint Abi Umayya, known as Umm Salamah, was among the first to migrate to Abyssinia and then to Madinah. When her husband Abu Salama died, she repeated the words the Prophet ﷺ had taught for hardship: "To Allah we belong and to Him we return. O Allah, reward me in my affliction and replace it with something better." She wondered who could be better than Abu Salama, and Allah replaced him with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, whom she later married.

At Hudaybiyyah, when the Companions were stunned by the terms of the treaty and did not move to sacrifice and shave as the Prophet ﷺ commanded, it was she who suggested that he should go out and do it himself without speaking to anyone. When he did, they all followed.
l: Patience in loss, with the words the Prophet ﷺ taught, can turn into an unexpected mercy.
Good counsel is given calmly and at the right moment; a simple action can do what a command could not.
The Prophet ﷺ consulted women and valued their opinion.
stories.src: Sahih Muslim 918; Sahih al-Bukhari 2731–2732 (Hudaybiyyah)

stories.title: Nusaybah bint Ka’b at Uhud
p: Nusaybah bint Ka’b, known as Umm ‘Umarah, was one of the two women who pledged allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ at al-‘Aqabah. At Uhud she came out with water and bandages for the wounded, but when the Muslim lines broke and the Prophet ﷺ was in danger, she took up a sword and fought in front of him.

According to the Sira, the Prophet ﷺ later said that wherever he looked, to his right or his left that day, he saw her fighting for him. She was wounded many times. Years later she fought in the war against the false prophet Musaylimah, in which she lost a hand.
l: Courage shows when others waver, and defending what is right is not restricted to one group.
Women in the first community were present at its hardest moments, not only at its calmest.
The Prophet ﷺ remembered and praised those who protected him.
stories.src: The classical biographies (Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Sa’d); the Uhud account is flagged as reported in the Sira

stories.title: Zaynab, the Prophet’s eldest daughter
p: Zaynab was the eldest daughter of the Prophet ﷺ and Khadijah. She married her cousin Abu al-‘As ibn al-Rabi‘, who did not accept Islam at first and fought with Quraysh at Badr, where he was taken prisoner. Quraysh sent ransom for their captives, and Zaynab sent a necklace that had been her mother Khadijah’s.

When the Prophet ﷺ saw it, he was deeply moved and asked the Muslims to release the prisoner and return the necklace if they were willing. They agreed. He asked Abu al-‘As, in return, to let Zaynab leave Makkah and come to Madinah. Years later, Abu al-‘As accepted Islam, and they were reunited.
l: A keepsake from a loved one carries more than its value; it carries a memory the Prophet ﷺ felt too.
The Prophet ﷺ showed tenderness in front of his Companions, and they responded with generosity.
Patience in a hard marriage and a long separation was rewarded with reunion.
stories.src: Sunan Abi Dawud 2692 (hasan); the classical biographies for the later events

stories.title: Khawlah, whose plea was heard
p: A woman came to the Prophet ﷺ to complain about her husband, who had said a phrase of pre-Islamic divorce (zihar) to her, comparing her to his mother. She spoke to him at length, and the Prophet ﷺ, who had no ruling yet, told her that she seemed to be forbidden to him. She kept saying: "I have little children; if I leave them with him they will starve."

Then Allah revealed Surah al-Mujadilah: "Certainly has Allah heard the speech of the one who argues with you concerning her husband and directs her complaint to Allah. And Allah hears your dialogue; indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing." The surah gave a ruling that protected her family.
l: Allah hears every plea, including those whispered in a corner of a room.
A woman’s voice mattered in the Prophet’s community, and the Qur’an itself replied to her.
Islam corrected an unjust custom and replaced it with a ruling of mercy and responsibility.
stories.src: Qur’an 58:1–4; Sunan Ibn Majah 188 (‘A’ishah’s statement), Sunan Abi Dawud 2214

stories.title: Umm Ayman, the Prophet’s second mother
p: Umm Ayman, named Barakah, was a servant in the household of the Prophet’s father and took care of him from his earliest years, after his mother Aminah died. She stayed with him all his life; he honoured her as family. She married Zayd ibn Harithah, and her son was Usamah.

After the Prophet ﷺ died, Abu Bakr and ‘Umar went to visit her, as the Prophet ﷺ used to. She wept. When they asked why, she said: "I know that what is with Allah is better for His Messenger. I weep because the revelation from heaven has ceased." They wept with her.
l: Loyalty and care for those who looked after us in childhood is part of faith.
Her grief was for the loss of revelation, not only for the loss of a person.
The Prophet ﷺ kept up the bonds of kindness his whole life, and so did his Companions.
stories.src: Sahih Muslim 2454 (narrated by Anas); the classical biographies for her earlier life

stories.title: Hafsa and the first copy of the Qur’an
p: Hafsa bint ‘Umar was the daughter of ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab and a wife of the Prophet ﷺ. After the Battle of Yamamah, where many reciters of the Qur’an were killed, ‘Umar urged Abu Bakr to have the Qur’an collected in one place. Zayd ibn Thabit gathered it from the written records and from the memories of the Companions.

The pages were kept first by Abu Bakr, then by ‘Umar, then by Hafsa. When ‘Uthman decided to produce standard copies for the cities, he borrowed those pages from her, and when the copies were made, he returned them to her.
l: Allah preserved the Qur’an through both memory and writing, by the hands of ordinary people.
The trust of the first complete copy was placed with a woman, and she kept it faithfully.
The Qur’an we read today is the one the Companions took care to preserve exactly.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 4986 and 4679 (narrated by Zayd ibn Thabit and Anas)

stories.title: Rufaydah, the first nurse in Islam
p: Rufaydah al-Aslamiyyah was a woman of the Ansar who is remembered in the Sira as having treated the wounded in a tent in the mosque of Madinah. When Sa’d ibn Mu’adh was wounded in the Battle of the Trench, the Prophet ﷺ ordered that he be placed in her tent, so that he could visit him from nearby.
The reports describe her as skilled in caring for the sick, and she trained other women, and cared for those who could not pay. She is often named as one of the first nurses in the history of Islam.
l: Caring for the sick is a service that the first Muslims valued and organised.
The mosque was a place for the whole community, including the injured.
The Prophet ﷺ made a place for a woman’s skill to serve the community.
stories.src: The classical biographies (Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Sa’d); the tent of Rufaydah is reported in the Sira

stories.title: Fatima al-Fihri and the Qarawiyyin
p: In the ninth century, a woman named Fatima bint Muhammad al-Fihri, from a family that had migrated from Qayrawan in Tunisia to Fez in Morocco, used her inheritance to found a mosque that grew into a centre of learning. It became known as al-Qarawiyyin, after her family’s home city, and its teaching circles grew into one of the oldest continuously operating educational institutions in the world.

Tradition says that she fasted until the building was complete. Her sister Maryam is said to have founded the mosque of al-Andalusiyyin in the same city. The Qarawiyyin library and school drew students and scholars from across the Muslim world and Europe for centuries.
l: Wealth used to build lasting knowledge continues to give reward long after its owner (sadaqah jariyah).
The first great institution of its kind was founded by a woman, from her own wealth.
A mosque in Islam is a school as much as a place of prayer.
stories.src: Later histories of Fez (al-Jaznai’s Zahrat al-As and the Rawd al-Qirtas, fourteenth century), summarised in modern works; details of her life come from tradition and are not well documented

stories.title: Al-Hasan al-Basri
p: Al-Hasan al-Basri was born in Madinah in the caliphate of ‘Umar and grew up among the Companions. His mother was a freed servant of Umm Salamah, who is reported to have cared for him as a child. He later settled in Basra, where his sermons and his example of detachment from the world drew a great number of students.

He is remembered as one of the great figures of the generation after the Companions, the tabi’un. His sayings about the Hereafter, the heart and sincerity were collected by later scholars, and many of the paths of spiritual education trace themselves back to him.
l: The knowledge of the Companions was passed on through personal company, not only through books.
A scholar’s authority came from how he lived as well as what he knew.
The reminder of death and the Hereafter is the centre of his teaching.
stories.src: Classical biographical works (Ibn Sa’d’s Tabaqat, al-Dhahabi’s Siyar A’lam al-Nubala’)

stories.title: Abu Hanifa
p: Al-Nu’man ibn Thabit, known as Abu Hanifa, was a cloth merchant of Kufa who became one of the foremost jurists in Islam. He studied for years under Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, and then taught himself in the same mosque, where a circle of students gathered around him.

He did not write a large body of books himself; his students, above all Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani, recorded and developed his legal reasoning. He is reported to have refused an offer of the post of chief judge, preferring his independence, and died in Baghdad in 150 AH. The Hanafi school, named after him, is today followed by a large part of the Muslim world.
l: A skilled trade can support independence in knowledge.
Careful reasoning from the sources, with respect for the views of others, was a mark of the early jurists.
Scholars may differ in method and each be sincere; later generations built on both.
stories.src: Classical biographies (al-Khatib al-Baghdadi’s Tarikh Baghdad, al-Dhahabi); the circumstances of his death differ between reports

stories.title: Malik ibn Anas
p: Malik ibn Anas lived his whole life in Madinah, the city of the Prophet ﷺ, and taught in his mosque for decades. He is the author of the Muwatta’, one of the earliest surviving collections of hadith and rulings, built around the practice of the people of Madinah.

He studied under many scholars of the generation after the Companions, among them Nafi’, the freed servant of Ibn ‘Umar, and Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri. His students included al-Shafi’i. It is reported that he held the Prophet’s city in such esteem that he avoided riding an animal in its streets.
l: Respect for the Prophet’s city and his Sunnah showed in the way the scholar lived.
A scholar says "I do not know" when he does not know.
The practice of a community that lived next to the Prophet ﷺ counted, for him, as evidence.
stories.src: Classical biographies (al-Qadi ‘Iyad’s Tartib al-Madarik; al-Dhahabi’s Siyar); the Muwatta’ itself

stories.title: Al-Shafi’i
p: Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi’i was born in Gaza, and his mother took him to Makkah when he was small. He was orphaned and poor, and is said to have written on bones and scraps because he could not afford paper. He memorised the Qur’an at a young age and then the Muwatta’ of Malik, before travelling to Madinah to study with Malik himself.

He later taught in Baghdad and finally in Egypt, where he wrote his major work, al-Risalah, which set out how the sources of Islamic law are to be used. He died in Fustat in 204 AH. He is regarded as the founder of the science of the foundations of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).
l: Poverty did not stop a determined student of knowledge.
He gave the Sunnah a defined place as a source of law next to the Qur’an, with clear rules.
A scholar who learned from many places made his view broader.
stories.src: Classical biographies (al-Bayhaqi’s Manaqib al-Shafi’i, al-Dhahabi); al-Risalah itself

stories.title: Ahmad ibn Hanbal and the trial
p: Ahmad ibn Hanbal was a hadith scholar of Baghdad who travelled widely to gather narrations, and compiled them in the Musnad. In his time the caliph al-Ma’mun and his successors tried to force scholars to say that the Qur’an was created, a doctrine of the Mu’tazila that the scholars of hadith rejected as contrary to what the Companions had said.

Ahmad refused to say it, was imprisoned and flogged under al-Mu’tasim, and held to his position until the policy was ended under al-Mutawakkil. His steadfastness is the reason many remember him as the "Imam of Ahl al-Sunnah".
l: Standing firm on the truth can cost something real.
He did not rebel against the ruler, but he would not say what he believed was false.
The people who admired him were those who saw that he kept to what the Companions had taught.
stories.src: Classical biographies (Ibn al-Jawzi’s Manaqib al-Imam Ahmad, al-Dhahabi, Ibn Kathir’s al-Bidayah); accounts of the beatings differ in detail

stories.title: Al-Bukhari and the Sahih
p: Muhammad ibn Isma’il al-Bukhari was born in Bukhara, in what is now Uzbekistan. He lost his father early, memorised hadith from a young age, and set out in his teens to collect reports from scholars in many cities. His Sahih, "The Authentic Collection", took some sixteen years to compile, and he is said to have prayed two rak’ahs before including each hadith.

He chose from a very large number of narrations the ones that met his strict conditions, and the book became, with Sahih Muslim, the most trusted collection of hadith. He died in 256 AH, in a village near Samarqand.
l: Preserving the Sunnah required years of travel, memory and checking.
He applied the same high standard to every report, including those he was fond of.
The effort of ordinary scholars preserved the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ.
stories.src: Classical biographies (al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, Ibn Hajar’s Hadi al-Sari); the numbers and anecdotes are traditional and are given as reported

stories.title: Al-Ghazali’s search for certainty
p: Abu Hamid al-Ghazali was the most famous professor in Baghdad, teaching at the Nizamiyya madrasa, when in 488 AH (1095 CE) he suffered a crisis. By his own account, he found he could no longer speak, his digestion failed, and he realised that his teaching was driven partly by the desire for fame. He left Baghdad, gave up his position, and spent years travelling and living in retreat.

He wrote about the experience in al-Munqidh min al-Dalal ("Deliverance from Error"), and during this period wrote his best-known work, Ihya’ ‘Ulum al-Din, "The Revival of the Religious Sciences". He later returned to teaching and died in Tus in 505 AH.
l: Even a great scholar must check his intentions.
Knowledge without a purified heart is incomplete.
He sought certainty honestly, and did not hide his doubts.
stories.src: Al-Ghazali’s own al-Munqidh min al-Dalal, and classical biographies (al-Subki, al-Dhahabi)

stories.title: Imam al-Nawawi
p: Yahya ibn Sharaf al-Nawawi was born in the village of Nawa, near Damascus, in 631 AH. He memorised the Qur’an as a child and, at nineteen, was sent to Damascus to study, where he lived in a simple room at the Rawahiyya school, attending a dozen lessons a day, as reported. He is the author of The Forty Hadith, Riyadh al-Salihin and a great commentary on Sahih Muslim.
He lived simply, refused gifts and a salary, and spoke frankly to rulers when he believed they were wrong. He died at forty-five, in his home village, in 676 AH. The Forty Hadith in this app are his.
l: A short life of focused effort left a library of lasting benefit.
Teaching without payment and living simply kept him free to speak the truth.
He gathered what is most important into forty hadith that anyone could memorise.
stories.src: Classical biographies (al-Sakhawi’s al-Minhaj al-Sawi, Ibn al-‘Attar, al-Dhahabi); the daily schedule is as reported by his student Ibn al-‘Attar

stories.title: How the Hijri calendar began
p: In the caliphate of ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab, the letters and documents of the growing state carried no year. A governor, reported to be Abu Musa al-Ash’ari, wrote that letters arrived from the caliph with no date, and he did not know which to follow. ‘Umar gathered the Companions to agree on a way of counting years.

They considered starting from the Prophet’s birth, from his first revelation, from his death, or from the Hijrah. It is reported that ‘Ali suggested the Hijrah, and they agreed, because it was the moment when the community became established. The first of Muharram that year became the beginning of the Hijri calendar.
l: The Muslims chose to date history by the moment of migration for Allah’s sake, not by a birth or a death.
A practical need, a missing date on a letter, led the Companions to consult one another.
The months follow the moon, as the Qur’an prescribes (9:36).
stories.src: Reports in al-Tabari’s Tarikh, Ibn Hajar’s Fath al-Bari and al-Hakim; the exact year (16 or 17 AH) is given differently by the sources

stories.title: ‘Umar enters Jerusalem
p: After a siege by the Muslim armies under Abu ‘Ubaydah and ‘Amr ibn al-‘As, the Christian patriarch of Jerusalem, Sophronius, agreed to surrender the city, but only to the caliph in person. ‘Umar travelled from Madinah. Reports say that he and his servant took turns riding the same animal, so that when they arrived it was the servant’s turn to ride and ‘Umar who walked, with mud on his clothes.

‘Umar granted the people of Jerusalem a covenant of safety for their lives, property, churches and crosses. When invited to pray in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, he is reported to have declined and prayed outside, so that later Muslims would not claim it as a mosque.
l: Victory was joined with a written promise of safety for those who surrendered.
The caliph travelled humbly and avoided any display.
He took care that his own act would not become an excuse to take away the places of other faiths.
stories.src: Al-Tabari’s Tarikh and other early histories; the text of the covenant is transmitted with some variation, so details are described as reported

stories.title: ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz
p: ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz was an Umayyad prince raised in luxury who became caliph in 99 AH (717 CE) and ruled for only about two and a half years. In that time he changed course: he gave up the comforts of the palace, took his own family’s unlawfully gained estates back to the public treasury, and ended the practice of cursing ‘Ali from the pulpits, replacing it with the verse of justice and kindness (16:90).

The reports say that in his reign the poor were so well cared for that it was hard to find anyone who would accept zakat. He died young, at about thirty-nine, in 101 AH. Later scholars often call him the fifth of the rightly guided caliphs, for his justice.
l: Power can be turned to justice by one sincere person.
He began with his own household before asking others to change.
A short reign with sincere effort left a long memory.
stories.src: Early histories (Ibn Sa’d, al-Tabari, Ibn ‘Abd al-Hakam’s Sirat ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz); the account of the zakat is transmitted by Yahya ibn Sa’id and is given as reported

stories.title: The House of Wisdom and the age of learning
p: From the eighth century, Baghdad became a centre of translation and original research. Scholars of different faiths, many of them Christians who knew Greek and Syriac, translated works of medicine, mathematics and philosophy into Arabic under the patronage of caliphs such as al-Ma’mun. The institution traditionally called the House of Wisdom is linked with this movement.

Muslim scholars did not simply translate: al-Khwarizmi wrote the book from which algebra takes its name, Ibn al-Haytham used experiment to study light, al-Zahrawi described surgical instruments, and Ibn Sina wrote the Canon of Medicine. The Qur’an’s first command, "Read", and its repeated call to reflect, were part of the background.
l: The first word revealed was "Read"; the community that took it seriously built libraries.
Knowledge grew through the work of many people across cultures.
Science and faith did not appear as opposites to these scholars.
stories.src: Standard histories of science in Islam; dates and the exact role of the "House of Wisdom" are discussed by historians, and the account below follows the broad consensus

stories.title: Salah al-Din and Jerusalem
p: Salah al-Din ibn Ayyub, known in the West as Saladin, was a Kurdish commander who rose in the service of Nur al-Din Zangi, took power in Egypt, and united Egypt and Syria. In 583 AH (July 1187 CE) he defeated the Crusader army at the Battle of Hattin, and in Rajab of the same year (October 1187) Jerusalem surrendered to him after a short siege.

The terms he gave were mild compared to what had happened in 1099 when the Crusaders took the city. Residents who paid a ransom were allowed to leave, and he and his brother freed many poor people. He died in Damascus in 589 AH (1193 CE), and his biographer reports that he left almost nothing.
l: A victory won with mercy is remembered longer than one won with revenge.
He kept his word, and the terms he set were generous.
A leader’s simplicity showed in how little he left behind.
stories.src: Baha’ al-Din ibn Shaddad’s al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya, Ibn al-Athir’s al-Kamil, and modern histories; details of the ransom and his estate are as reported by his contemporaries

stories.title: The fall of Constantinople
p: On 29 May 1453 CE (20 Jumada al-Awwal 857 AH), after a siege of fifty-three days, the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II took Constantinople, the capital of the Byzantine Empire. He was twenty-one years old. The city had been besieged by Muslim armies many times before, since the early caliphate, and it had long been the subject of a famous saying of the Prophet ﷺ.

The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said: "Constantinople will be conquered. How excellent is its commander and how excellent is that army." The report is in Musnad Ahmad and al-Hakim and some scholars grade it as acceptable while others weaken it. The conquest ended the Byzantine state and began a new period for the city, which became Istanbul.
l: Great events grow from long preparation: the siege came after many failed attempts over eight centuries.
The Muslims regarded a prophetic report about the city as a spur to effort, not a guarantee.
The new rulers kept the Orthodox Church in being, as a recognised community.
stories.src: Standard histories of the Ottoman state (Kritovoulos, Tursun Beg, Inalcik); the hadith is in Musnad Ahmad 18189 and al-Mustadrak, with a debated grading

stories.title: Ibn Battuta, the traveller
p: Muhammad ibn ‘Abd Allah ibn Battuta was born in Tangier in 1304 CE (703 AH). At twenty-one he set out to make the Hajj, and ended up travelling for about twenty-nine years, through North Africa, Egypt, Syria, Arabia, Iraq and Persia, East Africa, Anatolia, Central Asia, India, the Maldives, and further east, and later west Africa.

On his return he dictated his account, called the Rihla, to a scribe, Ibn Juzayy, in 1356. It describes the cities, rulers, scholars, customs and journeys of the Muslim world in the fourteenth century. Some of his claims are debated by historians, but the book remains one of the richest sources for its time.
l: Travel for the sake of knowledge and worship was a deeply rooted tradition in Islam.
A Muslim could find a welcome, a lodge and a scholar in most cities of the known world.
A traveller’s record should be read with care, as a mixture of observation and hearsay.
stories.src: The Rihla of Ibn Battuta (as dictated to Ibn Juzayy) and modern studies; the extent of his travels in the east, especially China, is debated by historians

stories.title: The blind man and the frown
p: A blind man, ‘Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, came to the Prophet ﷺ asking to be taught, while the Prophet ﷺ was talking with some of the leaders of Quraysh, hoping that they would accept Islam. The Prophet ﷺ turned away from the blind man and continued speaking to them. Allah revealed the opening of Surah ‘Abasa, a gentle reproach: "He frowned and turned away because there came to him the blind man."

The Prophet ﷺ took the correction to heart. It is reported that afterwards, whenever he saw Ibn Umm Maktum, he would say, "Welcome to the one on whose account my Lord rebuked me," and he honoured him with responsibility in Madinah.
l: Allah put in the Qur’an a correction of His own Messenger, so that it would never be hidden: the revelation is not shaped by his wishes.
The one who comes seeking Allah sincerely deserves attention before the one whose acceptance we hope for.
Disability does not lower anyone’s standing: Ibn Umm Maktum went on to call the adhan.
stories.src: Surah ‘Abasa 80:1–16; Sunan at-Tirmidhi 3331 (narrated by ‘A’ishah, hasan gharib)

stories.title: Ka’b ibn Malik and the three who stayed behind
p: When the Prophet ﷺ called the Muslims to march to Tabuk, in the hardest heat and with a long journey, three Companions stayed behind without a valid excuse: Ka’b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayyah and Murarah ibn al-Rabi‘. When the Prophet ﷺ returned, the hypocrites came with excuses and swore oaths. Ka’b chose to tell the truth.

The Prophet ﷺ ordered the Muslims not to speak to the three. For fifty days, Ka’b was shunned, even by those he loved most, and then Allah accepted their repentance: "And [He also forgave] the three who were left behind."
l: Telling the truth in a hard situation is a means of salvation, even when a lie seems easier.
The punishment was a social boycott that taught them, and it ended when they had shown sincere remorse.
Ka’b’s response to the news was gratitude and a vow of truthfulness for the rest of his life.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 4418 and Sahih Muslim 2769 (Ka’b ibn Malik’s own account); Surah at-Tawbah 9:117–119

stories.title: Ibrahim, Sarah and the tyrant king
p: Ibrahim and his wife Sarah once travelled into a land ruled by a tyrant, a king who took any beautiful woman he heard of. Ibrahim knew that if the king learned she was his wife, he might have him killed to take her. So he told Sarah to say that she was his sister, and he meant a sister in faith, since the two of them were then the only believers in that place.

The king sent for her. Ibrahim stood up to pray, and Sarah went in with nothing but her trust in Allah. What happened in that room is the heart of this account, and the Prophet ﷺ told it to his Companions as an example of how Allah defends those who turn to Him.
l: When every human way is closed, prayer is still open, and Allah answers the one who is wronged.
Sarah is shown as a woman of steady faith: she prayed, and she was not shaken.
Scholars explain Ibrahim’s words “she is my sister” as an allusion that was true in meaning, said only to protect a life.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of the Prophets) and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah

stories.title: The man who told his sons to burn him
p: A man among those before you had wronged himself greatly, and had done little good in his life. When he felt that his death was near, he called his sons and told them what to do with his body. They were to burn it, then crush what was left into powder, and scatter half on land and half over the sea on a windy day.

His reason was fear. He was sure that if Allah ever got hold of him, he would be punished as no one had ever been punished. What Allah said to him after that, and what He did, is why the Prophet ﷺ told this account to his Companions.
l: Fear of Allah can be a door to His mercy, even for a person who has sinned a great deal.
No one can escape Allah’s hold, and nothing, not fire, wind or sea, is beyond His command.
We should never be certain that someone is doomed, since Allah’s forgiveness is wider than the faults we can see.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah, Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri and Hudhayfah

stories.title: The voice in the cloud
p: A man was walking through an open stretch of land when he heard a voice from a cloud above him say: “Water the garden of so-and-so,” and it named a particular person. The cloud moved off to a rocky patch of black stone and poured out all its water there. The water gathered into one channel and began to flow.

The man followed it. He saw someone standing in a garden, working the water with a spade, directing it where it was needed. When he asked who the owner was, the name was the one he had heard in the cloud. Then he asked what the owner did with what the garden produced.
l: Rizq is written, and it often arrives by routes we do not see.
The garden owner divided his harvest in three: a share for sadaqah, a share for his family, and a share put back into the land. Giving and planning belong together.
Generosity does not reduce wealth in the end; Allah says that what you spend in His way He replaces.
stories.src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah

stories.title: Sulayman and the two mothers
p: Two women were walking, each with a baby son, when a wolf came and carried one of the babies away. Each woman then said to the other: “It was your son that was taken. Mine is the one that is left.” Neither would give way.

They took the quarrel to the prophet and king Dawud, and he decided in favour of the elder woman. They left, and passed before Dawud’s son Sulayman, who asked how they had been judged. When he heard, he called for something no one expected: a knife.
l: A mother’s love can reveal the truth when evidence alone cannot.
Allah gave understanding to Sulayman in this case and still praised both father and son, since each was given judgement and knowledge.
A wise judge looks at what the situation shows, and not only at the words spoken.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah

stories.title: The cow and the wolf that spoke
p: One morning, after leading the Fajr prayer, the Prophet ﷺ turned to the people and told them two things that had happened in the past. A man was driving a cow and then climbed onto its back and struck it. The cow turned and said: “We were not created for this. We were created for ploughing.”

The people were amazed and said: “Glory be to Allah! A cow speaking?” The Prophet ﷺ replied: “I believe in this, and so do Abu Bakr and ‘Umar.” Neither of them was in the mosque. He went on to a second account, about a shepherd and a wolf.
l: Allah is able to make any creature speak, and a believer accepts what is reliably reported without being troubled by how unusual it is.
The Prophet ﷺ trusted Abu Bakr and ‘Umar enough to speak for them, and their faith is described as complete.
Everything has its purpose: even an animal is reminded to be used for what it was made for.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah

stories.title: The babies who spoke
p: The Prophet ﷺ said that only three infants ever spoke while still at the breast. One was ‘Isa, the son of Maryam. Another was the child in the story of Jurayj the monk, who testified to his own father’s identity. The third was a baby whose words were heard by his mother as she nursed him.

This third baby was nursing when a handsome rider passed by on a fine horse. His mother said: “O Allah, make my son like him.” The baby let go of her breast, looked up at the rider and said: “O Allah, do not make me like him.” What he saw next makes the story.
l: Looks and show are poor guides to a person’s worth, and Allah sees what lies underneath.
The one who is accused unjustly and bears it with “Allah is enough for me” has more than the one who rides in power.
A mother’s wish for her child should be made carefully, for what we admire may not be what is good.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah

stories.title: Musa and the angel of death
p: The angel of death was once sent to the prophet Musa. He came in the form of a man and said that Musa’s Lord was calling him. Musa did not know who this stranger was, and he struck him on the eye with his hand and put it out. The angel went back to Allah and said: “You sent me to a servant who does not want to die.”

Allah gave back the angel’s eye and told him to return with a different message. What Musa was offered, and how he answered, is a story the Prophet ﷺ told his Companions, and it ends beside a road near a red dune in the Holy Land.
l: Even a prophet loves life, and a natural dislike of death is no sin.
The believer’s answer to the choice of long life is to prefer what is with Allah.
The report teaches how to understand strange-sounding hadith: look for how the scholars explained them, and do not reject what is authentic.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah

stories.title: The man who swore Allah would not forgive
p: Among those before you there were two men. One of them was devoted to worship, and the other was known for sinning. Whenever the first saw the second doing wrong, he said to him: “Stop.” The sinner would answer: “Leave me with my Lord. Were you sent to watch over me?”

One day the worshipper found him doing something wrong again and told him: “By Allah, Allah will never forgive you, and will never let you into Paradise.” What happened to the two of them afterwards, and what Allah said to each, is a warning that the Prophet ﷺ gave to his Companions.
l: No one has the right to decide who Allah will forgive and who He will not.
A single careless oath against Allah’s mercy can undo years of worship, so guard the tongue.
Advising someone to do right is good, but it must come with humility, since we do not know how we ourselves will be judged.
stories.src: Sahih Muslim, narrated by Jundub ibn ‘Abdillah; Abu Dawud, narrated by Abu Hurayrah

stories.title: The last man to enter Paradise
p: The Prophet ﷺ described a man who will be the last of all to leave the Fire and the last to enter Paradise. He will come out crawling, stumbling, with the flames having scorched him. Allah will tell him to go and enter Paradise, and he will approach it and imagine that it is full.

What he is offered, how many times he is told to go back, and what he says to his Lord are described in the longest and most hopeful of the reports about the Day of Resurrection. When the Prophet ﷺ finished it, he laughed so that his back teeth showed.
l: Allah’s generosity on the Last Day is beyond what any person can imagine, even for the least of those saved.
A believer who has come through the worst trial still has a place waiting, so no one should despair.
The man’s amazement shows how overwhelming Allah’s mercy is, and reminds us to ask for it.
stories.src: Sahih Muslim and Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by ‘Abdullah ibn Mas‘ud and Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri

stories.title: The prophet who asked the sun to wait
p: One of the earlier prophets set out with his people to fight, and he gave them an unusual order. He told them that three kinds of man should not come with him: a man who had married and wanted to be with his wife but had not yet done so, a man who had built a house but had not yet put the roof on, and a man who had bought sheep or pregnant camels and was waiting for them to give birth.

He went on and came to a town at about the time of the afternoon prayer. The day was running out, and the battle had to be finished before the sun went down. He spoke to the sun. What followed, and the surprising way the prophet found a hidden fault among his people, is one of the more dramatic stories the Prophet ﷺ told.
l: A mission needs hearts that are free for it; things half done pull a person back.
Even a small amount of stolen goods can block victory, and a community is accountable for its honesty.
Allah’s mercy to this ummah is shown in how He lightened for it what He made heavy for others.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Abu Hurayrah

stories.title: The ship and the people who would not stop the hole
p: The Prophet ﷺ gave his Companions an image they could easily picture. A group of people drew lots to decide who would sit where on a ship. Some of them got the upper deck, and some the lower. Those on the lower deck had to go up to fetch water, and in doing so they passed by those above them and disturbed them.

One of the lower group said: “Why don’t we make a hole in our part of the ship, and take our water directly, so we do not trouble the people above us?” What would happen to the ship, depending on whether the others stopped him or let him, is the point of the parable.
l: A community is like one ship: when a few people harm it, everyone suffers if no one steps in.
Forbidding wrong, with wisdom and gentleness, is a duty that protects everyone, including the one doing the wrong.
A harm may look like it is private, but it is not, when others share the same vessel.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by an-Nu‘man ibn Bashir

stories.title: Sulayman and the Queen of Saba’
p: Sulayman was a prophet and a king who could understand the speech of birds and ants, and who commanded the jinn and the wind. One day he inspected his birds and found the hoopoe missing. He threatened it with a harsh punishment unless it brought a clear excuse.

The hoopoe was not gone long. It came back with news from the land of Saba’, a woman ruling a great kingdom, who had a magnificent throne, and whose people bowed to the sun instead of to Allah. What followed was a letter, a royal gift refused, a throne carried across the desert in the blink of an eye, and a palace with a floor she mistook for water.
l: Power and wealth do not make a person right; the Queen was wise because she was willing to consult and listen.
Sulayman gave credit to Allah at every step: “This is from the favour of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful.”
The Queen’s turn to Allah came through reflection and not force, and she ends by saying: “I submit, with Sulayman, to Allah, Lord of the worlds.”

stories.title: The golden calf
p: Musa left his people at the foot of the mountain to speak with his Lord, and he put his brother Harun in charge of them. He was meant to be gone for thirty nights, and Allah added ten. During those forty nights, a man called as-Samiri took the gold the people had brought out of Egypt and made it into a calf that made a sound like lowing.

When Musa came back with the tablets, he found his people bowing to it. The anger and grief of that moment, and what he said to Harun and then to as-Samiri, are told in the Qur’an with great closeness. The calf, which people had said was their god, was burned and scattered in the sea.
l: A people can hear a prophet’s message, see miracles, and still turn to something they have made themselves.
Harun’s patience under pressure was an effort to keep the people together until Musa returned, and it is explained in his own words.
The calf could not speak, harm or help, and its worship had no basis; Allah forgave those who repented.

stories.title: The people of the Sabbath
p: There was a town by the sea whose people were told not to fish on the Sabbath. Allah tested them in a strange way. On the days when fishing was forbidden, the fish came to the surface and swam close to the shore for everyone to see. On the days when it was allowed, they were nowhere to be found.

Some people found a way around the command, and the town divided into three groups: those who broke the limit, those who warned them, and those who asked the warners why they were wasting their breath. The Qur’an tells what happened to each.
l: Clever excuses do not change what Allah has forbidden; He knows what is in the heart.
Those who warned are described as a group who saved themselves, and their reason is the model: “an excuse before your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him.”
To keep inviting people to good even when they seem not to listen is a duty, and the result is not in our hands.

stories.title: Ibrahim, the king and the four birds
p: Ibrahim once met a king who argued with him about his Lord, because Allah had given that king power. Ibrahim said: “My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death.” The king said: “I give life and cause death.” Ibrahim then put a challenge to him that left him speechless.

In a different place, Ibrahim asked Allah himself how He gives life to the dead. He was already a believer, and Allah knew it. What he was told to do with four birds is a lesson in how a believer can ask for more certainty, and how Allah answers.
l: The best answer to a tyrant’s argument is one that cannot be twisted, and Ibrahim chose the sun.
It is no weakness to ask Allah for more peace of heart: Ibrahim said “but to put my heart at ease,” and was given an answer.
Faith has levels, from knowing to seeing, and Allah knows how to take a servant from one to the next.
stories.src: Qur’an 2:258 and 2:260

stories.title: Ilyas and the people of Ba‘l
p: Ilyas was one of the messengers Allah sent to the descendants of Isra’il. His people worshipped an idol called Ba‘l, and he asked them a simple question: “Will you call upon Ba‘l and leave the best of creators, Allah, your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers?”

The Qur’an gives only a few verses about him, and then it adds a line that has made him loved by readers: “Peace upon Ilyasin.” What more is known comes from the traditions of the earlier scriptures, and scholars have always said to treat those details with care.
l: The oldest question of all prophets is the same: who deserves worship?
A prophet can be rejected and still be honoured by Allah for all time, as the “peace” upon Ilyas shows.
Where the Qur’an and Sunnah are silent, a Muslim does not have to fill in the details.

stories.title: The jinn who listened to the Qur’an
p: The Prophet ﷺ was on his way with some Companions to the market at ‘Ukaz. At a place called Nakhlah, he led them in the Fajr prayer, reciting aloud. At the same time, a group of the jinn who had been sent to find the reason why they had lately been barred from listening at the heavens passed by.

They heard the recitation and stopped. They said to each other: “Be quiet and listen.” When it was over, they went back to their people and said: “We have heard a wondrous Qur’an, which guides to the right way, and we have believed in it.” The Prophet ﷺ did not know they were there until Allah told him.
l: The Qur’an is a message for all those who are accountable, jinn as well as people.
The jinn who heard it recognised its truth at once, and their response was to believe and to warn their people.
No one, human or jinn, can protect a person from Allah, and nothing can be found as a refuge besides Him.
stories.src: Qur’an 72:1–15; 46:29–32; Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Ibn ‘Abbas

stories.title: The mosque built to do harm
p: Not long before the army set out for Tabuk, a group of men in Madinah came to the Prophet ﷺ with a request. They had built a mosque, they said, for the sick and the needy and for cold nights, and they wanted him to come and pray in it.

The Prophet ﷺ was about to leave on a long journey and said he would see them on his return. But on the road back, Allah revealed the truth about that mosque. It was a plan, and the Qur’an says exactly what it was for. The Prophet ﷺ then sent men ahead of him, and they did something that tells how seriously a place of worship can be abused.
l: The outward form of an act of worship does not make it sound; what matters is the intention behind it.
A place of worship built to divide the believers has no blessing in it, however it looks.
Compare it with the mosque of Quba, built on taqwa from its first day, and where “men love to purify themselves.”
stories.src: Qur’an 9:107–110; Sirah of Ibn Hisham (from Ibn Ishaq); tafsir of Ibn Kathir and at-Tabari

stories.era: c. 582 CE, on the road to Syria
stories.title: The monk Bahira and the boy from Makkah
p: When Muhammad was about twelve years old, his uncle Abu Talib prepared a trading caravan for Syria. The boy asked to come, and Abu Talib, moved by his attachment, took him along. It was the first long journey of his life, across the desert to the town of Busra, where the caravan stopped near the cell of a monk.

The monk, whom the sources call Bahira, had spent years watching caravans go by without taking notice of them. That year he did, and he prepared a meal for all of them. The reasons he gave for the invitation, and what he asked about the boy, are told by Ibn Ishaq and in a hadith of at-Tirmidhi.
l: The signs of a prophet were known to those who studied the earlier scriptures, long before the first revelation.
Abu Talib’s protection of his nephew began early, and Bahira’s advice was to guard him from harm.
Muhammad ﷺ did not seek status; he stayed with the baggage while the others went to eat.
stories.src: Sirah of Ibn Ishaq (in Ibn Hisham); Sunan at-Tirmidhi (narrated by Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari), where the story is graded hasan gharib, though scholars note a problem with one detail

stories.title: The palm trunk that cried
p: In the first years in Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ gave his Friday sermon standing beside a trunk of a date palm that was part of the mosque’s structure. He would lean against it as he spoke. One day, a man of the Ansar suggested making a pulpit for him, so that more people could see and hear him. It was built, and the Prophet ﷺ began to speak from it.

From that Friday, the people in the mosque began to hear a sound. The trunk made a noise like a camel crying for her young. The Prophet ﷺ stepped down from the pulpit, went over to it and held it. What he said afterwards is one of the best-known reports about the love of nature for the Prophet ﷺ.
l: A piece of wood missed the Prophet ﷺ; a person has more reason to long for him.
The Prophet ﷺ was gentle even with a trunk of wood, so he is an example in mercy to all creatures.
Remembrance of Allah is a presence that even inanimate things notice.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah, Ibn ‘Umar and Anas ibn Malik; also Sunan Ibn Majah and Musnad Ahmad

stories.title: The covenant of Madinah
p: When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah, he found a city that had been torn by years of war between its two main Arab tribes, the Aws and the Khazraj, with Jewish clans living alongside them and allied to one side or the other. Now there was a third group too: the Muhajirun, who had come from Makkah with almost nothing.

The sources say that he wrote a document that set out how these groups were to live together. It is called the Sahifah, or the covenant or constitution of Madinah. It is among the earliest written agreements of its kind in the Islamic tradition, and its text has been preserved by Ibn Ishaq and others.
l: A just society needs agreed rules about rights and duties, written and known to everyone.
Those who share a city share its defence, and an attack on it is an attack on all who live there.
People of different religions can live together by agreement, each keeping their own faith, as the document says.
stories.src: Sirah of Ibn Ishaq, in Ibn Hisham; Abu ‘Ubayd, Kitab al-Amwal; related hadith in Sahih Muslim and Musnad Ahmad on the sanctuary of Madinah

stories.title: The tug at the cloak
p: Anas ibn Malik was walking with the Prophet ﷺ, who was wearing a Najrani cloak with a rough, thick border. A Bedouin came up behind him and pulled the cloak so hard that Anas could see the edge of it had left a mark on the Prophet’s neck. The man said: “O Muhammad, give me something from the wealth of Allah that you have.”

There was nobody to stop the man, and no one would have blamed the Prophet ﷺ for being angry. What he did is recorded in the Sahih of al-Bukhari. A second story, about a rabbi who tested the Prophet’s patience, has a more disputed chain but a similar ending, and it is told after it with care.
l: The Prophet ﷺ answered harshness with a smile, and with a gift; this is the highest form of patience.
Mercy shown to the rude and the ignorant can bring people closer than any argument.
In the second report, a rabbi reportedly tested what he had read about the Prophet’s character, and it held; it is told here as a report whose chain scholars discuss.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (the Bedouin and the cloak, narrated by Anas); the account of Zayd ibn Sa‘nah is in at-Tabarani, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim, with a chain that scholars discuss

stories.era: On the return from an expedition, c. 5–6 AH
stories.title: The lost necklace and the gift of tayammum
p: On the way back from a military expedition, the army halted for the night in a place without water. In the morning, ‘A’ishah, who was travelling with the Prophet ﷺ, found that her necklace had fallen from her neck. It was a necklace she had borrowed from her sister Asma’, and she could not leave it behind.

The Prophet ﷺ stopped the army and sent men to look for it. Nobody had water, and the time of prayer was close. The whole of the community depended on a small piece of jewellery, and the result was a ruling that people have used since in every place without water.
l: A small, ordinary event can be the occasion of a great mercy for the ummah.
Tayammum shows that the religion is built on ease: when water is not there, the earth is enough.
Abu Bakr’s family is remembered for being a blessing, as Usayd ibn Hudayr said.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Tayammum) and Sahih Muslim, narrated by ‘A’ishah

stories.title: Abu Basir and the clause of the treaty
p: The treaty of Hudaybiyyah included a clause that had upset many Muslims: if anyone from Quraysh came to Muhammad ﷺ as a Muslim without the permission of his guardian, he would be returned to them. If anyone from the Muslims went to Quraysh, they would not be returned. ‘Umar had protested. The Prophet ﷺ had accepted it.

Soon after the treaty was signed, a man named Abu Basir escaped from Makkah and arrived in Madinah as a Muslim. Quraysh sent two men to claim him. The Prophet ﷺ kept his word and handed him over. What happened on the road back to Makkah showed how Allah can open a way through a clause that looked like a defeat.
l: Keeping a treaty, even one that seems unfavourable, is part of integrity, and the Prophet ﷺ kept it.
Allah opened a way for the believers that no one had planned, and the clause turned out to hurt Quraysh.
What looks like a loss in the short term can be a victory in the long term, as Hudaybiyyah showed.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Conditions), narrated by al-Miswar ibn Makhramah and Marwan; Sirah of Ibn Ishaq

stories.title: Khaybar: the banner and the fortresses
p: About two months after the return from Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet ﷺ set out for Khaybar, an oasis about a hundred miles north of Madinah, with some fourteen hundred men. It was a land of date palms and strong fortresses, and many Jewish clans from Madinah, who had incited the tribes against the Muslims in the Battle of the Trench, now lived there and were preparing for another attack.

The army came at night and waited until morning, so as not to attack while they slept. When the farmers came out with their baskets and tools, they saw the army and shouted: “Muhammad and the army!” and ran back inside. The siege of Khaybar had begun, and it would last for weeks, with the most famous day being the day of the banner.
l: The Prophet ﷺ gave the banner to the one who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love.
Success in this conflict came from patience and planning, and the Prophet ﷺ fought only after warning and calling to Islam.
Those who surrendered were treated with terms, and were left on their land under an agreement, which shows how the Prophet ﷺ handled the conquered.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (Book of Maghazi), narrated by Anas, Sahl ibn Sa‘d and Salamah ibn al-Akwa‘; Sirah of Ibn Ishaq

stories.era: After Hunayn and Ta’if, Dhu al-Qa‘dah, 8 AH
stories.title: What the Prophet ﷺ said to the Ansar
p: After the battle of Hunayn, an enormous amount of booty was collected: thousands of camels, sheep and silver. The Prophet ﷺ began to divide it. He gave a hundred camels each to some of the leaders of Quraysh and other tribes who had only recently become Muslim or who had been enemies until days before, hoping to win their hearts to the faith.

The Ansar, who had given up everything for him, were given nothing. Some of the younger men said something that was reported to the Prophet ﷺ. He gathered them in a leather tent, and what he said to them is one of the most moving speeches in the whole sira.
l: Loyalty can be tested by what seems like being overlooked, and the Ansar passed the test.
The Prophet ﷺ acknowledged their sacrifice openly and did not belittle their feelings.
The greatest wealth is to have the Messenger ﷺ with you, as the Ansar chose.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (Book of Maghazi and Book of Zakat), narrated by Anas ibn Malik, ‘Abdullah ibn Zayd and Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri

stories.title: The death of Ibrahim and the eclipse
p: In the tenth year after the Hijrah, the Prophet’s infant son Ibrahim, born to Maryam the Copt, fell ill and died. He was about a year and a half old. He had been nursed in the outskirts of Madinah by the wife of a blacksmith, and the Prophet ﷺ used to visit him there, with the house full of smoke from the forge.

On the day he died, the sun eclipsed. People began to say that it had been darkened for the death of the Prophet’s son. The Prophet ﷺ went out and told them something that has shaped Muslim understanding of such events ever since, after having spoken about his grief in words that people remember.
l: The Prophet ﷺ wept, and said that tears are mercy; grief is not a lack of faith.
He refused to benefit from a coincidence that people took as a sign for him, and he corrected a mistaken belief at once.
The sun and the moon are signs of Allah, to be met with prayer and remembrance, not with superstition.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Anas ibn Malik, al-Mughirah ibn Shu‘bah and ‘A’ishah

stories.title: ‘Abd ar-Rahman ibn ‘Awf, the merchant who feared his wealth
p: ‘Abd ar-Rahman ibn ‘Awf arrived in Madinah with nothing. He had left his property in Makkah, and the Prophet ﷺ paired him with a man of the Ansar named Sa‘d ibn ar-Rabi‘, who offered him half of his wealth, and even one of his two wives. ‘Abd ar-Rahman answered with a sentence that has been remembered ever since: “May Allah bless you in your family and your wealth. Show me the market.”
