In a short time he became one of the richest men of Madinah, and one of the most generous. But the Companions also remembered something else about him: a day when food was put before him and he began to weep.
l: Honest work and generosity can go together, and wealth is a trust when it is spent for Allah.
Pride in one’s own effort is a risk; ‘Abd ar-Rahman chose the market and not the gift.
The fear of having already received one’s reward in this life is the mark of a heart that is alive.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Manaqib al-Ansar and Book of Funerals); Sahih Muslim; Musnad Ahmad; Siyar A‘lam an-Nubala’ of adh-Dhahabi

stories.title: Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib, the father of the poor
p: Ja‘far was the older brother of ‘Ali, and a cousin of the Prophet ﷺ. He was one of the earliest Muslims and the one the Muslims chose as their speaker before the Negus of Abyssinia. Many years later, he marched to Mu‘tah carrying the banner, and he fell there with fifty wounds on the front of his body.

He is remembered, however, for something that Abu Hurayrah noticed while he was living in hunger in Madinah. Of all the people he knew, he said, the best to the poor was Ja‘far. And the way that the Prophet ﷺ responded when he heard of Ja‘far’s death gave a rule to Muslims that they still follow.
l: Generosity to the poor is as good a measure of a person as courage in battle.
The Prophet ﷺ showed that the families of the bereaved should be fed, as they are not able to look after themselves.
Martyrdom is described as a reward with wings, and the Prophet ﷺ spoke of him as “the one who flies in Paradise.”
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Maghazi and Book of Manaqib); Musnad Ahmad; Sunan Abi Dawud and at-Tirmidhi (food for the bereaved); Sirah of Ibn Ishaq

stories.title: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, the Prophet’s first host in Madinah
p: When the Prophet ﷺ entered Madinah, every family wanted him to stay in their house. They took hold of his camel’s halter and invited him, and he told them to leave her alone because she was commanded. She walked on until she knelt in front of a house that belonged to Abu Ayyub, of the Banu an-Najjar.

Abu Ayyub carried the Prophet’s saddle-bags inside and became his host for months. Decades later, as an old man, he died on a campaign and was buried at the foot of the walls of a city that he never saw captured. The place is still visited.
l: The honour of hosting the Prophet ﷺ fell to the one with whom the camel stopped, showing it was Allah’s choice.
Respect for the Prophet ﷺ can be seen in the smallest act, as when Abu Ayyub wiped up water with his own quilt.
A believer goes where he can serve until his last day.
stories.src: Sirah of Ibn Ishaq; Sahih Muslim (Book of Drinks, on the Prophet’s food); al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak; Ibn Hajar, al-Isabah

stories.title: Abu Talha, the shield of the Prophet ﷺ
p: At the battle of Uhud, when the Muslim lines broke and the Prophet ﷺ was exposed, a man of the Ansar stood in front of him, raised his chest to the arrows, and said: “My neck before your neck, O Messenger of Allah. May my face be a shield for your face.” His name was Zayd ibn Sahl, known as Abu Talha.

He was also a man of a very different kind of generosity. He owned the best garden in Madinah, and when a verse was revealed that spoke of what a person loves, he went straight to the Prophet ﷺ with an offer. What the Prophet ﷺ told him, and a night when his family went hungry for a guest, are among the finest stories of the Ansar.
l: To give what we love most is the test of the verse: “You will not attain righteousness until you spend from what you love.”
Putting oneself between the Prophet ﷺ and harm showed a love that did not count the cost.
Preferring a guest over one’s own family’s hunger is praised by Allah in the Qur’an.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Zakat, Book of Maghazi, Book of Manaqib al-Ansar); Sahih Muslim; al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak; Ibn Hajar, al-Isabah

stories.title: ‘Ammar ibn Yasir, whom the Prophet ﷺ promised Paradise
p: ‘Ammar was one of the first to enter Islam and one of the first to be tortured for it. His father Yasir and his mother Sumayyah were killed, and he was made to endure what no one should. On one occasion, after he had been pushed to the limit, he said words that they wanted him to say. He came back to the Prophet ﷺ in tears, afraid that he had destroyed himself.

The Prophet ﷺ wiped his eyes and asked him how he found his heart. He said it was at rest in faith. A verse of the Qur’an was revealed concerning him, and from that moment, it became the basis for a ruling that millions of Muslims have relied on in times of oppression.
l: Allah does not hold a person responsible for what is forced from the tongue when the heart stays firm.
The Prophet ﷺ comforted those who suffered by naming their reward: “Patience, family of Yasir, for your promise is Paradise.”
A believer can carry a heavy load of work and still be remembered as the one who shared the effort.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Salah, on the building of the mosque); al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak; at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir on 16:106; Sunan at-Tirmidhi

stories.title: Ubayy ibn Ka‘b, the one the Prophet ﷺ recited to
p: One day the Prophet ﷺ said to Ubayy ibn Ka‘b: “Allah has commanded me to recite the Qur’an to you.” Ubayy asked: “Did He mention me by name?” The Prophet ﷺ said: “Yes.” Ubayy began to cry. Few men have been told that their own name was spoken in the heavens in connection with the Qur’an.

Ubayy was one of the scribes of revelation, and the Prophet ﷺ called him the most skilled of his community in recitation. ‘Umar, who led the Muslims after him, said that Ubayy was the best of them in recitation. He also asked a question about the Qur’an which has been remembered ever since.
l: The Qur’an is a gift to be memorised, understood and recited with feeling.
The Prophet ﷺ taught people by asking questions that made them think, and by encouraging them.
A person given knowledge should be humble before it, as Ubayy wept when he was named.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Tafsir and Book of Fadail al-Qur’an); Sahih Muslim (Book of Salat al-Musafirin); Sunan at-Tirmidhi

stories.title: Zayd ibn Thabit, the young man who collected the Qur’an
p: Zayd ibn Thabit was a boy of eleven when the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah. He came with a few chapters already memorised, and the Companions were amazed. The Prophet ﷺ made him one of his scribes, and Zayd wrote down the revelation as it came, at the Prophet’s dictation.

After the Prophet ﷺ died, and after a battle in which many reciters were killed, ‘Umar went to Abu Bakr with a worry that no one had yet faced: the Qur’an existed in the hearts of the men and on scattered pieces of writing. Abu Bakr then called for Zayd, and asked him to do something that he said felt heavier than moving a mountain.
l: The Qur’an has been preserved by the effort of people who treated it with great care, and Zayd’s method was strict.
Youth is no barrier to trust: the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr both chose him for his ability and honesty.
Respect for the people of knowledge is a mark of the Companions, shown when Ibn ‘Abbas held Zayd’s stirrup.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Fada’il al-Qur’an, hadith on the collection of the Qur’an); Sunan at-Tirmidhi; al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak

stories.title: ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Abbas, the scholar of the ummah
p: ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Abbas was a boy when the Prophet ﷺ died, barely thirteen. Yet he came to be called the “ocean of the ummah” and the interpreter of the Qur’an. The Prophet ﷺ had prayed over him as a child: “O Allah, give him understanding in the religion and teach him the meaning of the Book.”

He did not become a scholar by being a prince of the family. He earned it by going to the doors of other Companions and waiting. What ‘Umar asked him once about one of the shortest chapters of the Qur’an shows what that waiting produced.
l: The prayer of the Prophet ﷺ and the effort of the student worked together to make him a scholar.
A person who wants knowledge must humble himself before those who hold it, as Ibn ‘Abbas did at the doors of the Ansar.
Understanding the Qur’an goes beyond reading: it includes noticing what a verse points to.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Knowledge, Book of Tafsir, Book of Wudu’); Sahih Muslim; Musnad Ahmad; Ibn Sa‘d, at-Tabaqat; al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak

stories.title: Talha ibn ‘Ubaydillah, the walking martyr
p: At Uhud, when the lines broke and the Prophet ﷺ was wounded, a small group of Muslims stayed around him. One of them was Talha ibn ‘Ubaydillah. He shielded the Prophet ﷺ with his own body and with his hand, taking spear and sword blows on it. His hand was cut and stayed lame for the rest of his life.
Abu Bakr never forgot it. When Uhud was mentioned, he used to say: “That day was entirely Talha’s.” And the Prophet ﷺ gave him a name that has stayed with him ever since.
l: There are moments in life that decide everything, and a person who is ready for them is already prepared by his character.
Talha’s hand was spent for the Prophet ﷺ, and it became a lifelong honour.
Generosity was part of his nature, and he was known as Talha al-Fayyad, the overflowing.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Manaqib, hadith of Qays ibn Abi Hazim and Abu ‘Uthman an-Nahdi); Sunan at-Tirmidhi; Ibn Sa‘d, at-Tabaqat; adh-Dhahabi, Siyar A‘lam an-Nubala’

stories.title: Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas, the one whose prayers were answered
p: Sa‘d was seventeen when he became a Muslim, one of the first handful. His mother was so angry that she swore not to eat or drink until he gave up Islam. She starved herself for days, and her family brought out a stick to open her mouth and pour water into it. Sa‘d said to her something that no one could have expected.

He later commanded the army that broke the Persian empire at Qadisiyyah. The Prophet ﷺ had prayed that his supplications would be answered, and the Companions remembered that every time he prayed against someone or for someone, it was fulfilled.
l: Obedience to parents does not extend to disobeying Allah, but kindness to them remains.
A prayer made with sincerity can reach beyond any army.
Leaving one’s heirs well provided for is better than leaving them in need, as the Prophet ﷺ told him.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Manaqib, Book of Wasaya, Book of Maghazi); Sahih Muslim (Book of the Merits of the Companions); Sunan at-Tirmidhi; Ibn Sa‘d, at-Tabaqat

stories.title: Abu ad-Darda’, the merchant who became a scholar
p: Abu ad-Darda’ was a businessman of Madinah, a man with a shop and a house, who had not yet accepted Islam when most of the Ansar did. His close friend ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah, who had become a Muslim, went into his house one day while he was out and broke the wooden idol he kept in it.

When he came home, his wife told him what had happened. He was angry at first, then he looked at the broken pieces and thought: if this could not defend itself, how could it have helped him? He went to the Prophet ﷺ and became a Muslim. He is remembered as a man who turned from trade to worship and learning without giving up the world’s needs.
l: The idol that cannot protect itself cannot protect anyone, and a clear mind sees this at once.
Worship should be balanced with rights of the body and family: “Give everyone with a right his right.”
A person can be a scholar and a worker; Abu ad-Darda’ taught in Damascus after leaving his trade.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Fasting, on Salman and Abu ad-Darda’); Musnad Ahmad; Siyar A‘lam an-Nubala’; Ibn Sa‘d, at-Tabaqat

stories.title: ‘Abdullah ibn Salam, the rabbi who recognised the truth
p: ‘Abdullah ibn Salam was the leading rabbi of Madinah, respected by the Jews as a scholar and the son of a scholar. When he heard that the Prophet ﷺ had arrived, he came to him in the crowd and looked carefully at his face. What he saw, and the first words he heard, were enough: “I knew that his face was not the face of a liar.”

But he also knew what his own people were like. He asked the Prophet ﷺ to question them about him before they learned that he had accepted Islam. What they said, and what they said afterwards, is one of the clearest accounts of how the truth can be hidden by envy.
l: A person who knows the earlier scripture sincerely recognises the Prophet ﷺ as one recognises his own child.
Envy and group pride can blind even learned people to what they know.
The first words the Prophet ﷺ said in Madinah are a summary of a whole way of life.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Manaqib al-Ansar, Book of Anbiya’); Sunan at-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah (the Prophet’s first words in Madinah); Sahih Muslim

stories.title: At-Tufayl ibn ‘Amr, who stuffed cotton in his ears
p: At-Tufayl was a poet and a chief of the tribe of Daws, a man of influence who came to Makkah on business. The leaders of Quraysh, who feared the effect of the Prophet’s words on visitors, came to him and said: “Take care that he does not speak to you. His words are like magic. They separate a man from his father and his family.”

At-Tufayl took their advice so seriously that he stuffed cotton in his ears before he went to the Ka‘bah. But then he saw the Prophet ﷺ praying near it, and a few words reached him. He thought: “Shame on me. I am a poet, and I understand the difference between good and bad speech. What is to stop me from listening?”
l: A person who is prepared to judge fairly can recognise truth when he hears it.
The Prophet ﷺ prayed for guidance for a people who had disobeyed him, and not against them.
Opposition that warns people off the truth often draws attention to it.
stories.src: Sirah of Ibn Ishaq (in Ibn Hisham); Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (the Prophet’s prayer for Daws, narrated by Abu Hurayrah)

stories.title: Khubayb ibn ‘Adi and the razor
p: Khubayb ibn ‘Adi was one of a group of ten Companions who were sent out in 4 AH and were ambushed by a hundred archers from the tribe of Hudhayl. Most of them were killed fighting. Khubayb and two others accepted the offer of safety and were sold to Quraysh in Makkah, where Khubayb was held for a time in the house of a family whose father he had killed at Badr.
A woman of the household watched him during these days. What she saw, and what she remembered afterwards, is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, and the way he was killed became part of Islamic history.
l: A believer’s trust in Allah gives him calm at the edge of death.
Khubayb did not take revenge on a child, even though he held a razor, and his integrity was noticed by his enemies.
He is remembered as the first to establish the practice of praying two rak‘ahs before being put to death.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Maghazi, the expedition of ar-Raji‘; Book of Jihad), narrated by Abu Hurayrah and others

stories.title: Nu‘aym ibn Mas‘ud and the night the alliance broke
p: In the siege of Madinah, ten thousand men from Quraysh, Ghatafan and other tribes camped outside the trench, while inside the city, the Banu Qurayzah, who had a treaty with the Prophet ﷺ, were being pressed to join them. If they did, the Muslims would be attacked from both sides.

In the middle of this, a man called Nu‘aym ibn Mas‘ud came to the Prophet ﷺ at night and said: “I have become a Muslim, but my people do not know it. Order me as you wish.” What he did over the next day is one of the stories told about the Battle of the Trench, and the Prophet ﷺ gave it a short sentence of approval.
l: The Prophet ﷺ approved of using a plan that sows doubt among the enemy: “War is deception.”
Mistrust between allies can undo a strong coalition faster than force.
A single person, if he is sincere and thinks carefully, can change the course of a siege.
stories.src: Sirah of Ibn Ishaq (in Ibn Hisham), with a chain that Ibn Hajar and others describe as hasan or mursal; Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim for “War is deception”

stories.title: ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un, whom the Prophet ﷺ kissed
p: ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un was one of the earliest Muslims, a man of great devotion who had given up alcohol in the days of ignorance. He was the first of the Emigrants to die in Madinah. When he died, the Prophet ﷺ bent over his body, kissed him on the forehead, and wept so that his tears fell on ‘Uthman’s cheek.

In his life, the Prophet ﷺ had also once stopped him from doing something that he intended out of love for worship. The story of what he refused to accept, and the strange statement the Prophet ﷺ made at his death, show how closely the two were bound.
l: The religion does not ask a person to give up marriage or the body’s rights to be devoted.
A believer’s protection comes from Allah, and ‘Uthman gave up a human protector to prove it.
Even the Prophet ﷺ said he did not know what would happen to him, in Allah’s hands, as a lesson in humility.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Marriage, Book of Manaqib al-Ansar); Sunan Abi Dawud and at-Tirmidhi (the Prophet’s kiss); Sirah of Ibn Ishaq

stories.title: ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah, the poet and the honest assessor
p: ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah was one of the leaders of the Ansar, a poet, and one of those who pledged himself at ‘Aqabah. He was one of the Prophet’s poets, and the third commander named when the army marched to Mu’tah.

The Prophet ﷺ also trusted him with a task that needed a very honest man: to estimate the date harvest of Khaybar and divide it between the Muslims and the people who farmed it. A story told about the day he did so shows why he was trusted.
l: Justice is shown most clearly when love and hatred pull the other way.
A believer’s faith is shown in the heat as well as in comfort: he fasted when no one else did.
Poetry in the service of truth is praised, and Ibn Rawahah’s verses were a form of devotion.
stories.src: Sahih Muslim (Book of Fasting, narrated by Abu ad-Darda’); Muwatta’ Malik and Musnad Ahmad (the Khaybar appraisal); Sirah of Ibn Ishaq (Mu’tah); Sahih al-Bukhari (Mu’tah)

stories.title: Al-Bara’ ibn Malik and the Garden of Death
p: Al-Bara’ ibn Malik was the brother of Anas ibn Malik, and one of those whom the Prophet ﷺ described in a short phrase: “There may be a man with dust-covered hair, turned away from doors, who, if he swears by Allah, Allah will fulfil it for him. Among them is al-Bara’ ibn Malik.”

He is best remembered for the battle of Yamamah, in 12 AH, when the Muslim army faced Musaylimah and a large force of the tribe of Hanifah, who had taken refuge behind the walls of a large walled orchard. It was a battle so fierce that the garden was later called the Garden of Death.
l: Reputation with Allah is not the same as reputation with people: a man turned away from doors may be someone Allah answers.
Courage is often combined with prayer, and al-Bara’ asked for martyrdom and it was written for him.
Great victories can come from one person who dares to open a gate.
stories.src: Sunan at-Tirmidhi (hasan, narrated by Anas); Ibn Sa‘d, at-Tabaqat; at-Tabari, History; adh-Dhahabi, Siyar A‘lam an-Nubala’

stories.title: Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh, for whom the Throne shook
p: Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh was the leader of the tribe of Aws in Madinah. When Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr came with the Qur’an, Sa‘d heard of him through his cousin Usayd. He went to see the visitor, listened, and became a Muslim at once. Then he went back to his people and said: “O Banu ‘Abd al-Ashhal, how do you see me among you?” They said: “You are our leader.”

He said: “Then speaking to your men and women is forbidden to me until you believe in Allah and His Messenger.” By evening, not one of them remained who was not a Muslim. Years later, when he died of a wound, the Prophet ﷺ said that the Throne of the Most Merciful shook for him.
l: A leader’s sincerity can bring an entire people with him in a day.
Sa‘d prayed that he would live to see justice done and that his wound would stay open until then: an example of a believer’s purposeful prayer.
The honour Allah gives a believer after death can be great: the Throne shook, and the angels attended his funeral.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (Book of Manaqib, Book of Maghazi); Sunan at-Tirmidhi; Sirah of Ibn Ishaq

stories.title: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, the keeper of secrets
p: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman was known as the keeper of the Prophet’s secret. The Prophet ﷺ had told him the names of those among the Madinans who were hypocrites, something he told no one else. After the Prophet ﷺ died, ‘Umar used to ask whether his name was among them, and if Hudhayfah was at a funeral, ‘Umar would look to see if he was present before praying.

On the coldest night of the siege of Madinah, with the wind blowing and the enemy camp in darkness, the Prophet ﷺ called for someone to go out and bring back news of the enemy. The man he called by name was Hudhayfah.
l: The Prophet ﷺ taught that good is learned by asking about evil as well, so one can avoid it.
Obedience to an order in discomfort, with no fear, was honoured with the Prophet’s own care.
Keeping a confidence is a trust, and Hudhayfah kept his until his death.
stories.src: Sahih Muslim (Book of Jihad, the Battle of the Trench); Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Manaqib, Book of Fitan); Ibn Sa‘d, at-Tabaqat

stories.title: Anas ibn Malik, who grew up at the Prophet’s side
p: When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah, a woman named Umm Sulaym brought her ten-year-old son to him. She said: “O Messenger of Allah, all the men and women of the Ansar have given you a gift, and I have nothing to give but this boy of mine. Take him, and let him serve you as you wish.”

Anas served the Prophet ﷺ for ten years. When he was an old man, people asked him what he remembered. His answer, one of the most quoted in the collections, is about the way the Prophet ﷺ spoke to a child who must have made mistakes.
l: The Prophet ﷺ never scolded a child who served him, and this gentleness shaped a great scholar.
A mother’s offering of her son to the service of the Prophet ﷺ gave the ummah a major source of hadith.
A prayer for blessing from the Prophet ﷺ was seen in wealth, children and a very long life.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Adab, Book of Da‘awat, Book of Manaqib); Sahih Muslim; Sunan at-Tirmidhi; Ibn Sa‘d, at-Tabaqat

stories.title: Safiyyah bint ‘Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet’s aunt
p: Safiyyah was the Prophet’s paternal aunt and the sister of Hamzah. She was among the early Muslims, one of the few members of his family who accepted the message early. At Uhud, she came to the battlefield when she heard what had happened to her brother.

The Prophet ﷺ told her son az-Zubayr to turn her back, so that she would not see Hamzah’s body, which had been mutilated. She asked why, and said she knew what had happened to him, and that it was for Allah’s sake. What she said and did afterwards is one of the great examples of patience in the sira.
l: Patience at the first shock is the true patience, and Safiyyah showed it at her brother’s body.
The Prophet ﷺ taught his own family that kinship does not replace deeds: “I cannot help you with Allah in anything.”
Courage is found among women too, and Safiyyah is remembered for defending the fort at the Trench.
stories.src: Sirah of Ibn Ishaq; Sahih al-Bukhari (the Prophet’s warning to his relatives); Musnad Ahmad; Ibn Hajar, al-Isabah; Ibn Sa‘d, at-Tabaqat

stories.title: Al-Khansa’, the poet who gave her sons to Qadisiyyah
p: Tumadir bint ‘Amr, known as al-Khansa’, was the greatest woman poet of the Arabs. In the days of ignorance she lost her two brothers, Mu‘awiyah and Sakhr, in tribal fighting, and her poetry of mourning for Sakhr was said to be the finest elegy in the language.

When Islam came, she came with her tribe, the Banu Sulaym, to the Prophet ﷺ, and he asked her to recite. Later, in the Battle of Qadisiyyah, she did something that was passed down in the books of history. She spoke to her four sons on the eve of the battle.
l: A person who is known for grief in one stage of life can become known for patience in the next.
A mother’s advice to her sons to be brave and to seek what is with Allah is a model of faith over attachment.
The Prophet ﷺ valued good poetry, and he asked her to continue.
stories.src: Ibn Hajar, al-Isabah; Ibn ‘Abd al-Barr, al-Isti‘ab; Ibn al-Athir, Usd al-Ghabah; al-Asma‘i and others for her poetry. The Qadisiyyah account is from the biographies and its chain is not strong.

stories.title: Zaynab bint Jahsh, married by Allah’s command
p: Zaynab bint Jahsh was the Prophet’s cousin, a woman of noble family, known for her skill with her hands and her generosity. The Prophet ﷺ had proposed her marriage to his adopted son Zayd ibn Harithah. She and her brother did not like the idea, until a verse of the Qur’an said that a believer has no choice once Allah and His Messenger have decided.

The marriage did not last, and some years later the Qur’an itself told the Prophet ﷺ to marry her, as a way of ending a custom of the days of ignorance. It is the only marriage that the Qur’an names directly, and she used to say something about it to the other wives that they never forgot.
l: Submission to what Allah decrees is a sign of faith, even when a person’s own feelings differ.
The Prophet ﷺ praised her for working with her hands and giving the proceeds to the poor.
Reality is formed by Allah’s command, not custom: adoption does not create blood ties.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Tafsir, Book of Tawhid, Book of Nikah); Sahih Muslim (Book of Fada’il as-Sahabah); Musnad Ahmad; Ibn Sa‘d, at-Tabaqat

stories.title: Sawdah bint Zam‘ah, who gave her day away
p: After the death of Khadijah, the Prophet ﷺ was grieving, and a woman called Khawlah bint Hakim suggested that he marry again. One of the two women she named was Sawdah bint Zam‘ah, a widow of the early Muslims who had gone to Abyssinia with her husband and returned to Makkah alone.

She was no longer young, and not famous for beauty or lineage. The Prophet ﷺ married her, and she stayed his wife until his death. Late in her life, she did something for ‘A’ishah that the sources record as one of the generous acts in the household.
l: A marriage can be a mercy: the Prophet ﷺ honoured a lonely widow and gave her a home.
Giving up a right for the sake of the household’s peace is a form of generosity.
Allah’s revelation in 4:128 recognises the value of reconciliation: “Reconciliation is better.”
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Nikah, Book of Hajj); Sahih Muslim; Sunan Abi Dawud; Ibn Sa‘d, at-Tabaqat; Musnad Ahmad

stories.title: Ruqayyah and Umm Kulthum, the daughters who married ‘Uthman
p: The Prophet ﷺ had four daughters: Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum and Fatimah. Ruqayyah and Umm Kulthum were married before Islam to the sons of Abu Lahab, ‘Utbah and ‘Utaybah. When Surah al-Masad was revealed, condemning Abu Lahab, he told his sons to divorce them, and they did.

The Prophet ﷺ then married Ruqayyah to ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan, and after her death, he married ‘Uthman to Umm Kulthum, so that ‘Uthman was called “the one with two lights.” The first couple to emigrate for the sake of Allah was ‘Uthman and Ruqayyah, and the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said of them: “They are the first household to migrate for the sake of Allah since Ibrahim and Lut.”
l: The Prophet’s own daughters shared the hardships of the early Muslims.
Staying beside a sick wife can outweigh joining a battle, as ‘Uthman was told.
The Prophet ﷺ wept for his daughters, and taught that weeping is mercy.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Fard al-Khums, Book of Manaqib); Musnad Ahmad; Ibn Sa‘d, at-Tabaqat; Sirah of Ibn Ishaq

stories.title: Umm Haram and the sea they would sail
p: Umm Haram bint Milhan was the aunt of Anas ibn Malik, and the Prophet ﷺ often visited her house and ate there. She would also look through his hair. One day, he lay down in her house and fell asleep. Then he woke up smiling.
She asked him why he was smiling. What he said, and what she asked of him, led to a journey many years later, across a sea that the Muslims of Madinah had never seen, and to a grave on an island.
l: A person’s hope for a good end, asked sincerely, can be answered in a distant time and place.
The Prophet ﷺ gave glad tidings of the first naval expedition, long before it happened, which shows his knowledge by revelation.
Even a small act of hospitality can be remembered for generations.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Jihad, Book of Isti’dhan) and Sahih Muslim (Book of Imarah), narrated by Anas ibn Malik

stories.title: Umm Waraqah, the woman who knew the Qur’an
p: Umm Waraqah bint ‘Abdullah al-Ansariyyah was one of the women of Madinah who learned the Qur’an in the Prophet’s lifetime. When the Prophet ﷺ went to Badr, she asked to go with him, saying she would help the wounded and perhaps be a martyr. He told her to stay at home, for Allah would grant her martyrdom there.

The Prophet ﷺ used to visit her house, and call her “the martyr.” He also gave her a permission that has been a subject of scholarly discussion to this day, since the report is only in Abu Dawud and has been graded differently.
l: A woman’s knowledge of the Qur’an was honoured in the Prophet’s time, and he visited her.
Allah can grant martyrdom in unexpected ways, and the Prophet ﷺ said it of her.
Good treatment of those under one’s care matters, since her end came from servants she meant to free.
stories.src: Sunan Abi Dawud (Book of Salah, on a woman leading her household); Musnad Ahmad; Ibn Sa‘d, at-Tabaqat. The chain of the main report is discussed by hadith scholars.

stories.title: Al-Tabari and the thirty thousand pages
p: Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari was born in Amul, in the mountains south of the Caspian Sea, in 224 AH (839 CE). He says that he memorised the Qur’an at seven, led the prayers at eight, and began to write down hadith at nine. At about twelve, he left home to study, and he never really went back.

He travelled through Rayy, Baghdad, Basra, Kufa, Syria and Egypt, and settled in Baghdad, where he spent the rest of his life writing a commentary on the Qur’an and a history of the world that are still read. The story of how he planned them is told by those who knew him.
l: Learning needs sacrifice: al-Tabari left home as a boy and lived simply for knowledge.
A scholar tests his project against the energy of his students, and trims it to what can be finished.
Even his last hour was spent on knowledge, as the reports say he asked for ink on his deathbed.
stories.src: al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, Tarikh Baghdad; Yaqut, Mu‘jam al-Udaba’; adh-Dhahabi, Siyar A‘lam an-Nubala’; Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa’n-Nihayah

stories.title: Imam Muslim and the basket of dates
p: Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj of Nishapur compiled a collection of hadith that is second only to al-Bukhari’s in the eyes of most scholars, and for some, equal to it. He says that he selected it from three hundred thousand hadiths he had heard, and that it took him fifteen years.
The way he died is one of the best-known stories among students of hadith. It is told by al-Hakim and others, and it concerns a hadith that he was asked about in a gathering and could not answer.
l: A scholar’s humility shows in what he admits he does not know.
Care in selecting and arranging the reports is a form of worship; Muslim’s work stands on this.
His devotion to a single question led him to forget himself, as the story says.
stories.src: al-Hakim an-Naysaburi, Ma‘rifat ‘Ulum al-Hadith (cited by Ibn Khallikan and adh-Dhahabi); Ibn as-Salah, Siyanat Sahih Muslim; adh-Dhahabi, Siyar A‘lam an-Nubala’

stories.title: Ibn Hajar al-‘Asqalani and the stone
p: Ahmad ibn ‘Ali ibn Hajar was born in Cairo in 773 AH (1372 CE) and lost both of his parents when he was a small child. His father died when he was about four. He was raised by a guardian, a merchant, who took him to Makkah when he was a boy, and then sent him to study.

He later became the most important scholar of hadith in the later centuries, and the author of Fath al-Bari, the commentary on Sahih al-Bukhari that all later scholars use. But there was a time in his youth when he was so discouraged that he nearly gave up. What changed his mind is a story he told his students.
l: Persistence wears down what seems impossible, as water wears down a rock.
An orphan can become a leader of the community when someone guides and he works.
The best commentary was the result of twenty-five years of slow, careful work.
stories.src: as-Sakhawi, al-Jawahir wa’d-Durar fi Tarjamat Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Hajar; Ibn Hajar, Raf‘ al-Isr; al-Shawkani; Brockelmann for dates

stories.title: Ibn Kathir, the orphan of Busra
p: Isma‘il ibn ‘Umar ibn Kathir was born around 701 AH (1301 CE) in a village near Busra, in southern Syria. His father, a preacher, died when he was about three. His older brother took him to Damascus, and there the boy grew up among the great scholars of the day.

He became one of the most widely read commentators on the Qur’an, and a historian whose chronicle begins with creation and runs to his own time. The way that he approached both reflects what he learned from two of his teachers, who are among the most famous of the age.
l: The Qur’an is best explained by the Qur’an itself, then by the Sunnah, then by what the Companions said.
A historian can distinguish between what is reliable and what comes from earlier scriptures, as Ibn Kathir tried to do.
Scholarship is a lifetime’s work, and he continued even after he lost his sight.
stories.src: Ibn Hajar, ad-Durar al-Kaminah; Ibn Hajji, Dhayl; adh-Dhahabi, al-Mu‘jam al-Mukhtass; Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa’n-Nihayah and Tafsir al-Qur’an al-‘Azim

stories.title: Al-Qurtubi, who carried Cordoba with him
p: Abu ‘Abdillah Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Ansari al-Qurtubi, “of Cordoba,” was born in the early thirteenth century in the greatest city of Muslim Spain. In 1236, when he was a young man, Cordoba fell to the armies of Castile after a siege. The city that had been the capital of the Umayyads for centuries was lost.

Al-Qurtubi left, as many others did, and went east. He ended in Upper Egypt, in a small town on the Nile. There he wrote a commentary that begins from the rulings of the Qur’an and has been used by jurists ever since. He never returned to his city.
l: Loss of a homeland can become the cause of a work that lasts for centuries.
The Qur’an is a source of legal wisdom as well as spiritual guidance, and al-Qurtubi collected its rulings.
A scholar can live simply and leave behind a library for the world.
stories.src: Ibn Farhun, ad-Dibaj al-Mudhahhab; al-Maqqari, Nafh at-Tib; adh-Dhahabi; the introductions to al-Qurtubi’s Jami‘ li-Ahkam al-Qur’an and at-Tadhkirah

stories.title: Al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyad, the highway robber who became a teacher
p: The biographers say that al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyad, who was born in Khurasan in the second century of Islam, was in his youth a highwayman, one who attacked caravans on the road between Abiward and Sarakhs. He was strong and feared. One night, he climbed a wall to meet a girl he was in love with.

As he was climbing, he heard a man in the house reciting a verse of the Qur’an. The verse spoke to him directly, and what he said in reply, and where he spent the rest of that night, is the beginning of the story of one of the great ascetics and teachers of hadith of the early period.
l: No one is beyond repentance, and one verse can open the door.
Repentance involves making peace with those one has wronged, as al-Fudayl did.
He who has feared Allah in secret can become a source of fear and hope for everyone.
stories.src: adh-Dhahabi, Siyar A‘lam an-Nubala’; Abu Nu‘aym, Hilyat al-Awliya’; Ibn al-Jawzi, Sifat as-Safwah. The account of his early life is from the biographies and its chains are not strong.

stories.title: Yarmouk: six days on the border of Syria
p: In the summer of 636 CE (Rajab, 15 AH), the Muslim army in Syria, a fraction of the size of the Byzantine force sent against it, gathered by the river Yarmouk, east of the Sea of Galilee. The emperor Heraclius had sent the best of his armies to take back the province, and the Muslims had given up some of the towns they had taken, returning the taxes they had collected, because they could not protect them.

The fighting went on for about six days, and ended in a rout that decided the fate of Syria. It is told by at-Tabari and later historians, and the details, including the numbers, are uncertain, but the main shape of the battle is clear.
l: Skill in command and unity decide battles more than numbers do.
The old enemies of Islam became some of its most steadfast fighters, as ‘Ikrimah did.
The Muslims returned taxes when they could not protect people, which Syrians remembered.
stories.src: at-Tabari, Tarikh; al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa’n-Nihayah; modern studies note that the sources differ on numbers and dates

stories.title: Tariq ibn Ziyad and the crossing to al-Andalus
p: In 92 AH (711 CE), a force of about seven thousand men, mostly Berbers of North Africa, crossed the narrow strait that separates Africa from Spain. They landed at the foot of a great rock, which has carried the name of their leader ever since: Jabal Tariq, the Mountain of Tariq, in Spanish Gibraltar.

Their commander, Tariq ibn Ziyad, was a freedman and a Berber, a lieutenant of the governor of North Africa, Musa ibn Nusayr. A famous story says that he burned the ships to prevent retreat, and gave a speech that began with the words: “The enemy is in front of you and the sea is behind you.” Historians treat that story with caution.
l: A single decision, made on the shore, can turn the course of centuries.
Berbers and Arabs together built Islamic Spain, and Tariq’s own origins show the diversity of the early community.
Historians must separate what the early sources say from what later centuries added.
stories.src: Ibn ‘Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr wa’l-Maghrib wa’l-Andalus; al-Baladhuri; Ibn ‘Idhari; al-Maqqari, Nafh at-Tib (17th century, for the speech). Modern historians discuss the dates, numbers and the speech.

stories.title: ‘Ayn Jalut: the day the Mongol advance stopped
p: In 1258 CE, the Mongol army under Hulagu took Baghdad, killed the last Abbasid caliph, and destroyed much of the city. In 1260 they took Aleppo and then Damascus. Between them and Egypt stood only the Mamluk sultanate, ruled by a young sultan, Qutuz.

Hulagu sent envoys demanding surrender. Qutuz had them killed, and then he did something unusual: he marched out to meet the Mongols in Palestine, rather than waiting for them in Egypt. On the 25th of Ramadan 658 AH (3 September 1260), the two armies met at a spring called ‘Ayn Jalut.
l: A seemingly unstoppable force can be beaten by preparation, unity and courage.
The community stood together in the crisis, with scholars helping to raise funds.
The victory preserved the heartlands of the Muslim world: Egypt, Hijaz and Syria.
stories.src: al-Maqrizi, as-Suluk; Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa’n-Nihayah; Ibn Taghribirdi; modern studies on the Mamluk–Mongol conflict. The dating and some details are discussed.

stories.title: Mansa Musa’s pilgrimage and the price of gold
p: In 1324 CE, the ruler of the empire of Mali, Mansa Musa, set out for Makkah. He travelled from the Niger across the Sahara to Cairo, then to the Hijaz. He took with him a caravan so large that people spoke of it for generations: thousands of attendants and a quantity of gold that astonished everyone it passed.

In Cairo, he gave away so much gold that, according to a scholar who visited the city twelve years later, its price fell in the markets, and did not recover for a long time. The story is told by al-‘Umari, who talked to people who had seen it.
l: Hajj is a duty that Muslims from every corner of the world have always undertaken, from West Africa to Southeast Asia.
Wealth was used for charity and for building: he returned with scholars and architects.
The accounts remind us that Africa had empires of great wealth and learning in the fourteenth century.
stories.src: al-‘Umari, Masalik al-Absar; Ibn Khaldun, Kitab al-‘Ibar; Ibn Battuta, Rihlah; Timbuktu chronicles (Ta’rikh as-Sudan). Numbers in these sources vary widely.

stories.title: Ibn al-Haytham and how we see
p: Before Ibn al-Haytham, many scholars, following Euclid and Ptolemy, believed that we see because rays come out of the eye and touch the objects around us. Others, following Aristotle, thought that something travelled from the object to the eye. Nobody had a way to decide.

Ibn al-Haytham, who was born in Basra in about 965 CE and worked in Cairo, took a different approach. He did experiments. In a long book on optics, written between 1011 and 1021, he showed that we see because light comes from objects into the eye, and he proved it with careful tests that others could repeat.
l: The Qur’an calls on people to observe and reason, and Ibn al-Haytham did so.
The truth must be tested, even against the great authorities: he wrote a book of “Doubts” against Ptolemy.
The best minds worked with patience, often under difficult conditions.
stories.src: Ibn Abi Usaybi‘ah, ‘Uyun al-Anba’; al-Qifti, Ta’rikh al-Hukama’; Ibn al-Haytham, Kitab al-Manazir (as edited and studied by Sabra and others); A. I. Sabra’s introduction

stories.title: Al-Zahrawi, the surgeon of Cordoba
p: Abu al-Qasim Khalaf ibn al-‘Abbas al-Zahrawi lived in Cordoba in the tenth century, in the time of the Umayyad caliphs. He was the court physician of al-Hakam II and spent most of his life in or near Madinat az-Zahra’, the palace city outside the capital.

He wrote an encyclopaedia of medicine in thirty parts. The last part, on surgery, included drawings of about two hundred instruments, descriptions of operations, and advice to surgeons. In Latin translation, it was a textbook in European universities for hundreds of years.
l: A physician must know anatomy and learn his craft by practice, not only by reading.
Careful drawings and clear descriptions made the knowledge of one man a resource for many.
Medicine is a service to people, to be given to the poor as to the rich.
stories.src: al-Zahrawi, Kitab at-Tasrif li-man ‘ajaza ‘an at-ta’lif; Ibn Abi Usaybi‘ah; the editions and studies by Spink and Lewis, Hamarneh, Campbell, and others

stories.title: Al-Khwarizmi and the book of restoring
p: Around 820 CE, in Baghdad, a scholar named Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote a short book on calculation. It was meant, he said, to help people with the most ordinary problems: dividing inheritances, settling legacies, measuring land, digging canals and trading.

The book was called al-Kitab al-Mukhtasar fi Hisab al-Jabr wa’l-Muqabalah. The word al-jabr, “restoring,” became “algebra,” and the author’s own name, in its Latin form Algoritmi, became the word “algorithm.” It is rare for a person to give their name to two words in this way.
l: The greatest ideas are often born from practical needs, as algebra came from inheritance and land.
The call of the Qur’an to the law of inheritance with exact fractions helped to inspire the study of arithmetic.
Learning travels: Greek, Indian and Persian ideas met in Baghdad and went on to Europe.
stories.src: al-Khwarizmi, Kitab al-Jabr wa’l-Muqabalah (ed. Rosen, 1831; Rashed, 2007); Ibn an-Nadim, al-Fihrist; Ibn al-Qifti; Latin translations by Robert of Chester and Gerard of Cremona

stories.title: Ibn Sina, the prodigy who wrote the Canon
p: Abu ‘Ali al-Husayn ibn ‘Abdillah ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was born in about 980 CE in a village near Bukhara, in what is now Uzbekistan. By ten he had memorised the Qur’an. By sixteen, he says, he was teaching medicine to physicians. At seventeen, he was called to treat the Samanid ruler of Bukhara, who had a disease that the court doctors could not cure.

He is the author of the Canon of Medicine, which was the main textbook in the medical schools of the Muslim world and Europe for more than five hundred years. In his own account of his life, he tells a story about a book that he could not understand, and how he finally did.
l: Great learning needs patience: he read a book forty times without understanding it.
He gave thanks by giving charity when he understood it, an example of gratitude.
A physician’s work is guided by observation and by the rules of health, and these remain at the base of medicine.
stories.src: Ibn Sina’s autobiography, completed by his student al-Juzjani (in Ibn Abi Usaybi‘ah, ‘Uyun al-Anba’, and Ibn al-Qifti); modern studies by Gutas and others

stories.title: Cordoba, the ornament of the world
p: In the tenth century, Cordoba was the largest and most refined city in western Europe. It was the capital of the Umayyad caliphate in Spain, ruled from 929 by ‘Abd ar-Rahman III. A German nun, Hrotsvit of Gandersheim, who had heard of it from travellers, called it “the ornament of the world.”

Its streets were reportedly paved and lit, its mosque was one of the wonders of the age, and its libraries held more books than all the libraries of Christian Europe combined, according to later Muslim writers. The accounts are partly exaggerated, but the city’s importance is not in doubt.
l: A civilisation that gives knowledge a home can reach far, as Cordoba did.
Muslims, Christians and Jews lived and studied together, though not without strain.
Great cities rise and fall, and what remains is the learning they preserved.
stories.src: Ibn Hayyan; al-Maqqari, Nafh at-Tib; Ibn Hazm; modern studies by Kennedy, Fletcher, Menocal and others. Figures for population and books are estimates by medieval writers and later historians.

stories.title: Julaybib: “He is from me and I am from him”
p: Julaybib was a man of the Ansar whom people did not much notice. He was short, according to the description in the narrations, with a plain appearance and no family of note. The Prophet ﷺ once went to a man of the Ansar and asked for the hand of his daughter, but not for himself. He asked for Julaybib.

The father hesitated, and went to ask his wife. What the daughter said when she overheard them, and what the Prophet ﷺ said when Julaybib was missing after a battle, make one of the most moving stories of the Madinan period.
l: The Prophet ﷺ valued people by faith and not by looks or lineage, and he made sure the overlooked had a place.
The daughter’s answer shows trust in Allah’s Messenger as a form of faith: “Do not reject what the Prophet ﷺ asks.”
His death, and the words of the Prophet ﷺ over him, honoured a man whom no one had expected.
stories.src: Musnad Ahmad (the proposal, narrated by Anas and Abu Barzah al-Aslami, graded sahih by al-Albani and others); Sahih Muslim (the battle, narrated by Abu Barzah)

stories.title: The young man who asked permission to sin
p: A young man came to the Prophet ﷺ in the mosque and said: “O Messenger of Allah, give me permission to commit fornication.” The people around the Prophet ﷺ were shocked. They turned on him and said: “Stop! Stop!”

The Prophet ﷺ told them to leave him alone. He called the young man to come closer, and then began to ask him questions. By the end of the conversation, the young man’s whole attitude to the thing he had asked for had changed.
l: The way to correct a person is by reasoning with him gently and appealing to his own conscience.
The Prophet ﷺ asked questions that made the young man answer himself, and he finished with a prayer.
A shock to the listeners is no reason to lose patience with the one who asks.
stories.src: Musnad Ahmad, narrated by Abu Umamah al-Bahili (graded sahih by al-Albani); also reported with a similar chain by at-Tabarani

stories.title: The Abyssinians with their spears in the mosque
p: It was a festival day in Madinah, and some Abyssinians were performing a display with spears and shields in the courtyard of the mosque. ‘A’ishah, who was a young wife at the time, wanted to watch. The Prophet ﷺ stood in the doorway of her room and held up his cloak so that she could see.

She rested her cheek on his shoulder and watched for as long as she wished, until she was tired and he asked if it was enough. ‘Umar came and tried to stop the display, and the Prophet ﷺ told him to leave them alone.
l: Joy on festival days is part of the religion, and the Prophet ﷺ allowed permitted play even in the mosque grounds.
He gave his wife time and attention, and showed that kindness within marriage is an act of faith.
“Leave them, ‘Umar”: not every expression that surprises is wrong.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Prayer, Book of the Two Festivals) and Sahih Muslim (Book of the Two Festivals), narrated by ‘A’ishah and Abu Hurayrah

stories.title: “Eat with your right hand”: ‘Umar ibn Abi Salamah at the table
p: ‘Umar ibn Abi Salamah was a boy being raised in the Prophet’s house, the son of Umm Salamah by her earlier husband. One day, as he was eating with the Prophet ﷺ, his hand wandered across the dish, taking from here and there.
The Prophet ﷺ spoke to him. What he said was only three short pieces of advice, yet ‘Umar remembered it for the rest of his life and said that he ate in that way ever afterwards.
l: Good manners are taught with kindness, in the moment, using short words a child can remember.
The three sunnahs of eating, naming Allah, using the right hand and eating from what is near, are the basis of table manners.
A child brought up in a home of faith carries what he learned all his life.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Food) and Sahih Muslim (Book of Drinks), narrated by ‘Umar ibn Abi Salamah

stories.title: Mu‘awiyah ibn al-Hakam, the man who spoke in prayer
p: Mu‘awiyah ibn al-Hakam as-Sulami was a new Muslim who had come from the desert and did not yet know all the rules. He was praying behind the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah when a man in the row sneezed. Mu‘awiyah said, aloud: “May Allah have mercy on you.”

The people next to him looked at him sternly and began to slap their thighs to silence him. He was upset and wanted to answer, but held back. When the prayer was over, the Prophet ﷺ spoke to him. Mu‘awiyah never forgot it.
l: The Prophet ﷺ taught the unknowing with gentleness, and excused those who acted from ignorance.
The ruling is plain: speech of the people is not permitted in prayer, which is for glorification, takbir and recitation.
A teacher’s kindness leaves a deeper mark than harshness.
stories.src: Sahih Muslim (Book of Mosques and Places of Prayer), narrated by Mu‘awiyah ibn al-Hakam as-Sulami

stories.title: “Go back and pray, for you have not prayed”
p: A man came into the mosque while the Prophet ﷺ was sitting there, and prayed two rak‘ahs quickly. Then he came and greeted the Prophet ﷺ, who returned his greeting and said: “Go back and pray, for you have not prayed.”

The man went and prayed again in the same way, came back and greeted him, and heard the same words. This happened a third time. Then the man said: “By the One who sent you with the truth, I cannot do better than this, so teach me.” What the Prophet ﷺ taught him is the basis of the description of how to pray.
l: The Prophet ﷺ let the man try until he asked, so that the teaching would be wanted when it came.
Calmness (tuma’ninah) in each part of the prayer is a requirement, not an extra.
To teach a person is to accept his honest admission that he does not know.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Adhan) and Sahih Muslim (Book of Prayer), narrated by Abu Hurayrah and others

stories.title: A race on the road, and “this one for that one”
p: ‘A’ishah once went with the Prophet ﷺ on a journey when she was still a slim young woman. He told the people to go on ahead of them, and then he said to her: “Come, let us race.” She raced him and won.

Years later, on another journey, he again told the people to go ahead and challenged her. By then she had put on weight and had forgotten that they had raced. This time he won, and what he said as he did it is a small and happy scene from their life.
l: The Prophet ﷺ made time for fun with his wife, and playfulness is part of a good marriage.
He sent people ahead so that the moment would be private, which shows his consideration for her feelings.
The best of men are the best to their families, and that includes laughter.
stories.src: Sunan Abi Dawud (Book of Jihad), Sunan Ibn Majah and Musnad Ahmad, narrated by ‘A’ishah (graded sahih by al-Albani and others)

stories.title: The Jewish boy who served the Prophet ﷺ
p: A young Jewish boy used to serve the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah, bringing him water and doing small tasks. One day he did not come, and the Prophet ﷺ asked about him. They told him that he was ill. The Prophet ﷺ went to visit him.
He sat down by the boy’s head and spoke to him. What the boy did, and what his father said, and what the Prophet ﷺ said as he left, are recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari by Anas ibn Malik, who was there.
l: The Prophet ﷺ visited a sick child of another faith, which shows that kindness is not limited to Muslims.
He invited the boy to Islam gently, in the presence of his father, and left the choice to him.
His thanks to Allah on leaving showed what mattered to him most: the safety of a soul.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Funerals), narrated by Anas ibn Malik; also Sunan Abi Dawud

stories.title: Umm Zar‘ and the eleven women
p: ‘A’ishah told a story to her students, which she had heard from the Prophet ﷺ himself. Eleven women of Yemen, it says, sat down together and made a pledge not to hide anything about their husbands. Each in turn describes hers, with a vivid image, in the poetic Arabic of the time.

The eleventh, Umm Zar‘, speaks longest. She tells of a husband who was generous and then left her, and of a second one who was kind but never matched the first. At the end, the Prophet ﷺ said something to ‘A’ishah that has been quoted by husbands and wives since.
l: The Prophet ﷺ listened to long stories and told them to his family, and found a lesson of gratitude in them.
The women’s descriptions of their husbands show how marriages can differ, and what women value: kindness, generosity and company.
Gratitude for one’s spouse is shown in how one speaks of them, and what one remembers.
stories.src: Sahih al-Bukhari (Book of Nikah) and Sahih Muslim (Book of Virtues of the Companions), narrated by ‘A’ishah; commentary by Ibn Hajar and al-Qadi ‘Iyad. The Arabic has many rare words, and the explanations of some phrases differ.

facts: Son of Ibrahim and Sarah, a prophet (19:49, 37:112–113)
Son of Ishaq, also named Isra’il; a prophet (19:49)
"We will worship your God and the God of your fathers" (2:133)

t: Angels came to Ibrahim in the form of men and greeted him, "Peace." He answered, "Peace," and soon brought a roasted calf. Seeing that their hands did not reach for it, he became wary of them. They said: "Do not fear. We have been sent to the people of Lut." His wife was standing there and laughed, and they gave her glad tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya’qub (11:69–71).

She said: "Woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this, my husband, is an old man? Indeed, this is a strange thing!" They said: "Are you amazed at the decree of Allah? May the mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, people of the house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Honourable." (11:72–73)

Ya’qub had twelve sons. The Qur’an says that Ibrahim and Ya’qub both left their children a testament: "O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims." (2:132) And as Ya’qub lay dying: "Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya’qub, when he said to his sons, What will you worship after me? They said: We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma’il and Ishaq, one God. And we are Muslims [submitting] to Him." (2:133)
It is a clear statement that the prophets from Ibrahim on shared one religion, submission to Allah (Islam), and this is why the Qur’an calls them all Muslims.

When Yusuf was lost, then Binyamin, Ya’qub said: "Rather, your souls have enticed you to something, so patience is most fitting. Perhaps Allah will bring them to me all together." And he turned away from them and said, "Oh, my sorrow over Yusuf," and his eyes became white from grief, and he was suppressing [his sorrow] (12:83–84). His sons said he would ruin his health. He said: "I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know." (12:86)

Then: "O my sons, go and find out about Yusuf and his brother and despair not of relief from Allah. Indeed, no one despairs of relief from Allah except the disbelieving people." (12:87) His patience was never a surrender of hope. The Prophet ﷺ said that being patient is at the first shock; he wept when his son Ibrahim died, so crying is not against it.

The Qur’an says: “All food was lawful to the Children of Israel, except what Israel had made unlawful for himself before the Torah was revealed.” (3:93) “Israel” is Ya‘qub. A hadith explains the reference. Ibn ‘Abbas reports in the Musnad of Ahmad and at-Tirmidhi that a group of Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him questions, among them what Ya‘qub had forbidden himself. The Prophet ﷺ asked them to swear by Allah, then said: “Do you know that Israel fell gravely ill, and that his illness lasted long, so he vowed to Allah that if He cured him, he would forbid himself the food and drink that he most loved? That was camel meat and its milk.” They said: “Yes, by Allah.”

This is how the Qur’an and Sunnah explain a point of law of the earlier community: that it was a personal vow which became a rule for his descendants. The lesson drawn by scholars is that making a hardship for oneself is not what Allah asks, and that the religion of Muhammad ﷺ came with ease. “He did not place upon you in the religion any hardship.” (22:78)

Ya‘qub is part of a line of four generations of prophets: Ibrahim, Ishaq, Ya‘qub and Yusuf. The Prophet ﷺ spoke of it in a hadith recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari. He was asked: “Who is the most honoured of people?” He said: “The most honoured of them in the sight of Allah is the one with the most taqwa.” They said: “We do not ask you about this.” He said: “Then Yusuf, the prophet of Allah, son of the prophet of Allah, son of the prophet of Allah, son of the Friend of Allah.” In another version: “The noble son of the noble son of the noble son of the noble, Yusuf ibn Ya‘qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim.”

It is a short genealogy and it gives a sense of what a house of prophecy looks like. Each generation passes on what it has received, as Ya‘qub did when he asked his sons on his deathbed what they would worship after him. They answered: “We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma‘il and Ishaq, one God, and to Him we submit.” (2:133)

facts: Musa, and older by some accounts
"Appoint for me a minister from my family: Harun, my brother" (20:29–30)
"You are to me as Harun was to Musa, except there is no prophet after me"

t: At the burning bush, Musa asked Allah to help his task: "My Lord, expand for me my breast [with assurance] and ease for me my task and untie the knot from my tongue that they may understand my speech. And appoint for me a minister from my family: Harun, my brother. Increase through him my strength and make him my partner in my task, that we may exalt You much and remember You much." (20:25–34) Allah said: "You have been granted your request, O Musa." (20:36)
And in Surah Maryam, Allah says: "And We gave him out of Our mercy his brother Harun as a prophet." (19:53) It is remembered as the greatest gift anyone has been given by another’s dua.

Musa left for the appointed meeting with Allah, and told Harun: "Take my place among my people and do right and do not follow the way of the corrupters." (7:142) The Samiri, a man among them, collected their jewellery, melted it and shaped it into a calf that lowed. He said: "This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot." (20:88) Harun told them: "O my people, you are only being tested by it, and indeed, your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my order." They said: "We will not cease to remain devoted to it until Musa returns to us." (20:90–91)

Musa returned, angry and sorrowful, threw down the tablets and seized his brother by the head and pulled him toward him. Harun said: "O son of my mother, indeed the people oppressed me and were about to kill me, so let not the enemies rejoice over me and do not place me among the wrongdoing people." (7:150) In Surah Ta-Ha, he adds: "I feared that you would say, You caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word." (20:94) Musa prayed: "My Lord, forgive me and my brother and admit us into Your mercy, and You are the most merciful of the merciful." (7:151)

The Prophet ﷺ praised Harun’s role when he told ‘Ali on the way to Tabuk: "Are you not content to be to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there is no prophet after me?" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

When the Prophet ﷺ set out for Tabuk in 9 AH, he left ‘Ali ibn Abi Talib in charge of his family in Madinah. Some of the hypocrites said that he had left ‘Ali behind because he found him a burden. ‘Ali was hurt and went after the Prophet ﷺ to tell him. Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas reports in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim that the Prophet ﷺ said to him: “Are you not pleased to be to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there is no prophet after me?”

The words show how the Prophet ﷺ saw Harun: as a brother and a deputy who is left in charge when the leader goes out. In the same way that Musa left Harun among his people at the foot of Mount Sinai, the Prophet ﷺ left ‘Ali in his city. Scholars note the exception that the Prophet ﷺ himself added: there would be no prophet after him. The comparison was for trust and for the place of a deputy, not for prophethood.

When Maryam came to her people with her baby, they said to her: “O sister of Harun, your father was not a man of evil and your mother was not unchaste.” (19:28) A question came up later. Harun lived long before ‘Isa, so how could Maryam have been his sister? Al-Mughirah ibn Shu‘bah reports in Sahih Muslim that when he was sent to the Christians of Najran, they put the objection to him. He did not know the answer, and he asked the Prophet ﷺ when he returned.

The Prophet ﷺ said: “They used to name their children after the prophets and the righteous people who came before them.” The explanation fits another possible reading: that she was called “sister of Harun” because she came from his line, as one says “brother of Tamim” for a man of that tribe, or because she was named after a righteous man of her own time. It is a small example of the Prophet’s approach to questions about the Qur’an: to give a short, clear answer.

facts: Not given in the Qur’an; tradition calls them Habil (Abel) and Qabil (Cain)
Envy after an offering was accepted from one and not the other
The first murder, and the first burial
"No soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Adam has a share of its blood" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

t: "And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam, in truth, when they both offered a sacrifice [to Allah], and it was accepted from one of them and was not accepted from the other. Said [the latter], I will surely kill you. Said [the former], Indeed, Allah only accepts from the righteous [who fear Him]." (5:27) The Qur’an does not say what each offered or how acceptance was shown; the narrations are from earlier traditions. What matters is the reason given: acceptance depends on taqwa.

"If you should raise your hand against me to kill me, I would not raise mine against you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds. Indeed, I want you to obtain [thereby] my sin and your sin so you will be among the companions of the Fire. And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers." (5:28–29) Scholars explain that he did not mean to submit to being killed in all circumstances, but that he chose not to start violence against his own brother, even at his own cost, and that it was a statement of restraint before a crime, not a rule for self-defence.

"And his soul permitted to him the murder of his brother, so he killed him and became among the losers. Then Allah sent a crow searching in the ground to show him how to hide the disgrace of his brother. He said: Woe to me! Have I failed to be like this crow and hide the disgrace of my brother? And he became of the regretful." (5:30–31)
His regret was not repentance: the verse says he became "of the regretful," not "of the repentant."

Because of this, Allah says: "We decreed upon the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul unless for a soul or for corruption [done] in the land, it is as if he had slain mankind entirely. And whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved mankind entirely." (5:32) The Prophet ﷺ said: "No soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Adam has a share of its blood, because he was the first to establish killing." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

facts: "A good land and a forgiving Lord"
The flood of al-‘Arim, the dam
"They scattered like the people of Saba’" (tafarraqu aydi Saba’)

t: "There was for [the tribe of] Saba’ in their dwelling place a sign: two [fields of] gardens on the right and on the left. [They were told], Eat from the provision of your Lord and be grateful to Him. A good land and a forgiving Lord." (34:15) Historians connect Saba’ to the kingdom of southern Arabia that built a great dam at Ma’rib to irrigate its fields. They also had safe, linked towns along the incense road: "And We placed between them and the cities which We had blessed [many] visible cities and determined between them the [length of] journey: Travel between them safely by night and day." (34:18)

"But they turned away, so We sent upon them the flood of the dam and replaced their two gardens with two gardens having bitter fruit and tamarisk and something of sparse lote trees." (34:16) Then the Qur’an adds what they said: "They said: Our Lord, lengthen the distance between our journeys, and wronged themselves. So We made them narrations and dispersed them in total dispersion. Indeed in that are signs for everyone patient and grateful." (34:19)

Commentators describe how they became bored of easy journeys and wished for harder ones to appear more important, a kind of arrogance toward ease. When the dam gave way they scattered across Arabia; tribes that later appear in Madinah and the north, such as Aws and Khazraj, are said to be among their descendants.

The verse says the sign is for "everyone patient and grateful." The believer’s state is exactly these two: patient in hardship, grateful in ease. The Prophet ﷺ said: "How wonderful is the affair of the believer..." (Sahih Muslim), which applies the same pair to a life.

A man named Farwah ibn Musayk once asked the Prophet ﷺ about Saba’, in a hadith recorded in at-Tirmidhi and graded hasan. He said: “O Messenger of Allah, tell me about Saba’. Is it a land or a woman?” The Prophet ﷺ said: “It is neither a land nor a woman. It is a man who had ten sons among the Arabs. Six of them settled in the south, and four of them in the north (Sham).” He then named the tribes that came from them.

It confirms that “Saba’” was both the name of an ancestor and the name given to a people and kingdom descended from him, and that the Arabs of Yemen were thought of as his descendants. It also explains the Arabic saying “scattered like the people of Saba’” (tafarraqu aydi Saba’), used of a group that has broken up and gone in all directions, which comes from the end of the story in the Qur’an: “and We scattered them in total dispersion.” (34:19)

The “flood of the dam” (sayl al-‘arim) is linked by historians to the great dam at Ma’rib, in what is now Yemen. It was a work of ancient engineering that stored the water of the seasonal floods and fed an irrigated plain. Inscriptions in the old South Arabian script found at Ma’rib record repairs to the dam over the centuries.

One of them, from the sixth century CE, records repairs carried out by Abraha, the Abyssinian governor of Yemen, in about 543 CE. It is the same Abraha who later marched on Makkah in the year of the Prophet’s birth. The dam broke for the last time in that same century, according to historians, and the area, which had been a land of gardens, became dry. The scholars say that the Qur’an does not date the event, and that this historical background helps one to picture the place, but it does not add to what is needed from the verses.

facts: Al-Baqarah (2:67–73), which is named after it
"Allah commands you to slaughter a cow"
Asking questions that narrowed the command
A dead man revived by a strike with part of the cow
Allah "shows you His signs that you might reason"

t: "And [recall] when you killed a man and disputed over it, but Allah was to bring out that which you were concealing. So We said, Strike him with part of it. Thus does Allah bring the dead to life, and He shows you His signs that perhaps you will understand." (2:72–73) The command, before this, was: "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow." They said: "Do you take us in ridicule?" He said: "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant." (2:67)

They said: "Call upon your Lord to make clear to us what it is." Musa said: "[Allah] says, It is a cow neither old nor virgin, but median between that." So do what you are commanded. They said: "Call upon your Lord to show us what is her colour." He said: "A yellow cow, bright in colour, pleasing to the observers." They said: "Call upon your Lord to make clear to us what it is. Indeed, all cows look alike to us. And indeed we, if Allah wills, will be guided." He said: "He says, It is a cow neither trained to plough the earth nor to irrigate the field, one free from fault with no spot upon her." They said: "Now you have come with the truth." And they slaughtered her, but they could hardly do it. (2:68–71)

Commentators note that had they slaughtered any cow when first told, they would have done it. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Leave me as I leave you. Those before you were destroyed because of their many questions and their disagreements with their prophets. If I forbid you something, avoid it, and if I order you something, do as much of it as you can." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). This was a lesson on obedience and about how many a hardship is created by those who ask for details after the matter was clear.

The lesson of excessive questioning has an example in the life of the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Hurayrah reports in Sahih Muslim that the Prophet ﷺ gave a sermon and said: “O people, Allah has made the Hajj obligatory upon you, so perform it.” A man asked: “Every year, O Messenger of Allah?” The Prophet ﷺ was silent. The man asked three times. Then he said: “If I had said yes, it would have become obligatory, and you would not have been able to do it.”

He then said: “Leave me as I leave you. Those before you were destroyed only because of their many questions and their disagreement with their prophets. If I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can, and if I forbid you something, leave it.” The Qur’an says the same: “O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if made plain to you, would distress you.” (5:101) The people of the cow could have fulfilled the command with the first animal they saw. Each question added a condition until the command became hard to fulfil.

facts: "That we may eat from it and our hearts be reassured"
"That it may be for us a festival"
A severe punishment for any who disbelieve afterwards

t: "[Mention] when the disciples said, O ‘Isa, son of Maryam, can your Lord send down to us a table [spread with food] from the heaven? He said: Fear Allah, if you should be believers. They said: We wish to eat from it and to have our hearts reassured and to know that you have been truthful to us and be among its witnesses." (5:112–113) Their statement is difficult: "can your Lord" is understood by scholars as a request, not doubt, though ‘Isa’s answer shows he thought it a risky one.

‘Isa, son of Maryam, said: "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table [spread with food] from the heaven to be for us a festival for the first of us and the last of us and a sign from You. And provide for us, and You are the best of providers." (5:114) Allah said: "Indeed, I will send it down to you, but whoever disbelieves afterwards from among you, then indeed will I punish him with a punishment by which I have not punished anyone among the worlds." (5:115)

The Qur’an does not say what the table contained or what became of the people after; its point is the statement of Allah’s generosity and the seriousness of ingratitude after witnessing a sign. Later reports give details of loaves and fish, and a punishment of those who disbelieved, but they are not found in authentic hadith, so we leave them. The Qur’an then turns to the scene on the Day of Resurrection when ‘Isa is asked about what his followers said of him (5:116–118).

The word the Qur’an uses for ‘Isa’s companions is al-hawariyyun. Allah says: “When ‘Isa sensed disbelief from them, he said: ‘Who are my helpers to Allah?’ The disciples said: ‘We are the helpers of Allah. We have believed in Allah, and bear witness that we are Muslims.’” (3:52) In another place the Qur’an tells believers to be “helpers of Allah, as ‘Isa the son of Maryam said to the disciples.” (61:14)

Commentators explain the word in different ways: as those who wore white clothes, as washers of clothes, or simply as the sincere ones. What they agree on is that the disciples were his closest followers. The request for the table was therefore made by people who already believed. They wished for a sign to settle their hearts, as Ibrahim had, and they were told that after such a sign, the standard of accountability would be higher.

The Qur’an does not describe what was on the table. Some reports in the commentaries say that it carried bread and fish, and others that it carried bread and meat, and that the disciples were told not to hoard the food or carry it away. Some of these reports are attributed to the Companions, and one, in at-Tirmidhi, is traced to ‘Ammar ibn Yasir, but at-Tirmidhi himself points out that it was reported as the saying of a Companion and not safely as the Prophet’s.

It is better to hold to what the Qur’an says, which is the main point: that ‘Isa asked that the table be “a festival for the first of us and the last of us”, a day to remember Allah’s favour, and that Allah said: “I will send it down to you, but whoever disbelieves afterwards, I will punish him with a punishment I have not given to anyone in the worlds.” (5:115) The seriousness of the warning is in proportion to the greatness of the gift.

facts: The Qur’an does not name him or the town
"How will Allah bring this to life after its death?"
The food unspoiled, the donkey revived

t: "Or [consider such an example] as the one who passed by a township which had fallen into ruin. He said: How will Allah bring this to life after its death? So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years; then He revived him. [Allah] said: How long have you remained? He said: I have remained a day or part of a day. [Allah] said: Rather, you have remained a hundred years. Look at your food and your drink; it has not changed with time. And look at your donkey; and We will make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones [of the donkey] how We raise them and then We cover them with flesh. And when it became clear to him, he said: I know that Allah is over all things competent." (2:259)

His words are not a denial but wonder. Commentators say they were a question to see how Allah would restore a population from a ruin, and that Allah answered by doing it to him. Commentators note that the Qur’an does not identify him because the point is the sign. Some earlier traditions say he was ‘Uzayr or Irmiya; neither is established.

Right after it, Ibrahim asks to see: "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." [Allah] said: "Have you not believed?" He said: "Yes, but [I ask] only that my heart may be satisfied." He said: "Take four birds and incline them to yourself, then put on each hill a portion of them; then call them; they will come to you in haste. And know that Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise." (2:260) The Prophet ﷺ said: "We are more worthy of doubt than Ibrahim," meaning he asked not out of doubt, and that if Ibrahim doubted, we would have more reason (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim), explaining that the request was for greater certainty.

facts: The Arabian Peninsula: Hijaz, Najd, Yemen, the Gulf coast
The Byzantine and Persian empires, Abyssinia
Winter caravans to Yemen and summer caravans to Syria (106:1–2)
Idols around the Kaaba, alongside the memory of Ibrahim and a few hanifs
Four sacred months in which fighting was forbidden

t: Society was organised by tribe and clan. A person’s protection, identity and justice rested on their kin, which is why those without a strong tribe suffered so much when Islam came. Honour was guarded fiercely; a killing could lead to a blood feud lasting decades, such as the war of Basus between two tribes, or the Day of Bu’ath that left Aws and Khazraj weary. Poetry was the highest art, and the markets of ‘Ukaz held contests where poets recited. Language mattered, and that is why the Qur’an’s challenge to produce something like it was so pointed.

Makkah lay in a barren valley, yet it flourished because it held the Kaaba and the well of Zamzam. Quraysh controlled both and the pilgrim trade; they were called "the people of Allah" and respected by all tribes. They made treaties with neighbouring peoples that allowed their caravans to run safely, a favour the Qur’an reminds them of: "For the accustomed security of Quraysh, their accustomed security [in] the caravan of winter and summer, let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them, [saving them] from hunger and made them safe, [saving them] from fear." (106:1–4)

By then the House built by Ibrahim and Isma’il was filled with idols. According to the Sira, ‘Amr ibn Luhayy brought idols to Makkah from Syria; the Prophet ﷺ said he saw him dragging his intestines in the Fire, because he was the first to dedicate animals to the idols (Sahih al-Bukhari). People worshipped al-Lat, al-‘Uzza and Manat, as well as Hubal, and saw them as intercessors. They still believed Allah created the heavens and the earth (29:61, 31:25), but addressed others for their needs.

The Qur’an describes what it came to correct: burying infant girls alive (81:8–9, 16:58–59), killing children for fear of poverty (17:31), interest and unjust treatment of orphans, and the exploitation of the weak. Gambling and drinking were common. There was no common authority. Slaves were bought and sold, and women had little protection under law.

It was also a place of seekers. A few men, the hanifs, such as Waraqah ibn Nawfal and Zayd ibn ‘Amr ibn Nufayl, rejected idols and sought the religion of Ibrahim; Zayd would lean on the Kaaba and say: "O Quraysh, none of you is on the religion of Ibrahim but me." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

To the north, the Byzantines ruled Syria; to the east, the Sasanian Persians ruled Iraq and the Gulf. They were fighting a long and exhausting war during the Prophet’s ﷺ time, and the Qur’an itself refers to a Byzantine defeat and the promise of a later victory: "The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land. But they, after their defeat, will overcome within three to nine years." (30:2–4) To the south, the kingdom of Himyar had fallen to Abyssinian rule, and then to Persian control. Arabia lay in the shadows of these powers, so unimportant to them that when Islam emerged they hardly noticed.
