(Sahih al-Bukhari). The Prophet ﷺ was looking for the answer of the Ansar, since their pledge at ‘Aqabah was to protect him in Madinah, not abroad. Sa’d ibn Mu’adh stood and said: "If you led us into this sea, we would plunge in with you; not one of us would stay behind. We are patient in war and sincere in battle." The Prophet ﷺ was delighted and said: "March on, and be glad."

Allah sent rain that night. It firmed the sand beneath the Muslims and turned the ground beneath Quraysh to mud, and gave them a light sleep that took away their fear: "[Remember] when He covered you with drowsiness, security from Him, and sent down upon you from the sky rain to purify you and remove from you the evil of Satan and to bind your hearts and plant firmly thereby your feet." (8:11)

The Prophet ﷺ spent the night praying beneath a tree. In the morning he lined up the ranks and made a long dua: "O Allah, if this band of Muslims is destroyed today, You will not be worshipped on the earth." He stretched out his hands until his cloak fell from his shoulders, and Abu Bakr put it back, saying, "Enough, O Messenger of Allah, you have implored your Lord urgently, and He will fulfil what He promised you." (Sahih Muslim)

It began with single combat. Three Makkan champions, ‘Utbah, Shaybah and al-Walid, challenged the Muslims. Three Ansar stepped forward, but they said they wanted their own cousins. The Prophet ﷺ sent Hamzah, ‘Ali and ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, and the first two quickly killed their opponents and helped ‘Ubaydah, who was wounded and died later (as ‘Ali narrates, Sahih al-Bukhari).

In the general fighting the Muslims prevailed; the Qur’an says angels fought with them: "When you asked help of your Lord, and He answered you: I will reinforce you with a thousand angels, following one another." (8:9) Abu Jahl was struck down by two young Ansar, Mu’adh ibn ‘Amr ibn al-Jamuh and Mu’awwidh ibn ‘Afra’, and ‘Abdullah ibn Mas’ud found him dying and finished him (Sahih al-Bukhari).

Seventy were taken captive. The Prophet ﷺ asked Abu Bakr and ‘Umar. Abu Bakr suggested ransom, since they were kin and the money would strengthen the Muslims, and ‘Umar suggested execution. He inclined to Abu Bakr’s view. The next day Allah revealed 8:67–68 in the direction of ‘Umar’s stricter view, that it was not for a prophet to take prisoners until he had established his authority; but the ransom was allowed (Sahih Muslim). Prisoners were to be treated well; some were reportedly freed in exchange for teaching ten Muslim children to read and write (Musnad Ahmad).

The Muslims who fought at Badr were afterwards given great honour. When ‘Umar wanted to punish Hatib ibn Abi Balta’ah for sending a letter to Quraysh before the conquest of Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ said: "He took part in Badr. How do you know that Allah has not looked at the people of Badr and said: Do what you will, for I have forgiven you?" (Sahih al-Bukhari).

facts: The mountain of Uhud, north of Madinah
About 70, including Hamzah and Mus’ab ibn ‘Umayr

t: Quraysh wanted revenge for Badr, in which many of their leaders had died. They raised an army of about three thousand, with their wives to urge them on, and camped at Uhud. The Prophet ﷺ had a dream in which a cow was slaughtered and his sword was notched, which he interpreted as losses among his companions, and he preferred to defend inside Madinah. But the younger men who had missed Badr wanted to go out and fight, and he agreed. When he had put on his armour, many regretted having pressed him, but he said: "It is not for a prophet, once he has put on his armour, to take it off until Allah judges between him and the enemy." (Musnad Ahmad)
On the way, ‘Abdullah ibn Ubayy, the leader of the hypocrites, withdrew with about three hundred men, saying, "He listened to the youths and did not listen to me." (3:166–167)

The Prophet ﷺ lined up the army with the mountain at their backs and placed fifty archers under ‘Abdullah ibn Jubayr on a hill, with the instruction: "Protect us from behind. If you see us seized by birds, do not leave your place until I send for you. If you see that we have defeated the enemy and trampled them, do not leave your place." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

The Muslims began to push the enemy back, and the Makkans broke and fled, leaving their camp. When the archers saw the spoils, most said, "The battle is won; take the spoils." Their commander reminded them of the order, but many went down. Khalid ibn al-Walid, then still with Quraysh, saw the gap, rode around the hill and attacked from behind.

In the chaos, someone shouted that Muhammad had been killed. The Prophet ﷺ was struck by a stone, his lower right tooth was broken and a helmet ring was driven into his cheek. He fell into a pit dug by the enemy. Sahl ibn Sa’d described it: his face was wounded, his front tooth broken and his helmet smashed on his head. Fatimah washed the blood while ‘Ali poured water; when she saw that the water only made it bleed more, she burned a piece of a woven mat and pressed the ash onto the wound until the bleeding stopped. (Sahih al-Bukhari)

A small group stayed to protect him, including Abu Talhah, who shielded him with his body, Talhah ibn ‘Ubaydillah, Sa’d ibn Abi Waqqas, and Nusaybah bint Ka’b (as reported in the Sira). Ka’b ibn Malik recognised the Prophet ﷺ and shouted to the Muslims that he was alive, and the believers rallied around him.

About seventy Muslims were killed. Hamzah, the Prophet’s uncle and "the lion of Allah", was killed by Wahshi, an Abyssinian slave who had been promised freedom for killing him; the Prophet ﷺ was deeply grieved at the sight of his body (Sahih al-Bukhari). Mus’ab ibn ‘Umayr, who carried the banner, fell too. Anas ibn al-Nadr, who had missed Badr, fought until his body had over eighty wounds, and could be identified only by his sister by his fingertips (Sahih al-Bukhari).

As the Makkans left, Abu Sufyan called from the mountain: "Is Muhammad among you?" The Prophet ﷺ told them not to answer. Then he asked about Abu Bakr and ‘Umar. Finally he shouted, "These have been killed! If they were alive, they would have answered." ‘Umar could not hold himself: "You lie, O enemy of Allah! Allah has kept alive what will shame you." Abu Sufyan said: "A day for a day: war goes by turns." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

Al ‘Imran 3:121–179 discusses Uhud in detail, and its tone is mercy: "Do not weaken and do not grieve, and you will be superior if you are [true] believers. If a wound touches you, a similar wound has touched the others. And these days We alternate among the people." (3:139–140) It names disobeying the order as the cause (3:152), yet adds "He has already pardoned you" (3:152). And it describes those who, despite their wounds, responded to the call to pursue the enemy the very next day, at Hamra’ al-Asad: "Those to whom the people said, The people have gathered against you, so fear them; but it increased them in faith, and they said, Sufficient for us is Allah, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." (3:173)

facts: Quraysh, Ghatafan and other tribes: about 10,000 men
A trench across the northern, open side of Madinah

t: After Banu al-Nadir, a Jewish tribe expelled from Madinah for plotting against the Prophet ﷺ, settled in Khaybar, their leaders travelled among the Arab tribes urging them to join Quraysh in a single decisive campaign. Roughly ten thousand men arrived outside Madinah, a force far beyond anything the city had faced.

Madinah is protected by lava fields and houses on most sides; the open side is north. Salman al-Farisi, who knew how Persian cities were defended, is reported to have suggested a trench. The Muslims dug it within days, in the cold, many of them hungry. The Prophet ﷺ dug alongside them and carried earth until his belly was covered in dust. When they chanted, he chanted with them: "O Allah, there is no good except the good of the Hereafter, so forgive the Ansar and the Muhajirun." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

Jabir ibn ‘Abdullah saw the Prophet ﷺ with a stone tied to his belly because of hunger and, going home, asked his wife what food they had. They had a small goat and a little barley. He invited the Prophet ﷺ quietly, but the Prophet called all the diggers, about a thousand. He blessed the pot and bread, and everyone ate until they were full, and the pot was still boiling with meat and the dough was still being baked as before (Sahih al-Bukhari).

The Arab armies arrived to find an obstacle they had never seen, which the horses could not cross. They camped in front of it and exchanged arrows for weeks. A few of their horsemen found a narrow point to cross, and ‘Ali killed ‘Amr ibn ‘Abd Wudd, their champion, in single combat (Sira).

The worst blow was inside the city. Banu Qurayza, a Jewish tribe bound by the Constitution of Madinah to defend it, were persuaded by Huyayy ibn Akhtab of al-Nadir to break the treaty and allow the army to attack from the south. The Qur’an describes the fear: "When they came at you from above you and from below you, and when eyes shifted and hearts reached the throats, and you assumed about Allah [various] assumptions." (33:10)

The Prophet ﷺ prayed: "O Allah, Revealer of the Book, swift in reckoning, defeat the confederates. O Allah, defeat them and shake them." (Sahih al-Bukhari). Na’im ibn Mas’ud, a newly Muslim man unknown to the besiegers, sowed distrust between Quraysh and Qurayza (Sira). Then Allah sent a cold wind that overturned their pots and tents and troops, and "an army you did not see" (33:9). Abu Sufyan ordered a retreat. The Prophet ﷺ said: "From now on we will march against them and they will not march against us." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

The Muslims then besieged Banu Qurayza for about twenty-five days. They surrendered and asked that their allies from Aws arbitrate; the Prophet ﷺ appointed Sa’d ibn Mu’adh, a leader of Aws. Sa’d judged that the fighting men be killed, the women and children taken and the property divided, a judgement the Prophet ﷺ said was in accord with Allah’s judgement (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). This is a difficult passage of the Sira. It was a wartime judgement on a tribe that had betrayed the city during an existential siege, delivered by their own chosen arbitrator, and it should be read in that context and not as a general rule.

facts: About 1,400, unarmed except for travel swords, with sacrificial animals
Al-Hudaybiyyah, at the edge of the sacred territory

t: The Prophet ﷺ saw in a dream that he was entering the Sacred Mosque and performing the rites. He announced it and set out with about fourteen hundred men, wearing the ihram and driving seventy sacrificial camels, to show clearly that they came for worship and not war. Quraysh sent out cavalry under Khalid ibn al-Walid to stop them, so the Prophet ﷺ took a rough mountain road. When they reached Hudaybiyyah his camel al-Qaswa knelt and would not rise. The Companions said she was stubborn. He said: "She is not stubborn; that is not her nature. She was stopped by the One who stopped the elephant. By Allah, whatever terms they ask me today that honour the sanctities of Allah, I will accept." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

Quraysh sent several envoys. ‘Urwah ibn Mas’ud, an experienced man, returned amazed: "O people, by Allah, I have been to Chosroes and Caesar and the Negus, and I have never seen a king whose companions revere him like Muhammad’s companions revere Muhammad. If he spits, it falls in someone’s hand and he rubs it on his face and body. If he orders them, they rush to do it. If he performs ablution, they nearly fight over his water. They lower their voices in front of him and do not look him in the eye out of reverence." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

The Prophet ﷺ sent ‘Uthman to Makkah, as he had kin to protect him. News spread that ‘Uthman had been killed. The Prophet ﷺ called the Muslims to pledge under a tree to fight to the death, and all except one man did so: "Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged to you under the tree." (48:18) It later turned out that ‘Uthman was safe.

Suhayl ibn ‘Amr arrived for Quraysh. The terms: a ten-year truce; the Muslims turn back this year and may return next year for three days; any Makkan who joins Muhammad without his guardian’s permission must be returned, but any Muslim who goes to Quraysh need not; and any tribe may ally with either side. When the Prophet ﷺ dictated "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," Suhayl objected: "We do not know this. Write, In Your name, O Allah." And when it said "Muhammad, Messenger of Allah," he said: "If we knew you were the Messenger of Allah, we would not have fought you. Write Muhammad ibn ‘Abdullah." The Prophet ﷺ agreed to both. When ‘Ali refused to erase the words "Messenger of Allah," the Prophet ﷺ asked where they were and erased them himself (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

The Muslims were deeply upset, and ‘Umar asked: "Are we not on the truth and they on falsehood? Why should we accept humiliation in our religion?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "I am the Messenger of Allah; I will not disobey Him, and He will help me." ‘Umar then went to Abu Bakr with the same questions, and got the same answer, and later said he gave charity and fasted and freed slaves to atone for his words that day (Sahih al-Bukhari).

He told the Companions to sacrifice and shave their heads. None moved, three times. He went to his wife Umm Salamah, upset. She said: "O Prophet of Allah, do you want this? Go out, do not say a word to anyone until you have slaughtered your animal and called your barber." He did, and they all rose, sacrificing and shaving until they nearly crushed each other (Sahih al-Bukhari).

On the way back, Surah al-Fath was revealed: "Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest" (48:1). He told the Companions that a surah had been revealed to him that night that was dearer to him than everything the sun rises upon (Sahih al-Bukhari). The truce allowed the Arabs to meet Muslims in peace; many saw their character and converted. Khalid ibn al-Walid and ‘Amr ibn al-‘As accepted Islam in the following months.

Abu Basir, who had escaped Quraysh and had to be returned under the treaty, killed one of his guards on the way and settled at the coast, where others who fled joined him, and began intercepting Quraysh trade caravans. Quraysh themselves asked the Prophet ﷺ to take them in and drop the clause (Sahih al-Bukhari). Within two years, the treaty was broken by Quraysh’s allies, which led to the conquest of Makkah.

facts: A silver ring engraved "Muhammad Rasul Allah"
Heraclius, Khosrow, the Negus, the Muqawqis and others
The campaign of Khaybar, Muharram 7 AH

t: When it was suggested that rulers only read sealed letters, the Prophet ﷺ had a silver ring made, engraved with three lines: "Muhammad / Rasul / Allah" (Sahih al-Bukhari). He sent envoys to Heraclius, the Byzantine emperor; Khosrow Parviz of Persia; the Negus of Abyssinia; the Muqawqis, ruler of Egypt; and the leaders of several Arab kingdoms, inviting them to Islam.

The letter to Heraclius began: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. From Muhammad, the servant of Allah and His Messenger, to Heraclius, ruler of the Byzantines. Peace be upon whoever follows the guidance. I invite you to the call of Islam. Accept Islam and you will be safe, and Allah will give you your reward twice. If you turn away, then upon you is the sin of the peasants." and the verse "Say, O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you: that we will not worship except Allah." (3:64)

Heraclius happened to be in Jerusalem, and asked whether any Arabs from the prophet’s people were nearby. Abu Sufyan, in Syria on a trading trip and still an enemy, was brought in. Heraclius asked him questions through an interpreter: What is his family like? Did any of his family claim prophethood before? Did he have a king among his ancestors? Do the nobles follow him or the weak? Do his followers increase or decrease? Does anyone leave in anger? Has he ever betrayed? Have you ever accused him of lying before he claimed this? What does he command? Abu Sufyan answered honestly, although he later said he would have lied if he had not been ashamed of being called a liar.

Heraclius replied: "I asked about his lineage, and you said he is of noble lineage, and that is how prophets are sent. I asked if he lied before, and you said no; he would not lie about people and then lie about Allah. If what you say is true, he will rule the ground beneath my feet. I knew he would appear, but I did not think he would be from among you. If I could reach him, I would wash his feet." The court erupted and he had them thrown out. Heraclius did not convert, but he honoured the Prophet’s ﷺ letter. (Sahih al-Bukhari)

Khosrow tore up the letter in rage; when the Prophet ﷺ heard, he said: "May Allah tear his kingdom to pieces." (Sahih al-Bukhari). The Sira reports that the Negus answered respectfully and accepted Islam, and that the Muqawqis replied politely, sending gifts, among them Maryam al-Qibtiyyah, who bore the Prophet’s ﷺ son Ibrahim, and the white mule Duldul.

In Muharram 7 AH the Muslims marched on Khaybar, a fortified oasis of Jewish clans some 150 km north of Madinah, from which the exiled leaders of Banu al-Nadir had helped organise the coalition against Madinah. Only those who had been at Hudaybiyyah were permitted to go (48:15, 48:18–20). After several of its forts fell over a number of weeks, the Prophet ﷺ said he would give the banner the next day to a man whom Allah and His Messenger love, and it was given to ‘Ali (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

The people were allowed to remain and farm the land in return for half of the harvest. One of the women of Khaybar, Zaynab bint al-Harith, served the Prophet ﷺ a roasted, poisoned sheep. He spat out the first bite, and one Companion, Bishr ibn al-Bara’, who ate it, died (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sunan Abi Dawud). Ja’far and the emigrants of Abyssinia arrived back around the time Khaybar ended, and the Prophet ﷺ kissed Ja’far between the eyes and said he did not know which was the cause of greater joy: Khaybar’s conquest or Ja’far’s arrival (as reported in the Sira).

facts: Mu’tah, east of the Jordan, in the Byzantine sphere
A far larger force of Byzantines and allied Arab tribes
Zayd ibn Harithah, Ja’far ibn Abi Talib, ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah

t: The Prophet ﷺ had sent an envoy, al-Harith ibn ‘Umayr al-Azdi, with a letter to the ruler of Busra. Shurahbil ibn ‘Amr al-Ghassani, a Byzantine-allied chieftain, killed him, which was a grave breach of the rule that messengers are not harmed. The Prophet ﷺ sent three thousand men north to hold the killers to account.

He appointed three commanders in order: "If Zayd is killed, Ja’far takes command; if Ja’far is killed, ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah." (Sahih al-Bukhari). Zayd was his freed servant and adopted son; Ja’far, his cousin, who had led the migrants to Abyssinia; ‘Abdullah, a poet of the Ansar. Their appointment together shows he judged people by capacity, not tribe.

At Mu’tah the Muslims found a force of Byzantine troops and Arab allies many times larger than theirs. After two nights of debate, ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah reminded them: "By Allah, what you hate is the very thing you came out for: martyrdom. We do not fight people by number, strength or large numbers but by this religion Allah has honoured us with. Go, for it is one of two excellent things: victory or martyrdom."

Zayd carried the banner and fought until he was killed. Ja’far took it; when his right hand was cut off, he held it in his left, and when that was cut off, he clasped the banner to his chest until he was killed. ‘Abdullah took it, hesitated for a moment, then recited verses to himself and fought on until he fell. ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar later found Ja’far among the dead and counted over ninety wounds from spears and arrows in his body (Sahih al-Bukhari).

The Muslims chose Khalid ibn al-Walid, who had accepted Islam only a few months before. He held the army together through the day. The next morning he rearranged the ranks so that the enemy, seeing new faces and standards, believed reinforcements had arrived. After skirmishing, he withdrew in good order. Khalid said nine swords broke in his hand that day (Sahih al-Bukhari).

In Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ stood on the pulpit and told the people before any messenger arrived: "Zayd took the banner and was martyred; then Ja’far took it and was martyred; then Ibn Rawahah took it and was martyred," and his eyes were flowing with tears. "Then the banner was taken by a sword of the swords of Allah (Khalid), until Allah gave them victory." (Sahih al-Bukhari). He went to Ja’far’s family to comfort them, and told them to prepare food for them, since they were occupied with their loss (Sunan Abi Dawud).

facts: Quraysh’s allies broke the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah by attacking Khuza’ah

t: Two years into the Hudaybiyyah truce, Banu Bakr, allies of Quraysh, attacked Khuza’ah, allies of the Prophet ﷺ, and Quraysh helped them with weapons. Khuza’ah appealed to Madinah. Quraysh realised their mistake and sent Abu Sufyan to renew the treaty, but he failed. The Prophet ﷺ began to prepare in secrecy.

Hatib ibn Abi Balta’ah, a veteran of Badr with family left in Makkah, sent a woman with a letter warning Quraysh. The Prophet ﷺ learned by revelation, sent ‘Ali and al-Zubayr to intercept her, and read the letter. When ‘Umar asked to execute Hatib, the Prophet ﷺ asked him why he did it. Hatib said he had no tribal protection for his family and meant no betrayal. The Prophet ﷺ accepted his explanation and reminded ‘Umar that Hatib had fought at Badr. Surah al-Mumtahanah 60:1 was revealed (Sahih al-Bukhari).

About ten thousand set out. At Marr al-Zahran, a day from Makkah, they camped and lit ten thousand fires. Abu Sufyan, Hakim ibn Hizam and Budayl ibn Warqa’ went out to see and were stunned. Al-‘Abbas brought Abu Sufyan to the Prophet ﷺ, and he accepted Islam. Al-‘Abbas asked the Prophet ﷺ to give him some honour, and he declared: "Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe, whoever shuts his door is safe, and whoever enters the Sacred Mosque is safe." (Sahih Muslim)

The Prophet ﷺ entered riding his camel, his head so low in humility that his beard almost touched the saddle, reciting Surah al-Fath (Sahih al-Bukhari). He had told the commanders to avoid fighting unless attacked. There was a small clash at one entrance, where some Makkans fought Khalid’s column, and a few men were killed.

He went to the Kaaba, circled it, and with a stick struck the idols around it, one after another, reciting: "The truth has come, and falsehood has departed. Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to depart." (17:81) The idols fell. He entered the Kaaba, had the pictures inside removed and prayed (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). He took the key from ‘Uthman ibn Talhah, then handed it back to him and his family to keep, in line with the verse "Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to whom they are due." (4:58) (as reported in the Sira).

s.h: The people who had fought him
t: He stood at the door of the Kaaba and addressed Quraysh, who had been his enemies for twenty years, who had tortured the Muslims, driven them from their homes and fought them at Badr, Uhud and the Trench. The Sira reports that he asked: "O Quraysh, what do you think I will do with you?" They said, "Good. You are a noble brother, son of a noble brother." He said: "Go, for you are free." A very small number of people, whose crimes were exceptional, were excluded from the general amnesty, and some of them, like ‘Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, were pardoned afterwards when they came to seek forgiveness. Wahshi, who killed Hamzah, also accepted Islam, and the Prophet ﷺ asked only that he stay out of his sight.

Then he told the Muslims at the gathering: "Allah made Makkah sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth; it is sacred by Allah’s sanctity until the Day of Resurrection." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). Bilal climbed to the roof of the Kaaba and gave the adhan. He remained in Makkah for about nineteen days, shortening his prayers (Sahih al-Bukhari).

Surah al-Nasr was revealed: "When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest, and you see the people entering into the religion of Allah in multitudes, then exalt [Allah] with praise of your Lord and ask forgiveness of Him. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance." ‘A’ishah said that after it was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ said in his bowing and prostration very often: "Glory be to You, our Lord, and praise; O Allah, forgive me." (Sahih al-Bukhari). Ibn ‘Abbas and ‘Umar understood it as a sign that his work was nearly complete.

facts: Hawazin and Thaqif, led by Malik ibn ‘Awf
The valley of Hunayn, between Makkah and Ta’if

t: Hawazin and Thaqif gathered a large force and, according to the Sira, brought along their families and animals so that their men would not flee. They hid in the narrow valley of Hunayn. The Muslims, over twelve thousand strong, entered at dawn. Some of the new Muslims reportedly said, "We will not be defeated today because of our small numbers." The Qur’an remembers this: "And on the day of Hunayn, when your great number pleased you, but it did not avail you at all, and the earth, vast as it is, closed in on you, then you turned back, fleeing." (9:25)

Archers on the slopes struck, and the Muslim column broke in panic. The Prophet ﷺ stood firm on his white mule and said: "I am the Prophet, no lie; I am the son of ‘Abd al-Muttalib." Al-Bara’ ibn ‘Azib said: "When the fighting grew fierce we used to take shelter with the Prophet ﷺ, and the bravest of us was the one who stood next to him." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

Only a handful stayed with him: Abu Bakr, ‘Umar, ‘Ali, al-‘Abbas, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, and others. He told al-‘Abbas, who had a powerful voice, to call the Companions: "O Ansar! O people of the tree of pledge!" They replied, "Here we are!" and turned back like camels responding to the call of their young, until a hundred gathered and charged. He took a handful of dust, threw it at the enemy’s faces and said: "May the faces be disfigured!" and the battle turned (Sahih Muslim). The Qur’an says: "Then Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and sent down soldiers you did not see." (9:26)

The Muslims captured six thousand prisoners and a huge number of camels and sheep. The Prophet ﷺ besieged Ta’if for several weeks but did not take it, and lifted the siege. When urged to curse them, he prayed instead: "O Allah, guide Thaqif and bring them" (Sunan al-Tirmidhi), and they did come, the following year.

When the spoils were divided he gave very large shares to the recently converted leaders of Quraysh and others, to win their hearts. Some of the young Ansar said, "May Allah forgive the Messenger of Allah; he gives Quraysh and leaves us, though our swords still drip with their blood." He gathered the Ansar in a tent and asked about the remark. Then he said: "O Ansar, did I not come to you when you were astray and Allah guided you through me? Poor, and Allah enriched you through me? Enemies, and Allah united your hearts?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger are the most generous." He said: "Will you not answer me? If you wished you could say, and you would be telling the truth: you came to us rejected and we believed you; abandoned and we helped you; a fugitive and we sheltered you. Are you not pleased that others go away with sheep and camels while you go back with the Messenger of Allah to your homes? By the One in whose hand is my soul, were it not for the Hijrah I would be one of the Ansar. If people went one way and the Ansar another, I would go the Ansar’s way." The Ansar wept until their beards were wet and said: "We are content with the Messenger of Allah as our share and portion." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim; the fuller wording of his reply is in Musnad Ahmad.)

A delegation from Hawazin arrived, having accepted Islam, and asked for their captives and property. The Prophet ﷺ told them: "With me are those you see. The most beloved speech to me is the most truthful. Choose one of the two: the prisoners or the wealth." They chose the prisoners. He said that his own share and Banu ‘Abd al-Muttalib’s was theirs, and asked them to ask the Muslims to return the rest after Zuhr prayer. The Muhajirun and Ansar returned theirs, and all six thousand were released (Sahih al-Bukhari).

facts: Jaysh al-‘Usrah, the army of hardship

t: Reports reached Madinah that the Byzantines were assembling to attack. The Prophet ﷺ called an expedition at the most difficult time possible: the heat of summer, drought, the harvest and a long distance. For the first time, he announced where they were going so that they could prepare. Many sprang to give. ‘Umar brought half his wealth and Abu Bakr brought all of it, and when the Prophet ﷺ asked what he had left his family, he said, "Allah and His Messenger." ‘Uthman equipped a large part of the army, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Nothing will harm ‘Uthman after today." (Sunan al-Tirmidhi)

There were seven poor Companions who came asking for mounts but he had none to give, and they turned back with tears flowing, grieved that they had nothing to spend. They are known as al-Bakka’un, the weepers (9:92). On the march the Prophet ﷺ said: "In Madinah there are men who were with you in every mountain pass and valley; they were held back by excuse." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

Eighty or so hypocrites asked leave with excuses, and Allah exposed them in Surah al-Tawbah. A group built a mosque near Quba as a base for plotting, called Masjid al-Dirar, which the Prophet ﷺ ordered destroyed (9:107–110). He left ‘Ali in charge of his family, and the hypocrites whispered that he was being left because he was a burden. ‘Ali told him; the Prophet ﷺ said: "Are you not content to be to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there is no prophet after me?" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

The Muslims reached Tabuk after weeks of hardship. The Byzantines had withdrawn and no fighting took place. The Prophet ﷺ stayed about twenty days and made treaties with the chiefs of the area: Yuhannah ibn Ru’bah of Ayla, and the people of Jarba and Adhruh, who agreed to pay the jizyah in return for protection. Khalid was sent against Ukaydir, the Christian ruler of Dumat al-Jandal, who was brought to the Prophet ﷺ and also made a treaty. The expedition secured the northern frontier.

s.h: Ka’b ibn Malik and the two others
t: Ka’b ibn Malik narrates his own story in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. He had never missed a campaign, apart from Badr, and he was well off with two camels, for the first time. "I kept saying to myself: I will prepare tomorrow, I will prepare the day after, until the time passed and the army left and I was still not ready." He walked about Madinah and saw only hypocrites and the excused.

When the Prophet ﷺ returned, men who stayed behind came with excuses and swore oaths, and he accepted them and asked Allah to forgive them. Ka’b came, and the Prophet ﷺ smiled the smile of an angry man and asked, "What kept you?" Ka’b said: "By Allah, if I were sitting before any other person in the world I would get out of his anger with an excuse, for I have been given eloquence. But I know that if I lie to you and you accept it, Allah would soon make you angry with me; and if I tell you the truth, you will be angry with me but I hope for Allah’s forgiveness. By Allah, I never had an excuse; I was never stronger or richer than when I stayed behind." The Prophet ﷺ said, "This man has told the truth. Stand until Allah decides about you."

Two others, Murarah ibn al-Rabi’ and Hilal ibn Umayyah, also told the truth. The Prophet ﷺ forbade the Muslims to speak to the three of them. Ka’b said that the earth became strange to him, though it was the same earth. He went to the mosque and greeted the Prophet ﷺ, watching to see if his lips moved in reply. His cousin and dearest friend Abu Qatadah would not answer his greeting even when Ka’b begged him, only saying, "Allah and His Messenger know best." He wept alone.

After forty days they were told to separate from their wives. A letter came from the King of Ghassan: "We have heard that your master has treated you harshly; come to us and we will console you." Ka’b said: "This is also a trial," and threw it into the oven. On the fiftieth morning, after dawn prayer, as he sat on his roof, in the straitened state Allah describes ("the earth, vast as it is, had become narrow for them, and their souls had become narrow"), he heard a voice from the mountain: "O Ka’b ibn Malik, good news!" A man had climbed the mountain to shout it, faster than the rider who was racing to him. Allah had revealed the acceptance of their repentance (9:117–118).

People rushed to congratulate him, and Talhah ibn ‘Ubaydillah stood up and shook his hand. The Prophet ﷺ’s face was shining like a piece of the moon when he was happy, and he said: "Rejoice at the best day that has passed over you since your mother bore you." Ka’b said: "Is this from you or from Allah?" He said: "From Allah." Ka’b offered all his property as charity, and the Prophet ﷺ told him to keep some. Ka’b said: "O Messenger of Allah, Allah saved me through truthfulness, and part of my repentance is to speak nothing but the truth as long as I live." Allah then commanded: "O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with those who are truthful." (9:119)

In the tenth year the Prophet ﷺ announced that he would perform Hajj, and people poured into Madinah to go with him. Jabir ibn ‘Abdullah gave the fullest account in Sahih Muslim: they left Madinah five days before the end of Dhul-Qa’dah, and wherever he looked, all around him, as far as he could see, there were riders and people on foot. The Prophet ﷺ pronounced the talbiyah, "Labbayk Allahumma labbayk," and the people repeated it. He entered Makkah, kissed the Black Stone, circled the Kaaba, prayed behind the Station of Ibrahim and walked between Safa and Marwa, and told those who had not brought a sacrificial animal to end their ihram after ‘umrah, and said: "If I had known earlier what I know now, I would not have brought a sacrificial animal and would have made it an ‘umrah."

On the ninth he stopped at Namirah until the sun passed its zenith, then came to the valley of ‘Uranah and addressed the crowd from his camel. Jabir’s report (Sahih Muslim) records: "Your blood and your wealth are as sacred to you as the sacredness of this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this city of yours. Everything of the affairs of the days of ignorance is under my feet abolished. The blood of the days of ignorance is abolished. The first blood I abolish is the blood of Ibn Rabi’ah ibn al-Harith. The interest of the days of ignorance is abolished, and the first interest I abolish is that of my uncle al-‘Abbas ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib; it is abolished entirely.

Fear Allah concerning women, for you have taken them as a trust from Allah, and made their private parts lawful by Allah’s word. You have a right over them that they not allow anyone you dislike into your home; if they do, strike them in a way that does not injure. They have the right to be provided with food and clothing in a fair manner.

I have left among you something which, if you hold fast to it, you will never go astray: the Book of Allah. And you will be asked about me. What will you say?" They said: "We bear witness that you conveyed, fulfilled and gave sincere advice." He raised his index finger toward the sky and then pointed it at the people, three times, saying: "O Allah, be witness."

Other reports preserve parts of what he said at Arafah and Mina. In Musnad Ahmad (an authentic narration): "O people, your Lord is one and your father is one. No Arab is superior over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, nor a red person over a black person, nor a black person over a red person, except by piety (taqwa)." On the tenth, at Mina, he asked: "Which day is this?" "Which month?" "Which city?" and then declared their sanctity. He said: "Let those present convey to those absent, for perhaps the one it is conveyed to will understand better than the one who heard it." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)
He also said at Mina: "Take your rites from me, for perhaps I will not meet you again after this year." (Sahih Muslim)

On that day, standing at Arafah, was revealed: "This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you and have approved for you Islam as religion." (5:3) A Jewish man told ‘Umar that if such a verse had been revealed to them, they would have taken that day as an Eid. ‘Umar replied that he knew exactly when and where it was revealed: on the day of Arafah, a Friday, while the Prophet ﷺ was standing at Arafah (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

On the tenth, at Mina, he stoned the Jamrat al-‘Aqabah, then sacrificed. He slaughtered sixty-three camels with his own hand, as many as his years, and told ‘Ali to sacrifice the rest of the hundred. He had his head shaved. He returned to Makkah for the tawaf al-ifadah and drank Zamzam standing (Sahih Muslim).

facts: Monday, 12 Rabi’ al-Awwal, 11 AH (8 June 632 CE)
The room of ‘A’ishah beside the mosque, where he was buried
Abu Bakr led the prayer for several days
Nothing was left to inherit except his mule, his weapons and a piece of land given as charity

t: At the end of Safar, in the eleventh year, the Prophet ﷺ went one night to al-Baqi’, the cemetery of Madinah, to pray for the dead. On the way back he told ‘A’ishah, who had a headache, "I have a headache too" and then fell ill with a severe fever that lasted about ten days or more. He asked his wives’ permission to be nursed in ‘A’ishah’s house, which they gave (Sahih al-Bukhari).

Several days before he died, he told them to pour seven skins of water over him, and he went out to the Companions, sat on the pulpit and delivered a final address: a servant had been given the choice between this world and what is with Allah, and chose what is with Allah. Abu Bakr wept, understanding that the servant was the Prophet ﷺ himself (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

When it was time for prayer, he asked that Abu Bakr lead the people. ‘A’ishah, thinking that Abu Bakr would cry too much and not be heard, asked that ‘Umar be told. The Prophet ﷺ insisted, "Tell Abu Bakr to lead the people in prayer. You are like the women around Yusuf." Abu Bakr led the Muslims for the rest of the Prophet’s ﷺ life, which is why the Companions considered him the natural successor (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

On the Monday morning, the Muslims were at Fajr prayer behind Abu Bakr when the Prophet ﷺ lifted the curtain of ‘A’ishah’s room and looked at them standing in rows. Anas said: "He smiled, and his face was like a page of the Qur’an; we nearly gave up our prayer out of joy when we saw him." Abu Bakr stepped back, thinking he wanted to come out, but the Prophet ﷺ signalled that they should complete the prayer, let the curtain fall, and did not come out again (Sahih al-Bukhari).

‘A’ishah says that he died with his head resting between her chest and chin, and that Allah joined her saliva and his in his last moments: her brother ‘Abd al-Rahman entered with a toothstick, and the Prophet ﷺ looked at it; she softened it for him and he used it, "as nicely as I had ever seen him use one". He had a bowl of water, dipped his hand in it and wiped his face, saying "There is no god but Allah, indeed death has its agonies." Then he raised his finger and said: "With the highest companions" (three times), and his hand dropped (Sahih al-Bukhari).

Anas reports that Fatimah said, "O my father, he answered the call of his Lord. O my father, his abode is Paradise al-Firdaws. O my father, to Jibril we announce his death." When he was buried she asked: "Did your hearts permit you to throw dust on the Messenger of Allah?" (Sahih al-Bukhari)

The news hit Madinah. ‘Umar stood in the mosque and said that the Prophet ﷺ had not died, but gone to his Lord as Musa had, and would return. Abu Bakr came, entered the room, uncovered his face and kissed him, saying, "May my father and mother be sacrificed for you. Allah will not make you taste two deaths; the death which was written for you, you have now tasted."

He went out and said: "O people, whoever used to worship Muhammad, Muhammad has died. Whoever worships Allah, Allah is Ever-Living and never dies." Then he recited: "Muhammad is not but a messenger. Other messengers have passed on before him. So if he was to die or be killed, would you turn back on your heels?" (3:144). ‘Umar said: "By Allah, as soon as I heard Abu Bakr recite it, I was stunned, my legs could not carry me, and I fell to the ground, realising that he had died." Ibn ‘Abbas said: "It was as if people had not known this verse had been revealed until Abu Bakr recited it, and then everyone was reciting it." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

The Companions disagreed where to bury him, until Abu Bakr remembered that he had heard the Prophet ﷺ say, "No prophet dies but is buried where he died." They dug his grave in ‘A’ishah’s room. He was washed by ‘Ali, al-‘Abbas, and others, in his clothes (as reported in the Sira); the Muslims prayed over him in groups, not led by an imam, and he was buried on the night before Wednesday.

‘A’ishah said: "The Prophet ﷺ died when his armour was pledged to a Jew for thirty sa’ of barley" (Sahih al-Bukhari). He said: "We, the prophets, do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). He had spent his life giving, and left behind a complete message and a community ready to carry it.

facts: The first human and the first prophet
Hawwa’ (Eve), created from the same soul (4:1)

t: The Qur’an begins the story with a conversation: "And [mention] when your Lord said to the angels, Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successor." The angels asked, "Will You place upon it one who causes corruption and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?" Allah said: "Indeed, I know that which you do not know." (2:30)

He then taught Adam the names of all things, presented them to the angels, and asked them to name them. They said: "Exalted are You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us." Adam named them. What distinguished the human being was knowledge, and the ability to learn, understand and choose (2:31–33).

Allah commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, a prostration of honour, not worship. They all did, "except Iblis; he refused and was arrogant and became of the disbelievers" (2:34). Asked why, he said: "I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay." (7:12) It was the first act of pride and the first of racism: judging worth by substance and origin, not by obedience.

Iblis asked for respite until the Day of Resurrection and vowed to mislead humanity from every side. He received it, and Allah told him that over His sincere servants he would have no authority (15:36–42, 7:14–17).

Adam and his wife lived in Paradise and were told: "Eat from wherever you will, but do not approach this tree, lest you be among the wrongdoers" (2:35). Satan whispered to them: "Your Lord did not forbid you this tree except that you become angels or become immortal," and swore that he was a sincere advisor to them (7:20–21). Adam forgot (20:115); both ate, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they covered themselves with leaves.

The Qur’an makes a point of the difference between the two responses. Iblis, when confronted, defended himself and blamed Allah: "Because You have put me in error" (7:16). Adam and Hawwa’ said: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers." (7:23) "Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance. Indeed, it is He who is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful." (2:37)

They were sent down to earth, "for a time and provision." But with them went a promise: "Whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve" (2:38). Earth was where the test was to be lived. In a hadith, the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah created Adam sixty cubits tall and gave him and his descendants the greeting of "As-salamu ‘alaykum" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).
The story ends with the first fruits of the human family, Habil and Qabil, which the Qur’an tells in Surah al-Ma’idah (5:27–31).

facts: "We raised him to a high station"
Met in the fourth heaven (Sahih al-Bukhari)
Scholars differ on identifying him with figures in other traditions

t: There are only two places that mention Idris. In Surah Maryam: "And mention in the Book, Idris. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet. And We raised him to a high station." (19:56–57) In Surah al-Anbiya’, he is listed beside Isma’il and Dhul-Kifl as among the patient, whom Allah admitted into His mercy and who were among the righteous (21:85–86).

In the long hadith of the Mi’raj, the Prophet ﷺ met Idris in the fourth heaven, and Idris welcomed him: "Welcome to the righteous prophet and the righteous brother." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

Many popular stories about Idris, such as that he invented writing or sewing, or that he lived in Egypt and was taken up alive, come from later commentators and from earlier traditions. They are not in the Qur’an or the authentic hadith. The Qur’anic account is short because the Qur’an does not tell us everything: it gives what we need. In his case it is a verdict, not a biography: truthful, a prophet, patient, raised in rank.

s.h: Where the Prophet ﷺ met him
t: The only authentic report that adds something about Idris is in the account of the Prophet’s night journey and ascent. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Anas reports from Abu Dharr that the Prophet ﷺ described how he was taken up through the heavens and met a prophet in each. In the fourth heaven he met Idris. The Prophet ﷺ said that Idris greeted him with: “Welcome, righteous prophet and righteous brother.”

The same hadith lists the others he met: Adam in the first heaven, Yahya and ‘Isa in the second, Yusuf in the third, Harun in the fifth, Musa in the sixth and Ibrahim in the seventh, leaning on the Frequented House. It is worth noticing what Idris says. He does not call the Prophet ﷺ a “son”, as Adam and Ibrahim do, but a brother. It is the language of someone who stands in a line of messengers, and who recognises the one who comes after.

The verse says: “And We raised him to a high station.” Some of the early commentators, among them Ibn ‘Abbas and Mujahid, understood this to mean that he was lifted to the heavens, and linked it to the hadith of the fourth heaven. Others, including Ibn Kathir in his commentary, say that the verse speaks of the high rank Allah gave him and need not mean that he was physically taken up.

The scholars add that there is no sound report that he was lifted up alive, and that the stories that he did not die come from earlier traditions. A believer can leave it at what the Qur’an gives: that he was truthful, that he was a prophet, and that his rank with Allah is high.

facts: The first messenger sent to a people who had fallen into idolatry
Wadd, Suwa’, Yaghuth, Ya’uq and Nasr (71:23)

t: Ibn ‘Abbas explained in Sahih al-Bukhari that the names Wadd, Suwa’, Yaghuth, Ya’uq and Nasr (71:23) were righteous men among Nuh’s people. When they died, Satan whispered to their people to set up statues in their gathering places and name them. They did so, and they were not worshipped until the original generation had died and knowledge was forgotten; then they were. It is a lesson about how excess in honouring righteous people can slide into worship.

Allah sent Nuh with a simple message: "Worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him." (7:59) He called them "night and day," "secretly and publicly" (71:5–9), and promised that if they asked forgiveness, Allah would send rain and increase their wealth and children. But "every time I invited them to Your forgiveness, they put their fingers in their ears, covered themselves with their garments, persisted and were arrogant." (71:7) The Qur’an says: "He remained among them a thousand years less fifty." (29:14)

The leaders objected that he was only a human like them and that only the lowest had followed him. Nuh answered that he would not drive away the believers, "for they will meet their Lord" (11:29), and that he did not claim to own treasures or know the unseen. They told him: "O Nuh, you have disputed with us and been excessive in dispute; so bring us what you promise if you are truthful." (11:32)

When Allah told him, "No one will believe from your people except those who have already believed," (11:36), and so he stopped hoping, and he was told to build the ark under Allah’s eyes and inspiration. Whenever the elders passed by him, they mocked. He answered: "If you ridicule us, then we will ridicule you as you ridicule." (11:38)

The sign was given: "the oven overflowed" (11:40). Nuh was told to carry in it a pair of every kind, his family, except those against whom the word had gone forth, and those who had believed. "And none had believed with him except a few." (11:40) He said: "Embark therein; in the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage." (11:41)

As the ark sailed through waves like mountains, Nuh saw his son standing apart and called: "O my son, come aboard with us and do not be with the disbelievers." He answered: "I will take refuge on a mountain to protect me from the water." Nuh said: "There is no protector today from the decree of Allah, except for him upon whom He has mercy." And a wave came between them and he was among the drowned (11:42–43).

Nuh turned to Allah, "My Lord, my son is of my family, and Your promise is true." Allah said: "O Nuh, indeed he is not of your family; indeed, he is [one whose] work was other than righteous. So do not ask Me for that about which you have no knowledge. I admonish you, lest you be among the ignorant." Nuh answered: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking that of which I have no knowledge." (11:45–47) It is a moving image of the limit of a father’s love and a prophet’s obedience.

It was said: "O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold [your rain]." The water subsided, the matter was concluded, and the ark came to rest on al-Judi (11:44). Nuh was told to descend in peace, with blessings upon him and upon nations from those with him (11:48). He is among the five greatest messengers, the ulu al-‘azm, and in Surah Nuh his supplication is recorded: "My Lord, forgive me and my parents and whoever enters my house a believer and the believing men and believing women." (71:28)

facts: ‘Ad, a people of al-Ahqaf, "Iram of the pillars" (89:6–8)
"Who is mightier than us in power?" (41:15)
A furious wind for seven nights and eight days (69:6–7)
"I put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord" (11:56)

t: ‘Ad were the successors of Nuh’s people (7:69). Allah had increased them in stature. They built monuments on every high place and fortresses, "as if you will live forever" (26:128–129). The Qur’an describes the city of Iram "of the pillars, the like of which had never been created in the land" (89:7–8). They were the dominant power of their age, and became tyrants: "When you seize, you seize as tyrants." (26:130)

Their brother Hud told them: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Then will you not fear Him?" (7:65) He asked them for no wage (11:51) and told them: "Ask forgiveness of your Lord and then repent to Him; He will send [rain from] the sky upon you in showers and increase you in strength upon your strength." (11:52)

Their leaders replied: "Indeed, we see you in foolishness, and indeed, we think you are among the liars." (7:66) Then: "We only say that one of our gods has struck you with evil." Hud’s answer, in the face of the whole nation, is one of the most confident in the Qur’an: "I call Allah to witness, and witness [yourselves] that I am free from what you associate with Allah. So plot against me all together, then do not give me respite. Indeed, I have relied upon Allah, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a path [that is] straight." (11:54–56)

When the punishment came, they saw a cloud rising on the horizon and said, "This is a cloud bringing us rain." Hud told them: "Rather, it is that for which you were impatient: a wind within which is a painful punishment, destroying everything by command of its Lord." (46:24–25) Surah al-Haqqah gives more: "A screaming, violent wind which He imposed upon them for seven nights and eight days in succession, and you would see the people therein fallen as if they were hollow trunks of palm trees." (69:6–7) The ‘Aishah report in Sahih al-Bukhari adds that whenever the Prophet ﷺ saw clouds, his face changed, and he feared it might be like the cloud of ‘Ad, who thought it was bringing rain.

s.h: The Prophet ﷺ and the cloud
t: ‘A’ishah reports in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim that when the Prophet ﷺ saw a cloud on the horizon, or a strong wind, the expression of his face changed. She said to him: “O Messenger of Allah, when people see a cloud, they are glad, hoping for rain, but when I see it, I see unease on your face.” He said: “O ‘A’ishah, what would assure me that it does not contain punishment? A people were punished by a wind, and they saw the punishment and said: ‘This is a cloud that will bring us rain.’”

He was speaking of the people of ‘Ad, whose story the Qur’an tells in the words: “So when they saw it as a cloud approaching their valleys, they said: ‘This is a cloud bringing us rain.’ Rather, it is what you asked to be hastened: a wind within which is a painful punishment.” (46:24) It shows how the Prophet ﷺ read the Qur’an: as a living warning. A man who knew that Allah had forgiven all his past and future sins still turned in fear at the sight of a cloud. When the rain came he used to say: “O Allah, a beneficial downpour.”

The Qur’an says that Hud warned his people “at al-Ahqaf”, the word for long curved sand dunes. (46:21) The commentators place al-Ahqaf in the south of Arabia, in the sands between Oman and Hadramawt and Yemen. It also speaks of “Iram, with the pillars, the likes of which had never been created in the land.” (89:6–8) Scholars have discussed whether Iram is a city, a tribe or an ancestor, and the Qur’an does not decide.

The commentaries often mention a tomb of Hud in Hadramawt, in the Yemeni valley that still bears his name. Visitors have gone there for centuries. As with many tombs of ancient prophets, the identification rests on tradition, and the early sources do not give a sure location. What the Qur’an gives is the lesson: that the strongest civilisation is as weak as a dry palm trunk before the command of Allah.

facts: The Prophet ﷺ passed their ruins on the way to Tabuk

t: Allah made Thamud successors after ‘Ad: "He settled you in the land, taking for yourselves palaces from its plains and carving from the mountains, homes." (7:74) Their civilisation was wealthy and artistic. But they too were arrogant. Their leaders told Salih: "You were among us a man of promise before this" (11:62), referring to the respect they had for him before his call. Then they rejected him, since he told them to leave what their fathers worshipped.

They asked for a sign. Salih said: "This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you. So let her feed upon Allah’s earth and do not touch her with harm, or you will be seized by a painful punishment." (7:73) There was a share of water for her on one day and for them on another (26:155). They were warned: "Do not touch her with harm, or there will seize you a punishment on a terrible day." (11:64)

But a group of nine men, the Qur’an says, were spreading corruption in the land (27:48). The wretched man among them, in the words of Allah’s Messenger ﷺ, "rose, the most wicked of the people" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, on 91:12), and they hamstrung the camel and defied the command of their Lord. Salih said: "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied." (11:65)

Then a cry seized them, "and morning found them fallen prone in their homes, as if they had never prospered therein." (11:67–68) Salih left them, saying: "O my people, I have conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you, but you do not like advisors." (7:79)

Their dwellings still stand at al-Hijr (Mada’in Salih). When the Prophet ﷺ passed there on the way to Tabuk, he told the Companions not to drink its water or use it for dough, and said: "Do not enter the dwellings of those who wronged themselves unless weeping, lest what struck them strike you." He covered his head and hurried through the valley (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

In Surah an-Naml the Qur’an adds a detail that the other surahs leave out. “And there were in the city nine individuals who spread corruption in the land and did not reform. They said: ‘Swear by Allah that we will attack him and his family by night; then we will say to his protector: We did not witness the destruction of his family, and indeed we are truthful.’ And they planned a plan, and We planned a plan, while they did not perceive.” (27:48–50)

So while the she-camel was still in the land and Salih was still warning them, a small group of leaders was plotting to kill him and his family at night and deny it afterwards. The Qur’an says that Allah’s plan was ahead of theirs. This is how the scholars read the end of the story: the people were not destroyed because of a single act of cruelty against an animal, but because their leaders had made up their minds to get rid of the messenger.

s.h: When the Prophet ﷺ passed their ruins
t: On the march to Tabuk in 9 AH, the army passed through al-Hijr, the land of Thamud, in the north of Arabia. Ibn ‘Umar reports in Sahih al-Bukhari that the Prophet ﷺ told his Companions: “Do not enter the dwellings of those who wronged themselves, unless you are weeping, lest what struck them strike you.” Then he covered his head with his cloak and urged his mount on until he had crossed the valley.

The Companions had already drawn water from the wells of the place and kneaded their dough with it. The Prophet ﷺ told them to pour out the water and feed the dough to the camels, and to draw their water from the well where Salih’s she-camel had drunk. It is the only passage in the hadith that tells us how a believer is to behave at a place of divine punishment: not with curiosity or a photograph, but with fear, humility and tears.

facts: Khalilullah (the friend of Allah, 4:125) and Abu al-Anbiya’ (father of the prophets)

t: His father, Azar in the Qur’an, carved and sold idols. Ibrahim asked him gently: "O my father, why do you worship that which does not hear and does not see and will not benefit you at all?" (19:42) He addressed him with respect, "O my father" repeatedly, and offered him knowledge: "Indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to an even path." (19:43) His father threatened to stone him and told him to leave. Ibrahim answered: "Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you of my Lord." (19:47)

Surah al-An’am tells how he reasoned with his people (6:74–79). He saw a star and said, "This is my lord," but when it set, he said, "I do not like those that set." The same with the moon and the sun. Then: "Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who created the heavens and the earth, inclining toward truth, and I am not of those who associate others with Allah." The argument does not show him as someone without knowledge but as someone modelling, in public, how to test a claim.

He secretly planned a response. When the town left for a festival, he went into the temple, asked the idols, "Do you not eat?" "What is the matter with you that you do not speak?" and struck them down, "except the largest of them, that they might return to it" (21:58). When they returned, they asked who did it. They knew who: "We heard a young man mention them who is called Ibrahim." He said: "Rather, this, the largest of them, did it, so ask them, if they should [be able to] speak." They turned to themselves and said, "Indeed, you are the wrongdoers," then fell back to their old position: "You have known that these do not speak." He said: "Then do you worship instead of Allah that which does not benefit you at all or harm you?" (21:62–66)

They said, "Burn him and support your gods." But Allah said: "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim." (21:68–69) Ibn ‘Abbas said that the last words of Ibrahim as he was thrown into the fire were: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs" (Sahih al-Bukhari).

Ibrahim left his people: "Indeed, I will go to my Lord; He will guide me." (37:99) He met a ruler who claimed to give life and death by executing one prisoner and freeing another. Ibrahim said: "Indeed, Allah brings up the sun from the east, so bring it up from the west," and the disbeliever was dumbfounded (2:258). He asked Allah to show him how He gives life to the dead, "but to satisfy my heart" (2:260), and was told to take four birds and place a part of them on each hill, then call them; they came flying.

In his old age he was given a son. The Qur’an tells the greatest test. He saw in a dream that he was sacrificing his son; the dreams of prophets are revelation. He told his son: "O my son, indeed I have seen in a dream that I am slaughtering you, so see what you think." He said: "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, of the steadfast." When they had both submitted and he laid him down upon his forehead, Allah called: "O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision. Indeed, We thus reward the doers of good. Indeed, this was the clear trial." And He ransomed him with a great sacrifice (37:102–107). This is remembered in the sacrifice of ‘Id al-Adha.

Ibrahim and Isma’il raised the foundations of the Kaaba, saying: "Our Lord, accept [this] from us. Indeed, You are the Hearing, the Knowing. Our Lord, and make us Muslims [in submission] to You and from our descendants a Muslim nation [in submission] to You. And show us our rites and accept our repentance. Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful. Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses and teach them the Book and wisdom and purify them." (2:127–129) The last of these supplications was answered with Muhammad ﷺ.

He was commanded: "And proclaim to the people the Hajj; they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel" (22:27), and the pilgrimage rites continue to follow his example, which is why the Muslim prayer includes blessings on Ibrahim and his family.

facts: The valley of Makkah, then without people, water or plants
Zamzam, the sa’i between Safa and Marwa
Raised among them, learned Arabic, and became a prophet

t: Ibn ‘Abbas narrates that Ibrahim brought Hajar and her infant son Isma’il to the place of the Kaaba, under a large tree near where Zamzam is now, and left them with a bag of dates and a skin of water. He turned back, and Hajar followed, asking, "O Ibrahim, where are you going, leaving us in this valley where there is no one and nothing?" She said it several times, and he did not look back. Then she asked: "Has Allah commanded you to do this?" He said, "Yes." She said: "Then He will not let us be lost."

When he reached the pass where they could no longer see him, he faced the House, raised his hands and prayed the words in 14:37: "Our Lord, I have settled some of my descendants in an uncultivated valley near Your Sacred House, our Lord, that they may establish prayer. So make hearts among the people incline toward them and provide for them from the fruits that they might be grateful." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

When the water ran out and her baby began to writhe from thirst, Hajar could not bear to watch. She climbed Safa, the nearest hill, and looked for anyone. She saw no one, came down, gathered her dress, and ran across the valley like someone in distress until she reached Marwa. She climbed it and looked. This she did seven times. The Prophet ﷺ said: "This is the origin of the sa’i that people do between them."

On the last run she heard a sound and said, "Be quiet" to herself, then heard again, and said: "You have made me hear; is there any help with you?" And there was the angel by the place of Zamzam, who struck the ground with his heel or wing until water came out. She began to dam it and to scoop it into her skin. The Prophet ﷺ said: "May Allah have mercy on Isma’il’s mother; had she left Zamzam alone, or not scooped, it would have been a flowing spring." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

Soon a party of the tribe of Jurhum passed through and, seeing birds circling in a place without water, sent scouts, who found the spring. They asked her for permission to settle there. She said they could, but they would have no right to the water. They agreed. They settled and brought their families. Isma’il grew among them, learned their Arabic, and was loved by them; they gave him a wife. Ibrahim visited from time to time. In one of these visits, he and Isma’il built the Kaaba (Sahih al-Bukhari).

Everything in this account is something Muslims re-live in Hajj: the sa’i between Safa and Marwa, the water of Zamzam, the Kaaba, the prayer for a city of believers. The Qur’an says: "Indeed, Safa and Marwa are among the symbols of Allah" (2:158). The story shows trust not as passivity but as effort, in that she ran seven times, and Allah’s provision as arriving at the end of her effort.

facts: Nephew of Ibrahim, who believed with him (29:26)
The towns of Sodom, in the area of the Dead Sea (as commonly identified)
A shameful act that "no one in the worlds preceded you in" (7:80), and robbing travellers (29:29)

t: Lut told his people: "Do you commit such immorality as no one has preceded you with from among the worlds? Indeed, you approach men with desire, instead of women. Rather, you are a transgressing people." (7:80–81) They also stalked travellers and "committed in your gatherings [all manner of] wrongdoing" (29:29). His message was the same as all the others: "So fear Allah and obey me. And I do not ask you for it any payment." (26:162–164)

Their answer was not an argument but a threat: "Expel them from your city. Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure." (7:82) The Qur’an points to this: those who are known for being clean are punished for it by those who are not.

Angels came to Ibrahim first, as men, with the news of Ishaq, and told him that they were sent against the people of Lut (11:69–76, 15:51–60). Then they came to Lut as handsome young men. He was distressed: "This is a trying day." (11:77) His people rushed upon him, and he said: "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you a man of reason?" (11:78) And: "If only I had against you some power or could take shelter in a strong support." (11:80)

Then the angels said: "O Lut, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So set out with your family during a portion of the night and let not any among you look back, except your wife; indeed, she will be struck by that which strikes them. Indeed, their appointment is the morning. Is not the morning near?" (11:81)

When Our command came, We made the highest part of the city its lowest and rained upon it stones of layered baked clay, marked from your Lord (11:82–83). The Qur’an reminds the Quraysh that they pass by the ruins at morning and at night (37:137–138; 15:76). Lut’s wife, who was with the wrongdoers in sympathy, is mentioned beside the wife of Nuh in Surah al-Tahrim as an example that being married to a prophet does not save anyone (66:10).

When the angels came to Ibrahim and told him they were going to the people of Lut, the Qur’an says: “And when the fright had left Ibrahim and the good news had reached him, he began to argue with Us concerning the people of Lut. Indeed, Ibrahim was forbearing, grieving and often turning in repentance.” (11:74–75) In Surah al-‘Ankabut he says: “Indeed, Lut is among them.” The angels answer: “We are more knowing of who is there. We will surely save him and his family, except his wife; she is of those who remain behind.” (29:32)

The angels told him: “O Ibrahim, give up this plea. The command of your Lord has come, and there will come upon them a punishment that cannot be turned back.” (11:76) The detail shows the heart of Ibrahim, who pleaded even for the people of a town far away. It also shows that, once Allah’s command has been given, even a prophet’s intercession does not change it.

The Qur’an uses Lut’s wife, and the wife of Nuh, as a pair of examples: “Allah presents an example of those who disbelieved: the wife of Nuh and the wife of Lut. They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them, so those two did not avail them against Allah at all.” (66:10) Ibn ‘Abbas explained that the betrayal was not adultery, which no prophet’s wife has committed, but that she did not believe and used to tell the wrongdoers about the guests who came to Lut’s house.

The point is that closeness to a righteous person does not save anyone. Each is answerable for his own faith. The Qur’an immediately follows with the opposite example, the wife of Fir‘awn, who believed in the house of the worst of tyrants.

When the men of the town rushed to his house, Lut cried out: “If only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in a strong support.” (11:80) The Prophet ﷺ commented on this, as Abu Hurayrah reports in Sahih al-Bukhari: “May Allah have mercy on Lut. He used to take refuge in a strong support,” meaning Allah.

The scholars have pointed out the gentleness of the remark. Lut had said that he wished for a human protector, and the Prophet ﷺ reminded his Companions that the real support he had was Allah, the strongest of all. The story is also taken as a reminder that a believer in a place where he is in the minority can feel that he has no one, and that he is always in the shelter of someone who is stronger than any tribe.

facts: Ya’qub (Jacob), son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim
Eleven; Binyamin was the full brother
Raised in the house of the ‘Aziz; prisoner; then treasurer
"The noble, son of the noble, son of the noble, son of the noble, Yusuf" (Sahih al-Bukhari)

t: He told his father: "I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me." His father told him not to tell his brothers, lest they plot against him (12:4–5). The brothers said: "Yusuf and his brother are more beloved to our father than we, while we are a group. Indeed, our father is in clear error." (12:8) They suggested killing him or throwing him in a faraway land, but one said to throw him in the bottom of a well instead, "some travellers will pick him up" (12:10). They took him for a day of play and threw him in, then came back at night weeping, with his shirt stained with false blood. Ya’qub said: "Rather, your souls have enticed you to something, so patience is most fitting." (12:18)

A caravan found him and sold him for a low price to a man of standing, the ‘Aziz, who told his wife: "Make his residence comfortable; perhaps he will benefit us, or we will adopt him as a son." (12:21) When Yusuf reached maturity, Allah gave him judgement and knowledge. The wife of the ‘Aziz sought to seduce him; she locked the doors and said, "Come, you." He said: "[I seek] the refuge of Allah. Indeed, he is my master, who has made good my residence. Indeed, wrongdoers will not succeed." (12:23) He ran for the door and she tore his shirt from behind, and they met her husband at the door. The proof was the tear from behind. The ‘Aziz told him to keep quiet and told her to ask forgiveness.

Then the women of the city gossiped, and she invited them, gave each a knife and a fruit, and had Yusuf come out before them. They were so struck they cut their hands, saying "Allah forbid, this is no mortal; this is none but a noble angel." (12:31) Yusuf asked Allah: "My Lord, prison is more dear to me than that to which they invite me." (12:33) And he was imprisoned, though the evidence of his innocence was known.

In prison two men told him their dreams. Before explaining, Yusuf gave them da’wah: "I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah... and I have followed the religion of my fathers, Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya’qub." (12:37–38) He told one he would serve wine to his lord and the other that he would be crucified, and asked the first to mention him to the king. Satan made the man forget, so Yusuf stayed in prison for several more years (12:42).

s.h: The king’s dream and the treasury
t: The king dreamed of seven fat cows eaten by seven lean, and seven green ears and others dry. The man who had been released remembered Yusuf, who explained: seven years of sowing as usual, leaving the harvest in its ears except a little for eating, then seven years of hardship consuming what was saved, then a year of rain. The king asked for him. Yusuf refused to leave until the matter of the women was investigated, and the Prophet ﷺ praised his patience and steadiness, saying: "Had I stayed in prison as long as Yusuf stayed, and then the caller had come, I would have responded" (Sahih al-Bukhari). The wife of the ‘Aziz admitted: "Now the truth has become evident. It was I who sought to seduce him, and indeed, he is of the truthful." (12:51)
Yusuf asked the king: "Appoint me over the storehouses of the land; indeed, I will be a knowing guardian." (12:55) He was given authority and prepared for the famine.

During the famine, his brothers came from Canaan to buy grain. He recognised them; they did not. He asked them to bring their other brother, and when they returned with Binyamin, he told his brother who he was and had a drinking cup put in Binyamin’s bag so he could keep him. The brothers pleaded for Binyamin. Ya’qub, who had gone blind from sorrow, said: "O my sons, go and find out about Yusuf and his brother and do not despair of relief from Allah." (12:87)

When they came to him a third time, the brothers said: "O ‘Aziz, adversity has touched us and our family, and we have come with goods of poor quality, so give us full measure." He said: "Do you know what you did with Yusuf and his brother when you were ignorant?" They said: "Are you indeed Yusuf?" He said: "I am Yusuf, and this is my brother. Allah has certainly favoured us. Indeed, he who fears Allah and is patient, indeed, Allah does not allow to be lost the reward of those who do good." They said, "By Allah, certainly has Allah preferred you over us, and indeed, we have been sinners." He said: "No blame will there be upon you today. May Allah forgive you; and He is the most merciful of the merciful." (12:89–92)

He sent his shirt to be laid on his father’s face, and his sight returned (12:93–96). The family came to Egypt and he raised his parents on the throne, and they all fell in prostration, an act of respect then permitted. He said: "O my father, this is the interpretation of my vision of before. My Lord has made it reality." (12:100) And he made one of the most beautiful duas in the Qur’an: "My Lord, You have given me [something] of sovereignty and taught me of the interpretation of dreams. Creator of the heavens and earth, You are my protector in this world and in the Hereafter. Cause me to die a Muslim and join me with the righteous." (12:101)

facts: Illness and the loss of wealth and family (as commonly understood)
"Indeed, We found him patient, an excellent servant. Indeed, he was one repeatedly turning back [to Allah]" (38:44)
"Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful" (21:83)
Strike the ground; a spring to wash and drink (38:42)

t: The Qur’an says only: "And [mention] Ayyub, when he called to his Lord, Indeed, adversity has touched me, and you are the most merciful of the merciful. So We responded to him and removed what was upon him of adversity. And We gave him [back] his family and the like thereof with them as mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers [of Allah]." (21:83–84) And in Surah Sad: "Remember Our servant Ayyub, when he called to his Lord, Indeed, Satan has touched me with hardship and torment." (38:41)

The Qur’an links his trial to a form of hardship and suffering. It does not say precisely what afflicted him. Later accounts mention a long illness, the loss of children and property, and his wife’s devotion. These details are not in the Qur’an or authentic hadith, and scholars warn against the more extravagant versions. What is certain is the attitude: he did not complain against Allah, he asked Him.

Allah said: "Strike [the ground] with your foot; this is a cool bath and drink." (38:42) Then He gave him back his family and as many again, "as a mercy from Us and a reminder for those of understanding." (38:43) There was also an oath he had sworn, and Allah told him to take a bundle of twigs and strike with it, to fulfil it without harm (38:44).

Ayyub says only: "Adversity has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful." He does not ask for anything by name. He states his need and names Allah’s mercy. Scholars have noted that this is the model of making dua in distress: describe the state, praise Allah, and leave the response to Him. The Qur’an says that this is "a reminder for the worshippers" (21:84), meaning that his story is for everyone who faces hardship, not just for prophets.

There is one more scene in an authentic hadith. Abu Hurayrah reports in Sahih al-Bukhari that the Prophet ﷺ said: “While Ayyub was bathing naked, a swarm of golden locusts began to fall around him. He started to gather them into his garment. His Lord called to him: ‘O Ayyub, have I not made you free from need of what you see?’ He said: ‘Yes, by Your might, but I cannot do without Your blessing.’”

The hadith adds to the picture. After years of loss, Ayyub is given wealth as a sudden gift, and his first act is to take it with both hands. Yet when Allah asks him a gentle question, he does not pretend that he is above wanting it. He says that he cannot do without Allah’s blessing, and thereby shows that to want more of Allah’s gifts is not a fault. The scholars say that the hadith supports the idea that a person may keep seeking lawful provision.

s.h: His wife, and the length of the trial
t: The Qur’an does not name Ayyub’s wife or say how long the illness lasted. Ibn Kathir and others report that she stayed with him when others left, and that she worked for people to earn food for them. A report in the collection of Ibn Hibban and others, with a chain that scholars discuss, says that the illness lasted eighteen years and that all his friends abandoned him except two men. These details are told in the commentaries as reports, and they cannot be treated as established.

What the Qur’an says is enough to see the effect on later readers. When Allah restored his family and the like with them, the verse says that it was “a mercy from Us and a reminder for the people of understanding.” Ayyub’s story has been told to the sick and the grieving in every century, because he is shown calling on his Lord quietly and without protest, and being answered.

facts: Cheating in measure and weight; highway robbery
