An earthquake (7:91), a cry (11:94), or the shadow of a day of gloom (26:189)
Musa lived with Shu’ayb’s family in Madyan (28:22–28)

t: The people of Madyan were traders at a crossroads between Egypt, Syria and Arabia, with a strong economy and a weak sense of right. Shu’ayb’s first command was about worship: "Worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him." His second was about trade: "And do not decrease from the measure and the scale. Indeed, I see you in prosperity, but indeed, I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing Day. And O my people, give full measure and weight in justice and do not deprive the people of their due, and do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption. What remains [lawful] with Allah is best for you, if you should be believers. And I am not a guardian over you." (11:84–86)

The Qur’an links monotheism and fair dealing. The same people who bowed to idols took advantage of customers; the same faith that teaches us to give Allah what is His demands that we give people what is theirs.

They answered: "O Shu’ayb, does your prayer command you that we should leave what our fathers worship or [stop] doing with our wealth what we please? Indeed, you are the forbearing, the discerning!" (11:87), in sarcasm. He answered calmly: "O my people, have you considered: if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord and He has provided me with good provision from Him... I do not intend to differ from you in that which I forbid you; I only intend reform as much as I am able. And my success is not but through Allah." (11:88)

They threatened him: "Our people’s family is what protects you from stoning, and you have no power over us." He said: "O my people, is my family more respected with you than Allah?" (11:91–92) They said that if he did not stop they would drive him and the believers out. He said: "Even if we were unwilling? We would have invented against Allah a lie if we returned to your religion." (7:88–89)

When Allah’s command came, He saved Shu’ayb and those with him, "and the shriek seized those who had wronged, and they became within their homes motionless [in death], as if they had never prospered there." (11:94–95) Shu’ayb turned from them: "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and advised you. So how could I grieve for a disbelieving people?" (7:93)

The Qur’an mentions two groups to whom Shu‘ayb was sent: the people of Madyan, and, in Surah ash-Shu‘ara’ and elsewhere, “the companions of the Thicket” (Ashab al-Aykah). Their message and their sins were the same: giving short measure and weight and spreading corruption. In the surah, the verses read: “They denied him, so the punishment of the day of the shadow seized them. Indeed, it was the punishment of a terrible day.” (26:189)

Scholars have discussed whether the two were the same people or neighbouring peoples, and the commentaries mention both views. Either way, the same prophet was sent to both. The commentators say that Allah sent a very hot spell on them for seven days, after which a cloud came which they thought was shade; they gathered under it for relief, and the punishment came from it. It is another picture of the same pattern: they saw a cloud, thought it a mercy, and it was their end.

s.h: The two women at the well
t: When Musa fled from Egypt he came to Madyan, and the Qur’an tells how he found two women holding back their sheep from the well while the men drew water. He watered the sheep for them, withdrew to the shade and prayed: “My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me.” One of the women came to him “walking shyly” and said that her father wanted to repay him. Their father asked Musa to work for eight years, and, if he wished, ten, in return for marrying one of his daughters. (28:23–28)

The Qur’an does not name the father. Some of the Companions and early commentators said that he was Shu‘ayb, and many popular accounts take it as certain. Ibn Kathir notes that no authentic hadith names him, and that others said that he was a righteous man of Madyan. It is therefore best to say that it was a righteous man in the land where Shu‘ayb had been sent, and that, if it was Shu‘ayb himself, that adds an honour to his house.

facts: More than any other prophet, in over thirty surahs
Kalimullah (the one to whom Allah spoke, 4:164)
Harun, who was sent with him (20:29–36)

t: Fir’awn "exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing a group of them, slaughtering their sons and keeping their females alive" (28:4). Musa’s mother was inspired: "Nurse him; but when you fear for him, cast him into the river and do not fear and do not grieve. Indeed, We will return him to you and make him [one] of the messengers." (28:7) She put him in a chest and set it on the Nile, and told his sister to follow. The household of Fir’awn picked him up; his wife Asiyah said: "[He will be] a comfort of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him; perhaps he may benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son." (28:9)

Musa refused every wet-nurse, and his sister said, "Shall I direct you to a household that will rear him for you?" So he was returned to his mother, "that her eye might be content and not grieve" (28:13). The very tyrant who sought to destroy him raised him.

When he grew, Allah gave him judgement and knowledge. One day he found two men fighting, one from his people and one from the enemy. The Israelite called to him for help; Musa struck the other and killed him by accident. He said at once: "This is from the work of Satan. Indeed, he is a manifest, misleading enemy." (28:15) He prayed: "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, so forgive me," and Allah forgave him (28:16). The next day he saw the same man in a fight again, and a man from Fir’awn’s court came running: "O Musa, indeed the eminent ones are conferring about you to kill you, so leave; indeed, I am to you of the sincere advisers." (28:20) He left.

He reached the water of Madyan and found men watering their flocks and two women holding theirs back. He asked, "What is your circumstance?" They said: "We cannot water until the shepherds dispatch [their flocks]; and our father is an old man." So he watered for them, then went to the shade and prayed: "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You would send down to me, in need." (28:24) One of the women came walking shyly and said: "My father invites you that he may reward you for having watered for us." Their father told him not to fear and later offered Musa one of his daughters in marriage in return for eight years of service, or ten if he wished (28:27). Musa agreed.

On the journey back, in the dark and cold, he saw a fire by the mountain. He told his family to wait. When he came to it, a voice called from the right side of the valley, from the tree: "O Musa, indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds." (28:30) In Surah Ta-Ha: "Indeed, I am your Lord, so remove your sandals. Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa. And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed. Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance." (20:12–14)

He was shown the first signs: his staff became a serpent, and his hand shone white. He was afraid, and said that he had killed a man and that his brother Harun was more eloquent. He asked: "My Lord, expand for me my breast [with assurance] and ease for me my task and untie the knot from my tongue that they may understand my speech. And appoint for me a minister from my family: Harun, my brother. Increase through him my strength and make him my partner in my task." (20:25–32) Allah answered: "You have been granted your request, O Musa." (20:36)

He and Harun were told: "Go to Fir’awn. Indeed, he has transgressed. And speak to him with gentle speech that perhaps he may be reminded or fear [Allah]." (20:43–44) Fir’awn asked: "And what is the Lord of the worlds?" and Musa answered with the world around them. Fir’awn threatened him with prison. Musa threw his staff, and it was a serpent; he drew out his hand, and it was white. Fir’awn called the magicians of the land for a public contest. They threw their ropes and staffs, and the people were awed. Musa threw his staff, and it swallowed what they had made. The magicians fell in prostration: "We have believed in the Lord of Harun and Musa." (20:70) Fir’awn threatened to cut off their hands and feet and crucify them, and they answered: "We will never prefer you over what has come to us of clear proofs and [over] He who created us. So decree whatever you are to decree. You can only decree for this worldly life." (20:72)

After years of calling, Fir’awn and his chiefs refused. Allah sent signs: drought, floods, locusts, lice, frogs and blood (7:130–133). Finally Musa was told to leave at night with his people. Fir’awn pursued. At the sea, with the enemy behind, Banu Isra’il said: "Indeed, we are to be overtaken!" Musa said: "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me." Allah told him: "Strike with your staff the sea." And it split, "and each portion was like a great towering mountain" (26:61–63). They crossed. Fir’awn followed and was drowned; when he saw it, he said: "I believe that there is no deity except that in whom the Children of Israel believe." Allah said: "Now? And you had disobeyed before and were of the corrupters? So today We will save you in body that you may be to those who succeed you a sign." (10:90–92)

The Qur’an tells what followed: the people who asked for an idol to worship as soon as they saw people devoted to idols (7:138), the forty nights at Mount Sinai, the calf made by al-Samiri while Musa was away (20:85–97), the request to see Allah, "You will not see Me" (7:143), the cow (2:67–73), their refusal to enter the holy land, which led to forty years of wandering (5:20–26).

The Prophet ﷺ said of Musa when he was hurt by criticism: "May Allah have mercy on Musa; he was hurt with more than this and was patient." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). The story is told so often because it is the pattern for the struggle between tyranny and faith.

facts: King and prophet; given the Zabur (4:163)
Iron softened, mountains and birds in praise (Dawud); wind, jinn, speech of animals (Sulayman)
The Prophet ﷺ said the dearest prayer to Allah is the prayer of Dawud (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

s.h: The young man and the giant
t: When the elders of Bani Isra’il asked their prophet for a king, Allah made Talut king. Among his army was a young man, Dawud. When the armies faced each other, "Dawud killed Jalut, and Allah gave him kingship and wisdom and taught him from that which He willed." (2:251) A young shepherd who faced a giant became a prophet-king. In Surah Sad, Allah says: "Be patient over what they say and remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength; indeed, he was one repeatedly turning back [to Allah]." (38:17)

Allah made the mountains and birds glorify with him in the morning and evening (38:18–19, 21:79), "and We made the iron soft for him" (34:10) so that he could make coats of mail. He ate only from the work of his hands: the Prophet ﷺ said: "No one has ever eaten better food than that which he earned by his own labour; and the Prophet of Allah Dawud used to eat from the earnings of his own hands." (Sahih al-Bukhari). He fasted on alternate days and slept a part of the night and prayed a part of it (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim), which the Prophet ﷺ called the most beloved fasting and prayer to Allah.

Surah Sad tells of two men who climbed the wall of his prayer chamber, startling him. One said, "This is my brother; he has ninety-nine ewes and I have one, and he said, Entrust her to me, and overcame me in speech." Dawud said: "He has wronged you in demanding your ewe [in addition] to his ewes." Then he realised that it was a test, asked forgiveness of his Lord, fell down bowing, and turned to Him. Allah forgave him and said that he had nearness and a good place of return (38:21–25). The lesson the Qur’an draws: "O Dawud, indeed We have made you a successor upon the earth, so judge between the people in truth and do not follow [your own] desire." (38:26) Scholars note it teaches a judge to hear both sides before giving a verdict.

Sulayman inherited from Dawud. In a case of crops destroyed by sheep, "We gave understanding of it to Sulayman, and to each We gave judgement and knowledge" (21:79). He said: "O people, we have been taught the language of birds, and we have been given from all things. Indeed, this is evident bounty." (27:16) Wind and jinn served him (21:81–82, 34:12). Once, marching with his army, he passed a valley of ants; one said: "O ants, enter your dwellings that you not be crushed by Sulayman and his soldiers while they perceive not." He smiled, amused at her words, and said: "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents and to do righteousness of which You approve." (27:18–19)

The hoopoe reported a queen ruling Saba’ with a great throne, whose people prostrated to the sun. Sulayman sent a letter, "In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Do not exalt yourselves against me, but come to me in submission [as Muslims]." (27:30–31) Bilqis consulted her council, sent a gift to test him, and he rejected it: "What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you." (27:36) One with knowledge of the Scripture brought her throne before a blink of an eye, and Sulayman said: "This is from the favour of my Lord to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful." (27:40) He had her palace floor made of glass over water, which she mistook for a pool, and uncovered her legs. He told her it was a palace smoothed with glass. Then she said: "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I submit with Sulayman to Allah, Lord of the worlds." (27:44)

Allah says that when He decreed Sulayman’s death, nothing indicated it to the jinn "except a creature of the earth eating his staff. And when he fell, it became clear to the jinn that if they had known the unseen, they would not have remained in humiliating punishment." (34:14) He had been leaning on his staff, and they went on working, thinking he was alive, until a termite ate the staff and he collapsed. It is a graphic proof that even those who could command jinn did not know what was happening in front of them.

facts: Dhun-Nun and Sahib al-Hut (the one of the fish)
A hundred thousand or more (37:147); the commentaries name Nineveh
"Sent to a hundred thousand or more" (37:147)
"La ilaha illa anta subhanaka inni kuntu min al-zalimin"

t: After a long time of preaching and being rejected, Yunus left his people angrily. The Qur’an says: "And [mention] the man of the fish, when he went off in anger and thought that We would not decide anything against him." (21:87) The Prophet ﷺ said: "It is not right for any servant to say that I am better than Yunus ibn Matta" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim), a reminder that this was a slip of a great prophet, and that no one should look down on him.

He boarded a laden ship. The ship was overloaded, and lots were drawn among the passengers to see who would be thrown overboard. The lot fell on him: "And he drew lots and was among the losers." (37:141)

"Then the fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy." (37:142) In the darkness of the night, the darkness of the sea and the darkness of the fish’s belly, he called out: "There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers." (21:87) Allah says: "Then We responded to him and saved him from the distress. And thus do We save the believers." (21:88) The Prophet ﷺ said of this dua: "The supplication of Dhun-Nun when he called upon his Lord in the belly of the fish: There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers. No Muslim ever calls upon his Lord with it for anything except that Allah responds to him." (Sunan al-Tirmidhi)

Allah says: "And had he not been of those who exalt Allah, he would have remained inside its belly until the Day they are resurrected." (37:143–144) The fish cast him onto a barren shore, ill, and "We caused to grow over him a gourd vine" (37:145–146).

In the meantime, his people had believed. The Qur’an remarks on it as unique: "So why was there not [a single] city that believed so its faith benefited it except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in worldly life and gave them enjoyment for a time." (10:98) It is said, in the commentaries, that when they saw the signs of the punishment approaching, they came out to the open with their children and animals and sincerely repented. Allah then "sent him to a hundred thousand or more, and they believed, so We gave them enjoyment for a time" (37:147–148).

Allah told the Prophet ﷺ: "So be patient for the decision of your Lord, and be not like the companion of the fish when he called out while he was distressed. Had not a favour from his Lord overtaken him, he would have been thrown onto the naked shore while he was blamed. But his Lord chose him and made him of the righteous." (68:48–50) The Prophet ﷺ was in a similar position, being rejected, and Allah told him to carry on, rather than to leave in frustration.

facts: A prophet and the guardian of Maryam (3:37)
Given wisdom as a child (19:12); "a prophet from among the righteous" (3:39)
"My Lord, do not leave me alone [with no heir]" (21:89)
Three nights without speaking to people (3:41, 19:10)

t: Maryam was entrusted to Zakariyya. "Every time Zakariyya entered upon her in the prayer chamber, he found with her provision. He said: O Maryam, from where is this to you? She said: It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah gives provision to whom He wills without account." (3:37) Seeing the provision, which was out of season, Zakariyya was moved, and "there Zakariyya called upon his Lord; he said, My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring. Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication." (3:38)

Surah Maryam gives the dua in its fullest form: "When he called to his Lord a private call. He said: My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened, and my head has filled with white, and never have I been in my supplication to You, my Lord, unhappy. And indeed, I fear the successors after me, and my wife has been barren, so give me from Yourself an heir who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya’qub. And make him, my Lord, pleasing." (19:3–6) His heir was a spiritual, not material, one: the Prophet ﷺ said that the prophets do not leave wealth as inheritance.

The angels called to him while he stood praying in the prayer chamber: "Allah gives you good tidings of Yahya, confirming a word from Allah, and [who will be] honourable, chaste and a prophet from among the righteous." (3:39) He was amazed: "My Lord, how will I have a boy when I have reached old age and my wife is barren?" He said: "Thus does Allah do what He wills." (3:40) He asked for a sign. Allah said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gesture." (3:41)

"O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination." And We gave him judgement [while yet] a boy, and affection from Us and purity, and he was fearing of Allah, and dutiful to his parents, and he was not a tyrant or disobedient. And peace be upon him the day he was born and the day he dies and the day he is raised alive. (19:12–15) The Qur’an describes him as "honourable" (sayyid), "chaste" (hasur) and "fearing Allah." He was a boy of serious character. Of how the lives of Zakariyya and Yahya ended, the Qur’an says nothing, and the accounts that say they were killed come from later reports.

facts: The only woman named in the Qur’an; Surah 19 and a surah of her family (3)
Without a father, by Allah’s command "Be" (3:59)
Not killed or crucified; raised to Allah (4:157–158)

t: The wife of ‘Imran vowed her unborn child to Allah; when she gave birth to a girl, she said, "My Lord, I have delivered a female," and Allah says: "and Allah was most knowing of what she delivered, and the male is not like the female." She named her Maryam and asked protection for her and her offspring from Satan (3:35–36). Allah "accepted her with good acceptance and caused her to grow in a good manner" (3:37), and Zakariyya took her care.

The angels told her: "O Maryam, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds. O Maryam, be devoutly obedient to your Lord and prostrate and bow with those who bow [in prayer]." (3:42–43) The Prophet ﷺ named her among the best women of all time: "The best of the women of her time was Maryam, and the best of the women of her time was Khadijah." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

She withdrew from her family to a place toward the east, and put up a screen. Allah sent Jibril to her "in the form of a well-proportioned man." She said: "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, [so leave me] if you should be fearing of Allah." He said: "I am only the messenger of your Lord to give you [news of] a pure boy." She said: "How can I have a boy while no man has touched me and I have not been unchaste?" He said: "Thus [it will be]; your Lord says, It is easy for Me, and We will make him a sign to the people and a mercy from Us. And it is a matter [already] decreed." (19:17–21)

She conceived and withdrew to a remote place. The pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree. She said: "Oh, I wish I had died before this and was in oblivion, forgotten." But a voice called to her from beneath her: "Do not grieve; your Lord has provided beneath you a stream. And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you ripe, fresh dates. So eat and drink and be contented. And if you see from among humanity anyone, say, Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful abstention, so I will not speak today to any human being." (19:23–26)

She came with the child to her people, who said: "O Maryam, you have certainly done a thing unprecedented. O sister of Harun, your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother unchaste." She pointed to the baby. They said: "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle a child?" He said: "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet. And He has made me blessed wherever I am and has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah as long as I remain alive. And [made me] dutiful to my mother, and He has not made me a wretched tyrant. And peace is on me the day I was born and the day I will die and the day I am raised alive." (19:27–33)

He was sent to Bani Isra’il: "I have come to you with a sign from your Lord in that I design for you from clay [what is] like the form of a bird, then I breathe into it and it becomes a bird by permission of Allah. And I cure the blind and the leper, and I give life to the dead by permission of Allah. And I inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses." (3:49) Those who believed were the disciples (al-hawariyyun): "We are supporters for Allah. We have believed in Allah and testify that we are Muslims [submitting to Him]." (3:52)

The Qur’an corrects errors about him, as it does for all: "The Messiah, son of Maryam, was not but a messenger; [other] messengers had passed on before him. And his mother was a supporter of truth. They both used to eat food." (5:75) On the Day of Resurrection, he will be asked: "O ‘Isa, son of Maryam, did you say to the people, Take me and my mother as deities besides Allah?" He will say: "Exalted are You! It was not for me to say that to which I have no right." (5:116)

s.h: The end of his time on earth
t: The plot against him is described: "And [for] their saying, Indeed, we have killed the Messiah, ‘Isa, the son of Maryam, the Messenger of Allah. And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but [another] was made to resemble him to them. And indeed, those who differ over it are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption. And they did not kill him, for certain. Rather, Allah raised him to Himself." (4:157–158)

The Prophet ﷺ said that ‘Isa will return before the end of time and "judge among you with justice, break the cross, kill the swine, and abolish the jizyah" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). And he said: "I am the closest of people to ‘Isa, the son of Maryam, in this world and the next. The prophets are brothers from one father with different mothers, and their religion is one." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

facts: Young men who believed in their Lord (18:13)

t: The Qur’an describes them as "youths who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance" (18:13). They lived among a people who worshipped others besides Allah, and a ruler who, according to the commentators, forced it on them. When they stood up, they said: "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. Never will we invoke besides Him any deity. We would have certainly spoken then an excessive transgression." (18:14)

They spoke it among themselves: "These, our people, have taken gods besides Him. Why do they not bring for them a clear authority? And who is more unjust than one who invents about Allah a lie?" (18:15) Then, with no way to practise freely, they agreed: "And when you have withdrawn from them and that which they worship other than Allah, retreat to the cave. Your Lord will spread out for you of His mercy and will prepare for you from your affair facility." (18:16)

"So We cast [a cover of sleep] over their ears within the cave for a number of years." (18:11) Allah turned them over to the right and left, so that their bodies would not decay, and their dog lay with its paws stretched at the entrance. The Qur’an says that anyone who looked would have turned in flight and been filled with terror, as protection (18:18). The sun rose and set away from the cave, so they lay in the open part of it but were shaded (18:17).

They woke and asked each other: "How long have you remained?" They said: "We have remained a day or part of a day." Others said: "Your Lord is most knowing of how long you remained. So send one of you with this silver coin of yours to the city and let him look to which is the purest food and bring you provision from it. And let him be cautious and let no one be aware of you." (18:19)

When the man went to buy food, the coin gave him away; it belonged to a time long gone. "And similarly, We caused them to be found that they [who found them] would know that the promise of Allah is truth and that of the Hour there is no doubt." (18:21) The people disagreed. Some said to build a structure over them; those with authority said: "We will surely take over them a mosque." (18:21) The Qur’an adds that people dispute how many they were: "three, the fourth being their dog," "five, the sixth being their dog," "seven, and the eighth being their dog." Say: "My Lord is most knowing of their number. None knows them except a few." (18:22) It tells the Prophet ﷺ not to argue over it, since the number is not the point.

Commentators say that the story was told to answer a question put to the Prophet ﷺ by the Jews of Madinah at the instigation of Quraysh, along with the questions about Dhul-Qarnayn and the soul. The lesson on the Hour, resurrection and trusting Allah’s promise is the real answer.

The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever recites Surah al-Kahf on Friday will have a light illuminate for him between the two Fridays (al-Hakim, al-Bayhaqi). He also said that whoever memorises the first ten verses of the surah is protected from the Dajjal, in another narration the last ten (Sahih Muslim). The surah has four stories, which scholars connect to four trials: faith (the cave), wealth (the two gardens), knowledge (Musa and Khidr), and power (Dhul-Qarnayn).

facts: "The one with two horns" or "two eras"; commentators differ on who he was
West, east, and between two mountains
A barrier against Ya’juj and Ma’juj
The Qur’an does not give his dates or nation

t: The Qur’an starts: "And they ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn. Say: I will recite to you about him a report. Indeed, We established him upon the earth, and We gave him to everything a way." (18:83–84) Scholars differ over who he was. Some say Alexander of Macedon, others a righteous king of Himyar or a Persian ruler. The Qur’an itself gives no name, since the point of the story is the character of a believing ruler, not his identity.

He followed a way until he reached the setting of the sun, and found it, as it appeared to him, setting in a spring of dark water, and near it a people. Allah said: "O Dhul-Qarnayn, either you punish [them] or else adopt among them [a way of] goodness." He said: "As for one who wrongs, we will punish him. Then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment. But as for one who believes and does righteousness, he will have a reward of the best [i.e. Paradise], and we will speak to him from our command with ease." (18:86–88)

Then he went east to a people who had no shelter from the sun, and dealt with them similarly (18:89–91). The Qur’an describes his policy with the same words twice: justice for the wrongdoer and kindness for the doer of good.

He then reached a place between two mountains, where he found a people who "could hardly understand [his] speech." They said: "O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Ya’juj and Ma’juj are [great] corrupters in the land. So may we assign for you an expenditure that you might make between us and them a barrier?" He said: "That in which my Lord has established me is better [than your payment], so help me with strength; I will make between you and them a dam. Bring me sheets of iron," until, when he had made it level between the two mountain-walls, he said, "Blow," until when he had made it [like] fire, he said: "Bring me, that I may pour over it molten copper." So they [Ya’juj and Ma’juj] were unable to climb it, nor were they able [to effect] in it any penetration. He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord; but when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level, and the promise of my Lord is ever true." (18:94–98)

Dhul-Qarnayn is the model of a powerful believer. He credits every success to Allah ("This is a mercy from my Lord"), refuses payment for a public good, asks the people to contribute labour so the work is theirs, and ends by remembering that even his greatest work will be levelled when Allah wills. The Prophet ﷺ mentioned that the barrier is breached in the last days, and Ya’juj and Ma’juj will emerge (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

facts: Musa, with a servant of Allah "to whom We had given mercy and taught knowledge" (18:65), named al-Khidr in the hadith
The boat, the boy, the wall
Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (Ubayy ibn Ka’b)

t: Ubayy ibn Ka’b narrates from the Prophet ﷺ: Musa stood among Bani Isra’il and was asked, "Who is the most knowledgeable person?" He said, "I am." Allah rebuked him, since he did not return knowledge to Allah, and said: "There is a servant of Ours at the junction of the two seas who is more knowledgeable than you." Musa asked how to find him and was told to take a fish in a basket; where the fish was lost, there he would be. He set out with his servant Yusha’ ibn Nun (Sahih al-Bukhari).

They walked until they reached a rock where they rested. The fish came alive and slipped into the sea. The servant forgot to mention it. When they had gone farther, Musa said: "Bring us our morning meal. We have certainly suffered in this, our journey, fatigue." The servant said: "Did you see when we retired to the rock? Indeed, I forgot the fish." Musa said: "That is what we were seeking." They returned, following their footprints, and found him (18:62–64).

Musa asked: "May I follow you on the condition that you teach me from what you have been taught of sound judgement?" He said: "Indeed, with me you will never be able to have patience. And how can you have patience for what you do not encompass in knowledge?" Musa said: "You will find me, if Allah wills, patient, and I will not disobey you in any order." He said: "Then if you follow me, do not ask me about anything until I make to you about it mention." (18:66–70)

They boarded a boat, and its owners, who knew him, took them without charge. Al-Khidr made a hole in it. Musa said: "Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? You have certainly done a grave thing." He said: "Did I not say that with me you would never be able to have patience?" Musa said: "Do not blame me for what I forgot and do not impose upon me in my case any difficulty." (18:71–73)

Then they met a boy and he killed him. Musa said: "Have you killed a pure soul for other than [having killed] a soul? You have certainly done a deplorable thing." He said: "Did I not tell you that with me you would never be able to have patience?" Musa said: "If I should ask you about anything after this, then do not keep me as a companion." (18:74–76)

They reached the people of a town and asked for food, but they refused to host them. They found a wall about to collapse, and he set it straight. Musa said: "If you wished, you could have taken for it a payment." He said: "This is parting between me and you. I will inform you of the interpretation of that about which you could not have patience." (18:77–78)

"As for the ship, it belonged to poor people working at sea. So I intended to damage it, as there was after them a king who seized every [good] ship by force. And as for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would overburden them by transgression and disbelief. So we intended that their Lord should substitute for them one better than him in purity and nearer to mercy. And as for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and there was beneath it a treasure for them, and their father had been righteous. So your Lord intended that they reach maturity and extract their treasure, as a mercy from your Lord. And I did it not of my own accord. That is the interpretation of that about which you could not have patience." (18:79–82)

The Prophet ﷺ said: "We wish Musa had been patient, so that more of their story would have been told to us." And he said that the sparrow’s sip from the sea was all the knowledge of Musa and al-Khidr compared with Allah’s knowledge (Sahih al-Bukhari).

The three acts look like harm, murder and a favour for rude people, and each turns out to prevent a greater harm or provide for someone unseen. It does not teach that we may kill or damage by personal discretion: Khidr said he acted on a command ("I did it not of my own accord"), and the law of Allah for everyone else stays as it is. What it teaches is humility about what we cannot see, and that when something seems wrong in the world, our knowledge is incomplete.

facts: A wise man; scholars differ on whether he was a prophet
Tawhid, gratitude, parents, prayer, patience, humility

t: "And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom [and said], Be grateful to Allah. And whoever is grateful is grateful for [the benefit of] himself. And whoever is ungrateful, then indeed, Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy." (31:12) The first thing that Allah tells him after giving wisdom is to be thankful. In the Qur’an, wisdom begins with gratitude.

"O my son, do not associate [anything] with Allah. Indeed, association [with Him] is great injustice." (31:13) The first piece is the most important, and it was said with affection: "O my son." Then, in a break from his words, Allah mentions the rights of parents: "We have enjoined upon man [care] for his parents. His mother carried him, [increasing her] in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years. Be grateful to Me and to your parents; to Me is the [final] destination." But if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, "do not obey them but accompany them in [this] world with appropriate kindness." (31:14–15)

"O my son, indeed if it [i.e. a wrong] should be the weight of a mustard seed and should be within a rock or [anywhere] in the heavens or earth, Allah will bring it forth. Indeed, Allah is Subtle and Aware." (31:16) A reminder that nothing hidden is lost.
"O my son, establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and be patient over what befalls you. Indeed, that is of the matters [requiring] determination." (31:17)

"And do not turn your cheek [in contempt] toward people and do not walk through the earth exultantly. Indeed, Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful. And be moderate in your pace and lower your voice; indeed, the most disagreeable of sounds is the voice of donkeys." (31:18–19)

The advice moves from belief to family, to accountability, to worship, to society and finally to manners. A complete character is built in nine sentences. Notably, nothing in it asks the son for worldly success: it is about who he is.

facts: The people of Musa, who "oppressed them" (28:76)
Treasures whose keys alone were a burden to a strong band
"I was only given it because of knowledge I have"
The earth swallowed him and his home

t: His own people warned him: "Do not exult. Indeed, Allah does not like the exultant. But seek, through that which Allah has given you, the home of the Hereafter; and [yet], do not forget your share of the world. And do good as Allah has done good to you. And desire not corruption in the land. Indeed, Allah does not like corrupters." (28:76–77) It is a complete economic ethic: wealth is allowed, even with a share in this world, but it must be used for the next, and not spent on corruption.

He said: "I was only given it because of knowledge I have." (28:78) Allah answered: "Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him of generations those who were greater than him in power and greater in accumulation?" Qarun went out among his people in his adornment. Those who desired worldly life said: "Oh, would that we had the like of what was given to Qarun. Indeed, he is one of great fortune." But those who had been given knowledge said: "Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better for he who believes and does righteousness. And none are granted it except the steadfast." (28:79–80)

"So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home. And there was for him no company to aid him other than Allah, nor was he of those who [could] defend themselves. And those who had wished for his position the previous day began to say: Oh, how Allah extends provision for whom He wills of His servants and restricts [it]! If it had not been that Allah conferred favour on us, He would have caused it to swallow us. Oh, how the disbelievers do not succeed!" (28:81–82)

The Qur’an concludes with a general principle: "That home of the Hereafter We assign to those who do not desire exaltedness upon the earth or corruption. And the [best] outcome is for the righteous." (28:83)

The Qur’an mentions Qarun in more than one place, always with proud rulers. “And [We destroyed] Qarun and Fir‘awn and Haman. Musa had come to them with clear proofs, but they were arrogant in the land.” (29:39) The pairing is revealing: one man with money, one with power, one with an office. They stood together against the message.

The Prophet ﷺ spoke about the test that wealth brings. Ka‘b ibn ‘Iyad reports in at-Tirmidhi: “Every nation has a trial, and the trial of my nation is wealth.” But he also said, in a hadith in the Musnad of Ahmad, to ‘Amr ibn al-‘As: “How good is righteous wealth for a righteous man.” Wealth is neither good nor bad in itself. Qarun’s fault was not that he was rich but that he put all the credit on himself: “I was only given it because of knowledge I have.”

facts: "Indeed, We have tried them as We tried the companions of the garden"
To harvest at dawn, leaving nothing for the poor
"Glory to our Lord; indeed, we were wrongdoers"

t: The story was told to Quraysh as a warning, since Allah had given them prosperity as a test: "Indeed, We have tried them as We tried the companions of the garden, when they swore to harvest it in the early morning, and were not making exception." (68:17–18) "Making exception" means saying "if Allah wills." They were so sure of their plan that they did not acknowledge Allah’s will.

"So there came upon it a visitation from your Lord while they were asleep, and it became as though it had been reaped." (68:19–20) In the morning they called each other: "Go early to your crop if you would harvest." They set out, speaking in whispers: "No poor person will enter it today upon you." And they went early, determined, able. But when they saw it, they said: "Indeed, we are lost." Then they said: "Rather, we have been deprived." (68:21–27)

Then "the most moderate of them said: Did I not say to you, Why do you not exalt [Allah]?" They said: "Exalted is our Lord! Indeed, we were wrongdoers." They turned to blaming one another. "They said: O woe to us! Indeed, we were transgressors. Perhaps our Lord will substitute for us one better than it. Indeed, we are toward our Lord desirous." (68:28–32) The Qur’an concludes: "Such is the punishment [of this world]. And the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew." (68:33)

Two sins: the greed that denies the poor a share of what Allah gave, and the arrogance of planning without mention of His will. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever says, insha’allah, when he swears, will not be in breach." Allah directed in Surah al-Kahf: "And never say of anything, Indeed, I will do that tomorrow, except [with the addition], If Allah wills." (18:23–24)

The Qur’an says that the owners agreed that “no poor person should enter it upon you today.” (68:24) It seems that the garden’s owner, their father, used to give from the harvest to the poor, and that his sons decided to stop the practice. The Qur’an does not say that they intended to steal or do any great evil, but that they would deny a right to the poor. That was enough for the calamity.

The right is also stated elsewhere. “And give its due on the day of its harvest, and do not be excessive.” (6:141) The commentators explain that the “due” is the charity from the crop, which the Prophet ﷺ fixed as a tenth of what is watered by rain and a twentieth of what is irrigated. The story of the garden is a picture of what happens to a harvest that was gathered without giving it.

facts: The Year of the Elephant, c. 570 CE, the year the Prophet ﷺ was born
Abraha, governor of Yemen under the Kingdom of Aksum
Birds with stones of baked clay (105:3–4)

t: Abraha built a magnificent cathedral in Sana’a, intending to divert the Arab pilgrimage from Makkah. The Sira tells that an Arab man defiled it in anger. Abraha swore to destroy the Kaaba and marched north with a large army and several elephants, among them a big one named Mahmud. Several Arab tribes tried to resist and were defeated.

At the outskirts of Makkah, Abraha’s men seized two hundred camels belonging to ‘Abd al-Muttalib, the leader of Quraysh. He went to speak to Abraha, who was impressed by his appearance and asked what he wanted. He said: "I want my two hundred camels." Abraha said: "I was impressed by you when I saw you, and now I regret it. You speak to me about two hundred camels and say nothing about the House, which is your religion and your fathers’ religion, which I have come to destroy?" ‘Abd al-Muttalib said: "I am the owner of the camels, and the House has an Owner who will protect it." The Quraysh withdrew into the hills and prayed at the Kaaba.

When Abraha’s army was ordered to advance, the elephant knelt, and would not go toward the Kaaba, though it went when turned in other directions (as the Sira tells). Then, "He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of hard clay, and made them like eaten straw." (105:3–5) The Sira adds that Abraha was struck by a disease that made his body fall apart, and that he died soon after reaching Yemen.

Surah al-Fil begins: "Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?" The Prophet ﷺ’s generation could remember it. The Arabs counted time from this year, and the story shows how Allah protected the House before it had a prophet to defend it.

The Prophet ﷺ himself referred to the Year of the Elephant at a critical moment. In 6 AH, as he led the Muslims towards Makkah for ‘Umrah, his camel, al-Qaswa’, knelt down on the road near Hudaybiyyah and would not get up. The people said: “Al-Qaswa’ has become stubborn!” The Prophet ﷺ said, as al-Miswar ibn Makhramah reports in Sahih al-Bukhari: “Al-Qaswa’ has not become stubborn. It is not her nature. She was held back by the One who held back the elephant from Makkah.”

He then said: “By the One in whose hand is my soul, they will not ask me today for any plan that honours the sanctity of Allah, but I will agree to it.” This led to the treaty of Hudaybiyyah. The Prophet ﷺ saw in the halting of the camel the same hand that had stopped Abraha’s elephant, and he took it as a sign that the way to Makkah was not to be forced but opened by agreement. It shows how the Qur’anic story lived in his thinking, as an example of Allah’s protection of His House.

In the order of the Qur’an, Surah al-Fil is followed by Surah Quraysh: “For the accustomed security of Quraysh, their accustomed security in the caravan of winter and summer, let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear.” (106:1–4) Many early scholars, including those who copied the Qur’an, saw the two as closely related, and some early copies are reported to have run them together.

The meaning is that the safety of Quraysh as guardians of the Ka‘bah, which allowed them to trade in safety, was Allah’s gift, and that the way to show thanks was to worship the Lord of the House. The story of the elephants is therefore not told only as a miracle. It is told so that the people it was shown to would know whom to thank.

facts: A king, his sorcerer, a boy, a monk
"Be patient, mother, for you are on the truth"

s.h: The sorcerer, the boy and the monk
t: Suhayb reports that the Prophet ﷺ said: There was a king, and he had a sorcerer. When the sorcerer grew old, he asked the king to send him a boy to teach. The boy, on his way, would pass a monk, and sit and listen to him, and he liked what he heard. When he went to the sorcerer, he was beaten for being late, and when he went home, he was beaten for being late. He complained to the monk, who said: "When you fear the sorcerer, say, The people of my house held me up; and when you fear your family, say, The sorcerer held me up."

One day a huge animal blocked the road. The boy said: "Today I will know whether the sorcerer or the monk is better." He took a stone and said, "O Allah, if the way of the monk is more beloved to You than that of the sorcerer, kill this animal so that people may pass," and he threw it and killed it. The people passed. He told the monk, who said: "My son, today you are better than me; you have reached what I see. You will be tested; if you are, do not tell on me."

The boy healed the blind and the lepers, and cured people of illnesses. A blind courtier of the king, hearing of him, brought a large gift and asked to be healed. The boy said: "I do not heal anyone. Allah heals. If you believe in Allah, I will pray and He will heal you." The courtier believed and was healed. Then he sat before the king as he used to, and the king asked: "Who restored your sight?" "My Lord." "Do you have a lord other than me?" "My Lord and your Lord is Allah." The king tortured him until he told of the boy, then tortured the boy until he told of the monk. The king ordered the monk and the courtier to renounce their religion. They refused, and he had them sawn in two.

The king sent men to take the boy up a mountain and throw him from the top if he did not leave his faith. The boy prayed: "O Allah, save me from them as You wish," and the mountain shook, and they fell, and the boy walked back to the king. Then a boat sent to drown him in the middle of the sea. He prayed the same, and it capsized, and all drowned; he walked back to the king. The boy said: "You will not be able to kill me until you do as I command." The king asked: "What?" He said: "Gather the people in a single place, tie me to a trunk, take an arrow from my quiver and say, In the name of Allah, the Lord of the boy; then shoot me. If you do that, you will be able to kill me."

The king did, and placed the arrow in his bow, saying "In the name of Allah, the Lord of the boy." The arrow hit the boy’s temple. The boy put his hand to the wound and died. The people cried out: "We believe in the Lord of the boy!" three times.

The king’s courtiers said: "Do you see what you feared? By Allah, what you feared has come: the people have believed." So the king commanded for trenches to be dug at the entrances of the roads, and fires lit in them. He said: "Whoever does not return from his religion, throw him in it." They did, until a woman came with her baby, and she hesitated to fall in. The baby said: "O mother, be patient, for you are on the truth." (Sahih Muslim)

Surah al-Buruj says: "Destroyed were the companions of the trench, [containing] the fire full of fuel, when they were sitting near it and they, to what they were doing against the believers, were witnesses. And they resented them not except because they believed in Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy." (85:4–8) Then it promises: "Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds will have gardens beneath which rivers flow. That is the great success." (85:11)

facts: A believing man of Fir’awn’s household who hid his faith
"I entrust my affair to Allah. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of [His] servants"
Why the surah is called Ghafir

t: When Fir’awn said, "Let me kill Musa and let him call upon his Lord. Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption in the land," (40:26) a believer from among his own people, "who concealed his faith," spoke up: "Do you kill a man [merely] because he says, My Lord is Allah, while he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord? And if he should be lying, then upon him is [the consequence of] his lie; but if he should be truthful, there will strike you some of what he promises you. Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar." (40:28)

He used reason and he used history. First: "O my people, you have today [high] position in the land, [but] who would aid us against the punishment of Allah if it came to us?" Fir’awn answered: "I do not show you except what I see, and I do not guide you except to the way of right conduct." The man warned: "O my people, indeed I fear for you [a fate] like the day of the companions [of earlier prophets], like the custom of the people of Nuh and ‘Ad and Thamud and those after them." (40:29–31) Then of the Day of Resurrection, and Yusuf, who had come before with clear proofs, and they did not believe him until he died. (40:32–34)

He spoke to their conscience: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the way of right conduct. O my people, this worldly life is only [temporary] enjoyment, and indeed, the Hereafter is the home of [permanent] settlement." (40:38–39) And finally: "You will remember what I [now] say to you, and I entrust my affair to Allah. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of [His] servants." (40:44)

"So Allah protected him from the evils which they plotted, and there enveloped the people of Fir’awn the worst of punishment." (40:45) The Qur’an describes how they are brought before the Fire morning and evening in their graves, and that on the Day when the Hour is established, "Make the people of Fir’awn enter the severest punishment." (40:46) The believer is nameless in the Qur’an. Commentators give names, but they are not part of the revelation. What we have of him is a voice: courageous, rational, kind.

facts: A town the Qur’an does not name; commentators differ
Two, then a third to support them
A man from the farthest part of the city
Said on his entry to Paradise

t: "And present to them an example: [the story of] the people of the town, when the messengers came to it. When We sent to them two but they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third, and they said, Indeed, we are messengers to you." The people answered: "You are only human beings like ourselves, and the Most Merciful has not sent down anything. You are only telling lies." The messengers said: "Our Lord knows that we are messengers to you, and we are only responsible for clear notification." They said: "Indeed, we consider you a bad omen. If you do not cease, we will surely stone you, and there will surely touch you from us a painful punishment." They said: "Your omen is with yourselves. Is it because you were reminded? Rather, you are a transgressing people." (36:13–19)

"And there came from the farthest end of the city a man, running. He said: O my people, follow the messengers. Follow those who do not ask you for payment, and they are [rightly] guided. And why should I not worship He who created me and to whom you will be returned? Should I take other than Him as gods when, if the Most Merciful intends for me some adversity, their intercession will not avail me at all, nor can they save me? Indeed, I would then be in manifest error. Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me." (36:20–25)

The Qur’an does not describe how they killed him, only that "It was said, Enter Paradise." He said: "If only my people could know of how my Lord has forgiven me and placed me among the honoured." (36:26–27) Commentators note that even after what they did to him, his first thought was to wish them well.

Allah did not send an army from the heaven against them: "There was not but one shout, and immediately they were extinguished." (36:29) And: "How regrettable for the servants. There did not come to them any messenger except that they used to ridicule him." (36:30) The story ends in a few lines, because the lesson was in the man’s words and his unexpected generosity of heart.

facts: The elders of Bani Isra’il, from their prophet
A river: whoever drinks is not with me

t: The elders of Bani Isra’il, remembering their losses, asked their prophet: "Send to us a king, and we will fight in the way of Allah." The prophet said: "Might it be that if fighting was prescribed for you, you would not fight?" They said: "And why should we not fight in the cause of Allah when we have been driven out from our homes and from our children?" But when fighting was written upon them, they turned away, except for a few (2:246).

Their prophet said: "Indeed, Allah has sent to you Talut as a king." They said: "How can he have kingship over us while we are more worthy of kingship than he and he has not been given any measure of wealth?" He said: "Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and has increased him abundantly in knowledge and stature." The sign of his kingship was that the Ark would come to them, "in which is tranquillity from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun had left, carried by the angels" (2:247–248).

When Talut went out with the soldiers he said: "Indeed, Allah will be testing you with a river. So whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is indeed of me, except one who takes [from it] in the hand." They drank from it, except a few. When he and those who believed crossed it, they said: "There is no power for us today against Jalut and his soldiers." But those who were certain that they would meet Allah said: "How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of Allah. And Allah is with the steadfast." (2:249)

They prayed as they met the enemy: "Our Lord, pour upon us patience and plant firmly our feet and give us victory over the disbelieving people." (2:250) They defeated them by Allah’s permission, and Dawud killed Jalut. Allah gave him kingship and wisdom (2:251).

The story is about three tests: a test of obedience to a leader who is not rich, a test of discipline at the river, and a test of faith before an overwhelming force. And the Qur’an adds a principle for history: "If Allah had not checked the people, some by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted." (2:251)

facts: One rich and arrogant, one poor and a believer
"I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in numbers"
"Why did you not say, Ma sha’ Allah, la quwwata illa billah?"
The gardens ruined; he wrung his hands

t: "And present to them an example of two men: to one of them We granted two gardens of grapevines and bordered them with palm trees and placed between them [fields of] crops. Each of the two gardens produced its fruit and did not fall short of it in anything. And We caused to burst forth within them a river." (18:32–33) He said to his companion as they talked: "I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in manpower." (18:34)

He entered his garden, "while he was unjust to himself," and said: "I do not think that this will perish, ever. And I do not think the Hour will occur. And even if I should be brought back to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a return." (18:35–36) His companion told him: "Have you disbelieved in He who created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then proportioned you [as] a man? But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I do not associate with my Lord anyone." (18:37–38)

"And why did you, when you entered your garden, not say, What Allah willed [has occurred]; there is no power except in Allah? Although you see me less than you in wealth and children, it may be that my Lord will give me [something] better than your garden and will send upon it a calamity from the sky, and it will become a smooth, dusty ground." (18:39–40)

"And his fruits were encompassed [by ruin], and he began to turn his hands about [in dismay] over what he had spent on it, while it was bare on its trellises, and said: Oh, I wish that I had not associated with my Lord anyone." (18:42) There was no company to help him other than Allah. "There the authority is [completely] for Allah, the Truth. He is best in reward and best in outcome." (18:43–44)

The practical lesson became a saying of the Muslims: when you see something you like, say "Ma sha’ Allah, la quwwata illa billah." The Prophet ﷺ taught that "la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah" is a treasure from the treasures of Paradise (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

facts: Khadijah bint Khuwaylid ibn Asad of Quraysh
About 595 CE; she was the Prophet’s first wife
Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum, Fatimah, al-Qasim and ‘Abdullah
In the 10th year of prophethood, about three years before the Hijrah
"The best of the women of her time" (Sahih al-Bukhari)

s.h: A woman of business and character
t: Khadijah was known in Makkah as al-Tahirah, the pure. She had been widowed twice and ran a large trading business, hiring men to carry her goods. When she heard of the honesty of Muhammad ibn ‘Abdullah, she asked him to trade for her, and offered him more than she normally paid. On his return, her servant Maysarah told her what he had observed: his integrity, his courtesy and the way he dealt with people. She then proposed marriage through a friend. It was a marriage in which she, a woman of status, took the initiative, and it lasted twenty-five years.

After the first revelation, the Prophet ﷺ came home trembling. Her response, preserved in Sahih al-Bukhari, was not panic but reasoning from his character: "By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You maintain family ties, bear the burdens of the weak, give to those who have nothing, honour guests and help in cases of hardship." She believed before anyone else, and took him to Waraqah. For the next ten years, she shared in the opposition, the boycott in the valley of Abu Talib and the loss of her wealth, which she placed at his disposal.

‘A’ishah, who married him after Khadijah’s death, said: "I was never jealous of any of the wives of the Prophet as I was of Khadijah, though I never saw her, because of how much he mentioned her. Whenever he slaughtered a sheep he would say: Send some to the friends of Khadijah." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). Abu Hurayrah narrates that Jibril came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, here is Khadijah, with a vessel containing food and drink. When she comes, convey to her the greetings of her Lord, and my greetings, and give her glad tidings of a house in Paradise of pearl, in which is no noise and no toil." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

facts: ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Quhafah, of the clan of Taym
Al-Siddiq (the one who affirms the truth)
11–13 AH (632–634 CE), about two years and three months
In the cave of Thawr and at every major event

t: He was a wealthy, trusted and well-liked merchant of Makkah. When the Prophet ﷺ told him of the revelation, he accepted at once. The Prophet ﷺ said later: "I did not invite anyone to Islam except that he hesitated, was reluctant and thought, except Abu Bakr; he did not hesitate when I mentioned it to him." (as reported in the Sira). Through him, several of the great Companions accepted Islam, and he spent his wealth to free persecuted slaves: Bilal, ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah and others. A verse was revealed praising one "who gave and feared Allah and believed in the best" (92:5–7), which commentators connect to him.

s.h: In the cave and on the journey
t: In the Hijrah, the Prophet ﷺ chose Abu Bakr as his only companion on the road. In the cave of Thawr, he was afraid for the Prophet ﷺ and not for himself. The Qur’an names him by a phrase: "the second of two" (9:40). The Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no one who has been more generous to me in his company and his property than Abu Bakr. Had I taken a khalil other than my Lord, I would have taken Abu Bakr." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

‘Umar ibn al-Khattab reports that the Prophet ﷺ commanded charity at the time of Tabuk, and ‘Umar thought: "Today I will surpass Abu Bakr." He brought half his wealth. The Prophet ﷺ asked what he had left for his family; he said, "The same amount." Then Abu Bakr brought all he had. The Prophet ﷺ asked what he left for his family. He said: "Allah and His Messenger." ‘Umar said: "I will never compete with you in anything." (Sunan Abi Dawud and al-Tirmidhi)

At the Prophet’s ﷺ death, he steadied the people with the verse "Muhammad is not but a messenger" (3:144), and was chosen as the first caliph at the Saqifah of Banu Sa’idah. In his short rule he dispatched the army of Usamah that the Prophet ﷺ had prepared, put down the tribes that refused zakah and those who claimed prophethood, and ordered the collection of the Qur’an into a single volume after many reciters were killed at the Battle of Yamamah (Sahih al-Bukhari, Zayd ibn Thabit). In his first speech, he said: "Obey me as long as I obey Allah and His Messenger. If I disobey, you owe me no obedience."

facts: ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab, of the clan of ‘Adi
Al-Faruq (the one who distinguishes truth from falsehood)
13–23 AH (634–644 CE), about ten and a half years
Dhul-Hijjah, 23 AH, after being stabbed while leading Fajr prayer

t: The Sira tells of ‘Umar setting out with his sword to find the Prophet ﷺ. A man on the road, Nu’aym ibn ‘Abdullah, told him to put his own house in order, because his sister Fatimah and her husband Sa’id had accepted Islam. He went there and heard recitation, and struck his brother-in-law and hit his sister so that she bled. She said: "Do what you will, we have become Muslim." Seeing the blood, he felt ashamed and asked to see what they were reading. She told him to wash first. He read the opening of Surah Ta-Ha: "We have not sent down to you the Qur’an that you be distressed, but only as a reminder for those who fear [Allah]" and said: "How beautiful and noble is this speech." He went to the house of al-Arqam and declared his Islam. (As reported in the Sira.)
‘Abdullah ibn Mas’ud said: "We have been mighty since ‘Umar became Muslim." (Sahih al-Bukhari) Before him, the Muslims prayed secretly; after, they prayed at the Kaaba.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "If there were a prophet after me, he would be ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab." (Sunan al-Tirmidhi). He also said: "Satan does not meet ‘Umar on a path but he takes another path." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). Many verses were revealed in agreement with his view, including the Station of Ibrahim, the hijab and the prisoners of Badr. Yet he was also gently corrected: at Hudaybiyyah he questioned the terms of the treaty, and when the Prophet ﷺ died he at first could not bring himself to believe it.

During his time as caliph, Muslim rule reached Syria, Egypt, Iraq and Persia. He established the Hijri calendar, the diwan (a register that paid stipends from the treasury), and courts. His justice is remembered in stories: he patrolled Madinah at night; hearing a mother pretend to cook stones to quiet her hungry children, he carried a sack of flour on his own back to her house (as reported by early historians). He is reported to have said: "If a mule were to stumble in Iraq, I fear that Allah would ask me why I did not pave the road for it." He was stabbed by Abu Lu’lu’ah, a Persian slave, while leading the Fajr prayer, and he died three days later, asking to be buried beside the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr (Sahih al-Bukhari).

facts: Makkah, to an Abyssinian mother (Hamamah); a slave of Umayyah ibn Khalaf
The Prophet ﷺ heard his footsteps in Paradise (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

t: Bilal believed early. His master Umayyah ibn Khalaf took him out in the heat of the day, laid him on the burning sand, placed a huge rock on his chest and said: "You will stay here until you die or deny Muhammad and worship al-Lat and al-‘Uzza." He kept repeating: "Ahad, ahad" (One, One). Abu Bakr passed, and said to Umayyah: "Do you not fear Allah for this poor man? How long?" Umayyah said: "You corrupted him; save him." Abu Bakr said he would, and bought him with a stronger slave and freed him (as reported in the Sira). Years later at Badr, Bilal saw Umayyah among the captives and cried out, and the Muslims killed him.

In Madinah, when the adhan was introduced, the Prophet ﷺ told ‘Abdullah ibn Zayd to teach it to Bilal, "for he has a more beautiful voice than you" (Sunan Abi Dawud). He called the Muslims to prayer for the rest of the Prophet’s life. On the day Makkah was conquered, he climbed on the Kaaba and gave the adhan. A once-enslaved Abyssinian man gave the call to prayer on the holiest building in Islam, a point not lost on the Makkans who had tortured him.

The Prophet ﷺ said to Bilal at Fajr: "O Bilal, tell me of the best deed you have done in Islam, for I heard the sound of your footsteps in front of me in Paradise." Bilal said: "I have not done anything better, except that whenever I perform wudu at any time of day or night, I pray with that purity what Allah wills me to pray." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

After the Prophet ﷺ died, Bilal found it too painful to call the adhan in Madinah and went to Syria. The Sira tells that once he came back, and the Prophet’s ﷺ grandsons al-Hasan and al-Husayn asked him to give the adhan once more, and when he did, Madinah wept as it had when the Prophet ﷺ was alive.

facts: ‘Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet’s cousin

s.h: A child in the Prophet’s house
t: When Makkah suffered a famine, the Prophet ﷺ took ‘Ali, then a small boy, into his own household to relieve Abu Talib, who had many children. He grew up beside the Prophet ﷺ and accepted Islam at about ten. He was given the most dangerous job on the night of the Hijrah, to lie in the Prophet’s ﷺ bed, covered in his cloak, while the men of Quraysh watched. Then he stayed behind for three days to return the trusts people had left with the Prophet ﷺ, and followed on foot to Madinah.

At Khaybar the Muslims were struggling to take the fort. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Tomorrow I will give the banner to a man through whom Allah will grant victory, who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love." The Companions spent the night wondering who it would be. In the morning, he asked: "Where is ‘Ali?" They said he had a sore eye. The Prophet ﷺ applied his saliva to it and ‘Ali was healed as if he had never had pain. He gave him the banner, and told him to invite them to Islam before fighting, saying: "By Allah, if Allah guides one man through you, it is better for you than red camels." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

He was among the foremost jurists and judges of the Companions; It is reported that ‘Umar used to say, "May Allah not let me live in a predicament where ‘Ali is not present to solve it." He lived simply, even when he was caliph. As the fourth caliph he ruled in the most difficult time, when the community was divided after the killing of ‘Uthman. He was killed by Ibn Muljam, a Kharijite, while going to the Fajr prayer in Kufah, in Ramadan 40 AH.
The Prophet ﷺ said to him on the way to Tabuk: "Are you not content to be to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there is no prophet after me?" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

facts: Dhu al-Nurayn (possessor of two lights), for marrying two daughters of the Prophet
Generosity, modesty, and the standard copy of the Qur’an
In his house in Madinah, in 35 AH

t: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Should I not be shy of a man of whom the angels are shy?" (Sahih Muslim). ‘Uthman had given most of his time and wealth to Islam: he emigrated twice, to Abyssinia and Madinah. When the Muslims in Madinah lacked good water, the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever bought the well of Rumah would have Paradise. ‘Uthman bought it and made it available to everyone (Sunan al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa’i). At Tabuk he provided hundreds of camels with saddles and blankets and a thousand dinars, which he poured into the Prophet’s ﷺ lap, and the Prophet ﷺ said, "Nothing ‘Uthman does after today will harm him." (Sunan al-Tirmidhi)

During the conquest of Armenia and Azerbaijan, Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman saw Muslims from different regions disputing over recitation. He told ‘Uthman: "Save this nation before they differ about the Book as the Jews and Christians did." ‘Uthman asked Hafsah for the volume that had been compiled in Abu Bakr’s time, and appointed Zayd ibn Thabit, ‘Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, Sa’id ibn al-‘As and ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith to copy it, in the dialect of Quraysh in case of disagreement. Copies were sent to the major cities, and the other copies were burnt (Sahih al-Bukhari). The Qur’an read today follows that standard text, the same in every land.

In his last years, discontent grew among some of the provinces, partly over appointments of his relatives. Rebels came to Madinah and besieged his house for weeks. He had the strength and the Companions’ offer to fight, but he refused to shed Muslim blood to defend himself, saying that the Prophet ﷺ had told him that Allah may clothe him in a garment and people would want him to remove it, and not to remove it (Sunan al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah). He was killed while reading the Qur’an. His death opened a period of civil strife.

facts: About 2,210 hadith (the number counted by the hadith scholars)
Among them ‘Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, al-Qasim and Masruq
Ramadan, 58 AH (678 CE), buried in al-Baqi’
In her room, in her arms

t: Abu Musa al-Ash’ari said: "Whenever we, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, had difficulty over a matter and asked ‘A’ishah, we found she had knowledge of it." (Sunan al-Tirmidhi). She explained verses, issued legal verdicts and corrected other Companions where she thought they had misunderstood. Her student ‘Urwah said he had never seen anyone more knowledgeable in fiqh, medicine or poetry. Many details of the Prophet’s ﷺ private life and worship are known only because she narrated them.

She told how he used to be "in the service of his family", helping with household chores, mending his shoes and sewing his clothes, and "when the call to prayer came he would go out" (Sahih al-Bukhari). When asked whom he loved most, he said "‘A’ishah." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). They raced each other once, and she won; later, when she was heavier, he won, and said, "This is for that." (Sunan Abi Dawud).

On the way back from the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq, ‘A’ishah was left behind when her camel was loaded without her, and was brought back by Safwan ibn al-Mu’attal. The hypocrites, led by ‘Abdullah ibn Ubayy, spread a rumour. For a month the Prophet ﷺ received no revelation about it, and she wept constantly. When he came to her and said she should repent if she had sinned, she said she would say what Yusuf’s father said: "So patience is most fitting." Then revelation came: ten verses of Surah al-Nur (24:11–20) declared her innocence. She said: "I did not think that Allah would send down a revelation that would be recited about me." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

facts: In 621 CE, as the first envoy of Islam

t: He grew up in a rich home, with fine perfume and costly clothes, and the Sira says that Makkah had no young man of his age who was better dressed. When he accepted Islam in secret, his mother, who adored him, found out, locked him up and withheld food and comfort. He escaped and emigrated to Abyssinia, and when he returned, he was thin and in worn clothes. The Prophet ﷺ saw him in a wrapped cloak with patches, and said to the Companions: "Look at him, whose heart Allah has illumined. I saw him with his parents who gave him the best food and drink; he left it for love of Allah and His Messenger." (as reported in the Sira)

After the first pledge of ‘Aqabah, the Prophet ﷺ sent him to Yathrib. Staying with As’ad ibn Zurarah, he taught the Qur’an, led the prayer and visited homes. By the following hajj, he had so many Muslims with him that seventy-five of them made the second pledge. He was gentle and clear, not argumentative. He was the one who turned the leaders Sa’d ibn Mu’adh and Usayd ibn Hudayr, and with them most of the clans of Aws, to Islam.

He carried the banner of the Muslims at Badr and again at Uhud. When the Muslim line broke, he held the banner high and fought for the Prophet ﷺ until he was killed, in the reports, by Ibn Qami’ah, who thought he had killed the Prophet ﷺ since Mus’ab resembled him. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: "We emigrated with the Messenger of Allah seeking Allah’s face, and Allah owed us our reward. Among us were those who died without eating any of their reward, such as Mus’ab ibn ‘Umayr, who was killed at Uhud and did not leave anything but a striped cloak. When we covered his head with it, his feet were uncovered, and when we covered his feet, his head was uncovered. The Prophet ﷺ told us to cover his head and put some idhkhir grass over his feet." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

facts: About 615 CE, killed by Abu Jahl (as reported)

t: Yasir came from Yemen and settled in Makkah under the protection of Abu Hudhayfah of Banu Makhzum, who married him to his slave Sumayyah. Their son ‘Ammar was among the earliest Muslims. Because they were not of a powerful clan, they were exposed. Quraysh took them out to the burning plain of Makkah each day to force them to renounce Islam.

The Prophet ﷺ passed by them while they were being tortured and said: "Be patient, O family of Yasir, for your meeting place is Paradise." (as reported in the Sira and by al-Hakim). Yasir died under torture. The biographies say Sumayyah was killed by Abu Jahl, who speared her when she would not renounce her faith, which made her the first martyr of Islam. ‘Ammar, under duress, said words he did not mean, then came to the Prophet ﷺ in tears. He asked, "How do you find your heart?" ‘Ammar said, "Content with faith." The Prophet ﷺ said: "If they do it again, then say it again." (as reported by al-Bayhaqi, in connection with 16:106)

After Badr, the Prophet ﷺ told ‘Ammar: "Allah has judged your case against the killer of your mother." She is remembered as one of the great examples of steadfastness: a woman, enslaved, with no tribe to protect her, who stayed firm against one of the most powerful men in Makkah.

facts: Persia, in a Zoroastrian family (said to be from Isfahan or Ramhurmuz)
Persia → Syria → Mosul → Nisibis → Ammuriyah → Madinah

t: Salman told his own story to ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Abbas, which is preserved in Musnad Ahmad. As a boy, he was devoted to the fire temple. Passing a church one day, he saw Christians praying, and found it better than his religion, so he asked where it came from and learned that it was in Syria. He ran away, travelled to a bishop, and served him. When the bishop died, he found out that he had been hoarding charity money and told the people. He moved to another teacher, and each in turn directed him to the next, until the last, dying at Ammuriyah, told him that a prophet would come in the land of Arabia, between two lava fields with palm trees, who accepted gifts but not charity, and had a seal of prophethood between his shoulders.

He travelled with a caravan of Arab traders who took him and sold him as a slave. He ended up in Madinah. When the Prophet ﷺ arrived, he brought food as charity; the Prophet ﷺ said to his companions to eat, but did not eat himself. The next day he brought a gift; the Prophet ﷺ ate it. Then he saw the seal between the shoulders, and kissed it and wept, and accepted Islam. The Prophet ﷺ helped him buy his freedom from his master, by planting three hundred palm trees and giving some gold the size of a hen’s egg.

At the Trench, he suggested digging a ditch around the vulnerable side, as Persian armies did. Both the Muhajirun and the Ansar said "Salman is one of us"; the Prophet ﷺ said: "Salman is from us, the people of the house." (reported by al-Hakim; the chain is weak, but the esteem in which the Companions held him is well attested). He took part in the conquest of Persia, and under ‘Umar was made governor of al-Mada’in, but kept to a wage of five thousand dirhams, which he gave away, living by weaving palm leaves. He is remembered for his advice that people should be moderate in worship.

facts: A shepherd for ‘Uqbah ibn Abi Mu’ayt
The great reciter, faqih of Kufah
Directly by the Prophet ﷺ: 70 surahs from his mouth
32 AH in Madinah, about 60 years old

t: He was a small, thin young man with slender legs. One day, the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr, tired and thirsty, asked him for milk. He said he was entrusted with the sheep and could not. The Prophet ﷺ asked for a young ewe that had never been milked, and stroked its udder, and milk flowed. After they drank, the Prophet ﷺ told the udder to return to its place, and it did. Ibn Mas’ud said: "Teach me from this speech." The Prophet ﷺ stroked his head and said: "You are a learned boy." (Musnad Ahmad)

The Companions in Makkah were too afraid to recite the Qur’an in public. They said: "By Allah, Quraysh have never heard the Qur’an openly. Who will make them hear it?" Ibn Mas’ud said: "I will." They said they feared for him. He went to the Kaaba at midday, stood at the Station and began Surah al-Rahman. They hit him in the face, and he kept reciting as far as he could. His face was swollen when he returned. He said: "The enemies of Allah were never lighter in my eyes than today. If you wish I will do the same tomorrow." They said: "Enough." (as reported in the Sira)

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever loves to recite the Qur’an as fresh as it was revealed, let him recite according to the recitation of Ibn Umm ‘Abd (Ibn Mas’ud)." (Musnad Ahmad and Ibn Majah). One day he said to him: "Recite to me." Ibn Mas’ud said: "Shall I recite to you when it was revealed to you?" He said: "I like to hear it from others."
