He recited Surah al-Nisa’, and when he reached "How then if We bring from every nation a witness and We bring you against these as a witness?" (4:41), the Prophet ﷺ said: "Enough for now." Ibn Mas’ud looked and the Prophet’s ﷺ eyes were flowing with tears. (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

facts: Al-Rumaysa’ (or al-Ghumaysa’) bint Milhan of Banu al-Najjar
Malik ibn al-Nadr, who refused Islam
Anas ibn Malik, the Prophet’s ﷺ servant
Carried a dagger and tended the wounded

t: Umm Sulaym accepted Islam in Madinah at the hands of Mus’ab. Her husband, Malik, was angry and left for Syria, where he died. Abu Talhah, a well-off man and a famed archer, proposed. She answered: "O Abu Talhah, do you not know that the god you worship was carved from the earth by the slave of such a tribe? Are you not ashamed to worship a tree?" He said nothing. When he proposed again, she said: "I will not marry anyone but you, but you are a disbeliever. If you become Muslim, that will be my dowry, and I will ask nothing else from you." He became Muslim and they married. Thabit said he had never heard of a dowry better than Umm Sulaym’s: Islam. (Sunan al-Nasa’i)

s.h: The night of her son’s death
t: A famous account in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim (Anas) tells that her son by Abu Talhah fell ill and died while Abu Talhah was out. She washed and shrouded him and laid him in a room and told the household not to tell him. When he came home, she gave him dinner and then, to the extent that a woman could, prepared herself for him. Later she said: "O Abu Talhah, if some people lent something to a family, and then asked for it back, would they be right to refuse?" He said no. She said: "Then be patient for your son." He was angry and said: "You left me until I was impure and then told me of my son?" In the morning he went to the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "May Allah bless you both for your night." She conceived and gave birth to ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Talhah, whose descendants were all reciters.

At Hunayn, she was seen with a dagger tucked in her belt. Asked why, she said it was for any idolater who came near her. At Uhud, ‘A’ishah and Umm Sulaym were seen carrying water skins on their backs and pouring water into the mouths of the wounded (Sahih al-Bukhari). When her son Anas was ten, she brought him to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, he is your servant, pray for him." He prayed for his wealth and children and a long life, and Anas lived to over ninety with many children (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

facts: Anas ibn Malik and Abu Hurayrah
The Companions rushed to stop him
"Leave him, and pour a bucket of water over it"
You were sent to make things easy

t: Anas ibn Malik reports: "A Bedouin came and urinated in a corner of the mosque. The people shouted at him. The Prophet ﷺ said: Leave him alone. When he finished, the Prophet ﷺ asked for a bucket of water and had it poured over it." (Sahih al-Bukhari). Abu Hurayrah adds the Prophet’s ﷺ words: "You were sent to make things easy, and you were not sent to make things difficult." (Sahih al-Bukhari)

In Sahih Muslim (Anas), the Prophet ﷺ called the man and said: "These mosques are not suitable for any of this urine or filth. They are only for the remembrance of Allah, prayer and the recitation of the Qur’an," or words to that effect. The man, a new Muslim, was removed from a desert life where it was normal to relieve himself anywhere. The Companions’ reaction was natural, yet it would have interrupted him mid-stream and spread impurity more widely, and humiliated a newcomer to Islam.

s.h: Why the Prophet acted this way
t: Scholars, noting the wisdom of the method, say that stopping him would have caused a greater harm (spreading the impurity over his clothes and more of the mosque), and that gentle education is a more lasting cure than shouting. It is a model of how to correct an ignorant person: let the harm be contained, remove it, and then explain.

facts: Al-Aqra’ ibn Habis al-Tamimi, a chief
"Whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy"
The Prophet ﷺ carried his granddaughter Umamah while praying

t: The Prophet ﷺ kissed al-Hasan ibn ‘Ali, and al-Aqra’ ibn Habis al-Tamimi was sitting with him. Al-Aqra’ said: "I have ten children and I have never kissed any one of them." The Prophet ﷺ looked at him and said: "Whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). In another narration: "What can I do if Allah has removed mercy from your heart?"

He used to pray carrying his granddaughter Umamah bint Zaynab on his shoulder: when he bowed he placed her down, and when he stood he lifted her (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). When he was giving a sermon and al-Hasan and al-Husayn came stumbling in red shirts, he came down from the pulpit, picked them up and said: "Allah spoke the truth: Your wealth and your children are but a trial. I saw these two stumbling and could not stop myself." (Sunan Abi Dawud and al-Tirmidhi). When his grandson was dying, his eyes filled with tears, and when asked, he said: "This is mercy that Allah has placed in the hearts of whom He wishes among His servants." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

Another report shows how far the Prophet’s tenderness went. Shaddad ibn al-Had reports in the Sunan of an-Nasa’i and the Musnad of Ahmad that the Prophet ﷺ came out to lead one of the evening prayers, carrying either al-Hasan or al-Husayn. He put the child down, said the takbir, and began the prayer. In the course of it, he prostrated, and made the prostration very long.

Shaddad says: “I raised my head, and there was the child on the back of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he was in prostration. So I went back to my prostration.” When the prayer was over, the people said: “O Messenger of Allah, you made a prostration in the middle of the prayer so long that we thought that something had happened, or that you were receiving a revelation.” He said: “None of that. But my son made me his mount, and I did not want to hurry him until he had finished.”

facts: She did not recognise him and said "Leave me, you have not suffered what I have"

t: The Prophet ﷺ passed by a woman who was weeping by a grave. He said to her: "Fear Allah and be patient." She said: "Go away; you have not suffered what I have suffered." She did not know him. Someone told her, "That was the Prophet ﷺ." She was overcome with remorse and came to his door, and found no guards at it. She said: "I did not recognise you." He said: "Patience is only at the first shock." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

Scholars have noted three things. First, he gave advice to a stranger in grief, and did not hold her sharp reply against her. Second, "there were no guards at his door": the leader of the Muslims was accessible to any citizen. Third, he did not ask her to stop crying; his advice was about her words and her reaction, since tears are natural. He wept himself at the death of his son Ibrahim, and said: "The eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, but we say nothing except what pleases our Lord." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

facts: Jabir ibn ‘Abdullah and Sahl ibn Hunayf
Scholars differ on whether standing is still recommended

t: A funeral passed in front of the Prophet ﷺ and he stood. It was said to him, "It is the funeral of a Jew." He said: "Is it not a soul?" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). In another report, Sahl ibn Hunayf and Qays ibn Sa’d were sitting in Qadisiyyah when a funeral passed; they stood. They were told it was a funeral of one of the people of the land, a non-Muslim. They said that a funeral passed in front of the Prophet ﷺ and he stood, and when told that it was a Jew, he said: "Is it not a soul?" (Sahih al-Bukhari)

Whatever the person’s faith, the sight of death is a sign of what awaits every living thing: "Is it not a soul?" Some scholars take it as an act of respect for the dead, others as a reminder of the awe of death. It shows that the Muslim community, in Madinah, lived beside people of other faiths, and the Prophet ﷺ honoured their humanity.

The Companions understood the Prophet’s act as a rule, not just a gesture. Ibn Abi Layla reports in Sahih al-Bukhari that Sahl ibn Hunayf and Qays ibn Sa‘d were sitting in Qadisiyyah, in Iraq, when a funeral procession passed. They stood up. It was said to them: “It is the funeral of one of the people of the land,” meaning a non-Muslim under Muslim protection. They said that a funeral had once passed before the Prophet ﷺ and he stood. It was said to him: “It is a Jew.” He said: “Is it not a soul?”

The scholars say that standing is a respect for death and for what it reminds us of. The Prophet’s remark, “Is it not a soul?”, shows the reason behind it. A person who has died is a human being whose life belonged to Allah, and a believer who sees a funeral is reminded that his own time will come. The Companions carried the practice into new lands, among peoples of different faiths, at a time when they were the rulers.

facts: Against the Huraqah clan of Juhaynah
Said "La ilaha illa Allah" as the sword was raised
"Did you kill him after he said La ilaha illa Allah?"
The Prophet’s ﷺ beloved, whom he later made commander

t: Usamah says: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent us in a raid against al-Huraqah of Juhaynah. We attacked them in the morning and defeated them. I and an Ansari man caught up with one of them. When we overpowered him, he said La ilaha illa Allah. The Ansari man held back, but I stabbed him with my spear and killed him. When we returned, the news reached the Prophet ﷺ, who said: O Usamah, did you kill him after he said La ilaha illa Allah? I said: O Messenger of Allah, he said it only to save himself. He said: Did you kill him after he said La ilaha illa Allah? He kept repeating it until I wished I had not accepted Islam before that day." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)
In another narration: "Did you split open his heart so that you would know whether he said it from his heart or not?" (Sahih Muslim)

Faith is judged by what people say and do, and the heart is known to Allah. A person who says the shahadah is protected. Usamah’s grief, which he carried for the rest of his life, shows how serious it was. The Prophet ﷺ later appointed him commander over an army, in his last illness, at about eighteen.

facts: Ten years, from about the age of ten
He never struck anything with his hand except in the way of Allah
"You are of a great moral character" (68:4)

t: Anas said: "I served the Prophet ﷺ for ten years. By Allah, he never said ‘uff’ to me, and he never said to me about something I did, Why did you do it? or about something I did not do, Why did you not do it?" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). In another report, he says: "The Prophet ﷺ had the best character of all people. One day he sent me on an errand. I said, By Allah, I will not go, though in my heart I intended to do as the Prophet of Allah commanded. I went out until I passed some boys playing in the market. The Prophet ﷺ seized me from behind by the neck, and I looked at him, laughing. He said: O Unays, did you go where I commanded you? I said: Yes, O Messenger of Allah, I am going." (Sahih Muslim)

‘A’ishah said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ never struck anything with his hand, neither a woman nor a servant, except when fighting in the way of Allah. And he never took revenge for anything done to him, unless the limits of Allah were violated, in which case he would take revenge for the sake of Allah." (Sahih Muslim). Asked about his character, she said: "His character was the Qur’an." (Sahih Muslim)

The example shows that leadership does not require harshness. The servant was a child. The Prophet ﷺ corrected him with laughter, not with a rebuke. When Anas was an old man, he remembered the Prophet ﷺ saying: "Make things easy and do not make them difficult; give glad tidings and do not make people averse." (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

facts: About sixty riders of Najran, among them their bishop and leaders
In the Prophet’s mosque (as reported in the Sira)
A treaty of protection with Najran

t: In the ninth or tenth year, a delegation from the Christian city of Najran in Yemen, around sixty men including the bishop Abu Haritha and the leaders al-‘Aqib and al-Sayyid, travelled to Madinah. They came in fine robes and silk, and the Prophet ﷺ at first did not answer their greeting. When they changed to simple clothes, he did. When the time of their prayer came, the Sira reports that they started to pray in the mosque, and the Companions went to stop them; the Prophet ﷺ said: "Leave them." They prayed facing east.

They debated the nature of ‘Isa. The Prophet ﷺ recited Surah Al ‘Imran, including: "Indeed, the example of ‘Isa to Allah is like that of Adam. He created Him from dust; then He said to him, Be, and he was." (3:59) And he invited them: "Say: O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you: that we will not worship except Allah and not associate anything with Him and not take one another as lords instead of Allah." (3:64)

When the debate did not end, the verse of mubahalah was revealed (3:61), inviting each side to call down Allah’s curse upon the liars. The Najran delegation, after consulting each other, said, "You know he is a prophet. We will not do so" and asked for a treaty. The Prophet ﷺ agreed to protect their lives, churches and property in return for a tax, and sent with them Abu ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, "the trustworthy one of this nation".

facts: The Prophet ﷺ, as reported by Abu Hurayrah
Ibrahim, his wife Sarah, a tyrant king and the servant Hajar
A town ruled by a tyrant on Ibrahim’s travels, which some commentators place in Egypt

t: The Prophet ﷺ said that Ibrahim travelled with Sarah and came to a town where there was a tyrant, one of the kings who ruled by force. The people of that town told the king that a man had arrived with a woman of great beauty. Ibrahim understood at once what that meant. In a place where the ruler took what he liked and killed those who stood in his way, a husband was a danger to himself.

Ibrahim asked her to say that she was his sister. The hadith records what he told her: there was no believer on that land except the two of them, and so she was truly his sister in faith. That was the only reason he asked, and it was said to save both of them. Scholars explain that this was an allusion in which the meaning he intended was true, and not an ordinary lie. The Prophet ﷺ also said that Ibrahim did not speak a lie except three times, each for Allah’s sake, and he counted this among them.

Soldiers came for Sarah and took her to the king. Ibrahim did not follow in panic. He went to the place where he prayed and stood before Allah. He had done what he could, and what was left was in Allah’s hands.

Inside, the king reached out to take hold of her. The report says that his hand was seized at that moment and that he was struck down, so that he could not move his hand towards her. He cried out to her: “Pray to Allah for me, and I will not harm you.” Sarah prayed, and he was released. He tried again, and the same thing happened. He asked her again to pray, and again he swore to leave her alone. She prayed, and he was freed. The third time was the same.

s.h: “You did not bring me a human being”
t: Then the king called one of his guards and said: “You have not brought me a human being. You have brought me a devil.” He no longer wanted her anywhere near him. He sent her away, and, as if to make up for what he had tried, he gave her a gift, a servant named Hajar.

Sarah came back to Ibrahim, who was still standing in prayer. He turned slightly and asked with a gesture what had happened. She said: “Allah has driven back the plot of the unbeliever, and he gave me Hajar as a servant.” Abu Hurayrah, who reported the hadith, would end it by saying to the Arabs: “That is your mother, O sons of the water of the sky.” By “the water of the sky” he meant the Arabs, who lived by the rain, and by Hajar the mother of Isma‘il, from whom the Arabs of the north trace their line.

First, it shows how Allah looks after His servants when they are wronged. Sarah stood alone in front of a man with an army, and he was stopped by nothing he could see. Her only weapon was a prayer, and the hadith does not describe her as brave in a loud way. She was calm.

Second, the story answers a question many people ask about the three occasions on which Ibrahim is said to have spoken untruthfully. The scholars explain that these were allusions, called tawriyah, in which what is said has a true meaning that the hearer does not take. Saying “I am sick” meant sick of heart at the idolatry around him, and saying “their big idol did it” was an argument meant to make them think. Ibn Hajar and others say that the Prophet’s word “lie” here reflects how it might sound, and that it was a lie only in appearance. Third, from Hajar’s coming into Ibrahim’s household follows the story of Isma‘il and the building of the Ka‘bah, which the Qur’an tells at length.

facts: The Prophet ﷺ, in several narrations from different Companions
Someone from the earlier nations who had sinned against himself
To burn him, grind the remains, and scatter them on land and sea
Allah gathered him and forgave him because of his fear

t: In the narration of Abu Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said that a man had treated himself unjustly, and when death came he gave a strange instruction to his children. “When I die, burn me. Then grind me and scatter me in the wind and in the sea. By Allah, if my Lord gets hold of me, He will punish me with a punishment He has never given to anyone else.” In another narration he is described as a man who had never done any good.

His sons did as he asked. When he died they burned his body, crushed what remained, and on a day with a strong wind they scattered it into the air and the sea. As far as any person could tell, nothing of him was left in one place.

Then Allah commanded the land to give back what it had taken, and the sea to give back what it had taken. In the words of the hadith, the man was suddenly standing there, whole. Allah asked him: “What made you do what you did?”

He said: “Fear of You, my Lord.” In some narrations he adds: “And You know best.” And Allah forgave him. The conversation is short, and there is no argument in it. He did not claim to have done good, and he did not make excuses. He simply said that he had been afraid.

Scholars have discussed this hadith at length because the man’s plan seems to show that he doubted that Allah could bring him back. Ibn Taymiyyah, an-Nawawi and Ibn Hajar, among others, explain that he did not deny the resurrection, and that he is described as a believer who feared Allah. What he did not understand was the full extent of Allah’s power, and he was excused because of his ignorance on that point, joined to his sincere fear.

They also warn against the wrong lesson. The story does not say that anyone may be careless about what he believes. It says that Allah’s mercy meets even a person who has gone wrong, if the root of his heart is fear of Him. The Prophet ﷺ himself said, in another hadith, that Allah is more joyful at a servant’s repentance than a traveller who finds his lost camel. This is the same mercy seen from another side.

The Companions who heard the hadith would have felt both things at once. The man was weighed down by his fear, and that fear made him do something extreme, but it was also what saved him. The believer is taught to keep hope and fear together, like the two wings of a bird. If one is cut away, the bird falls.

It is also a reminder that no state of the body, however destroyed, is a problem for the One who created it the first time. The Qur’an says that He knows what the earth takes from the dead, and that with Him is a record that preserves. A man who burns to ash is no harder to gather than a man who was never made.

facts: The Prophet ﷺ, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
A man hears a voice in a cloud naming a farmer
A third as charity, a third for his family, a third back into the garden
Sahih Muslim, Book of Zuhd and Heart-softeners

s.h: The man, the cloud and the voice
t: The Prophet ﷺ said: “While a man was in an open land, he heard a voice in a cloud: ‘Water the garden of so-and-so.’ That cloud moved away, and it poured its water onto a stony black tract. There was a channel among the channels in that tract that took in all that water. The water flowed, and the man followed it.”

Nothing is told about who the man was, and that is deliberate: he could be anyone. What matters is that he happened to be there and that he heard something he was not expecting. Of all the places the cloud could have rained, it chose rough black ground, and from that ground a single channel carried the whole of the water in one direction. It is a small image of how provision is directed.

There at the end of the water stood a man in his garden, turning the flow with a spade. The traveller asked: “Servant of Allah, what is your name?” He gave a name, the very name that had been spoken in the cloud. Then he asked: “Why do you ask me my name?”

The traveller told him: “I heard a voice in the cloud whose water this is, saying ‘Water the garden of so-and-so’, and it was your name. What is it that you do with this garden?” The owner’s answer is what makes the story worth telling.

The farmer said: “Since you ask, I look at what comes out of it. I give a third of it in charity, my family and I eat a third, and I return a third to it.” The report in some wording says that he put it back into the land, into seed, labour or upkeep, so that the garden would keep producing.

This is a very ordinary kind of righteousness. He did not leave his work to make an unusual show of worship. He worked, he fed his household, he gave away, and he kept the thing running. Ibn Hajar and an-Nawawi both note that the hadith shows the virtue of earning honestly, spending on one’s family, and giving charity from what one has, all as one practice. Scholars also note that some read the account as one of the honours given to the righteous, an unusual sign, called a karamah, which comes from Allah as a gift and is neither claimed nor sought.

It is tempting to read this as only a story about charity, but there are at least three lessons in it. One is that provision is assigned by Allah, and the cloud knows the farmer’s name. Another is that the farmer did not leave work to wait for the sky, because he was still standing there with a spade, directing the water where it needed to go. The third is the pattern of his spending, which keeps three duties in balance: to Allah through giving, to the family through feeding them, and to the future through reinvestment.

The Qur’an uses a similar image: “The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a seed which grows seven ears; in every ear is a hundred grains.” The farmer lived this verse in a quiet way, and the cloud’s voice was Allah’s recognition of it.

facts: The Prophet ﷺ, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
The prophet Dawud, then his son Sulayman
A baby boy, one of two taken to the same quarrel
Qur’an 21:78–79, on Dawud and Sulayman and a case of judgement

t: The Prophet ﷺ said: “There were two women, each with her son. A wolf came and took the son of one of them. The one said to her companion: ‘It was your son that it took.’ The other said: ‘No, it was your son.’” With no witness to what had really happened, and each insisting, they went to Dawud.

Dawud was a prophet and a king in Israel, known for his justice. He judged between them and gave the surviving child to the elder woman. The reports do not tell us on what basis; scholars have suggested that he was ruling by what appeared to him, such as her possession of the child, or that she was the elder and had a stronger claim in the absence of proof. A judge must rule from what is in front of him.

The two women left the court and met Sulayman, Dawud’s son. He asked them what had been decided, and they told him. Then he said: “Bring me a knife, and I will cut the boy in two, and give half to each of you.”

The younger woman cried out: “Do not do it, may Allah have mercy on you! He is her son!” At that, Sulayman gave the child to the younger. She was the one who would sooner lose her child to someone else than see him harmed. The other had not spoken, or had accepted the idea of splitting him.

Abu Hurayrah added: “By Allah, I had never heard the word sikkin for a knife before that day. We only used to say mudyah.” It is a small and honest detail, and it shows how a Companion remembered the exact word the Prophet had used.

The Qur’an mentions Dawud and Sulayman when they judged a case concerning a field in which some people’s sheep had strayed at night. It then says: “We made Sulayman understand it, and to each We gave judgement and knowledge” (21:79). The verse does not blame Dawud. It says that Sulayman was given a more precise understanding, and that both were given right judgement and knowledge.

Scholars also use this hadith to discuss how a judge may use signs and circumstances, and not only formal proofs. Ibn al-Qayyim is among those who wrote about it in his book on judging, noting that the truth has marks which an alert judge can read. They also note that Sulayman did not intend to cut the child. It was a way of drawing out what was hidden, and he knew the real mother’s heart would not allow it.

facts: The Prophet ﷺ, after the Fajr prayer
A cow that spoke, and a wolf that spoke to a shepherd
“I believe in this, and so do Abu Bakr and ‘Umar”

t: Abu Hurayrah reports that the Prophet ﷺ prayed the morning prayer and then turned to the people. He said: “While a man was driving a cow, he rode on it and beat it. The cow said: ‘We were not created for this. We were only created for ploughing.’”

The people said: “Subhan Allah! A cow that speaks?” The Prophet ﷺ said: “I believe in this, and Abu Bakr and ‘Umar believe in it.” Abu Hurayrah adds that Abu Bakr and ‘Umar were not there. The Prophet ﷺ was so sure of their faith that he could answer for them. Scholars point to this as one of the clearest signs of the standing of these two men.

Then he said: “While a shepherd was with his sheep, a wolf attacked and carried off one of them. The shepherd ran after it and took the sheep back. The wolf said: ‘You have rescued it from me, but who will be its guardian on the day of the beasts of prey, when it will have no shepherd but me?’”
The people again exclaimed: “Subhan Allah! A wolf that speaks?” And he said once more: “I believe in this, I and Abu Bakr and ‘Umar.” Abu Hurayrah repeats that the two were not present.

Scholars have given two explanations for “the day of the beasts of prey.” One is that it refers to a time of trials, when people are left without protection and everyone preys on everyone else. Another reading is that it refers to a day on which the sheep would be left to the beasts because there was none to guard them. The meaning that most commentators accept is the first.

This report is sometimes treated as a mere curiosity, but the Prophet ﷺ told it to teach. The cow’s words show the purpose Allah gives to each creature, and that it is a wrong to use an animal for something it was not made for, such as riding a plough animal into exhaustion. The wolf’s words are a warning of a time when the weak will be abandoned to the strong.

The believer’s response is shown by the Prophet’s own: he did not ask how it was possible. The Qur’an records that on the Day of Resurrection, skins and hands and feet will speak, and that Sulayman understood the speech of birds and ants. If Allah gives speech to a creature, there is no difficulty for Him. What the hadith asks of us is the same ready acceptance.

facts: The Prophet ﷺ, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
‘Isa; the child in Jurayj’s story; and a nursing baby in this account
A mother, her baby, a rider, and a slave girl

t: The Prophet ﷺ said: “No one spoke in the cradle except three: ‘Isa, son of Maryam; the companion of Jurayj; and a baby who was at his mother’s breast.” The Qur’an tells how ‘Isa spoke from the cradle to his people when they accused Maryam: “Indeed I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet.”

The second is the infant in the account of Jurayj, a monk in Israel who was falsely accused of fathering a child. He touched the baby and asked: “Who is your father?” And the baby said: “My father is the shepherd.” That story is told in its own page. This page tells the third. Other reports mention further babies who spoke, such as the child of the woman in the story of the trench, and scholars explain the number three as those the Prophet ﷺ listed in this narration.

s.h: The rider and the slave girl
t: A woman was nursing her baby when a man passed by on a fine mount, dressed well and looking impressive. She said: “O Allah, make my son like this one.” The baby released the breast, looked towards him and said: “O Allah, do not make me like him.” Then he went back to nursing.

Abu Hurayrah said that it was as if he could see the Prophet ﷺ acting out how the baby sucked, putting his own finger in his mouth. Then a slave girl passed by, with people leading her along, striking her and saying: “You committed fornication, you stole.” She was saying: “Allah is enough for me, and He is the best protector.” The mother said: “O Allah, do not make my son like her.” And the baby left the breast and looked at the girl and said: “O Allah, make me like her.”

At that, the mother and the baby spoke to each other. She said: “Why did you say that?” He answered: “The rider was one of the tyrants. And this slave girl is being accused of fornication and theft, and she has done neither.” The baby had seen through both: the powerful man was unjust under his fine clothes, and the beaten girl was innocent under her chains.

The hadith does not say what became of the rider or the girl. It only gives the infant’s verdict, which is the only one that matters. Many scholars point to this as a lesson in not being impressed by outward things. Another reading draws out something about the mother’s duty to be careful of what she wishes for her child, since the appearance of power or ease can hide a bad end. The one who bears an unjust accusation patiently, and says “Allah is enough for me”, is on firmer ground than the one who has power and abuses it.

facts: The Prophet ﷺ, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
The prophet Musa, the angel of death, and Allah’s command
A year of life for each hair under his hand on the back of an ox
The Prophet ﷺ said it lies by the road near the red dune

t: The Prophet ﷺ said: “The angel of death was sent to Musa, peace be upon him. When he came to him, Musa struck him in the eye and put it out. The angel went back to his Lord and said: ‘You sent me to a servant of Yours who does not want to die.’”

The first question anyone asks is why Musa would strike an angel. Scholars have discussed it at length. The most common explanation, given by Ibn Khuzaymah and others and accepted by many, is that the angel came in the form of a man, with no announcement, and Musa had no knowledge of who he was. Musa, who was known for his strength and his quick defence of what was his, pushed away a stranger who had walked into his house and said he had come to take him. It was an act of self-defence by someone who did not know. Allah did not rebuke Musa, and He restored the angel’s eye, which shows that no wrong was held against him.

Allah restored the angel’s eye and said: “Go back to My servant and say: ‘Do you want life? If you do, put your hand on the back of an ox, and for every hair that your hand covers you will live one more year.’”

The angel returned and gave Musa the message. Musa asked: “O Lord, what is next?” “Then death.” Musa said: “Then now.” He chose to go to his Lord, not to stay for years in the world. The Prophet ﷺ said of him that he asked Allah to bring him close to the Holy Land, within a stone’s throw. A man who had spent his life leading his people towards that land, and who died before he could enter it, asked that at least his grave lie near it.

Then the Prophet ﷺ said: “If I were there, I would show you his grave beside the road, at the red dune.” Abu Hurayrah recorded these words, and it shows the closeness the Prophet felt to Musa, whom he had met during the night journey and seen praying in his grave. The exact spot is not known, and scholars say there is no benefit in assigning it to any particular place without a sound report.

It is worth seeing how the Prophet ﷺ spoke of Musa here. In another hadith he said: “Do not give me preference over Musa,” and in another that Musa will be found holding the leg of the Throne on the Day of Resurrection. The accounts show a deep respect between the two prophets.

Some people have found this hadith hard to accept because they imagine an angel as something that cannot be struck. Scholars answer that the angel was in human form, that Allah restored his eye in an instant, and that the report is in the two Sahihs, so it is to be accepted. The hadith does not describe the angel as weak or Musa as disobedient. It describes a test of readiness and a servant who, when the real question was put to him, did not choose the world.

There is also gentleness in it. Allah did not send the angel to take Musa’s soul by surprise. He sent a second message and gave him a choice. And the Qur’an says that when death arrives it is described as something every soul will taste, which is not a punishment but a passage to what is with Allah. Musa’s “then now” is what the believer hopes to say.

facts: The Prophet ﷺ, reported in Sahih Muslim (Jundub) and Sunan Abi Dawud (Abu Hurayrah)
A devoted worshipper and a man who sinned
“By Allah, Allah will not forgive so-and-so”
Allah forgave the sinner and erased the worshipper’s deeds

t: In the narration of Abu Dawud, the Prophet ﷺ said that there were two men in Banu Isra’il who were friends, or associates. One was a man who worshipped diligently, and the other sinned. The worshipper would see his companion committing a sin and say: “Stop.” The other would say: “Leave me and my Lord. Have you been sent as a watcher over me?”

It is a very familiar picture. The one who is serious about his religion is annoyed at the one who is not, and the one who is not serious resents being told. The first has good intention; the second has something to say too, since the Qur’an does not appoint any of us as a guard over another’s heart. But the story shows what happens when good advice sours into arrogance.

One day the worshipper found the other doing a sin he considered very serious, and said: “Stop!” The man replied again: “Leave me with my Lord. Were you sent as a watcher over me?” The worshipper said: “By Allah, Allah will never forgive you, and will never admit you into Paradise.”

Then Allah took the souls of both of them, and they met with Him. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ gives the sentence of Allah in the first person: “Who is it who swears by Me that I will not forgive so-and-so? I have forgiven him, and I have made your deeds worthless.” In Abu Dawud’s longer report, Allah says to the worshipper: “Were you able to prevent what was in My hand?” Then He says to the sinner: “Enter Paradise through My mercy,” and to the other: “Take him to the Fire.”

Abu Hurayrah, who narrated it, then said a sentence that has stayed in the memory of scholars: “By the One in whose hand is my soul, he spoke a word that destroyed his world and his Hereafter.” That is a heavy remark about a man who spent his life in worship, and it shows what the tongue can do. Years of effort were lost, in the hadith of Muslim, not for any act of the body but for a statement of certainty about something that belongs to Allah alone.

Scholars point out that the word used for such an oath, ta’alli, means to speak as though you had a claim on Allah. The believer is allowed to hope and to fear for others, to advise and to warn, but never to close the door of mercy on someone. The man’s sin was not in telling the sinner to stop. It was in swearing about the result.

This hadith is not meant to stop anyone from forbidding wrong. The Prophet ﷺ said that anyone who sees something wrong should change it with his hand, or his tongue, or at least in his heart. The difference is in how it is done and how the person thinks of himself afterwards. Advice given gently, with hope for the other and fear for oneself, is worship. Advice given with a sense of superiority and a certainty about the other’s fate is a danger to the one giving it.
The one who gives advice is wise to ask himself how he would fare in the same situation, and to fear for himself at least as much as for the other. That is the attitude this story points to.

facts: The Prophet ﷺ, as reported by Ibn Mas‘ud
The last of the people of the Fire to leave it
The like of the world and ten times as much
He laughed until his back teeth showed

t: Ibn Mas‘ud said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “I know the last of the people of the Fire to come out of it and the last of the people of Paradise to enter it. He is a man who will come out of the Fire crawling. Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, will say to him: ‘Go and enter Paradise.’”

The man will go to it and find that it looks to him as though everyone has already taken a place. He will come back and say: “My Lord, I found it full.” Allah will say to him again: “Go and enter Paradise.” He will go, and again he will think it is full. He will come back: “My Lord, I found it full.” A third time Allah says: “Go and enter Paradise, for you will have the like of the world and ten times as much,” or, in another wording, ten times the like of the world.

The man will say: “Do You mock me, or do You laugh at me, while You are the King?” Ibn Mas‘ud said: “I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ laugh until his back teeth showed.” Ibn Mas‘ud adds that it used to be said that this man is the lowest of the people of Paradise in rank.

There is something of a gentle humour here. The man had lived through the Fire and its terrors, and he has become so used to disappointment that when he is offered the world and ten times more, his first reaction is disbelief. He cannot imagine that someone like him is to be given so much, and he is wary, as someone is who has been burned. The Lord’s answer is a quiet one: it is real, it is yours.

The hadith is long and detailed, and it belongs to a group of reports about the people who are taken out of the Fire after the Day of Judgement, by Allah’s mercy and by the intercession of the prophets and others. They are people who died believing, with sins that had to be dealt with, and who are then brought out. Scholars use this to show that anyone who dies with faith, even a grain of it, will not stay in the Fire for ever.

It also gives a measure of what Paradise is. If the one who is lowest in rank receives the like of the world and ten times more, a person can begin to estimate what is kept for the others. The Prophet ﷺ said in another hadith, which he reported from Allah: “I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has imagined.” The believer reads the story of the last man in as a motive for hope, and for making the most of the time that is left before it begins.

facts: The Prophet ﷺ, narrated by Abu Hurayrah
One of the earlier prophets, not named in the hadith (some scholars say Yusha‘ ibn Nun)
A head of gold taken from the spoils against the rule
Spoils became lawful for this ummah

t: The Prophet ﷺ said: “A prophet among the prophets went to battle, and he said to his people: ‘A man who has married a woman and wants to consummate it, and has not done so, must not come with me; nor a man who has built houses and not yet put up the roofs; nor a man who has bought sheep or pregnant she-camels and is waiting for their young.’”

The point of the three conditions is the same. A fighter should go with a mind that is on the task. A man who is waiting for his bride, or the end of a half-built home, or the birth of his animals, has his attention turned somewhere else. The prophet was not asking anyone to give up good things. He was asking that nothing unfinished should be dragging at the hearts of the men he took with him.

He went on until he reached the town at the time of the afternoon prayer, or close to it. He said to the sun: “You are commanded, and I am commanded. O Allah, hold it back for us.” And the sun was held, until Allah gave him victory.

The hadith tells it simply, and it adds that this was a power given to a prophet in a particular case. The scholars note that this is a rare sign, a miracle, given to a prophet. Some commentators say the prophet here was Yusha‘ ibn Nun, the successor of Musa, though the hadith does not name him, and it is better to leave it as the Prophet ﷺ left it.

s.h: The fire that would not take it
t: After the battle, they gathered the spoils together, as was the practice then, so that fire would come down from the sky and consume it. That was the sign of an accepted offering. The fire came and did not take it.

The prophet said: “There is theft among you. Let one man from each tribe pledge to me.” They came forward, and the hand of one man stuck to the prophet’s hand. He said: “The theft is among you. Let your tribe come to me.” Then the hands of two or three men stuck to his. He said: “The theft is among you.” They brought out a head of gold like the head of a cow, and put it with the spoils. Then the fire came, and it consumed everything.

The Prophet ﷺ ended the story with a comment for his own community: “Then Allah made the spoils lawful for us. He saw our weakness and our inability, so He made them lawful for us.” In earlier times, spoils could not be used by the army and had to be left for the fire. This nation was given a lighter rule.

Scholars take three things from the report. First, that a community can be held back from success by even one concealed wrong, and that leaders are right to look for it. Second, that dishonesty in public property is a very serious matter, one that the Qur’an warns about: “Whoever steals will come on the Day of Resurrection with what he stole.” Third, that Allah has lightened our burdens, and a believer should be thankful for the ease of this religion.

facts: The Prophet ﷺ, narrated by an-Nu‘man ibn Bashir
A ship divided by lots into an upper and a lower deck
A hole cut in the hull to reach water
The one who keeps Allah’s limits and the one who breaks them

t: An-Nu‘man ibn Bashir heard the Prophet ﷺ say: “The example of the person who keeps within Allah’s limits and the one who falls into breaking them is like people who drew lots on a ship. Some of them got the upper part and some of them the lower part. When those in the lower part needed water, they had to pass by those above them. They said: ‘If we made a hole in our share, we would not disturb those above us.’”

The lots show that no one earned a place by merit, and that all were passengers in the same situation. People with the upper deck did not have a right over the others; they simply had a better position that day. The ones below were not wicked. Their plan came from convenience, and it was reasonable on its face: a hole in their own share would harm no one else.

Then the Prophet ﷺ gave the outcome in two parts: “If they leave them to do what they intend, they all perish. And if they take hold of their hands, they are saved, and everyone is saved.” The sea does not distinguish between the decks. A hole in one part of the ship lets the water in everywhere, and nobody can say it belongs only to the people who made it.

The word used for “those who take hold of their hands” suggests prevention by force of care: stopping a person from harming himself and others. It is not about humiliating him. A person standing in front of someone about to scuttle the boat does not need a theory. He only needs to put out a hand.

Scholars read the parable on two levels. On one, the person who breaks a command of Allah is harming himself, and if others see it and say nothing, the harm spreads to the whole society, as the Qur’an warns about those who did not forbid each other from wrongdoing. On the other, it applies to ordinary problems of shared life: a neighbour who dumps rubbish, an official who accepts bribes, or an office where wrongdoing is ignored because it is not our part of the ship.

The way to stop the hole is also taught elsewhere. A person who sees an evil should change it with his hand if he has the authority and ability, or else with his tongue, or else with his heart. The parable says that to say nothing is not neutrality, and that the safety of everyone is shared.

s.h: The house and the missing brick
t: The Prophet ﷺ gave another picture of his own role. He said that his example and the example of the prophets before him is like a man who built a house and made it beautiful and complete, except for the place of one brick in a corner. People walked around it, admired it, and said: “If only that brick were put in.” He said: “I am that brick, and I am the last of the prophets.”

Taken with the story of the ship, the two parables show a community held together by shared limits and brought to completion by a final message. Both are in Sahih al-Bukhari, and both are simple enough for a child to repeat.

facts: The prophet-king Sulayman, a hoopoe, a queen of Saba’, her council
Not given in the Qur’an; later tradition calls her Bilqis
Saba’ (Sheba), in the south of Arabia, commonly placed in Yemen
Surah an-Naml (27), with a short mention in Surah Saba’ (34)

t: The Qur’an says that Sulayman reviewed the birds and said: “Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent? I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or slaughter him, unless he brings me a clear reason.” A king who rules men, jinn and birds still notices when one small bird is not in its place. He gives it a chance to explain.

The hoopoe came soon and said something that sounds bold: “I have encompassed what you have not encompassed, and I have come to you from Saba’ with certain news.” Then it reported: “I found a woman ruling them, and she has been given from all things, and she has a great throne. I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah, and Satan has made their deeds attractive to them.”
The hoopoe’s speech is the first sign of what kind of story this is. The bird’s complaint is not about the Queen’s power. It is about what her people worshipped.

Sulayman did not simply send an army. He said: “We will see whether you have told the truth or are of the liars. Take this letter of mine and cast it to them; then turn away and see what they will return.” The hoopoe took the letter and dropped it before the Queen.

She gathered her chiefs and said: “O chiefs, a noble letter has been delivered to me. It is from Sulayman, and it says: ‘In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful: do not exalt yourselves against me, but come to me in submission.’” It is a short and polite message. It names Allah, it asks for no tribute, and it asks only for submission to Him.

Then she did something that shows her wisdom: she asked advice. “O chiefs, advise me in my affair. I am not one to decide a matter until you are present with me.” Her chiefs offered strength: “We are men of power and great might, but the command is yours, so see what you will command.” The Queen was more careful: “Kings, when they enter a city, ruin it and humiliate its noble people. And thus they do. But I am sending them a gift, and I will see what the messengers return with.”

When her envoys arrived with the gift, Sulayman said: “Do you provide me with wealth? What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you. But you rejoice in your gift.” Then he told the messengers: “Return to them, for we will come to them with forces they cannot face, and we will drive them out from there, humbled and disgraced.”

He was not interested in gold. The Queen had treated the matter as a diplomatic exchange, and Sulayman answered that it was about something else. This also shows that Sulayman’s wealth was not what drew her to him, and that his message was not a bargain. He ended it with a firm warning. Still, when she came, she was invited and not forced.

Before she arrived, Sulayman asked his court: “Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?” An ‘ifrit from among the jinn said: “I will bring it to you before you rise from your place. I am strong and trustworthy for this.” But a man who had knowledge of the Book said: “I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you.” When Sulayman saw it standing before him, he said: “This is from the favour of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful.”

The Qur’an does not name the man who had knowledge of the Book. Commentators have offered several names, and some say it was a righteous scholar of his court, but none of it is certain. What matters is the way the Qur’an places the credit: not in the jinn’s strength, not in the man’s learning, but in Allah’s favour, and Sulayman’s answer is gratitude. Then he ordered the throne to be disguised, to see whether she would recognise it.

When she came, she was asked: “Is your throne like this?” She said: “It is as though it were it.” She neither said yes nor no, and her answer was careful. Then she was told: “Enter the palace.” When she saw its floor, she thought it was a pool of water and uncovered her legs to wade through it. Sulayman said: “It is a palace paved with glass.”

At that moment she turned: “My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I submit with Sulayman to Allah, Lord of the worlds.” It is the end of the story. The Qur’an does not say which sign moved her most, but they come one after another: a letter that asked for submission and not for gold, a throne that arrived without a journey, a floor that was not what it seemed. Each one showed her that what she had taken for solid might be less than it looked, and that the power behind Sulayman was not his own.

facts: Musa, Harun, as-Samiri and Banu Isra’il
Made of the people’s jewellery, and it made a sound like lowing

t: The Qur’an says that Allah appointed thirty nights for Musa and completed them with ten, so that the term of his Lord was forty nights. Musa told his brother: “Take my place among my people, do right, and do not follow the way of the corrupters.” Then he went up. He was eager to meet his Lord, and when Allah asked him why he had hurried ahead of his people, he said they were close behind him and that he had hastened to please Him. At that moment, Allah told him that his people had been put to the test in his absence, and that as-Samiri had led them astray.

This is how the Qur’an tells it: the people had left Egypt behind, crossed the sea, and seen the drowning of Fir‘awn. They passed by people who were devoted to their idols, and asked Musa to make them a god like theirs. Even then, Musa told them that they were an ignorant people.

During Musa’s absence, as-Samiri took the ornaments the people had brought with them and shaped a calf out of them. “A body that had a lowing sound,” the Qur’an says. The people said: “This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot.” In Surah Ta-Ha, Allah replies to this: “Did they not see that it did not return to them a word, and had no power to harm or benefit them?”

The Qur’an does not explain the calf’s sound. Commentators have offered two ideas: that the wind passing through the cast hollow gave it a lowing noise, or that it was a trick that as-Samiri arranged. One more explanation, which many of them mention, connects it to the handful of dust he later says he threw in. The text leaves it, and it is better to hold to what it says: that the calf was a thing without power, and that it deceived the people because they wanted to be deceived.

Harun did warn them. “O my people, you are only being tested by it, and your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my order.” They said: “We will not cease to worship it until Musa returns to us.” They had set a condition and would not move. Harun was one man, and the people were many, and later he would say that they had thought him weak and had nearly killed him.

When Musa returned, angry and grieved, he threw down the tablets and took his brother by the head, pulling him towards him. Harun said: “O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard or by my head. I feared that you would say: ‘You have divided the children of Israel, and you did not wait for my word.’” This is one of the most human exchanges in the Qur’an. It shows a brother who had not abandoned his duty but who had judged that keeping the people together was the lesser harm than a split. Musa did not argue. He prayed: “My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy.”

Then Musa turned to as-Samiri: “What was your motive, O Samiri?” He said: “I saw what they did not see, so I took a handful from the track of the messenger and threw it, and thus my soul suggested to me.” The Qur’an does not say more. Commentators say the “messenger” was Jibril, and that the dust from beneath the hoof of his horse had life in it, but these are explanations and not words of the text.

Musa’s judgement was that he should be cut off from his people: “Go, for in this life you will have to say: ‘Do not touch me.’” The people were to avoid contact with him, as he would avoid them. Then he turned to the calf: “Look at your god to which you have been devoted. We will burn it, and then we will scatter it in the sea.” The thing the people had treated as divine was reduced to ash and then to nothing, and the Qur’an adds one line that brings it to its point: “Your god is only Allah, the One for whom there is no deity except Him. He has encompassed all things in knowledge.”

The story does not end with punishment. In Surah al-Baqarah, Allah reminds Banu Isra’il that after the calf He forgave them, so that they might be grateful. Repentance was accepted from those who turned back. In Surah al-A‘raf, Musa chooses seventy men to go with him for an appointment, and when they are shaken, he prays that Allah will not destroy them for what the foolish among them have done.

It is a story about how quickly a group of people can slide into error when their leader is away, and about the price of that error. It is also about patience under accusation, in Harun, and about the way that a prophet’s anger gives way to prayer. Musa picked the tablets up again. In them, the Qur’an says, was guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord.

facts: The inhabitants of a coastal town of Banu Isra’il
Not to fish on the Sabbath
Those who broke the rule, those who warned, and those who asked why
Not given in the Qur’an; some early commentators said Ayla, on the Red Sea

t: The Qur’an tells the Prophet ﷺ to ask the Jews about the town that was by the sea, when its people transgressed concerning the Sabbath. “When their fish came to them openly on their Sabbath, and the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come. Thus We tried them for what they used to defy.”

The test was well suited to human weakness. The fish were plentiful when they were not allowed to be caught, and absent when they were. A person who was keeping the rule saw plenty in front of him and had to leave it, and then saw nothing when his hand was free. Many commentators describe how the people at first stayed within the limit and then began to look for ways around it.

The reports of the early commentators, such as Ibn ‘Abbas and others, say that some of them dug channels or ponds that the fish would enter on the Sabbath, and closed them off so that they were trapped. They would then take them on the day after. They told themselves that they had not fished on the Sabbath, since the catching was done on another day.

Ibn Kathir and others call this a legal trick, a hiyal, and the Qur’an treats it as a transgression because the people did what they were told not to do and only changed the form. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have warned in another hadith: “Do not do what the Jews did, making what Allah has forbidden permissible by the lowest of tricks.” Hadith scholars have discussed the chain of that report, but the principle it states is agreed.

The town divided. The Qur’an says: “And when a community among them said: ‘Why do you advise a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?’ They said: ‘As an excuse before your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him.’” So there were those who broke the Sabbath, those who warned them with the hope that they would turn, and those who had given up and thought it was no use.

The middle group gave two reasons for what they did. First, so that they could say to Allah, on the Day, that they had done their duty. Second, because there was still a chance that someone would listen. Both are lessons for anyone who has tried to correct a friend or family member and been ignored. The middle group did not stop. The ones who asked why they bothered were still in the town when what followed arrived.

The verse says: “And when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We saved those who forbade evil and seized those who wronged with a wretched punishment because they were defying.” Then: “And when they were insolent about what they had been forbidden, We said to them: ‘Be apes, despised.’”

Scholars have two views on this. Many early commentators, including Ibn ‘Abbas, held that the people were actually transformed in form. Others, including Mujahid, held that it was their hearts that were changed, and that “apes” describes the way they lived, without understanding or restraint. Both views are old and respected. What both agree on is that the Qur’an presents it as a warning, and says: “So We made it a deterrent for those present and those after it, and a lesson for the righteous.”

What happened to the middle group, the ones who asked the warners why they spoke, is not clearly stated. Reports say that Ibn ‘Abbas was at first unsure about this middle group, and that ‘Ikrimah argued that they too were among the saved, and Ibn ‘Abbas accepted it. The question is discussed among the commentators. The Qur’an’s emphasis falls on the warners, and the lesson that anyone who does the work of calling to good does so for the sake of Allah, not for the sake of results.

facts: Ibrahim, a king who disputed with him, and four birds
Not named in the Qur’an; later tradition calls him Namrud (Nimrod)
To bring the sun from the west

t: The Qur’an says: “Have you not considered the one who argued with Ibrahim about his Lord, because Allah had given him kingship?” The king was proud of his power, and he thought of it as his own. When Ibrahim said: “My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death,” the king replied: “I give life and cause death.”

The commentators explain how he did this. He had two prisoners brought. One he ordered to be killed, and the other he ordered to be freed. He then said that he had caused one to die and kept the other alive. It was an answer that played with the words and avoided the point, since the question was about the source of life and death, and not about the power to end a life or to spare it.

Ibrahim did not waste time on the trick. He moved to something that could not be answered with a performance: “Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west.” The king had no reply. The Qur’an says: “So the disbeliever was dumbfounded, and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.”

The argument is the one Ibrahim had already used with the stars, the moon and the sun, when he looked for the truth as a young man. Everything that rises and sets is under a command. A king who rules a country does not rule the sky. It is also an example of how to argue: let the other side set out his claim, and then ask for the one thing that it cannot do.

The second scene is a private prayer. “And when Ibrahim said: ‘My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.’ He said: ‘Have you not believed?’ He said: ‘Yes, but to put my heart at ease.’” Allah’s question was not a reproach. It brought out what everyone should hear: that Ibrahim already believed, and that what he was asking for was something more.

The Prophet ﷺ is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim to have said: “We have more right to doubt than Ibrahim, when he said: ‘My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.’” Scholars explain that this was a humble way of saying that if there were doubt in Ibrahim’s question, we would be more deserving of it, and that there was none. It was a request for a deeper certainty, the kind that comes from seeing.

Allah said: “Take four birds and incline them to yourself. Then place on every hill a part of them, then call them, and they will come to you in haste. And know that Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise.” Ibrahim was to take the birds, and the commentators say he cut them up and mixed their parts, then divided them over the hills around him.

Then he called, and the parts came together, and the birds came flying to him. The Qur’an gives only the instruction and its end, and does not describe the scene. It is enough. The man who had been asked to break his own comfort at every turn, to leave his land and nearly sacrifice his son, was given a sight which fixed the idea of resurrection in his heart. And the closing words of the verse, “Exalted in Might and Wise”, tell why it is possible and why it has a purpose.

facts: Ilyas, listed among the righteous in Surah al-An‘am
Only a few verses, in Surah as-Saffat
Often identified with the prophet Elijah of the earlier scriptures

t: In Surah as-Saffat Allah says: “And indeed, Ilyas was among the messengers. When he said to his people: ‘Will you not fear Allah? Do you call upon Ba‘l and leave the best of creators, Allah, your Lord and the Lord of your first forefathers?’ But they denied him, so they will be brought forth, except the chosen servants of Allah. And We left for him a good mention among the later generations: ‘Peace upon Ilyasin.’ Indeed, thus We reward the doers of good. Indeed, he was of Our believing servants.’”

Everything certain about him is in those verses and in a single line in Surah al-An‘am, where he is counted among the righteous with Zakariyya, Yahya and ‘Isa. “Ba‘l” in the Semitic languages means lord or master, and was the name of a god worshipped in the lands of Sham. The commentators say the idol was in a city in the north of Sham, which some name as Ba‘labak, but the Qur’an does not.

The phrase “Peace upon Ilyasin” is recited in more than one way. In the common recitation it is read as two words, “Il Yasin”, and in other recitations as “Al Yasin” or as one word. Many early commentators understood it as another form of the name Ilyas, the way some names have a second form in Arabic. What matters here is that Allah chose to praise him, and that the praise was lasting.

The pattern is repeated for Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and Harun in the same surah: a verse that says “Peace upon” each, “thus We reward the doers of good.” These are among the few places where Allah speaks greetings upon prophets by name, in His own words.

The later commentators draw from the traditions of Banu Isra’il to say that Ilyas lived during the time of a king named Ahab, whose wife promoted the worship of Ba‘l, that a drought came upon the land, and that there was a gathering where the worshippers of Ba‘l and Ilyas each offered a sacrifice and waited for fire to come down. These details are found in the Hebrew Bible about Elijah, and in Ibn Kathir’s history. Ibn Kathir himself says that such reports are taken from the earlier tradition, and that they cannot be accepted as certain.

The Prophet ﷺ said: “If the People of the Book tell you something, do not confirm them and do not deny them.” That is the way to read this. If the details turn out to be true, the story only adds colour. If they are not, nothing in the faith is changed. The Qur’an’s point stands: Ilyas called people to the One who made them, and he is remembered with a peace from Allah.

facts: Nakhlah, between Makkah and Ta’if, on the way to the market of ‘Ukaz
In the Makkan period, before the Hijrah
Fajr, led aloud by the Prophet ﷺ

t: Ibn ‘Abbas reports: “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not recite to the jinn and did not see them. He set out with a group of his Companions towards the market of ‘Ukaz. At that time, the devils had been prevented from hearing news of the heavens, and shooting stars had been sent against them. The devils went back to their people, who asked what had happened. They said: ‘We have been prevented from news of the heavens, and meteors have been sent against us.’ Their people said: ‘Something has happened. Travel through the east and the west of the earth and see what has caused this.’”

Those who headed towards Tihamah, where the Prophet ﷺ was, came to him at Nakhlah while he was leading his Companions in the dawn prayer. They heard the Qur’an and they listened closely. They said: “This is what has come between us and the news of the heavens.” They returned to their people and said: “O our people, we have heard a wondrous Qur’an.” And Allah revealed to His Prophet the verses: “Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened.”

The Qur’an gives their words at length. “We have heard a wondrous Qur’an. It guides to the right way, and we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord.” They then said that their Lord is exalted and has not taken a wife or a son, and that the foolish among them used to say about Allah what was far from the truth.

They also admitted that some of them had acted wrongly. People used to seek refuge in the jinn, which, they said, only increased their pride. They had thought that no one would be sent after the death of earlier prophets, and then found the sky filled with guards and flames. Among them were people who were righteous and people who were not, in different groups.

The second passage, in Surah al-Ahqaf, tells what they said to their people when they returned: “O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Musa, confirming what was before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path. O our people, answer the caller to Allah and believe in him; He will forgive you some of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment.” They were already aware of the earlier revelation, and recognised the Qur’an as a continuation of it.

In Surah al-Jinn, Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ to say: “No one can protect me from Allah, and I will never find any refuge besides Him.” It is the Prophet’s own declaration of his dependence on Allah, made in a chapter that begins with unseen beings accepting his message. He did not hold power over any creature, seen or unseen, by himself.

There are two things the early Muslims took from this report. The first was that the Qur’an has an audience beyond humankind: the jinn are among those who are addressed, and some respond. The second was a protection against the beliefs of the time. People in Makkah used to say that the Prophet ﷺ was a poet or a person possessed by a jinn. Here, the jinn themselves recognise the Qur’an as truth.

Scholars also point out that the Prophet ﷺ did not know about the jinn until he was told. He was not a man who spoke to the unseen. What he knew, he knew by revelation, and the jinn’s own statement in the same surah is that none of them knows the unseen either: “Knower of the unseen, He does not reveal His unseen to anyone.”

facts: Madinah, in the neighbourhood of Quba
Around the time of the expedition to Tabuk, 9 AH
A group of hypocrites, with a man named Abu ‘Amir ar-Rahib in the background
The Prophet ﷺ had it demolished

t: The accounts of Ibn Ishaq, which Ibn Kathir and at-Tabari also give, say that a group of the Banu Salim and others built a mosque near Masjid Quba and then asked the Prophet ﷺ to pray in it, as a blessing. They said that it was for the weak, the ill, and for rainy and cold nights, when people could not reach the main mosque.

It was a reasonable-sounding request, and the Prophet ﷺ did not refuse outright. He said he was preparing for a journey and was busy, and that if Allah willed, he would come when he returned. He was going to Tabuk, a long and hard march against the Byzantines in the heat. He knew what the people had asked, and he did not yet know what they meant.

When he reached a place called Dhu Awan, a short distance from Madinah, the revelation came: “And there are those who took for themselves a mosque for causing harm and disbelief and division among the believers, and as a station for whoever had fought Allah and His Messenger before. They will surely swear: ‘We intended nothing but good.’ And Allah testifies that they are liars.”

Allah then added a command: “Do not ever stand in it. A mosque founded on taqwa from the first day is more worthy that you stand in it. In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves.” That described the mosque at Quba, where the Prophet ﷺ had prayed and which had been built on the first day of the Hijrah.

The phrase “a station for whoever had fought Allah and His Messenger before” refers, according to the early commentators, to Abu ‘Amir ar-Rahib, a man from Madinah who had been a monk in the days of ignorance and was known for his piety. When the Prophet ﷺ came, Abu ‘Amir turned against him out of jealousy, joined Quraysh, fought at Uhud, and left for Syria after the conquest of Makkah, where he hoped to get help from the Byzantines.

The plotters had built the mosque as a base. Abu ‘Amir was to send them letters and men, and the mosque would serve as a meeting place for those who wished to cause trouble. The Prophet ﷺ named him later, and the people called him al-Fasiq, the transgressor. He died in exile.

The Prophet ﷺ sent Malik ibn ad-Dukhshum and Ma‘n ibn ‘Adi (in some reports, his brother ‘Asim) to go to the mosque and destroy it. They set it alight, and it was razed. The place was left as a rubbish heap for some time.

The Qur’an closes the passage with a verse about the builders: “Their building which they built will not cease to be a source of doubt in their hearts, until their hearts are cut to pieces. And Allah is Knowing and Wise.” The story is often cited by scholars as proof that a mosque can be demolished if it was founded to divide, and as a warning to those who use religion as a front. It also teaches that Allah looks at the intention, and that He reveals what is hidden. The same Prophet ﷺ who had not rushed to judge before the revelation did not hesitate to act once it came.

facts: About twelve years, according to Ibn Ishaq
His uncle Abu Talib and a Quraysh caravan
Busra, in the south of Syria
Some details differ between versions, and some scholars question parts of the report

s.h: A boy on the caravan road
t: Ibn Ishaq says that Abu Talib was getting ready for a journey to Syria, and when he was about to leave, the boy Muhammad clung to him. Abu Talib was moved. He said he would take him with him, and that they would never be parted. The Prophet’s father had died before his birth and his mother when he was six. His grandfather ‘Abd al-Muttalib had raised him for two years and then also died. Abu Talib had taken the child in, and the attachment was real on both sides.

They crossed the desert in the slow rhythm of caravans, from water to water, for weeks. At a place called Busra, in the region of Sham, there was a monk in a cell, a man of learning who was known among the people as Bahira. He had a book that was passed down among the monks of his cell, and what it said, the sources say, had to do with a prophet who would appear.

s.h: The cloud, the tree, and the meal
t: Quraysh had passed that way many times, and Bahira had never spoken to them. This time, the sources say, as the caravan approached he saw a cloud that seemed to shade one person among them. When they stopped under a tree, the tree’s branches seemed to lean over to give him shade. Bahira came down from his cell and had a meal prepared. Then he sent a message: “I have prepared food for you, O men of Quraysh, and I would like you all to come, young and old, slave and free.”

One man said: “By Allah, you are doing something unusual today. Why?” He said: “You are right, but you are my guests, and I wanted to honour you.” They came, but they had left the youngest of them with the baggage, under the tree. Bahira looked at them and did not see what he was looking for. He said: “O men of Quraysh, let none of you stay behind.” They said: “Everyone who ought to come is here, except a boy, the youngest of us, who stayed with the baggage.” He told them to bring him.

When the boy came, Bahira looked at him closely, then began to ask about him, about his habits and his sleep. In the narration of Ibn Ishaq he asked him, by al-Lat and al-‘Uzza, to answer some questions. The boy replied: “Do not ask me by al-Lat and al-‘Uzza. By Allah, nothing is more hateful to me than those two.” Bahira said: “Then by Allah, tell me what I ask.” This is how Ibn Ishaq records the boy’s early dislike of the idols, a detail that fits with the later tradition that he was kept from them throughout his youth.

Bahira examined him and, according to the account, saw the mark between his shoulders which matched the sign of prophethood that he had read of. He then turned to Abu Talib and asked who the boy was. Abu Talib said he was his son. Bahira said that this boy’s father could not be alive. Abu Talib said that he was his nephew, and that his father had died while his mother was pregnant. Bahira said: “You are right.”

Then Bahira told Abu Talib to take him back to his country and to guard him carefully against the Jews, saying that if they saw what he had seen they would try to harm him, since a great matter was ahead of his nephew. Abu Talib, in the account, took him back to Makkah as soon as he had finished his trade in Syria.

Some scholars have questioned parts of this story. In the version in at-Tirmidhi’s collection, narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari, Abu Bakr and Bilal are mentioned as being there, which cannot be right since Abu Bakr was a child and Bilal was not yet born. Adh-Dhahabi and others raised this problem, and they concluded that the mention is a mistake by one of the narrators, while the main event may still have happened. Some also point out that the Qur’an says plainly that the Prophet was not expecting what was to come to him. In the traditional view, the story is accepted as likely in its outline and told with care, as it is here.

facts: The trunk he leaned on cried when the pulpit replaced it
He came down and embraced it, and it grew quiet

t: Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah reports: “The Prophet ﷺ used to stand on Fridays by a trunk of a palm tree that was in the mosque, to deliver the sermon. A woman of the Ansar, or in another version a man, said: ‘O Messenger of Allah, shall we make a pulpit for you?’ He said: ‘If you wish.’ So they made him a pulpit.’”

This was a practical request, since the mosque was filling, and the people at the back could not see him well. The Prophet ﷺ agreed. The mosque in Madinah at that time was a simple building with walls of mud brick and a roof of palm trunks and fronds. The trunk he had been leaning on was one of the posts that held up the roof.

Jabir says: “When it was Friday, he went to the pulpit, and the trunk on which he used to stand cried out like a child. The Prophet ﷺ came down and embraced it, and it kept making a sound like a child being quieted, until it settled.” In another narration, by Anas, the sound was like the lowing of a she-camel, and the whole mosque heard it.

It is reported in the sources that the people were listening when it happened. This is a point the scholars emphasise: the story is told by several Companions who were present, and it is found in more than one chapter of Sahih al-Bukhari. Ibn Hajar and other scholars treat it as one of the most widely narrated reports of the signs of the Prophet’s prophethood.

In some narrations, the Prophet ﷺ said: “It cried because of the remembrance it used to hear.” In another narration, reported in Ibn Majah and Ahmad, he said: “By the One in whose hand is my soul, if I had not embraced it, it would have continued like this until the Day of Resurrection, out of longing for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.” Later sources say that Ubayy ibn Ka‘b took the trunk and kept it in his house until it decayed.
It was a creature that grieved at being left. The Prophet ﷺ did not consider it unworthy of attention. He got down from his pulpit, in front of a full mosque, to comfort a piece of wood.

Al-Hasan al-Basri, the great scholar of the generation after the Companions, used to narrate this hadith and then cry. He said: “O servants of Allah, a piece of wood yearned for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ because of his position with Allah. You are more deserving of longing for meeting him.” This is how the scholars heard the story: not as a mere wonder, but as a call to the heart.

The Qur’an says that everything glorifies Allah, though we do not understand how they do it: “The seven heavens and the earth and all those within them glorify Him, and there is nothing except that it exalts with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification.” The trunk’s weeping is one of the times that this hidden speech reached human ears.

facts: Soon after the Hijrah, in the first year
The Muhajirun, the Ansar, and the Jewish clans of Madinah
Ibn Ishaq, Abu ‘Ubayd and others, with differences in wording
Historians discuss whether it was one document or several, and the dating of its parts

t: The Aws and the Khazraj had fought for a long time, most recently the Battle of Bu‘ath a few years before the Hijrah. That was one reason the people of Madinah had invited the Prophet ﷺ: they wanted someone who could settle the quarrels. There were also three main Jewish tribes, the Banu Qaynuqa‘, the Banu an-Nadir and the Banu Qurayzah, and smaller groups, many of them linked to the Arab clans by older pacts.

The first steps the Prophet ﷺ took were to build the mosque and to pair the Muhajirun with the Ansar as brothers. The document went further and set out the shape of the whole city. According to Ibn Ishaq, he wrote it between the Muhajirun and the Ansar, “and made a treaty and a covenant with the Jews, in which he confirmed them in their religion and their property, and laid down rights and duties for them.”

The text, as it is preserved, has about fifty clauses. Its opening says: “This is a document from Muhammad the Prophet between the believers and Muslims of Quraysh and Yathrib and those who follow them and join them and strive alongside them: they are one community (ummah), distinct from other people.” It then sets out how each clan is to deal with blood money and the ransom of prisoners according to the good custom they already had, so that every group would keep its own system of responsibility.

About the Jews it says: “The Jews of Banu ‘Awf are a community with the believers. The Jews have their religion and the Muslims have theirs, themselves and their allies.” It adds that those who do wrong, or commit treachery, harm only themselves and their families.
