It also provides that they would help each other against anyone who attacked the people of the document, and that the city of Yathrib would be a sanctuary for the people of the document.

Several clauses concern disputes. Any serious quarrel that might lead to violence was to be referred to Allah and to Muhammad, in other words to the Prophet as the final judge. No one was to give protection to a Quraysh fighter or his property. A neighbour who was under protection was to be treated like oneself, neither harmed nor wronged. No agreement of peace was to be made by one group without the others, and in a war against an outside enemy, they were to share both the costs and the effort.

The document therefore sets up a shared defence and a shared authority, but does not demand religious uniformity. Each group was to remain in its own faith and under its own customs, and the Prophet ﷺ was the point of reference for the city. It is an early form of what later jurists called dhimmah, mutual protection, though the wording in the text is different.

Scholars and historians discuss this document with care. Some note that Ibn Ishaq gives it as one text, but its style suggests that it may combine more than one agreement written over a period, with the Jewish clauses perhaps added later. Others point out that it is consistent with what is known from hadith: that the Prophet ﷺ declared Madinah a sanctuary (haram) between two mountains, and said that “the covenant of the Muslims is one.” There are also differences in the wording between the accounts. The right approach is to accept its main points as part of the sira, to note the differences, and to avoid reading modern political ideas into it.

What it shows is what the Prophet ﷺ did first when he had a city to organise. He did not begin with conquest. He set up a framework of mutual obligation and protection, built on existing customs and not on force, and invited all to take part. It is the basis of a city that, in the following years, would be tested by war, but which began with agreement.

facts: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Anas ibn Malik
The cloak’s border left a mark on the Prophet’s neck
Zayd ibn Sa‘nah, a rabbi, who later became a Muslim; the chain is disputed

t: Anas said: “I was walking with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he was wearing a Najrani cloak with a thick border. A Bedouin caught up with him and pulled his cloak violently. I looked at the side of the Prophet’s neck, and I saw that the edge of the cloak had left a mark on it because of the force of his pull. Then the man said: ‘O Muhammad, order that I be given something from the wealth of Allah that you have.’”

The man was a desert Arab, unused to the manners of a city, and he made a demand rather than a request. The cloak was heavy, with a rough hem, and it was dragged hard enough to scratch the skin of a man who was carrying the burden of a state. Someone watching would have expected a rebuke, or an order to remove him.

Anas goes on: “The Prophet ﷺ turned to him, laughed, and then ordered that he be given a gift.” That is all the hadith says. He laughed, and he gave. He did not lecture. He did not ask the man to apologise. He took the man’s rudeness for what it was, a habit of speech from a hard life, and answered it with generosity.

The Prophet’s dealings with Bedouins are often told in the sources. One of them urinated in the mosque, and the Companions rushed at him, but the Prophet ﷺ told them to leave him, to pour water over the place, and he taught the man gently afterwards. The Qur’an says of him: “It is by a mercy from Allah that you were gentle with them. If you had been rough and hard of heart, they would have dispersed from around you.”

s.h: A rabbi’s test (a report with a disputed chain)
t: A longer report, in at-Tabarani, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim, tells of Zayd ibn Sa‘nah, a rabbi of Madinah. He is said to have known from the Torah all the signs of the Prophet ﷺ except two that he had not been able to see: that his forbearance would come before his anger, and that the more he was treated with ignorance, the more forbearing he would become. So he decided to test them.

He had lent the Prophet ﷺ eighty dinars for a purchase of dates. Three days before the debt was due, he saw the Prophet ﷺ coming from a funeral with some Companions. He took hold of the Prophet’s clothes at the collar and said, with a hard face: “Pay me what you owe me, Muhammad. By Allah, you of Banu ‘Abd al-Muttalib are slow to pay.” ‘Umar rose against him, saying: “Enemy of Allah, do you say that to the Messenger of Allah? By the One who sent him with the truth, if I did not fear missing something I would strike your head.”

The Prophet ﷺ looked at ‘Umar calmly, smiling, and said: “O ‘Umar, he and I needed something other than this from you: that you tell me to pay well, and tell him to ask well. Take him, O ‘Umar, and pay him what is his, and give him twenty extra measures for having frightened him.” Zayd then said: “O ‘Umar, there was no sign of prophethood that I did not see in his face when I looked at him, except two which I had not tested: his forbearance preceding his ignorance, and that the harder the ignorance towards him, the more forbearance he shows. Now I have tested both. I call you to witness that I am content with Allah as my Lord, with Islam as my religion, and with Muhammad as my Prophet.” He gave half his wealth in charity and fought with the Muslims, and in the report he died as a martyr at Tabuk.

s.h: How to take the second report
t: Scholars of hadith have discussed the second report, and scholars differ about the strength of its chain. Its main point, however, agrees with a very large number of authentic reports that describe the Prophet’s forbearance. For this reason it is told here as a story with a note, and not as a main source. What is established, and what the Bedouin’s cloak shows, is enough: he was not moved to anger by rudeness aimed at himself, though he was strict when it came to the limits of Allah.

It is a picture of strength under control. ‘A’ishah said that he never took revenge for himself in a matter unless the limits of Allah were violated. The man who pulled the cloak and the man who seized his collar both found something different from what they expected.

facts: ‘A’ishah, in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim
A necklace she had borrowed from her sister Asma’
Tayammum, wiping the face and hands with clean earth when water is not available

t: ‘A’ishah said: “We went out with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on one of his journeys. When we reached Bayda’, or Dhat al-Jaysh, a necklace of mine was broken, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed to look for it, and the people stayed with him. They were not at a place with water, and they had no water with them.”

The army was large, and it was on the road home. The necklace was one that ‘A’ishah had borrowed from her sister Asma’. It was not hers, and she was anxious. She was a young wife, and what she felt was the embarrassment of losing something that belonged to someone else.

s.h: No water and the time of prayer
t: Some of the people went to Abu Bakr and said: “Do you not see what ‘A’ishah has done? She has made the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the people stay where there is no water, and they have none with them.” Abu Bakr came to ‘A’ishah while the Prophet ﷺ was resting with his head on her thigh. He said: “You have detained the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the people when there is no water and they have none with them.” She said: “He rebuked me and said what Allah willed he should say, and he poked me in the side with his hand. Nothing stopped me from moving except the position of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with his head on my thigh.”

The Prophet ﷺ slept until morning, when it was time to pray, and there was no water. At that point Allah revealed the verse of tayammum. The Qur’an says: “If you do not find water, then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and your hands with it. Allah does not want to place any difficulty on you, but He wants to purify you and complete His favour upon you, that you may be grateful.”

Usayd ibn Hudayr, one of the leaders of the Ansar, said: “This is not the first of your blessings, O family of Abu Bakr.” He meant that this family had often been the cause of good for the Muslims. They then made tayammum and prayed.

‘A’ishah’s own account of the end is gentle. She said: “We made the camel I was riding get up, and we found the necklace under it.” After all the effort of searching, it was lying where she had been sitting. The sources also say that Abu Bakr, who had been strict with her, then showed his joy at what had come about. Scholars say that this story is a sign of the honour of ‘A’ishah’s household.

Tayammum is a sign of how the law is designed. A person who cannot find water, or who would be harmed by using it, because of illness or cold, is not left without a way to pray. The earth takes the place of water for the purpose of purification. The Prophet ﷺ said: “The earth has been made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification.” That was one of the things given to him which had not been given to the prophets before.

Scholars point to the way that the ruling came about as part of the lesson. It was not announced in advance, and no scholar would have been able to deduce it. It came from a moment of difficulty, and answered the problem of the whole army. The next time any group of Muslims was without water, in the desert, on a ship, or in a hospital, they would find the answer in the same verse.

facts: Abu Basir ‘Utbah ibn Usayd, of Thaqif, an ally of Banu Zuhrah
Anyone from Quraysh who came as a Muslim was to be returned
On the way to Makkah at Dhu al-Hulayfah, then on the coast at al-‘Ays
A band of Muslims formed on the coast and cut Quraysh’s trade route

t: The treaty had been signed at Hudaybiyyah in Dhu al-Qa‘dah of the sixth year. The Prophet ﷺ and his Companions had come for ‘Umrah and been stopped outside Makkah. The treaty gave Quraysh a ten-year truce and a promise that the Muslims would return the next year. It also included the clause on the return of those who came from Quraysh. Many Companions felt it was unfair, and ‘Umar spoke to the Prophet ﷺ and to Abu Bakr about it.

Al-Miswar and Marwan report in Sahih al-Bukhari that after the Prophet ﷺ returned to Madinah, a man from Quraysh named Abu Basir came to him as a Muslim. Quraysh sent two men to find him, with a letter that said: “Keep your promise to us.” The Prophet ﷺ handed Abu Basir over to the two men, who took him out of Madinah and set off for Makkah.

When they reached Dhu al-Hulayfah, they stopped to eat some dates. Abu Basir said to one of them: “By Allah, I think that this is a fine sword of yours.” The man drew it and said: “Yes, it is a fine sword, and I have tried it many times.” Abu Basir said: “Let me look at it.” When the man let him take it, Abu Basir struck him until he was dead. The other man ran off to Madinah and entered the mosque running.

When the Prophet ﷺ saw him he said: “This man has seen something frightening.” The man said: “By Allah, my companion has been killed, and I will be killed too.” Then Abu Basir came and said: “O Messenger of Allah, Allah has fulfilled your pledge. You returned me to them, and Allah has saved me from them.” The Prophet ﷺ said: “Woe to his mother, he would kindle a war if he had men with him.” Abu Basir understood from this that the Prophet ﷺ would return him again, so he went out and settled on the coast, at a place called al-‘Ays.

Al-‘Ays lay on the road that Quraysh caravans used on the way to Syria. Others who had become Muslim and who could not be taken in by the Prophet ﷺ under the treaty began to join Abu Basir. The sources mention Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl, the son of the man who had negotiated the treaty for Quraysh, among them. They grew to around seventy men by some accounts, and others say more.

Whenever a Quraysh caravan passed, they intercepted it, killed some of those with it and took their goods. The clause that Quraysh had insisted on now worked against them. The men on the coast were outside the Prophet’s control, so he was not in breach of the treaty, and they could not be returned. Quraysh was losing trade and had no one to hold responsible.

In time, Quraysh sent a message to the Prophet ﷺ asking him, in the name of kinship, to take these men in, and it is reported that they dropped the clause for those who came to him as Muslims. The Prophet ﷺ sent word to Abu Basir and his companions to come to Madinah. In a narration found in later sources, the letter reached Abu Basir as he was dying, and he died with it in his hand. This detail is not in the Sahih, and is told in the sira books.

What the Companions had feared as an humiliation turned out to be the opening of something. The treaty gave the Muslims safety, allowed the message to spread among the tribes during the truce, and within two years led to the opening of Makkah. Allah had called it “a clear victory” in Surah al-Fath. When ‘Umar later reflected on his own protest at Hudaybiyyah, he said he had kept giving charity and fasting and freeing slaves for fear of what he had said that day.

facts: Muharram of the seventh year, about two months after Hudaybiyyah
The Khaybar oasis, about 165 km north of Madinah
About 1,400 men who had been at Hudaybiyyah
The fortresses fell; the people stayed to farm and gave half their produce

t: When the Muslims left Hudaybiyyah, the Qur’an had promised them near victory and many spoils (48:18–21). Khaybar was the next stage. It was home to several of the families that had been expelled from Madinah, including the leaders of the Banu an-Nadir who had gone to the tribes to form the alliance of the Trench. The oasis had a number of fortresses, called Na‘im, as-Sa‘b, an-Natah, ash-Shiqq, al-Qamus, al-Watih and as-Sulalim, each of which had to be reduced in turn.

The Prophet ﷺ chose to march while Quraysh was bound by the truce and so could not help. He gave the order that only those who had been at Hudaybiyyah should come. When they arrived at night, he did not attack. He waited for the dawn, as his custom was when he came to a people at night.

Anas reports that when the Prophet ﷺ came to Khaybar at night, he did not attack until morning. When the people of Khaybar came out with their spades and baskets and saw the army, they said: “Muhammad, by Allah! Muhammad and the army!” The Prophet ﷺ said: “Allahu akbar! Khaybar is destroyed. When we come down to the courtyard of a people, evil is the morning of those who were warned.”

The attack began with the nearer forts. The first fell after a few days, others took longer. The sources note the difficulty of the siege, with hunger among the Muslims, who found little to eat, and the cost of taking a fortress on a high rock. Several Companions died, among them ‘Amir ibn al-Akwa‘, who was struck by his own sword in a duel by accident.

At one point the siege stalled. Sahl ibn Sa‘d reports that the Prophet ﷺ said on the evening before: “Tomorrow I will give the banner to a man at whose hands Allah will give victory, who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love.” The Companions spent the night wondering which of them it would be, and each of them hoped.

In the morning they came to the Prophet ﷺ, each hoping to be called. He asked: “Where is ‘Ali ibn Abi Talib?” They said that he had sore eyes. He sent for him, and he was brought. The Prophet ﷺ put some of his saliva on his eyes and prayed for him, and the pain went as though he had never had it. He gave him the banner. ‘Ali asked: “Shall I fight them until they are like us?” The Prophet ﷺ said: “Go on gently until you reach their courtyard, then call them to Islam and tell them what is due from them to Allah. By Allah, if Allah guides one man through you, it is better for you than red camels.”

The strongest fort, al-Qamus, fell after ‘Ali’s attack. Salamah ibn al-Akwa‘ reports that ‘Ali fought the champion Marhab and killed him. The remaining fortresses surrendered in the following days on terms: the people were allowed to keep their lives and to stay on the land and farm it, giving the Muslims half the produce each year. The Prophet ﷺ said that they would be left there as long as Allah allowed it. This arrangement lasted until the caliphate of ‘Umar, who later moved them out of the Arabian peninsula, as the Prophet ﷺ had said near the end of his life that two religions must not remain in it.

Two other things are told of the end of the siege. A Jewish woman, Zaynab bint al-Harith, brought the Prophet ﷺ a roasted sheep with poison, and Bishr ibn al-Bara’ died from eating it. And Safiyyah bint Huyayy, who had been among the captives, was freed and married the Prophet ﷺ, becoming one of the mothers of the believers. In the same days, Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib and the Muslims who had been in Abyssinia since the fifth year of the mission arrived at Khaybar. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said: “I do not know which of the two makes me happier: the conquest of Khaybar or the arrival of Ja‘far.”

facts: After the Battle of Hunayn, in 8 AH
Leaders of Quraysh and other tribes whose hearts were to be won
The Ansar, who had fought beside him
Anas, Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri and others

t: After Hunayn and the siege of Ta’if, the spoils were gathered at al-Ji‘ranah. They included many thousands of camels, sheep and goats, and a large amount of silver. The Prophet ﷺ distributed them in a way that surprised many. He gave a hundred camels to Abu Sufyan, to his son Mu‘awiyah, to Hakim ibn Hizam, to al-Aqra‘ ibn Habis, to ‘Uyaynah ibn Hisn and to Safwan ibn Umayyah, among others. They were men whose hearts needed to be reconciled to Islam, and whose tribes would follow them.

This giving was a policy of bringing hearts together, as the Qur’an provides in the share of those whose hearts are to be reconciled (9:60). It was not a judgement of rank, and the Prophet ﷺ said so afterwards.

Among the Ansar, there were those who spoke bitterly. Anas reports that one of them said: “May Allah forgive the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He gives to Quraysh and leaves us, when our swords are still dripping with their blood.” Another said that it was when things were hard that they were called, and when the booty came, it went to others. Sa‘d ibn ‘Ubadah, their leader, told the Prophet ﷺ what they were saying.

The Prophet ﷺ asked: “Where do you stand in this, Sa‘d?” He said: “I am only one of my people.” The Prophet ﷺ told him: “Gather your people for me in this enclosure.” When they were there, he came to them and said: “O Ansar, what is this that has reached me from you?” The older and wiser among them answered: “As for our leaders, O Messenger of Allah, they said nothing. But some of the younger among us said what you were told.”

The Prophet ﷺ said: “O Ansar, did I not find you astray, and Allah guided you through me? Did I not find you divided, and Allah brought your hearts together through me? Did I not find you poor, and Allah made you rich through me?” At each question they answered: “Allah and His Messenger are the most generous and bountiful.”

Then he said: “Will you not answer me, O Ansar?” They said: “What should we say, O Messenger of Allah?” He said: “If you wished, you could say, and you would be truthful and be believed: ‘You came to us rejected, and we believed you. You came to us abandoned, and we helped you. You came to us driven out, and we sheltered you. You came to us poor, and we comforted you.’ O Ansar, are you troubled in your hearts over some of the goods of this world, with which I won over a people so that they would become Muslims, while I entrusted you to the Islam you already have?”

Then came the sentences that people remember: “Are you not pleased that the people go away with sheep and camels, and you go back to your homes with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ? By the One in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, if it were not for the Hijrah, I would be one of the Ansar. If the people went one way and the Ansar went another, I would go the way of the Ansar. O Allah, have mercy on the Ansar, on the children of the Ansar, and on the grandchildren of the Ansar.”

The narrators say that the people wept until their beards were wet. They said: “We are pleased with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as our share and our portion.” Then the Prophet ﷺ added a last piece of advice to them, which was about the future: “After me you will see others preferred over you. Be patient until you meet Allah and His Messenger at the Pool (al-Hawd).” He did not need to explain what he meant. The wealth of the world would go to others, and the Ansar were promised something that would stay.

facts: Ibrahim, son of the Prophet ﷺ and Maryam al-Qibtiyyah
A solar eclipse on the same day, in 10 AH
“The sun and the moon are two signs of Allah; they do not eclipse for anyone’s death or life.”

t: Ibrahim had been born in Dhu al-Hijjah of the eighth year, to Maryam, a gift from the ruler of Egypt. The Prophet ﷺ was very happy. He had lost his sons Qasim and ‘Abdullah in infancy by Khadijah, and his other children were daughters. Ibrahim was given to a nurse in the ‘Awali, on the edge of Madinah. Anas ibn Malik says: “I have not seen anyone who was kinder to his family than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Ibrahim was being nursed in the high part of Madinah, and he would go there, and we would go with him. He would enter the house, which was full of smoke, since the nurse’s husband was a blacksmith. He would take him and kiss him, and then come back.”
When Ibrahim fell ill, the Prophet ﷺ was called. He took the child and held him in his lap. The boy was dying. The report of Anas says that the Prophet’s eyes were shedding tears.

‘Abd ar-Rahman ibn ‘Awf said to him: “And you, O Messenger of Allah?” The Prophet ﷺ said: “O Ibn ‘Awf, this is mercy.” Then he wept again and said the words that have been repeated by Muslims at every funeral for fourteen centuries: “The eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. We are saddened by your departure, O Ibrahim.”

In another narration, Anas adds that the Prophet ﷺ said that Ibrahim would have a nurse in Paradise to complete his nursing. The Prophet ﷺ was open about his sadness. He did not teach that faith meant not weeping. He wept, and then he said what a believer says: that the situation is Allah’s, and that the heart may grieve but the tongue should not complain.

On the day Ibrahim died, an eclipse of the sun took place. Al-Mughirah ibn Shu‘bah says: “The sun was eclipsed on the day Ibrahim died, and the people said: ‘The sun has been eclipsed for the death of Ibrahim.’” The Prophet ﷺ had no wish to use a coincidence in this way. He could have said nothing. He might have let people believe that heaven mourned with him.

Instead he went to the mosque and called the people to prayer. He gave a short address: “The sun and the moon are two signs among the signs of Allah. They are not eclipsed for the death of anyone, or for his life. When you see it, pray and call on Allah until it is cleared.” Then he led the prayer of the eclipse, which was long, with two bowings in each unit, and with so long a standing that some of the people fell down. He told them in his sermon what he had seen in it, including a reminder of the Fire and the Garden, and the abiding warnings.

There are three things in this report that scholars have drawn out. First, the Prophet’s humanity: he loved his son, he cried, and he did not hide it. Second, his honesty: at a moment when people were ready to attribute a miracle to him, he refused it out of concern for the truth, which is a clear proof of his sincerity. Third, a lesson on how to treat natural events. Muslims do not read the heavens as omens about births and deaths. They treat an eclipse as a sign of Allah’s power, and respond with prayer, remembrance, charity and repentance.

Ibrahim was buried in al-Baqi‘. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said at his grave: “He has a nurse in Paradise.” The same man who wept at that grave also set the example for everyone who has stood at one since.

facts: About ten years after the Year of the Elephant; died in 32 AH at Madinah
One of the first eight to accept Islam; migrated to Abyssinia and then to Madinah
One of the ten given the glad tidings of Paradise
Began again with nothing in Madinah, in the market

t: ‘Abd ar-Rahman was among the early Muslims of Makkah, accepting Islam, as the sources say, at the invitation of Abu Bakr. He migrated to Abyssinia, and then to Madinah. When the Prophet ﷺ established brotherhood between the Muhajirun and the Ansar, he was joined with Sa‘d ibn ar-Rabi‘, who was rich.

Anas ibn Malik reports in Sahih al-Bukhari that Sa‘d said to him: “I am the richest of the Ansar. I will share my property equally with you. And I have two wives; look at whichever pleases you more, and I will divorce her for you, and when she is free, marry her.” ‘Abd ar-Rahman said: “May Allah bless you in your family and your property. Show me the market.” He did not take a share. He asked for a place where he could trade.

He went to the market, bought and sold, and came back with some cheese and ghee as profit. Within a few days he was wearing perfume, and the Prophet ﷺ asked him what had happened. He told the Prophet ﷺ that he had married a woman of the Ansar, with a dowry of the weight of a date stone in gold. The Prophet ﷺ said: “Hold a wedding feast, even if with one sheep.”

He reportedly said later that he felt that if he lifted a stone, he expected to find gold or silver beneath it. His trade grew until his caravans were among the largest that came into Madinah. A report from ‘A’ishah, in Ahmad’s Musnad, tells of a caravan of seven hundred camels arriving in the city, so large that it shook the town, and that when she asked what it was, they told her it was the caravan of ‘Abd ar-Rahman ibn ‘Awf. This report has a weak chain and is told here only to show how the early Muslims remembered the scale of his business.

He used this wealth freely. For the army of Tabuk he gave a great sum. The sources say that in his will he left four hundred dinars to each of the surviving men of Badr and a large sum for the sake of Allah, and a garden for the Mothers of the Believers. Adh-Dhahabi adds that he once freed thirty slaves in a single day.

s.h: The food that made him cry
t: The following is in Sahih al-Bukhari. Food was brought to ‘Abd ar-Rahman ibn ‘Awf when he was fasting, and he said: “Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr was killed, and he was better than me. He was shrouded in a burda, and if his head was covered his feet would show, and if his feet were covered his head would show. Then Hamzah was killed, and he was better than me, and was found with nothing to shroud him but a cloak. Then the world was spread out before us, or he said that we were given from the world what we were given, and I fear that our rewards have been given to us early in this life.” He then began to cry, and left the food.

It is a short account, but it says much about him. He was among the richest men in Madinah, yet his reaction to his wealth was not pride but concern. He did not stop earning, and he did not renounce his money. He worried about whether the ease that came to him was a sign that his account was being settled early.

There is a distinction in his life that few others had. During the march to Tabuk, the Prophet ﷺ went away to relieve himself, and the time of the dawn prayer came. ‘Abd ar-Rahman led the people. The Prophet ﷺ came back, caught up with the second rak‘ah, and prayed behind him. After the prayer he got up and finished what he had missed. This is recorded in Sahih Muslim, and scholars count it among his distinctions.

He was also one of the six whom ‘Umar named on his deathbed as a council to choose the next caliph, and it was ‘Abd ar-Rahman who withdrew his own name so that he could manage the consultation. He spent three days and nights asking people, men and women, what they thought, and then chose ‘Uthman. He died in 32 AH at Madinah, at about seventy-two, and ‘Uthman is reported to have prayed over him. The man who had arrived with nothing left behind a large estate, much of which had already been given away.

facts: Son of Abu Talib; cousin of the Prophet ﷺ and brother of ‘Ali
To Abyssinia, then to Madinah in 7 AH, on the day Khaybar fell
At Mu‘tah, 8 AH, carrying the banner

t: Abu Hurayrah says in Sahih al-Bukhari: “The best of people to the poor was Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib. He used to take us home with him and feed us what was in the house. He would even bring out a leather container with nothing left in it but traces of ghee, and we would split it open and lick what was inside.” He was known as Abu al-Masakin, the father of the poor.

It is a vivid detail. Abu Hurayrah was one of the people of the Suffah, who lived on the edge of the mosque with almost nothing, and he remembered the exact vessel that was brought out. The man who had been the spokesman of Muslims before a king was not above emptying out his kitchen for those who had nothing.

The fullest account of what Ja‘far said in Abyssinia is in the Musnad of Ahmad, from Umm Salamah, who was among the emigrants. When the envoys of Quraysh came with gifts to ask the Negus to send the Muslims back, he called them in. He asked what this religion was which had made them leave their people. Ja‘far answered: “O king, we were people of ignorance, worshipping idols, eating carrion, doing shameful things, cutting off kinship and treating neighbours badly, with the strong among us eating the weak. Then Allah sent us a messenger from among us, whose lineage, truthfulness, trustworthiness and purity we knew. He called us to Allah, to worship Him alone and abandon the stones we had worshipped, and ordered us to speak the truth, return trusts, keep kinship, be good to neighbours, and stop forbidden things and bloodshed.”

The Negus asked: “Do you have anything of what he brought from Allah?” Ja‘far recited the opening verses of Surah Maryam. The Negus wept until his beard was wet, and his bishops wept until their scrolls were wet. He said: “This and what Musa brought come from the same lamp.” He told the envoys that he would not give them up. The Muslims stayed in Abyssinia in safety, and some of them remained until the early years of the Madinan state.

s.h: Khaybar, and the banner at Mu’tah
t: Ja‘far arrived in Madinah with the rest of the emigrants of Abyssinia, at about the time the Muslims captured Khaybar. (The Negus sent them back in two ships at the Prophet’s request.) The Prophet ﷺ met him and kissed him between the eyes, and said, according to a report, that he did not know which of the two events made him happier. The Prophet ﷺ said to him once: “You resemble me in appearance and in character.”

A year later, in 8 AH, the Prophet ﷺ sent an army to Mu’tah, on the Byzantine border, and appointed three commanders: Zayd ibn Harithah, then Ja‘far, then ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah. When Zayd was killed, Ja‘far took the banner. Ibn ‘Umar reports in Sahih al-Bukhari that when they found him afterwards, he had more than ninety wounds from spear and arrow, and none of them was in his back. According to the narrations, his right hand was cut off when he held the banner, then his left, and he held it to his chest until he fell.

The Prophet ﷺ, in Madinah, knew what had happened before any messenger came. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Anas reports that he told the people: “Zayd took the banner and was killed. Then Ja‘far took it and was killed. Then ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah took it and was killed.” His eyes were shedding tears. “Then the banner was taken by a sword from among the swords of Allah, and Allah gave them victory.” He was speaking of Khalid ibn al-Walid. In another report he said that he saw Ja‘far in Paradise “with two wings, soaked in blood.” This is why he is called at-Tayyar, the flyer, and dhu al-Janahayn, the one with two wings.

Then the Prophet ﷺ went to the house of Ja‘far. Asma’ bint ‘Umays, his wife, was making bread and washing her children. The Prophet ﷺ comforted her. And then he gave the instruction recorded in Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi: “Prepare food for the family of Ja‘far, for something has come to them which preoccupies them.” That is the origin of the practice, still observed, of neighbours and relatives taking food to a family that has lost someone.

facts: Khalid ibn Zayd, of the Banu an-Najjar of the Khazraj
Hosting the Prophet ﷺ on his arrival in Madinah
Badr, Uhud, the Trench and every battle with the Prophet ﷺ
About 52 AH, at the walls of Constantinople

t: The Prophet ﷺ came into Madinah on his camel, al-Qaswa’. As he passed the houses of the Ansar, people called to him: “Stay with us, O Messenger of Allah, with numbers, equipment and protection.” He said to each: “Leave her way, for she is commanded.” The camel walked until she came to where the Mosque of the Prophet ﷺ now stands, and knelt. Then she got up, walked a short way, and returned to the same place and knelt again.

The Prophet ﷺ asked: “Whose house is nearest?” Abu Ayyub said: “Mine, O Messenger of Allah. This is my house and this is my door.” The Prophet ﷺ said: “Go and prepare a resting place for us.” Abu Ayyub went to his wife, and they prepared the house. It had two floors, and Abu Ayyub made up the upper one.

The Prophet ﷺ said he would prefer to stay on the lower floor, as it would be easier for people who came to see him. Abu Ayyub and his wife spent the first night on the upper floor. During that night, a jar of water broke, and Abu Ayyub and his wife, Umm Ayyub, wiped up the water with their only quilt so that nothing would drip down onto the Prophet ﷺ below. They had no other cover, and it was a cold night.

In the morning, Abu Ayyub came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: “May my father and mother be your ransom. I do not like to be above you. Please come up, and let us be below.” The Prophet ﷺ agreed. When he moved to the upper floor, Abu Ayyub’s house stayed his home for some months, until the Mosque and the rooms beside it were built.

Abu Ayyub used to send food every day to the Prophet ﷺ. When the dish came back, he and Umm Ayyub looked for the place where the Prophet’s fingers had touched, and ate from there, hoping for blessing. One day the Prophet ﷺ sent it back untouched. Abu Ayyub came to him and asked if he had made something forbidden. The Prophet ﷺ said: “No, but it had garlic in it, and I dislike its smell.” Abu Ayyub said: “What you dislike, I dislike.” The Prophet ﷺ had made clear that it was not forbidden, only something he himself disliked.
It is a small domestic scene, and it shows the character of the household: a host who thought of how his guest felt, and a guest who answered with courtesy and without making a rule of it.

Abu Ayyub took part in every battle of the Prophet ﷺ, and many after him. In the year 49 or 50 AH, in the caliphate of Mu‘awiyah, the Muslims sent a naval and land expedition against Constantinople. Abu Ayyub, who was then over seventy, joined it. He is reported to have recited the verse: “Go forth, light and heavy,” and said that he could find himself among either.

He fell ill during the campaign, and when the commander, Yazid ibn Mu‘awiyah, came to visit him, he said he would like to be taken as far into the enemy’s land as possible and buried there. He died, and the army carried him with them to the walls of the city, and buried him there, in about 52 AH. A cemetery now surrounds the place in Istanbul. A tomb was identified after the Ottoman conquest in 1453, by a scholar named Aq Shams ad-Din, as the resting place of Abu Ayyub. The identification rests on tradition. What is sure from the early sources is that he died on that campaign and was buried at the city’s walls.

facts: Zayd ibn Sahl al-Ansari of the Khazraj
Shielded the Prophet ﷺ and broke his bow

t: Anas ibn Malik, who was Abu Talha’s stepson, describes the day in Sahih al-Bukhari. When the Muslims were scattered at Uhud, Abu Talha stood in front of the Prophet ﷺ, holding a shield. He was a strong archer, and he drew his bow so hard that he broke two or three bows that day. When a man passed by with a quiver of arrows, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Spread them out for Abu Talha.”

The Prophet ﷺ raised his head to look at the enemy, and Abu Talha said: “May my father and mother be your ransom! Do not look up, lest one of their arrows hit you. My neck is before your neck.” He stood with his chest before the Prophet ﷺ. Anas also reports that ‘A’ishah and Umm Sulaym were seen carrying water skins on their backs to the wounded that day. It was said that the voice of Abu Talha in the army was better than a hundred men, according to a report in al-Hakim.

Abu Talha owned more date palms than anyone among the Ansar, and the most loved of his properties was a garden called Bayruha’, which faced the Mosque of the Prophet ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ used to go there and drink its sweet water. When Allah revealed: “You will never attain righteousness until you spend from that which you love,” Abu Talha went to the Prophet ﷺ and said: “O Messenger of Allah, Allah says this, and the property I love most is Bayruha’. It is a charity for Allah, and I hope for its reward with Allah. Put it where Allah shows you.”

The Prophet ﷺ said: “Excellent! That is profitable wealth, that is profitable wealth. I have heard what you said, and I think that you should give it to your relatives.” Abu Talha said: “I will do so, O Messenger of Allah,” and he divided it among his relatives and cousins, including Hassan ibn Thabit and Ubayy ibn Ka‘b. He had not hesitated, and he did not keep it for himself.

The other well-known story is related in the two Sahihs. A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said he was hungry. The Prophet ﷺ sent to his wives, but they had only water. The Prophet ﷺ said: “Who will host this man tonight? Allah will have mercy on him.” A man of the Ansar said: “I will, O Messenger of Allah.” In some narrations of Muslim, he is named Abu Talha.

He took the guest to his wife and said: “Honour the guest of the Messenger of Allah.” She said: “We have only the children’s food.” He said: “Prepare your food, light the lamp, and put the children to sleep when they ask for dinner.” She did so. Then she stood as if to repair the lamp and put it out. They sat in the dark, making sounds as if they were eating, while the guest ate, and they went to bed hungry. In the morning, the man went to the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “Allah was pleased,” or “Allah laughed at what you did last night.” And Allah revealed: “And they prefer them over themselves, even if they are in need.”

Abu Talha remained devoted. After the Prophet ﷺ died, Anas said, he fasted continuously, except on the days of the festivals, for the rest of his life, and he kept fighting in the cause of Allah. He is reported to have died in 34 AH, and some say 51 AH, in a naval expedition or on land, and the early sources differ on this.

His household is also remembered for his marriage. Umm Sulaym, a widow and a believer, would not marry him while he was a polytheist, and told him that she would accept nothing as a dowry but his Islam. He became a Muslim, and Thabit says that Anas said he had never heard of a dowry more precious. It is a love story built on faith, and that story is told on its own page. Here it is enough to say that both of them were people who kept nothing back.

facts: Yasir and Sumayyah, both martyred in Makkah
Qur’an 16:106, on the one who is forced while his heart is at rest in faith
“Patience, family of Yasir, your appointment is Paradise”

t: Yasir came from Yemen to Makkah with his brothers, in search of one of them, and settled there under the protection of Abu Hudhayfah of Banu Makhzum. He married a slave woman of the same clan, Sumayyah, and had a son, ‘Ammar. When Islam began, the whole family accepted it. They had no tribe to protect them, so they were an easy target.

The Prophet ﷺ passed by them while they were being tortured in the heat of Makkah, and said: “Patience, O family of Yasir, for your promise is Paradise.” This is reported in al-Hakim’s Mustadrak with a chain that he graded sahih. Sumayyah was killed by Abu Jahl, and she is counted as the first martyr of Islam. Yasir died of his torture. ‘Ammar survived them, and was left alone.

In the tafsir of at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, the cause of revelation of the verse 16:106 is given as the case of ‘Ammar. The polytheists seized him, and would not let him go until he cursed the Prophet ﷺ and spoke well of their gods. When they let him go, he came to the Prophet ﷺ, who asked: “What is behind you?” ‘Ammar said: “Bad. I was not released until I spoke ill of you and spoke well of their gods.” The Prophet ﷺ asked: “How do you find your heart?” He said: “Content in faith.” The Prophet ﷺ said: “If they return to you, then return to what you said.”

And Allah revealed: “Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief, except one who is forced while his heart is at rest with faith, but those who open their breasts to disbelief, upon them is wrath from Allah and a great punishment.” The scholars used this to establish the rule that a person who is compelled under real duress may say words of disbelief with the tongue, while his heart is firm, and is not held guilty. They also say that to hold out and not speak, as Bilal did, is a higher choice, but a permitted one is not blameworthy.

When the Muslims built the Prophet’s Mosque in Madinah, they carried the bricks. Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri reports that they carried the bricks one by one, while ‘Ammar carried two at a time. The Prophet ﷺ passed by, wiped the dust from his head and said: “Woe to the son of Sumayyah! A rebellious group will kill him. He will call them to Paradise and they will call him to the Fire.”

This is in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri, who says that the Prophet ﷺ spoke these words while ‘Ammar was carrying his load. The Companions later remembered these words when ‘Ammar was killed at Siffin in 37 AH, fighting on the side of ‘Ali, at about ninety-three years of age. It was a painful time for the Muslims. Scholars of Ahl as-Sunnah say that Muslims should hold back from blaming any of the Companions, while recognising that ‘Ali was closer to the truth in that conflict.

The Prophet ﷺ honoured ‘Ammar in other ways. At-Tirmidhi reports that ‘Ali heard ‘Ammar asking permission to come in and the Prophet ﷺ said: “Let him in. Welcome to the good and purified one.” In another report, he said that ‘Ammar was filled with faith from the top of his head to the soles of his feet, and that faith had mixed with his flesh and blood.

He took part in all the battles with the Prophet ﷺ, and, according to some reports, was the first to propose building a mosque at Quba. He has remained a model of the believer who was tested as a young man and as an old one, and whose life was in the service of the community.

facts: Ubayy ibn Ka‘b, of the Khazraj, Abu al-Mundhir
The best of the Companions in recitation and a scribe of revelation
Allah commanded the Prophet ﷺ to recite Surah al-Bayyinah to him
Between 19 and 35 AH, with different reports

s.h: “Allah commanded me to recite to you”
t: Anas ibn Malik reports in the two Sahihs that the Prophet ﷺ said to Ubayy ibn Ka‘b: “Allah has commanded me to recite to you: ‘Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book...’” (Surah al-Bayyinah). Ubayy said: “Did He name me?” The Prophet ﷺ said: “Yes.” And Ubayy cried.

It was an honour that no scholar would argue with, and it has been taken as evidence of the value of learning the Qur’an from an expert. The Prophet ﷺ was not showing off Ubayy’s status. Scholars have given reasons for it: to honour Ubayy, to show that the Qur’an is learned by listening to a reciter, and to teach the nation to take it from those who know how to recite it.

Ubayy reports in Sahih Muslim that the Prophet ﷺ asked him one day: “O Abu al-Mundhir, do you know which verse of the Book of Allah is the greatest, with you?” He said: “Allah and His Messenger know best.” The Prophet ﷺ repeated it, and Ubayy said: “Allah, there is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting: that is, the Verse of the Throne.”

The Prophet ﷺ struck him on the chest and said: “May knowledge be easy for you, O Abu al-Mundhir!” It was a form of praise and a prayer, and Ubayy never forgot it. He went on to become one of the Companions to whom people went to learn.

The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said: “The most knowledgeable of my community in recitation is Ubayy ibn Ka‘b.” ‘Umar repeated it: “Ubayy is the best reciter among us, though we leave some of what he says,” as is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari. By this ‘Umar meant that Ubayy sometimes held on to a recitation that had been abrogated later, and that ‘Umar and others followed the final form.

Ubayy wrote down the revelation for the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah, and, with Zayd ibn Thabit, was among the scribes. He gave rulings, and ‘Umar consulted him on legal questions. When ‘Umar organised the congregational night prayer in Ramadan, he put Ubayy ibn Ka‘b in charge as the imam for men, a practice that remains in mosques to this day.

Ubayy was known for his sincerity and his emotion. A man came to him and asked for advice. He told him: “Take the Book of Allah as your guide and imam.” A well-known report shows how he thought of taqwa. ‘Umar once asked him what it meant, and Ubayy said: “Have you ever walked along a path full of thorns?” ‘Umar said that he had. “What did you do?” “I gathered up my clothes and watched every step.” Ubayy said: “That is taqwa.”

He died in Madinah, with the exact year disputed. Some say it was in the caliphate of ‘Umar in 19 or 22 AH, and others place it in the caliphate of ‘Uthman. It is reported that when he died, ‘Umar said: “Today the master of the Muslims has died.” The Qur’an that was recited to him by name in the Prophet’s own voice is now recited by every Muslim.

facts: Zayd ibn Thabit, of the Khazraj, Abu Sa‘id (or Abu Kharijah)
Scribe of the Prophet ﷺ; collected the Qur’an under Abu Bakr; led the copying under ‘Uthman

t: Zayd was born in Madinah and his father died when he was a child. At the Hijrah, he was brought to the Prophet ﷺ, with seventeen chapters learned. He was too young to take part at Badr, and the Prophet ﷺ sent him home. At Uhud also, he was sent back, and only later fought with the army. But he was good with writing, which was a rare skill, and the Prophet ﷺ gave him a task.

At-Tirmidhi reports that the Prophet ﷺ said to him: “Learn for me the writing of the Jews, for I do not trust them with my letters.” Zayd learned it in fifteen days, and wrote and read the letters for the Prophet ﷺ. Another report says that he also learned Syriac. He became the Prophet’s translator and one of the leading scribes of revelation.

The Battle of Yamamah, in 12 AH, took place against the false prophet Musaylimah. Many of the reciters of the Qur’an were killed in it. ‘Umar went to Abu Bakr and said he feared that if more were killed in other battles, much of the Qur’an would be lost, and he urged him to have it collected. Abu Bakr said: “How can I do something that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not do?” ‘Umar said: “By Allah, it is good,” and kept urging him until Abu Bakr came to agree.

Zayd reports in Sahih al-Bukhari that Abu Bakr then said to him: “You are a young and intelligent man, and we do not suspect you. You used to write down the revelation for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. So seek out the Qur’an and collect it.” Zayd says: “By Allah, if they had asked me to move one of the mountains, it would not have been heavier on me than what he asked me to do.” He asked: “How can you do something that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not do?” Abu Bakr said: “By Allah, it is good.” They kept going until Allah opened his heart to it.

Zayd searched for the Qur’an among the pieces of leather, palm stalks, thin white stones and the hearts of men. He did not accept a verse from a single person, even a reliable one. He required the written text and also that two witnesses testify that it had been written in front of the Prophet ﷺ. This is reported by Ibn Hajar and others as the standard he followed. He found the last two verses of Surah at-Tawbah only with Abu Khuzaymah al-Ansari (in some reports, Khuzaymah ibn Thabit), and was satisfied that they were from the Qur’an, because he also knew them from memory.

The pages were kept with Abu Bakr until he died, then with ‘Umar, and then with Hafsah, ‘Umar’s daughter. When the Muslims began to disagree over recitations in the armies of Armenia and Azerbaijan, Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman went to ‘Uthman and asked him to act before they differed as the Jews and Christians had. ‘Uthman asked Hafsah for the pages, and had Zayd and three men of Quraysh copy them into a number of copies, which were sent to the main cities. Zayd led both great efforts.

Zayd became the leading authority in Madinah in inheritance and judging. The Prophet ﷺ said: “The most knowledgeable of my community in inheritance is Zayd ibn Thabit.” When he rode, ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Abbas, the Prophet’s cousin and a great scholar, would walk beside him and hold the stirrup of his mount. Zayd tried to stop him, but Ibn ‘Abbas said: “This is how we have been told to treat our scholars.” Zayd then kissed his hand and said: “This is how we have been told to treat the family of our Prophet.”

When Zayd died in about 45 AH, Abu Hurayrah said: “Today the scholar of this ummah has died.” Ibn ‘Abbas said: “This is how knowledge goes: by the death of those who carry it.” The text which he gathered has been the Qur’an of every Muslim, from his day to ours.

facts: Three years before the Hijrah, in the valley where Banu Hashim were boycotted
Son of al-‘Abbas, the Prophet’s uncle
Hibr al-Ummah (the scholar of the ummah) and Turjuman al-Qur’an
At Ta’if, 68 AH, aged about seventy

t: Ibn ‘Abbas’s aunt was Maymunah, the Prophet’s wife, and he sometimes stayed in her house. One night he decided to watch how the Prophet ﷺ prayed at night. He lay across the width of the cushion, with the Prophet ﷺ and his wife along its length. The Prophet ﷺ got up in the last part of the night, wiped the sleep from his face, recited the last verses of Surah Al ‘Imran, and prayed.

Ibn ‘Abbas got up and stood at the Prophet’s left. The Prophet ﷺ took him by the ear and moved him gently to his right. This is in Sahih al-Bukhari, and it is the source of the ruling on where a single follower stands. In another report, the Prophet ﷺ put his hand on his shoulder and said: “O Allah, give him understanding of the religion and teach him interpretation.” The scholars say this prayer is the root of everything that followed.

After the Prophet ﷺ died, Ibn ‘Abbas was a young man, and he began to search for knowledge. He is reported to have said to a young man of the Ansar: “Come, let us ask the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, for they are many today.” The Ansari said: “Do you think people will need you, when there are so many of the Prophet’s Companions among them?” Ibn ‘Abbas left him and went on his own. If he heard that someone had a hadith, he went to his door.

He said: “I would find that he was having a nap, so I would spread my cloak at his door, and the wind would blow dust on me. If I had wished, I could have asked permission and he would have let me in, but I wanted to win his heart.” When the man came out and saw him covered in dust, he said: “O cousin of the Messenger of Allah, why did you not send for me?” Ibn ‘Abbas answered: “It is for me to come to you, for knowledge is sought out and does not come by itself.” The young Ansari who had mocked him lived to see people crowded around Ibn ‘Abbas with their questions, and said: “This young man was wiser than I.”

‘Umar used to include Ibn ‘Abbas in the council of the elders who had fought at Badr. Some of them felt uneasy about it, and one said: “Why do you bring this boy in with us, when we have sons like him?” ‘Umar replied: “He is one whom you know.” One day he called them and called Ibn ‘Abbas, and it appeared that he did it to show them something.

He asked them: “What do you say about the words of Allah: ‘When the help of Allah and the conquest come’ (Surah an-Nasr)?” Some said: “We are ordered to praise Allah and seek His forgiveness when we are given help and victory.” Others said nothing. ‘Umar turned to Ibn ‘Abbas: “Is that what you say?” He said: “No.” “Then what do you say?” He said: “It is the announcement of the end of the Messenger of Allah’s life, which Allah told him: when your help and the conquest come, that is the sign of your end, so glorify the praises of your Lord and seek His forgiveness, for He is ever-accepting of repentance.” ‘Umar said: “I know nothing about it but what you have said.” This is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari.

In later years his house in Makkah, and then in Ta’if, had rooms set aside for different subjects. One group would come for the Qur’an and its meanings, another for law, another for poetry and the Arabic language, and another for the battles and history. Ibn ‘Abbas would teach each in turn. He would explain a verse by pointing to a line of pre-Islamic poetry using the same word, and he is credited with beginning the habit of using poetry to explain rare words in the Qur’an.

There is a report in al-Hakim’s Mustadrak that ‘Ali sent him to debate the Khawarij at Harura’, and that he argued so well that thousands of them returned to the community. This report is accepted by many as an example of his persuasion by reason and the Qur’an. In his old age he lost his sight. He died in Ta’if in 68 AH, and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, who prayed over him, said: “Today the scholar of this ummah has died.”

facts: Talha ibn ‘Ubaydillah of Banu Taym, Abu Muhammad
One of the ten promised Paradise; “Talha al-Khayr” and “Talha al-Fayyad”
36 AH, at the Battle of the Camel

t: Qays ibn Abi Hazim says in Sahih al-Bukhari that he saw the hand of Talha, with which he had protected the Prophet ﷺ at Uhud, withered. When the Muslims were scattered and a rumour said the Prophet ﷺ had been killed, only a few stood by him. The sources name Abu Bakr, Abu ‘Ubaydah, Sa‘d, Abu Talha and Talha.

The Prophet ﷺ was struck on the face, his tooth was broken and a ring of his helmet was driven into his cheek. When the Prophet ﷺ tried to climb a rock and could not because of his heavy armour, Talha knelt and took him on his back and lifted him up. The Prophet ﷺ said: “Talha has earned it,” which the scholars take to mean Paradise. Az-Zubayr is reported to have heard the Prophet ﷺ say that day: “Talha has made it binding.”
Abu Bakr used to say that whenever Uhud was mentioned. Afterwards, the sources say, Talha was found to have dozens of wounds from spears, swords and arrows, and his hand was left withered.

The Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever would like to look at a man walking on the earth who has already given his life, let him look at Talha ibn ‘Ubaydillah.” This is in at-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan gharib. He is often called a martyr who walked among the living. It is in the list of the ten that the Prophet ﷺ mentioned by name as promised Paradise.

Talha was a rich trader. His business in Iraq produced an income that the reports put at a very large figure, and his nickname al-Fayyad, the Overflowing, refers to what he gave. A report in the Siyar says that in one evening he divided seven hundred thousand dirhams, and that when the money was in his house, he could not sleep until it was given away. This is a story told by later scholars, and the figures may be exaggerated, but they agree in the picture.

His wife Su‘da once found him sad and asked him what was wrong. He told her that he had a lot of money and it was weighing on him. She said: “Divide it.” He called his people and shared it all among them. It is an old story, and it is typical of what the Companions said about him: that he gave without being asked, and that he thought of the poor as those who did him a favour by accepting.

After the assassination of ‘Uthman, Talha was among those who believed that justice had to be done quickly for his death, and he marched to Basra with ‘A’ishah and az-Zubayr. At the Battle of the Camel in 36 AH, Reports say that ‘Ali met them and spoke to az-Zubayr, reminding him of something the Prophet ﷺ had said, and az-Zubayr left the field. Talha was struck by a stray arrow and died shortly after.

The reports say that ‘Ali later wept over him, and wiped the dust from his face, and said that he wished he had died twenty years earlier. Many scholars consider the details of this report weak, and it is not needed here. What is established is that those who were at odds in that conflict mourned each other, and that the Muslims remember Talha for his hand at Uhud and not for his last day.

facts: Sa‘d ibn Malik, of Banu Zuhrah, Abu Ishaq; uncle of the Prophet ﷺ on his mother’s side
The first to shoot an arrow in the cause of Allah; one of the ten promised Paradise
Qadisiyyah, c. 15 AH, against the Persians
About 55 AH, the last of the ten to die

t: Sa‘d reports in Sahih Muslim that when he accepted Islam, his mother, Hamnah bint Sufyan, swore that she would not speak to him until he left his religion, and would not eat or drink until she died, so that people would taunt him as the one who had killed his mother. Sa‘d said: “Do not do that, mother, for I will not give up my religion for anything.”

She stayed without food, and her family had to pour water into her mouth with a stick. In other reports, Sa‘d told her: “Mother, if you had a hundred lives, and they left you one by one, I would not give up this religion for anything. So eat if you wish, or do not eat.” Then she gave up and ate. And Allah revealed: “If they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, but accompany them in this world with kindness.” The verse separates the two things: no obedience in what goes against faith, and kindness that continues.

s.h: “Shoot, my father and mother be your ransom”
t: Sa‘d was an archer, and he is remembered as the first to shoot an arrow in the cause of Allah, in an early expedition before Badr. At Uhud, the Prophet ﷺ stood by him and gave him arrows, saying: “Shoot, may my father and mother be your ransom.” ‘Ali ibn Abi Talib said in Sahih al-Bukhari that he never heard the Prophet ﷺ promise both his parents to anyone but Sa‘d.

The Prophet ﷺ prayed for him: “O Allah, answer his prayer when he calls on You.” This is recorded in at-Tirmidhi, and the early Muslims spoke of Sa‘d as the one whose supplication was answered. One account is in Sahih al-Bukhari. When some people of Kufa complained about Sa‘d to ‘Umar, one of them, Usamah ibn Qatadah, accused him falsely. Sa‘d prayed that if the man was lying, Allah would give him a long life, long poverty and trials. The narrator says that he later saw the man very old, his eyebrows drooping over his eyes, and in trouble because of it.

In the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, Sa‘d fell very ill in Makkah. The Prophet ﷺ visited him. Sa‘d said: “O Messenger of Allah, I have a lot of wealth, and no one inherits from me but one daughter. Shall I give two thirds of it away in charity?” The Prophet ﷺ said: “No.” “Half?” “No.” “A third?” The Prophet ﷺ said: “A third. And a third is a lot. It is better to leave your heirs well off than to leave them in need, begging from people.”

The Prophet ﷺ put his hand on Sa‘d’s forehead and face, and wiped his stomach, and said: “O Allah, heal Sa‘d, and complete his migration.” Sa‘d says that he felt the coolness of the Prophet’s hand on his liver. He recovered, and lived another forty-odd years. This is the source of the rule that a Muslim may leave a third of his estate by will and no more, to a person who is not an heir.

In the caliphate of ‘Umar, the army that was sent against Persia was put under Sa‘d’s command. At Qadisiyyah, in about 15 AH, the Muslim army, much smaller than the Persian, fought a battle that lasted several days. Sa‘d was ill and had boils, and could not ride. He directed the battle from a litter, and the leaders on the field carried out his orders. The Persian army broke, and its general Rustam was killed.

Sa‘d went on to found the city of Kufa as a garrison town and was its first governor. ‘Umar later replaced him as governor, yet still named him among the six for the council. When the conflict between the Companions came after ‘Uthman’s death, Sa‘d kept apart and would not take sides. He died at about 55 AH in his house in the valley of al-‘Aqiq, and was brought to Madinah on the shoulders of men and buried at al-Baqi‘. He was the last of the ten to die.

facts: Salman al-Farisi, according to the Prophet’s pairing
Judge and teacher in Damascus under ‘Umar and ‘Uthman

t: Ibn Rawahah went to Abu ad-Darda’s house when he was out, and found the idol in a corner of the room. He took an axe and smashed it, saying: “Shall we not see what good is in you?” Then he left. This account is in the biographies, and not in the hadith collections. Abu ad-Darda’s wife, Umm ad-Darda’, saw him do it. When her husband came home, she said: “Your brother ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah came in, broke your god, and left.”

Abu ad-Darda’ was furious at first. He said he would get revenge. But when he looked at the pieces, he said: “If there had been any good in it, it would have defended itself.” This is how the account is given in Ahmad and in the Siyar, and it is a simple argument that resembles the one Ibrahim used with his people. He then went with ‘Abdullah to the Prophet ﷺ and declared Islam.

When the Prophet ﷺ paired the Muhajirun with the Ansar, Salman al-Farisi became the brother of Abu ad-Darda’. Salman visited him one day and found Umm ad-Darda’ in worn-out clothes. “What is the matter with you?” he asked. She said: “Your brother Abu ad-Darda’ has no need of this world.” When Abu ad-Darda’ came, he prepared food and told Salman to eat, saying that he was fasting. Salman said: “I will not eat until you eat.” So he ate.

At night, Abu ad-Darda’ got up to pray. Salman said: “Sleep,” and he slept. Later he got up again, and Salman said: “Sleep.” Only at the end of the night did Salman say: “Now get up,” and they prayed together. Then Salman said: “Your Lord has a right over you, your self has a right over you, and your family has a right over you. So give each one who has a right his right.” Abu ad-Darda’ went to the Prophet ﷺ and told him, and the Prophet ﷺ said: “Salman has spoken the truth.” This is in Sahih al-Bukhari.

Abu ad-Darda’ was known for memorising the Qur’an and for his wisdom, and Mu‘adh ibn Jabal is said to have trained him. He said of himself that when he became a Muslim, he wanted to combine trade with worship, but that he could not, so he left trade. ‘Umar sent him to Damascus as a judge and teacher in the new province of Sham, and the people there read to him in groups of ten, with hundreds in a circle.

His sayings were preserved, and some of them are collected in books of ascetic literature. He said: “Do not sit with those who do not remind you of Allah, and do not choose those who do not help you to do right.” He told a man: “Remember Allah in good times, and He will remember you in bad times.”
Abu ad-Darda’ died in Damascus, in the caliphate of ‘Uthman, around 32 AH. He is said to have been buried in Damascus, though the exact place is not certain.

He is a type of person who is found in every age: someone with an ordinary life, a shop and a family, who is moved by something small, the sight of a broken idol, to ask what is really worth his devotion. And who then holds on to that for the rest of his life, taking care to give everyone with a right what is theirs.

facts: Al-Husayn ibn Salam; the Prophet ﷺ named him ‘Abdullah
Banu Qaynuqa‘, of the descendants of Yusuf
The Prophet ﷺ said that he would die on the firm handle of Islam

t: ‘Abdullah ibn Salam says: “When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to Madinah, people rushed towards him, and it was said: ‘The Messenger of Allah has come.’ I went among the people to see him. When I looked at his face, I knew that it was not the face of a liar. The first thing I heard him say was: ‘O people, spread peace, feed food, keep family ties, and pray at night while people are asleep, and you will enter Paradise in peace.’” This is in at-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah.
He did not declare his Islam at once. He went to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him three questions that, he said, only a prophet could answer.

Anas reports in Sahih al-Bukhari that ‘Abdullah ibn Salam heard of the Prophet’s arrival while he was on his date palm, picking fruit, and he came down quickly. He said: “I will ask you about three things that only a prophet knows. What is the first sign of the Hour? What is the first food of the people of Paradise? And why does a child sometimes resemble its father, and at other times its maternal uncles?” The Prophet ﷺ said: “Jibril has just told me about them.” ‘Abdullah said: “That is the enemy of the Jews among the angels.”

The Prophet ﷺ answered: “The first sign of the Hour will be a fire that gathers the people from the east to the west. The first food of the people of Paradise will be the extra lobe of the liver of a fish. As for the child: if a man’s fluid precedes the woman’s, the child resembles the father, and if the woman’s precedes, the child resembles her.” ‘Abdullah said: “I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that you are the Messenger of Allah.”

Then he said: “O Messenger of Allah, the Jews are a people who invent lies. If they hear that I have accepted Islam before you ask them about me, they will slander me. So hide me in one of your rooms, then send for them and ask them about me.” The Prophet ﷺ hid him, and sent for the Jews, and asked: “What kind of man is al-Husayn ibn Salam among you?” They said: “He is our master, and the son of our master. He is our best and the son of our best. He is our scholar and the son of our scholar.”

The Prophet ﷺ asked: “What if he were to become a Muslim?” They said: “May Allah protect him from that.” He repeated it, and they said the same. Then ‘Abdullah came out and said: “I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.” They said at once: “He is the worst of us, and the son of the worst of us,” and they began to slander him. He said: “O Messenger of Allah, this is what I feared.” The story is in Sahih al-Bukhari.

The Qur’an refers to a witness from the Children of Israel who testified that the Qur’an is like what was before it: “And a witness from the Children of Israel has testified to something similar and believed, while you were arrogant.” Many commentators, including Ibn Kathir, say it refers to him, though others say the verse was revealed in Makkah and so refers to the principle.

Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas said: “I never heard the Prophet ﷺ say of anyone walking on earth that he was of the people of Paradise, except ‘Abdullah ibn Salam.” In another report in Sahih al-Bukhari, Qays ibn ‘Ubad describes a dream that ‘Abdullah ibn Salam had, and the Prophet ﷺ interpreted it: that he would hold fast to the firm handle until he died. He lived a long life as a scholar and teacher of the early community, and died in about 43 AH.

facts: A poet, and a leader of his people
As a martyr at Yamamah in 12 AH

t: Ibn Ishaq says that At-Tufayl came to Makkah, and that men of Quraysh came to him and spoke to him: “O Tufayl, you have come to our city, and this man in our midst has ruined us. He has split our unity and divided our affairs. His speech is like magic, and he divides a man from his father, his brother and his wife. We are afraid for you and for your people. So do not speak to him and do not listen to what he says.”

At-Tufayl says: “By Allah, they kept on at me until I decided not to listen to anything he said, and not to speak to him. When I went to the Ka‘bah in the morning, I stuffed cotton into my ears, for fear that some of his speech would reach me without my wanting it.” He was a sensible man and he wanted to protect himself and his tribe.

At the Ka‘bah, he saw the Prophet ﷺ standing in prayer. He went close, and, he says, Allah wanted him to hear some of what he said, and he heard speech that was good. He told himself: “What is the matter with me? I am a poet and a man of reason. The good and the bad of speech are not hidden from me. What prevents me from hearing what this man says? If it is good, I will accept it, and if it is bad, I will leave it.”

He waited until the Prophet ﷺ went home and followed him. He told him what had happened, and what the people of Quraysh had said to him, and how he had put cotton in his ears. Then he said: “Present your message to me.” The Prophet ﷺ presented Islam to him and recited the Qur’an. At-Tufayl says: “By Allah, I never heard words better than these, or a matter more upright.” He accepted Islam and testified to the truth.

At-Tufayl asked the Prophet ﷺ for a sign to help him invite his people. The sources say that he was given a light on his forehead, which he asked to have moved elsewhere in case his people took it as a punishment, and so it appeared at the end of his whip. This detail comes from the sira books, and its chain is weak, but it is told by Ibn Ishaq. What is fully established is the next part.

He went back to Daws and called them to Islam. His father and his wife accepted it, but the others delayed. He came back to the Prophet ﷺ and said, as Abu Hurayrah reports in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim: “O Messenger of Allah, Daws have been stubborn and have refused. Pray against them.” The Prophet ﷺ turned to face the qiblah and raised his hands, and the people feared that he would pray against them. He said: “O Allah, guide Daws, and bring them.”

The Prophet ﷺ then told At-Tufayl: “Go back to your people, be gentle with them, and call them.” He returned and kept calling. Years later, in 7 AH, when the Prophet ﷺ was at Khaybar, At-Tufayl arrived with some eighty families of Daws, all Muslims. Among them was Abu Hurayrah, who became the most prolific narrator of hadith.

At-Tufayl took part in the conquest of Makkah, and was sent to destroy the idol of ‘Amr ibn Humamah, which he burned. He fell as a martyr at Yamamah in 12 AH, as the sources say. The man who had put cotton in his ears is the reason that one of the largest tribes of southern Arabia came to Islam together, and that Abu Hurayrah’s memory entered the ummah. The Prophet ﷺ had prayed for Daws, and the whole group responded.

facts: The expedition of ar-Raji‘, in Safar of 4 AH
Zayd ibn ad-Dathinnah, who was also captured and killed in Makkah

t: The Prophet ﷺ sent ten men as scouts, under the command of ‘Asim ibn Thabit. When they reached a place between ‘Usfan and Makkah, about a hundred archers of Hudhayl, who had followed their traces by the date stones they left, surrounded them. The ten climbed a small hill. The enemy called to them: “Come down and give yourselves up, and we promise you that we will not kill any of you.”

‘Asim said: “As for me, I will not come down under the protection of a disbeliever. O Allah, tell Your Prophet about us.” They shot him with arrows, killing seven of the party. Khubayb, Zayd ibn ad-Dathinnah and one other accepted the pledge and came down. When they were bound, the third man said: “This is the first betrayal,” and refused to follow them. They dragged him, and when he would not go, they killed him.

The Hudhayl wanted to cut off ‘Asim’s head and sell it to Sulafah bint Sa‘d, who had vowed to drink wine from his skull, because ‘Asim had killed her sons at Uhud. But a swarm of bees, or hornets, came and covered his body, and they could not get to it. They said: “Let us wait until night, when they will go, and then we will take it.” The valley filled with a torrent in the night and carried his body away.

‘Asim had said earlier that he would not let a polytheist touch him, nor touch one, and It is reported that ‘Umar, when he heard of this, said: “Allah protects His believing servant after his death as He protected him in his life.” The bees were called ad-dabr in the account. Khubayb and Zayd were taken to Makkah and sold.

Khubayb was bought by the sons of al-Harith ibn ‘Amir, whose father he had killed at Badr. He was kept in their house until the sacred months ended. A woman of the household, whose account is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, said: “I never saw a prisoner better than Khubayb. I saw him eating from a bunch of grapes in his hand, though he was in iron chains, and there was no fruit in Makkah at that time. It was nothing but provision that Allah gave him.”

When they decided to kill him, he asked to borrow a razor to clean himself. She gave it to him. She says: “A little boy of mine crawled to him while I was not paying attention, and he sat him on his thigh. When I saw him, I was terrified, and Khubayb saw it in my face. He said: ‘Are you afraid that I would kill him? I would not do that.’ By Allah, I have never seen a prisoner better than Khubayb.” He held a razor in his hand with a child on his lap, in a house of people who meant to kill him, and did nothing.

They took him out of the Sanctuary to al-Tan‘im, outside the sacred area, to execute him. He said: “Let me pray two rak‘ahs.” They let him, and he prayed two short units. Then he said: “By Allah, if I did not think that you would suppose that I was afraid, I would have made them longer.” This is why scholars say that Khubayb was the first to establish the two rak‘ahs before being killed, as Abu Hurayrah reports.

Then he said: “O Allah, count them one by one, kill them one by one, and do not leave any of them.” And he recited the lines that are quoted in Sahih al-Bukhari: “I do not care, as long as I am killed a Muslim, on which side my death falls for Allah. That is for the sake of God, and if He wills, He will bless the cut limbs.” ‘Uqbah ibn al-Harith killed him. The Prophet ﷺ in Madinah is reported to have learned of it, and to have told the Companions on the day it happened. Khubayb’s place among the martyrs is firm, and the story is told whenever Muslims speak of patience under captivity.

facts: The Battle of the Trench (al-Ahzab), Shawwal 5 AH
The details are from the sira books, not the Sahih collections

t: Ibn Ishaq reports that Nu‘aym ibn Mas‘ud came to the Prophet ﷺ during the siege and said: “O Messenger of Allah, I have become a Muslim, and my people do not know it. Order me what you wish.” The Prophet ﷺ replied: “You are only one man among us, so go and discourage the people from us if you can, for war is deception.”

Nu‘aym was well placed for this. Before Islam he had been a friend of both Quraysh and Banu Qurayzah, and had often visited the Qurayzah settlement and drunk with them. They trusted him and did not know that anything had changed.

He went first to Banu Qurayzah. He said: “You know my love for you and my care for you. But the Quraysh and Ghatafan are not like you. This is your country, your property and your wives and children. If Quraysh see an opportunity they will take it, and if they do not, they will go home, leaving you alone with Muhammad, who will take revenge. So do not fight alongside them until you take some of their nobles as hostages, so that they do not abandon you.” The Qurayzah said: “That is good advice.”

Then he went to Quraysh and said to Abu Sufyan and the others: “You know my loyalty to you. I have heard something that I think I should tell you, but you must keep it secret. The Jews have regretted breaking their pact with Muhammad, and have sent word to him: ‘Would you be pleased if we took some of the nobles of Quraysh and Ghatafan and handed them over to you, so that you could kill them? Then we will be with you against them.’ If the Jews send you a message asking for hostages, do not give them a single man.” He said the same to Ghatafan.

On the Saturday night, Abu Sufyan sent a message to Banu Qurayzah, saying that they should come out and fight the next day. The Qurayzah replied that it was the Sabbath and they could not fight, and that they would not fight until the Quraysh gave them hostages. The Quraysh and Ghatafan said: “Nu‘aym told us the truth.” They sent word that they would give no hostages. The Qurayzah said: “Nu‘aym told us the truth.” The alliance was in doubt on both sides, and neither would act.

That night, Allah sent a cold wind and a storm. The fires of the camp were put out, the tents were torn up, and the cooking pots were overturned. Abu Sufyan stood up and said: “O Quraysh, we are not in a place to stay. Our horses and camels are dying, and Banu Qurayzah have broken their word.” They left in the night. The Qur’an describes it: “Allah sent upon them a wind and forces you did not see.”

The story of Nu‘aym is told in the sira books, and its chain is not of the grade of the Sahih collections. Ibn Hajar and others treat it as an acceptable report for history. It is not needed for any ruling. The line the Prophet ﷺ said, “War is deception,” is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, and it is the basis for the ruling that clever measures that do not break a promise or a trust are allowed in war.

Scholars note the limit. Nu‘aym did not break a treaty, since he was not a party to one, and he did not lie about a covenant. He used the enemy’s own fears. The Prophet ﷺ himself forbade treachery, and he kept his agreements, even with those who had wronged him. It is also worth remembering that the Qur’an gives the decisive role to Allah: the wind and the unseen forces. Human planning played a part, but Allah ended the siege.

facts: To Abyssinia and then to Madinah
The first Emigrant to die in Madinah, and the first buried at al-Baqi‘

s.h: The man who returned his protection
t: When the Muslims suffered in Makkah, ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un went to Abyssinia, and when he came back he was given protection by al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, a leader of Quraysh. He walked in safety in Makkah. But as he watched his fellow Muslims being beaten and insulted, while he went about unharmed, he felt that something was wrong.

He went to al-Walid and said: “O Abu ‘Abd Shams, you have kept your word. But I do not want anyone’s protection but Allah’s.” Al-Walid said: “Perhaps someone has harmed you.” ‘Uthman said: “No, I am content with the protection of Allah and I do not want to seek anyone else’s.” They went to the mosque, and al-Walid announced that he had withdrawn his protection at ‘Uthman’s request. This is told by Ibn Ishaq.

Ibn Ishaq also tells that the poet Labid ibn Rabi‘ah was reciting to a gathering of Quraysh, and said: “Truly, everything other than Allah is false.” ‘Uthman said: “You have spoken the truth.” Labid then said: “And every bliss will certainly vanish.” ‘Uthman said: “You have lied. The bliss of Paradise will not vanish.” Labid said angrily: “O people of Quraysh, I was never insulted at your gatherings like this. Since when has this been done?” A man struck ‘Uthman on the eye and blackened it.

Al-Walid, who saw it, said: “By Allah, nephew, your eye was not in need of this. You were in a secure protection.” ‘Uthman said: “By Allah, my other eye needs what has happened to this one, in the way of Allah. And I am under the protection of One who is stronger and more powerful than you, Abu ‘Abd Shams.”

Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas says in Sahih al-Bukhari: “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ rejected tabattul (giving up marriage) for ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un.
