If he had allowed him, we would have castrated ourselves.” ‘Uthman wanted to give up marriage and worldly life entirely, to pray the whole night and fast all the days. The Prophet ﷺ came to him and said: “O ‘Uthman, I was not commanded to take up monasticism. Is it not a good example for you to follow me? By Allah, I am the most fearful of you towards Allah and the one who best keeps His limits.”

He taught him a balance. In another report, the Prophet ﷺ told him: “Your wife has a right over you, and your body has a right over you, and your guest has a right over you.” The Qur’an addresses the same thing: “Do not forbid the good things Allah has made lawful for you.” ‘Uthman accepted the correction.

s.h: “I do not know what will be done with me”
t: ‘Uthman died in Madinah in 2 AH. ‘A’ishah reports in the collections of Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi that the Prophet ﷺ kissed him after he died, and wept, so that she saw the tears running on his cheeks.

A woman of the Ansar, Umm al-‘Ala’, said at the time: “O Abu as-Sa’ib, may Allah’s mercy be upon you. I testify that Allah has honoured you.” The Prophet ﷺ said: “How do you know that Allah has honoured him?” She said: “May my father and mother be your ransom, then who?” He said: “As for him, certainty has come to him from his Lord, and I hope good for him. But by Allah, I do not know, though I am the Messenger of Allah, what will be done with me.” This is in Sahih al-Bukhari. Umm al-‘Ala’ said: “By Allah, after that I never declared anyone pure.”

He was buried at al-Baqi‘, the first of the Companions to be buried there. The Prophet ﷺ marked the grave with a stone, according to a report in Abu Dawud whose chain is weak, to know where his brother lay. The scholars remember this account as a lesson in the right way to speak about the dead: to hope for them, not to pronounce sentence on them.

facts: A poet of the Prophet ﷺ and a pledger at ‘Aqabah
Appraised the date crop for the shares of the harvest
At Mu’tah, 8 AH, as the third commander

s.h: A man who fasted in the heat
t: Abu ad-Darda’ says in Sahih Muslim: “We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a journey on a very hot day, so hot that a man would put his hand over his head because of the heat. None of us was fasting except the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah.”

It is a single sentence, and it tells us what kind of person he was: one who did not wait for ease to be devoted. He was also the friend who broke Abu ad-Darda’s idol, in the account told on another page, and a man of the community who set himself to do more than he had to.

After Khaybar was conquered, the people who lived there, who were Jews, were allowed to stay and farm the land on condition of giving half the produce to the Muslims. Each year the Prophet ﷺ sent ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah to estimate the dates when they ripened, so that the Muslim share could be calculated before the people ate any of the harvest. He did this for some time, as Malik records in the Muwatta’.

The Jews wanted to be treated leniently. They collected some of their women’s jewellery and brought it to him, saying: “This is for you. Lighten the load on us and be generous in the division.” He said: “O Jews, by Allah, you are the most hated of Allah’s creatures to me. But that does not lead me to be unjust to you. As for what you have offered me, it is a bribe, and bribes are forbidden, and we do not take them.” They said: “It is because of this that the heavens and the earth stand.” This is related in the Muwatta’ and the Musnad of Ahmad.

In 8 AH, the Prophet ﷺ sent an army of three thousand to the Syrian border, and told them that Zayd ibn Harithah was the commander; if he was killed, Ja‘far, and if Ja‘far was killed, ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah. Ibn Ishaq tells that when the Muslims reached Ma‘an and heard how big the Byzantine and Arab army was, some of them said that they should send word to the Prophet ﷺ for more men or instructions.

‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah answered: “O people, by Allah, what you dislike is the very thing you came out to seek: martyrdom. We do not fight people by numbers, strength or multitude. We fight them with this religion, with which Allah has honoured us. So go forward: it is one of two good outcomes, victory or martyrdom.” The people said: “By Allah, Ibn Rawahah has spoken the truth.” They went on.

When Zayd and then Ja‘far were killed, ‘Abdullah took the banner. Ibn Ishaq says that he hesitated for a moment, and then he recited verses to himself, which began: “O soul, I swear you must go down to the fight, willingly or by force. If the people have gathered and raised the shout of battle, why do I see you disliking Paradise?” He then dismounted, took a piece of meat to eat, and heard the sounds of battle, and said to himself: “And you are still in the world?” He threw it down, took his sword, and fought until he was killed.

The Prophet ﷺ in Madinah saw it, as Anas reports in Sahih al-Bukhari, and told the people the order of the three, with tears in his eyes. The man who had been the Prophet’s poet in life had turned his last poems into action. Verses of his had been chanted at the Trench, as the Muslims dug and the Prophet ﷺ carried earth with them: “By Allah, if it were not for Allah, we would not have been guided, nor given charity, nor prayed.”

facts: Al-Bara’ ibn Malik of Banu an-Najjar, brother of Anas
The Prophet ﷺ said that if he swore by Allah, Allah would fulfil it
Opening the gate at the Garden of Death in the Battle of Yamamah
20 AH, at the siege of Tustar

t: Anas ibn Malik reports that the Prophet ﷺ said: “How many a man with dishevelled and dusty hair, who is turned away from doors, if he were to swear by Allah, Allah would fulfil it: and among them is al-Bara’ ibn Malik.” At-Tirmidhi gave this report the grade hasan.

Al-Bara’ was a man of strong voice and a good singer of the cameleers’ songs, and the sources say that he used to chant in the journeys of the Prophet ﷺ. He fought in Uhud, the Trench and all the battles after. According to Anas, he was the sort who, when others hesitated, went forward.

After the Prophet’s death, a man named Musaylimah, who had claimed to be a prophet during his lifetime, gathered thousands of the tribe of Banu Hanifah at Yamamah in central Arabia. Abu Bakr sent Khalid ibn al-Walid against them. The first day went badly for the Muslims, who were pushed back to their camp. On the next, they rallied, and the enemy retreated into a big walled garden.

The sources say that the walls were high and the gate was shut. The Muslims could not enter. Then al-Bara’ said: “Put me on a shield, raise it on spears, and throw me over the wall to them.” They hesitated, but he insisted. They lifted the shield and threw him over the wall. He landed among the enemy, fought his way to the gate, and opened it. The Muslims poured in. Musaylimah was killed, and with him many of his men. The garden became known as Hadiqat al-Mawt, the Garden of Death.

The reports, which come in at-Tabari and Ibn Sa‘d, say that al-Bara’ was wounded more than eighty times in that action. Khalid ibn al-Walid nursed him for a month, and he recovered. Many companions fell at Yamamah, including a number of those who knew the Qur’an by heart, which led to the collecting of the Qur’an under Abu Bakr, as told in the story of Zayd ibn Thabit.

The number of wounds and the details of how he entered the garden vary between the accounts, and they were written down in later centuries. Historians accept the main outline, that he was among the first to enter and that he was badly hurt, while treating the details cautiously.

He died in 20 AH at the siege of Tustar in Persia. The Persians let down iron chains with red-hot hooks to catch the Muslims, and one of them seized Anas. Al-Bara’ jumped up and grabbed the chain with his hands, holding it until the skin of his palms burned. He freed Anas and fell back, his hands badly burned.

When the Muslims asked him to swear that Allah would give them victory over the Persians, he said: “O Allah, grant them victory over us, and make me a martyr.” In the reports he was killed that day. The Muslims won, and the Prophet’s description of him became part of the way he was remembered. His brother Anas, who lived for nearly a century more, carried the memory of him.

facts: Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh, chief of the Aws, of Banu ‘Abd al-Ashhal
At Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr’s hands, before the Hijrah
By an arrow at the Battle of the Trench
Shortly after the siege of Banu Qurayzah, 5 AH

s.h: The day he became a Muslim
t: Ibn Ishaq tells that As‘ad ibn Zurarah brought Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr to a garden of Banu Zafar, where he was teaching. Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh told Usayd ibn Hudayr to go and drive the two away. Usayd went with his spear, and Mus‘ab said to him: “Will you sit and listen? If you like what you hear, accept it; if you dislike it, we will leave.” He sat, listened, and became a Muslim.

Then he went to Sa‘d, who saw him coming and said: “I swear he has come back with a different face.” Usayd said he had spoken to the two, and had found nothing wrong in them. He added that the Banu Harithah were going out to kill As‘ad, who was Sa‘d’s cousin, because they knew he was protected. Sa‘d got angry and took his spear. He found the two sitting calmly. He understood that Usayd wanted him to listen. He did, and he accepted Islam.

s.h: A whole clan in a day
t: Sa‘d returned to his people and asked: “O Banu ‘Abd al-Ashhal, how do you know me among you?” They said: “You are our chief, the best in judgement and the most blessed in leadership.” He said: “Then I will not speak to any man or woman among you until you believe in Allah and His Messenger.” Ibn Ishaq says that by evening, there was not a man or woman among Banu ‘Abd al-Ashhal who was not a Muslim, except one man.

It was a leader using the trust that his people had in him. It was also the start of the Ansar becoming a community that could receive the Prophet ﷺ. Not long after, the delegation of seventy-three met the Prophet ﷺ at ‘Aqabah, and the Hijrah followed.

At the Battle of the Trench, Sa‘d was hit in the arm by an arrow. ‘A’ishah reports in Sahih al-Bukhari that he prayed: “O Allah, You know that there is nothing I love more than to fight a people who denied Your Messenger and expelled him. O Allah, if You have put an end to the war between us and Quraysh, then make this wound burst, and let me die from it. But do not let me die until my eyes are comforted by the fate of Banu Qurayzah.”

The Banu Qurayzah, who had a treaty with the Prophet ﷺ, had broken it during the siege and had been on the point of joining the besiegers. After the siege ended, they were besieged in their forts. They agreed to accept the judgement of Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh, who had been their long-time ally from the Aws. He was brought on a donkey, wounded. The Prophet ﷺ told the Ansar: “Stand for your chief.” They asked him to treat his allies kindly. Sa‘d judged that their fighting men be killed, the women and children taken captive, and their wealth divided. The Prophet ﷺ said: “You have judged by the judgement of Allah, from above seven heavens.” This is in the two Sahihs. The scholars note that this was a punishment for treason in wartime according to a law the people themselves had agreed to, and that historians differ about numbers.

After judging, his wound opened and he died. Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah reports that the Prophet ﷺ said: “The Throne of the Most Merciful shook at the death of Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh.” This is in the two Sahihs. At-Tirmidhi reports that seventy thousand angels attended his funeral, who had never come down before. The Prophet ﷺ himself led the funeral prayer.

One more remark is in Sahih al-Bukhari. Some silk garments were brought to the Prophet ﷺ, and the people marvelled at their softness. He said: “Do you marvel at this? The handkerchiefs of Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh in Paradise are better and softer than this.” The man who had said to his people: “I will not speak to you until you believe” was now spoken of by the Prophet ﷺ with the highest praise.

facts: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, of ‘Abs, an ally of the Ansar
Sahib sirr rasul Allah, the keeper of the secret of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ
Spying on the Quraysh camp on the night of the Trench

t: Ibrahim at-Taymi reports from his father that a man said to Hudhayfah: “If I had been with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, I would have fought with him and served him.” Hudhayfah said: “Would you?” And then he told what happened on the night of the Trench. This is in Sahih Muslim.

“We were at the trench on a night of fierce wind and cold. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: ‘Who will go and bring me news of the enemy, and Allah will make him my companion in Paradise?’ No one of us stood up. Then he said it again, and then a third time, and none of us stood. Then he said: ‘Get up, Hudhayfah, and bring me news of the people.’ When he called me by name, I had to get up.”

The Prophet ﷺ said: “Go and bring me news of the enemy, and do nothing until you come back to me.” Hudhayfah says: “I went, and it was as if I were walking in a warm bath, not feeling the cold. I came to the enemy camp. Abu Sufyan was warming his back by the fire. I took out an arrow and set it on my bow, to shoot him. Then I remembered the Prophet’s words: ‘Do nothing until you come back.’ I put it down.”

Abu Sufyan stood up and addressed the people: “O Quraysh, let each of you look at who is sitting beside him.” Hudhayfah quickly took the hand of the man next to him and said: “Who are you?” The man said: “So-and-so, son of so-and-so.” He was safe. Abu Sufyan said: “O Quraysh, you are not in a safe place. The horses and camels are perishing, and Banu Qurayzah have deserted us. The wind has done what you see. Let us go.” He mounted his camel, though it was tied, and they began to leave.

Hudhayfah went back. The Prophet ﷺ was praying, wearing a blanket belonging to one of his wives. When he finished, Hudhayfah told him what he had seen, and that the enemy was leaving. The Prophet ﷺ drew him in and made him sit at his feet, and covered him with the end of his own blanket. “I stayed there,” he says, “until the morning.” When morning came, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Get up, O sleeper.”
In the Qur’an, Allah says of that night: “O you who have believed, remember the favour of Allah upon you when armies came to you and We sent upon them a wind and armies you did not see.”

Hudhayfah said in Sahih al-Bukhari: “The people used to ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the good, and I used to ask him about evil, for fear that it might reach me. I said: ‘O Messenger of Allah, we were in ignorance and evil, and Allah brought us this good. Is there evil after this good?’ He said: ‘Yes.’ I said: ‘And after that evil, is there good?’ He said: ‘Yes, and in it is some smoke.’” The conversation continued through the times of trial that would follow.

When Hudhayfah asked what he should do if he lived to see such times, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Stay with the main body of the Muslims and their imam.” He asked what if there was none, and the Prophet ﷺ said: “Then leave all those groups, even if you have to bite on the root of a tree until death comes to you.” This is why Hudhayfah is remembered as a source of knowledge about trials. He died in 36 AH, forty days after ‘Uthman’s killing, having kept his secret to the end.

facts: Anas ibn Malik an-Najjari, Abu Hamzah
About ten years, from the Hijrah to the Prophet’s death
About 91–93 AH in Basra, the last of the Companions to die there

t: Anas was ten when the Prophet ﷺ came to Madinah. His mother, Umm Sulaym, who had accepted Islam early and been widowed from her first husband, offered him as a servant. He did small tasks: he brought water, prepared the Prophet’s ablution, went with him on errands, and learned from being near.

He later said: “I served the Prophet ﷺ for ten years, and he never said ‘uff’ to me, and never said to me about something I had done: ‘Why did you do that?’ nor about something I had not done: ‘Why did you not do that?’” This is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. He also said that he had never touched any silk or brocade softer than the palm of the Prophet’s hand, and never smelled a perfume sweeter than the Prophet’s scent.

The Prophet ﷺ teased him affectionately and called him “O one with the two ears,” according to a report in Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi. Anas was also sent on errands, and Anas says that one day the Prophet ﷺ sent him on a task, and he went out and found children playing in the market. He stopped to play. The Prophet ﷺ came up from behind and took him by the back of the neck. Anas turned and saw him laughing, and the Prophet ﷺ said: “O Anas, did you go where I told you?” He said: “Yes, I am going, O Messenger of Allah.” This is in Sahih Muslim.

His mother asked the Prophet ﷺ to pray for him. The Prophet ﷺ said: “O Allah, increase his wealth and his children, and bless him in what You have given him.” Anas said: “By Allah, my wealth is great, and my children and grandchildren number over a hundred,” and that his date garden bore fruit twice in the year, as at-Tirmidhi reports. And he lived long, to the age of about a hundred, according to most reports.

After the Prophet ﷺ died, Anas settled in Basra, where ‘Umar had sent him to teach. He narrated more than two thousand hadiths, which is among the most of any Companion, and his reports are found in all the major collections. His students said that he prayed in the manner of the Prophet ﷺ, and that he kept some of the Prophet’s belongings, including a pair of leather sandals and a wooden cup, as Sahih al-Bukhari mentions.

He kept three hairs of the Prophet ﷺ, and asked that they be put in his mouth, or under his tongue, when he was buried. This is told in the early biographies, and its chain is not strong, and is mentioned here only to show how he was remembered. He was the last of the Companions to die in Basra, and when he died in his nineties, the city had lost its last living link to the Prophet ﷺ.

The reports of Anas show the Prophet ﷺ at home. He tells how the Prophet ﷺ would greet the children in the street, how he would visit a sick Jewish boy who used to serve him, how he never took revenge for himself, and how he prayed. He described the Prophet’s eating, his clothing, and his kindness to everyone from the lowest servant to the highest chief.

It is the memory of a person who watched closely from the age of ten to twenty, an age at which impressions last. When he told a story, as in the one about the Bedouin and the cloak on another page, he told it as one who stood beside the Prophet ﷺ, and saw the mark on his neck.

facts: Paternal aunt of the Prophet ﷺ; mother of az-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam
Hamzah, the lion of Allah, killed at Uhud
Came to the field after the battle

t: After Uhud, the Muslims counted their dead. Hamzah’s body had been cut open by Hind, Abu Sufyan’s wife, and mutilated. Safiyyah, hearing the news, set out from Madinah, according to Ibn Ishaq, with two shrouds in her hands. The Prophet ﷺ told az-Zubayr: “Meet your mother and take her back, so that she does not see what has been done to her brother.”

Az-Zubayr told her: “Mother, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ orders you to go back.” She said: “Why? I have heard that my brother has been mutilated, and that is for the sake of Allah. We accept whatever happens. I will be patient and expect the reward, God willing.” When az-Zubayr told the Prophet ﷺ, he said: “Leave her.” She went to her brother, prayed for him, said “We belong to Allah and to Him we return,” and asked forgiveness for him.

She had brought two pieces of cloth to wrap Hamzah. But next to Hamzah lay a man of the Ansar who had been killed in the same way, and who had no shroud. The Muslims felt that it was not fair that Hamzah should have two while the other man had none. They drew lots, and each of the two was wrapped in one piece. This is told in the Musnad of Ahmad, and in Ibn Ishaq’s account.

The Prophet ﷺ stood over Hamzah and wept. He had loved him as an uncle and a foster-brother. He said that he had never been in a place that made him angrier than the place where he saw him. Safiyyah stayed as long as she could, and the Prophet ﷺ prayed for her as well.

When the verse was revealed: “Warn your closest kindred,” the Prophet ﷺ stood on Safa and called the clans of Quraysh by name. In the hadith of Sahih al-Bukhari from Abu Hurayrah, he named his own family: “O Safiyyah, aunt of the Messenger of Allah, I cannot help you in anything against Allah. O Fatimah, daughter of Muhammad, ask me for whatever you want of my property, but I cannot help you in anything against Allah.”

It is a striking line, said by a nephew to his aunt. The Prophet ﷺ was not setting up his family as a protected class. He was making sure that no one believed that lineage would substitute for deeds. Safiyyah had taken this to heart: her actions at Uhud were the kind of response that the words ask for.

The Trench is remembered for the story that Ibn Ishaq tells about her, with a chain that is not strong, so it is given here with that note. The women and children of Madinah were placed in a fortress, and Hassan ibn Thabit, the poet, who was ill or unwilling to fight, was with them. A Jewish man came and began to move around the fort, to find out whether it was undefended. Safiyyah said to Hassan: “Go down and kill him.” He said: “May Allah forgive you, you know I am not a man for that.”

She took a tent pole, went down, and struck the man until he was dead. She then went back and told Hassan to strip the body. He said he had no need of the man’s belongings. So she cut off his head and threw it down to the Jews who were outside. They said: “We knew that Muhammad would not have left the women unprotected,” and went away. Some scholars have doubted the story, but it was told as part of her memory. She is remembered as a woman who stood up when she was needed, and who lived to be an old woman in Madinah, dying in the caliphate of ‘Umar.

facts: Tumadir bint ‘Amr ibn ash-Sharid, of Banu Sulaym
Her elegies for her brothers Sakhr and Mu‘awiyah
In about 9 AH, with a delegation of her tribe
About 24 AH, in the caliphate of ‘Uthman, according to most reports

t: Al-Khansa’ was born in Najd to a noble family. She was married and had children, but her great loss was her brother Sakhr, who was known for his generosity and was wounded in a raid and died after a long illness. She wept for him for a year and wore a hair garment. She wrote that “he was a mountain that guides by his light, with a fire on its head.” The line, with its image of a hill with a beacon for travellers, is still memorised.

The Arabs held a competition at the fair of ‘Ukaz, and the poet an-Nabighah ad-Dhubyani reportedly told her that if Abu Basir (al-A‘sha) had not recited before her, he would have said she was the best poet of all the jinn and men. According to the sources, she replied that she was a better poet than he was, and a better poet than any man. Whatever the details, her place was recognised.

She became a Muslim at the hands of the Prophet ﷺ, in a delegation of Banu Sulaym, in about 9 AH. The reports say the Prophet ﷺ liked to hear her poetry and used to say, “Go on, Khunas,” after each poem, which is a diminutive of her name. She had lost her brothers before Islam, and she is reported to have said that she had wept for them in the days of ignorance and that, as a Muslim, she had found something better.
She had four sons. When the Muslims were preparing for the Battle of Qadisiyyah in about 15 AH, she went with them.

s.h: Advice on the eve of battle
t: The biographers report that on the eve of the battle she said to her sons: “O my sons, you became Muslims willingly, and you migrated by choice. By the One other than whom there is no god, you are the sons of one man, as you are the sons of one woman. I did not betray your father, I did not shame your maternal uncle, I did not disgrace your lineage, and I did not change your descent. You know what reward Allah has prepared for the Muslims in fighting the unbelievers. Know that the everlasting abode is better than the passing one. Allah says: ‘O you who believe, be patient, outdo others in patience, be ready, and fear Allah so that you may succeed.’ When you wake tomorrow, God willing, in good health, go to the enemy with determination and seek help from Allah against them. When you see that the war has been fought to its height and the fire has been kindled, then go into its thick, grasp the lead of its leaders, and you will win Paradise and honour in the home of permanence.”

Her sons went out in the morning and fought, one after the other, reciting verses of their mother’s advice, until each was killed. When the news was brought to her, she said: “Praise be to Allah, who honoured me with their deaths. I hope that my Lord will gather me with them in the abode of His mercy.” ‘Umar, it is said, gave her the pension of each of her sons for the rest of her life.

Some of the details come from later biographers, and the sources do not agree on all of them. The core of the story, that she encouraged her sons to fight and that all four died as martyrs and that she bore it with patience, is in most of the early biographical works. Scholars of the Sunnah have always said that she embodied the teaching that the Prophet ﷺ gave about the patience at the first shock.

Her poems, collected in a diwan, are still taught in Arabic literature. One of the more discussed features of her life is the shift: the poet who had been known for unrestrained mourning was a mother who, as a Muslim, gave her sons to a cause she believed in and accepted their loss with the words “To Allah we belong.” This is how her story is told: not as a loss of feeling, but as a turn of it towards what lasts.

facts: Zaynab bint Jahsh, of Banu Asad ibn Khuzaymah
Cousin of the Prophet ﷺ; sister of ‘Abdullah ibn Jahsh
20 AH, the first of his wives to die after him

t: Zayd ibn Harithah had been a slave of Khadijah, and the Prophet ﷺ had freed him and adopted him. In the days before Islam, he had been known as “Zayd ibn Muhammad.” The Prophet ﷺ wished to show that in Islam, all believers were equal, and that a freed slave could marry into a noble family. He asked Zaynab, who was of Quraysh and a granddaughter of ‘Abd al-Muttalib, to marry Zayd.

She and her brother, ‘Abdullah, did not want it. They said: “We are of a better lineage.” Then Allah revealed: “It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, to have any choice in their affair.” Zaynab said: “I am content, O Messenger of Allah.” They married. The marriage was not a happy one. Zayd came repeatedly to the Prophet ﷺ to say he wanted to divorce her. The Prophet ﷺ told him: “Keep your wife and fear Allah.”

After the divorce, Allah revealed: “So when Zayd had no further need of her, We married her to you, so that there would be no difficulty for the believers in marrying the wives of their adopted sons when they have no further need of them.” The Prophet ﷺ had been told that this would happen, and had hidden what was in himself out of concern for what people would say, as the Qur’an says: “and you feared the people, while Allah has more right that you should fear Him.”

It was a marriage with a purpose: to end a custom in which adopted sons were treated as true sons for the purposes of marriage and inheritance. Anas reports that Zaynab used to boast to the other wives, saying: “Your families married you off, and Allah married me from above seven heavens.” This is in Sahih al-Bukhari. At her wedding feast, the verses of hijab and manners in the Prophet’s house were revealed, since some guests stayed on after the meal.

‘A’ishah reports in Sahih Muslim that some of the Prophet’s wives asked him: “Which of us will be the first to follow you?” He said: “The one with the longest hand.” They began to measure their arms against a wall. But, ‘A’ishah says, it turned out to be Zaynab, who died first. They realised that what he meant was not the length of a limb but giving. Zaynab was a woman who worked with her hands, who tanned hides and sewed, and used to give what she earned in charity.

‘Umar sent her her annual stipend, and she gave it away at once. When the money was set in front of her, she covered it with a cloth and told Barzah bint Rafi‘, who was with her, to put her hand in and take a handful for certain families. When she was done, all but a few dirhams had gone. She said: “O Allah, do not let ‘Umar’s gift reach me another year.” She died that year.

Zaynab died in 20 AH, aged about fifty-three. ‘Umar led the funeral prayer, and she was buried in al-Baqi‘, the first of the wives to die after the Prophet ﷺ. Before her death she had prepared her own shroud, and had said that if ‘Umar sent a shroud, she wanted one of the two used for charity.

‘A’ishah said of her: “I have never seen a woman better in religion than Zaynab, more fearful of Allah, more truthful in speech, more keeping of family ties, or more generous in charity.” She said this despite the fact that Zaynab had been a rival among the wives. It is a testimony that came from someone who knew her closely.

facts: Sawdah bint Zam‘ah of Banu ‘Amir ibn Lu’ayy
As-Sakran ibn ‘Amr, with whom she went to Abyssinia
In Shawwal of the tenth year of the mission, in Makkah
Late in the caliphate of Mu‘awiyah (c. 54 AH), according to many reports

s.h: A widow of the first Muslims
t: Sawdah and her husband as-Sakran were among the early Muslims. They went to Abyssinia, and when they returned to Makkah, as-Sakran died. She was left without protection among relatives who were still polytheists. In the year of sorrow after Khadijah’s death, Khawlah bint Hakim went to the Prophet ﷺ and said: “O Messenger of Allah, will you not marry?” He asked: “Whom?” She said: “If you wish, a virgin, and if you wish, a woman who has been married before.” He asked who the second was, and she named Sawdah.

The Prophet ﷺ asked her to approach Sawdah. Her father, who was old, said that if she was willing, he agreed. Sawdah accepted. The marriage gave her a home and a position as one of the Mothers of the Believers. For some years, she was the only wife he had, and she looked after his daughters Umm Kulthum and Fatimah at home.

‘A’ishah reports in Sahih Muslim and al-Bukhari: “Sawdah bint Zam‘ah gave her day to ‘A’ishah, and the Prophet ﷺ used to give ‘A’ishah her day and the day of Sawdah.” Sawdah had grown old and feared that the Prophet ﷺ might divorce her. She said: “O Messenger of Allah, keep me, and I give my day to ‘A’ishah.” He agreed. ‘A’ishah says that the verse “If a woman fears ill-treatment or neglect from her husband, there is no blame upon them if they make terms of settlement between themselves, and settlement is best” was revealed about such a case.

There is nothing in the reports to suggest that the Prophet ﷺ wanted to divorce her. It was she who wished to stay on, and she gave up her time with him to secure her place among his wives. ‘A’ishah is quoted as saying: “I never saw a woman whom I would rather be in her skin than Sawdah, a woman with a sharpness in her,” by which she meant a straightforwardness, and she then said that Sawdah had given her day.

At the Farewell Pilgrimage, the Prophet ﷺ spent the night at Muzdalifah. ‘A’ishah reports: “Sawdah was a heavy woman, and she asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to leave Muzdalifah before the rush of the people. He gave her permission, and she left before the others, and we stayed until morning and left with the Prophet ﷺ.” ‘A’ishah says: “If I had asked for permission as Sawdah did, it would have been dearer to me than anything.” This is in Sahih al-Bukhari. It is the origin of the ruling that the weak, the old and those who care for them may leave Muzdalifah in the later part of the night.

The reports also describe her as lively and amusing. They say that she prayed behind the Prophet ﷺ one night and told him afterwards that he had bowed for so long that she was afraid her nose would bleed, and she held it. This is in the Tabaqat of Ibn Sa‘d, with a weak chain, and the Prophet ﷺ is said to have laughed. She was a woman of generosity: ‘Umar once sent her a bag of dirhams, and she distributed them at once.

Sawdah died late in the caliphate of Mu‘awiyah, though some reports give the year as 22 AH, in ‘Umar’s time. After the Prophet’s death, she stayed at home, and, according to reports, she did not go on Hajj again, saying: “I have performed the Hajj and ‘Umrah, and Allah has commanded me to remain in my house.” Many of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ are reported to have done the same.

What the Muslims have drawn from her life is the value of quiet loyalty. She was not a scholar like ‘A’ishah, a political advisor like Umm Salamah, or a woman who had a strong place in the history like Khadijah. She was the one who came when she was needed, and who gave up something of her own to keep a household in harmony.

facts: Married ‘Uthman; migrated to Abyssinia and Madinah; died in 2 AH
Married ‘Uthman after Ruqayyah, in 3 AH; died in 9 AH
Dhu an-Nurayn, “the one with two lights”

t: Ruqayyah and Umm Kulthum were engaged or married to ‘Utbah and ‘Utaybah, the sons of Abu Lahab, the Prophet’s uncle and one of his fiercest opponents. When Allah revealed Surah al-Masad, “May the hands of Abu Lahab perish,” Abu Lahab said to his sons: “My head and yours are forbidden to each other unless you divorce the daughters of Muhammad.” They did. Ibn Ishaq and others tell that ‘Utaybah then came to the Prophet ﷺ and said something insulting, and the Prophet ﷺ prayed that Allah would set one of His dogs on him. Years later, on a journey to Syria, a lion killed ‘Utaybah.
The Prophet’s daughters returned to their father’s house, and, soon after, ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan, one of the early believers, a man known for his modesty and wealth, asked for Ruqayyah’s hand.

When the Muslims suffered in Makkah, ‘Uthman and Ruqayyah left for Abyssinia. The Prophet ﷺ did not hear from them for some time, and a woman arrived in Makkah and told him: “I saw them: ‘Uthman has put her on a donkey and is leading her.” The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said: “May Allah be their companion. ‘Uthman is the first to migrate with his family after Lut.” They later returned, and then migrated again, to Madinah.

In Madinah, in 2 AH, the Muslims left for Badr. Ruqayyah fell ill with measles. The Prophet ﷺ told ‘Uthman to stay behind and look after her. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn ‘Umar says that the Prophet ﷺ told ‘Uthman: “You will have the reward and share of a man who was at Badr.” ‘Uthman is the only Companion who, though he did not attend the battle, was counted among the men of Badr.

s.h: The day of Badr and the day of grief
t: Ruqayyah died while the army was away. According to Ibn Ishaq, Usamah ibn Zayd says that the news of the Muslim victory at Badr reached Madinah at the same time that they were burying Ruqayyah. Zayd ibn Harithah arrived on the Prophet’s camel, al-Qaswa’, announcing the victory, as they finished the burial. Usamah, who was a boy, says that he heard the cries of joy as they smoothed the earth over the grave of the daughter of the Messenger of Allah.

So the Prophet ﷺ came back from the first great victory of Islam to find that he had lost a daughter. ‘Uthman, who had stayed to nurse her and had been given the reward of Badr, had been at her side to the end. The sources do not record many words of the Prophet ﷺ at that time. It is one of the many places in the sira where joy and sorrow arrived on the same day.

After Ruqayyah’s death, the Prophet ﷺ married his other daughter, Umm Kulthum, to ‘Uthman, in 3 AH. She lived with him for six years, and died in Sha‘ban of 9 AH. The Prophet ﷺ led the funeral prayer, and as they were putting her in the grave, he asked who would go down. Abu Talhah went down. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Anas says that he saw the Prophet’s eyes shedding tears at her grave.

Neither daughter left any children who survived. Ruqayyah’s son ‘Abdullah, born in Abyssinia, died at about six years old, according to reports. Their lives show how the Prophet’s family was joined to the hardships of the early community: forced divorce, migration, illness, early death. The ummah remembers ‘Uthman’s title, “the one with two lights,” which refers to his marriage to two daughters of a Prophet.

facts: Umm Haram bint Milhan of Banu an-Najjar, sister of Umm Sulaym
Among the first to cross the sea for the sake of Allah

t: Anas ibn Malik reports in the two Sahihs that the Prophet ﷺ used to visit Umm Haram, who was married to ‘Ubadah ibn as-Samit. She used to feed him and look over his head. One day he came, she gave him food, and then she sat and looked through his hair. He slept, then woke laughing. She asked: “What makes you laugh, O Messenger of Allah?” He said: “Some people of my community were shown to me as fighters in the cause of Allah, riding on the back of this sea like kings on thrones.”

She said: “O Messenger of Allah, ask Allah to make me one of them.” He prayed for her. Then he lay down again, slept, and woke up laughing, and she asked him the same thing. He gave the same answer, and she asked again that she be among them. He said: “You are among the first.”

The Prophet ﷺ died, and so did Abu Bakr and ‘Umar. During the caliphate of ‘Uthman, Mu‘awiyah, who was governor of Sham, asked for permission to attack Cyprus by sea. ‘Umar had refused to allow it, for fear of the sea. ‘Uthman gave permission on condition that no one be forced to go. In 27 or 28 AH, the Muslims built ships and set out. ‘Ubadah ibn as-Samit went, and his wife Umm Haram went with him.

Anas says she was with the expedition. When they came to Cyprus, and landed, a riding animal was brought for her to ride. She mounted it, and it threw her. Her neck was broken, and she died. She was buried there. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the narrator says that she went with her husband and joined those who fought on the sea.

She is buried near Larnaca, on the island of Cyprus, at a place now called Hala Sultan Tekke, beside a salt lake. A mosque was built there by the Ottomans, and her grave is visited as that of the first woman to die in the Muslim fleet. The identification of the grave rests on a long tradition, and no one in the early sources contradicted it.

The Prophet’s words in this hadith are also taken by scholars as a sign of the value of the sea expedition, and of his knowledge of what was to come. Sahih al-Bukhari adds that the Prophet ﷺ also spoke of the first army of his community to attack the city of Caesar, saying that they would be forgiven. Umm Haram asked whether she would be among them, and he said: “No.” The two promises fit together: she was among the first who sailed, and she died on the sea expedition, before the later one.

facts: Umm Waraqah bint ‘Abdullah ibn al-Harith al-Ansariyyah
Knowing the Qur’an by heart or by large part, in the Prophet’s time
In the caliphate of ‘Umar, killed by two of her servants

t: Umm Waraqah says, in the report found in Abu Dawud and Ahmad: “When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out to Badr, I said to him: ‘O Messenger of Allah, allow me to go with you, to nurse your sick and treat your wounded, and perhaps Allah will give me martyrdom.’ He said: ‘Stay in your house, for Allah the Exalted will give you martyrdom.’” From then on, she was called “the martyr.”

The report says that she had learned the Qur’an, and that the Prophet ﷺ gave her permission to have a mu’adhdhin call to prayer for her. According to the report, he also told her to lead the people of her household in prayer. This is why she is cited by scholars who discuss whether a woman may lead other women, or in some views her household, in prayer.

The hadith is in Abu Dawud. Some scholars, including al-Albani, consider it hasan by its various routes, and others point to weakness in one narrator. The scholars have differed on what it allows. Many say that it shows that a woman may lead women in prayer, as ‘A’ishah and Umm Salamah are reported to have done. Some applied it to the house of Umm Waraqah only, and others take it more widely, including a household that has men in it who cannot recite. The majority of the schools allow a woman to lead other women, and it is a matter of discussion whether she could lead men.

It is told here as part of her biography, with the note that the ruling is discussed. What is not in doubt is that she had learned the Qur’an and was regarded as a person of knowledge, and the Prophet ﷺ visited her at home.

Umm Waraqah had two servants, a male and a female, whom she had promised to free upon her death. One night, they thought that they could not wait, and they strangled her with a cloth and ran away. This was in the caliphate of ‘Umar. The next morning, he heard her voice missing in the house, as she used to recite at night, and he said: “I think that the aunt has been done wrong.” He went to her house and found her dead.

Then he said: “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ spoke the truth. He used to say: ‘Come with us to visit the martyr.’” They searched, found the two servants and brought them. ‘Umar had them crucified or executed, and in the sources it is said that they were the first to be executed in Madinah in this way. The report of ‘Umar’s words is in the Tabaqat of Ibn Sa‘d.

Her story is one of a woman who stayed in her home, and whose reputation for the Qur’an and her place among the early Muslims was such that people remembered not only her knowledge but also what the Prophet ﷺ had said about her end. It is a reminder to those who feel left out of the large events that Allah’s ways of giving a reward are many.

facts: Jami‘ al-Bayan (the commentary on the Qur’an) and Tarikh ar-Rusul wa’l-Muluk (the history)
He founded a legal school of his own, the Jariri, which did not survive

t: His father, a man of some means, supported him in his first years. A report says that he dreamed that his son stood before the Prophet ﷺ with a bag of stones and was throwing them out of the way, and the dream-interpreters said that he would defend the religion. His father therefore encouraged him to learn. Al-Tabari went to Rayy to study hadith and history, and then he planned to go to Baghdad to study with Ahmad ibn Hanbal. But when he arrived in 241 AH, Ahmad had just died.

He did not turn back. He went on to Basra and Kufa, where he studied with the scholars of those cities, and to Syria and Egypt. In Egypt, he is said to have run out of money. A report in the biographies, which is not very well documented, says he sold the sleeves of his shirt to buy food, and that Allah later opened wealth to him. What is certain is that he lived frugally all his life, and that he kept to his books.

The best-known story is in al-Khatib’s history of Baghdad and in other works. Al-Tabari said to his students: “Are you ready to write a commentary on the Qur’an?” They said: “How long would it be?” He said: “Thirty thousand pages.” They said: “That would take a lifetime before it was finished.” He said: “Verily we belong to Allah! Ambitions have died!” And he shortened it to about three thousand pages. When he proposed to them a history of the world from Adam to his own day, he had the same conversation, and with the same result: he cut the thirty thousand to three thousand.

The commentary that came out, Jami‘ al-Bayan, is in about thirty volumes in its modern editions. It gathers the sayings of the Companions and the early scholars on each verse, with their chains, and then he gives his preferred opinion, with reasons. It became the base of everything that came after. The history, Tarikh ar-Rusul wa’l-Muluk, goes up to 302 AH, and is the main source for the early centuries of Islam.

His students said that he wrote forty pages every day for forty years. The estimate is based on the total of his works and may be an exaggeration, but it gives the sense of his steadiness. He ate simply, and lived without a household for much of his life, and he turned down offers of public office from the viziers. Reports say that when ministers offered him posts, including that of a judge, he refused them.

He was a man of independence and some pride. He held opinions that did not belong to any of the four schools that were taking shape, and had his own school of law. He was also in a conflict with some Hanbalis, who, according to reports, were angry with him, perhaps over a remark of his on the status of Ibn Hanbal as a jurist as opposed to a hadith scholar. The details are disputed.

He died in Shawwal 310 AH. The accounts say that he asked for an inkwell and paper shortly before his death, and when someone told him to rest, he said: “It is better that a man should not give up learning until he dies.” He then wrote a supplication, and died soon after. The story is in Yaqut’s dictionary of writers.

The funeral was difficult. A number of people had gathered at his house, and, according to some reports, the crowd was so large, or so unruly, that he was buried in his own house at night. It is a sad ending for a man who had given so much, but his books reached everyone. Later commentators, Ibn Kathir among them, drew on it constantly, and it is still the first reference for scholars who want to know how the earliest generations understood a verse.

facts: Nishapur, about 204–206 AH; died 25 Rajab 261 AH
Al-Musnad as-Sahih, known as Sahih Muslim
Included Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh and al-Bukhari

t: Nishapur, in northeastern Iran, was a centre of learning, and Muslim grew up in a family of scholars. He began to study hadith as a boy, and travelled to Iraq, the Hijaz, Syria and Egypt. His teachers included Yahya ibn Yahya an-Naysaburi, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh and many others, and from the age of about twenty he began to collect.

He says in the introduction to his book that he has arranged his collection with care, by putting the hadith that are more sure first, and then those that supplement them. He did not use chapter headings in the original, though later editors added them. He placed all the routes of a hadith together, so that a reader can compare. His own comment on the book, as reported in it, was: “Not everything that is sound in my view have I put here. I have put here only what the scholars agreed upon.”

In 250 AH, al-Bukhari arrived in Nishapur. Muslim, who had admired him from afar, attached himself to him. Al-Hakim reports that Muslim came to al-Bukhari, kissed him between the eyes, and said: “Let me kiss your feet, O master of the masters, leader of the hadith scholars, and physician of the hidden defects in hadith.” It is a report of deep respect between two men who were in different generations, and who have since been named together as the authors of the two Sahihs.

A dispute then arose in the city over whether one’s pronunciation of the Qur’an is created, and a leading scholar there, Muhammad ibn Yahya adh-Dhuhli, told people to avoid those who said it. Al-Bukhari was forced to leave. Muslim stood with al-Bukhari, and went to adh-Dhuhli, brought back all the manuscripts he had written from him, and put them on the back of a camel. He never narrated from him again.

s.h: The question he could not answer
t: Al-Hakim and others tell of the end. Muslim was at a gathering of scholars when someone asked him about a hadith. He did not know it. He went home and lit a lamp. He told his household that no one was to enter, and that he did not want to be disturbed. Someone said that a basket of dates had been given to them. He said: “Bring it to me.” They brought it, and he began to search for the hadith in his books while he ate from the basket, taking one date at a time.

He kept at it through the night. By morning, he had found the hadith, and the basket was empty. He had eaten so many dates that, according to the report, he became ill, and he died from it. It was said in later generations that he died from the pursuit of knowledge, which scholars have often described as a blessed death. The report is told by al-Hakim with a chain, and it is accepted in the biographies, though it is sometimes treated with caution. He died on 25 Rajab 261 AH, at around fifty-five, and was buried in Nasrabad, a suburb of Nishapur.

Sahih Muslim has about four thousand hadiths without repetition, in the main text. Scholars have praised it for its arrangement and its careful wording. Ibn as-Salah said that it was better arranged than al-Bukhari’s in one respect, since the different routes of a hadith are in one place. Al-Bukhari’s, he said, was stronger in the rigour of its conditions and in the depth of its legal remarks.

The ummah has accepted both books, and most scholars consider that what the two agree on is the most reliable of all the hadith. It is customary to say that a hadith is “in the two Sahihs” to mean that its strength is beyond question. Imam Muslim also left a method that students still learn, and a lesson in humility: that when he did not know, he went home and looked, and kept looking until the morning.

facts: Cairo, 773 AH; died in Cairo, Dhu al-Hijjah 852 AH
Fath al-Bari, commentary on Sahih al-Bukhari, in about 13 large volumes
Amir al-Mu’minin in hadith; chief judge of the Shafi‘is in Egypt
Al-Isabah, Tahdhib at-Tahdhib, Bulugh al-Maram, Lisan al-Mizan

t: Ibn Hajar’s father, ‘Ali, had been a merchant and a poet, and a man of some learning. When he died, he left the boy to the care of Zaki ad-Din al-Kharrubi, a wealthy trader of Egypt. His guardian saw to his education. At the age of five he entered a school and then memorised the Qur’an at nine, in Makkah. He went on to memorise a short book on the legal rulings of hadith, ‘Umdat al-Ahkam, and several other texts.

He was clever but not remarkable as a child. The biographers say that he progressed more slowly than his friends in the early years. He turned to poetry and to literature in his teens. It was only in his early twenties that he turned towards hadith, under the guidance of his teacher, Zayn ad-Din al-‘Iraqi, a distinguished scholar. He sat with al-‘Iraqi for about ten years, and learned the sciences of hadith under him.

Al-Sakhawi, Ibn Hajar’s student and his biographer, writes that his master used to tell this story. In the early period he found his studies hard, and he was ready to give them up. One day, as he was leaving the place, he was passing by a cave or a rock face in which water was dripping, and he noticed that the rock had been worn away by it. He said to himself: “If this soft water, with its constant dripping, can make a mark in a hard rock, then my effort must be able to make a mark in my own heart.” He went back, and persisted.

The anecdote is told by the biographers, and is not found in a hadith, but it was widely repeated by students of the generation after him. It carries something that the scholars hold dear, that the one who stays with a subject for long enough will master it. “He who keeps knocking will enter,” as the Arabic saying goes.

Ibn Hajar began to write his commentary on Sahih al-Bukhari in 817 AH, when he was in his early forties, and finished it in 842, a span of about twenty-five years. He dictated it in sessions to groups of students, and each session was followed by corrections. The result was a work in which he dealt with the text of each hadith, its chain, its linguistic points, and the legal conclusions of the scholars. He aimed at completeness and precision.

When it was finished, al-Sakhawi and others report, a gathering was held for its completion, at which hundreds of scholars and officials attended. The reading was concluded and Ibn Hajar spent a large sum on a feast. The figure given is five hundred dinars. It was said that the book was valued at three hundred dinars when a copy was sent to a ruler in the East. The figures are reported by his students, and the accuracy is not certain, but they are an index of the esteem in which it was held.

Ibn Hajar served as the chief judge of the Shafi‘is in Egypt for about twenty-one years, with several breaks, and was a figure of authority in Cairo. He was known for his wit and for the clarity of his memory. He dictated his books at set times, taught hadith in a number of colleges, and trained many students, among them al-Sakhawi, who wrote his biography.

He died in Cairo in Dhu al-Hijjah of 852 AH, after an illness. The funeral was said to have been attended by a very large crowd, including the sultan and the caliph of the time. A remark often quoted about his book, attributed to ash-Shawkani, is “there is no hijrah after the conquest,” a play on the title (fath means conquest) and on the Prophet’s words about Makkah. It means that after Fath al-Bari, no one needs to travel in search of a better commentary on al-Bukhari.

facts: Near Busra, about 701 AH; Damascus, 774 AH
Tafsir al-Qur’an al-‘Azim and al-Bidayah wa’n-Nihayah
Ibn Taymiyyah, al-Mizzi, adh-Dhahabi and others
The daughter of his teacher al-Mizzi

t: After his father’s death in his third year, his brother ‘Abd al-Wahhab took him to Damascus in about 706 AH. There he learned the Qur’an, at about ten, and studied the books of hadith and law. He was a student in the Shafi‘i school, but later also studied hadith with the great scholars of the time.

His most important teachers were Ibn Taymiyyah, whom he accompanied closely, and al-Mizzi, the famous critic of narrators, whose daughter he married. He also studied with adh-Dhahabi, the historian of the Muslims. When Ibn Taymiyyah was imprisoned in the Citadel of Damascus in 726 AH, Ibn Kathir was among those who loved and defended him, and he was later criticised for it.

His commentary starts with a plain statement of the method. The best way to explain the Qur’an, he says, is by the Qur’an itself, since what is stated briefly in one place is stated at length in another. Then by the Sunnah, since it is an explanation of the Qur’an. Then by the sayings of the Companions, who saw the revelation and knew the context, and then by the Successors. He says that he will quote the chains of narrators for what he reports, and will say what he thinks is stronger.

In practice, this means that for each verse he lists the other verses on the same theme, then the relevant hadith, then the sayings of the Companions, and finally comments on points of language. He is careful about stories drawn from the People of the Book. He often says: “This is from Isra’iliyyat, and we narrate it for reference, not as proof,” and, at times, he warns that an account is unlikely to be true.

Ibn Kathir’s al-Bidayah wa’n-Nihayah, “The Beginning and the End,” starts with the creation, and the story of the prophets, goes through the life of the Prophet ﷺ and the history of the Muslims to about 767 AH, and then covers the signs of the Last Hour and the Day of Judgement. It is the longest of its kind and a source for the Mamluk period, which he lived through.

Unlike some historians, he made it a point to distinguish between the reports that are solid and those that are not, and he said so in the text. He also added an account of Mongol invasions from the point of view of one who lived in Damascus, which had suffered from them. His writings are consulted today by both Muslims and non-Muslim historians.

He held teaching posts in Damascus, including the Umm Salih school and, later, the Dar al-Hadith al-Ashrafiyyah. He taught for years, and wrote a number of other works, including a short book on the science of hadith.

At the end of his life, his eyesight failed, and the biographers say that this was from working late at night on his book on hadith, the Jami‘ al-Masanid. He died in Sha‘ban 774 AH, in Damascus, and was buried next to Ibn Taymiyyah, as he had asked, in the cemetery of the Sufis. He had lived about seventy-three years. His book on the Qur’an has gone into more homes than almost any other, and its simple, trustworthy method has made it a first stop for Muslims who wish to understand a verse.

facts: Cordoba, about 600 AH; Minya, Upper Egypt, 9 Shawwal 671 AH
Al-Jami‘ li-Ahkam al-Qur’an and at-Tadhkirah fi Ahwal al-Mawta wa Umur al-Akhirah
Cordoba fell to Castile in 1236 CE (633 AH)

t: Cordoba had been the city of ‘Abd ar-Rahman III, with its great mosque, the palace of Madinat az-Zahra’ and a library that was famous in Europe. By al-Qurtubi’s lifetime its glory had faded, but it was still a home of scholars. In 633 AH (1236 CE), King Ferdinand III of Castile took the city, and the great mosque was made into a cathedral.

Al-Qurtubi was in his thirties by that time, and he had already studied with the scholars of Andalusia, including Abu al-‘Abbas al-Qurtubi, who wrote a summary of Sahih Muslim. He left for the East, and eventually travelled through Egypt. Like many refugees from Andalusia, he found that scholars of the east welcomed him.

He settled in Minya, on the east bank of the Nile in Upper Egypt, which at that time was a quiet place. He taught there, and wrote his large commentary, al-Jami‘ li-Ahkam al-Qur’an, which is also called Tafsir al-Qurtubi. He says that his purpose was to write a commentary based on the rulings, explaining the legal matters of each verse and the reasons for the differing opinions of the scholars.

The work is long, in about twenty volumes today. For each verse that has a legal ruling, he lists the points of law, quotes from Maliki, Shafi‘i, Hanafi and Hanbali scholars, and gives the evidence for each. He also explains the language and the readings, and tells the circumstances of revelation. He is open about his sources, and gave credit where it was due, which he said was part of the blessing of knowledge: “It is part of the blessing of knowledge to attribute a saying to the one who said it.”

He also wrote a book of a very different kind, at-Tadhkirah, “The Reminder, on the states of the dead and the matters of the Hereafter.” It collects the verses and hadiths on death, the grave, the Resurrection, the Reckoning, the Bridge, Paradise and the Fire. It was written to help readers prepare their hearts, and it is one of the main sources for later books on the subject.

The two books reflect two parts of al-Qurtubi: the jurist who was careful with the details of law, and the believer who wished to remind people of the end. He is described by the biographers as a man of devotion, simple in dress, and so busy with worship and writing that he spent his days between them.

He died in Minya in Shawwal 671 AH (1273 CE), and was buried there. His tomb is still pointed out, and there is a mosque near it which bears his name. He never saw Cordoba again. The fall of the city, which must have been a great grief, led to his work as a teacher, and to the book that is among the most widely used references in Islamic law and Qur’anic scholarship today.

There is also a gentle detail: at the start of his commentary, he gave the reason for writing. He said that he wished to write a work that would be a memory for himself, a means of drawing near to Allah and a source of guidance for others. In a life that had been broken by the loss of a city, he built something that was passed on.

facts: Khurasan, about 105 AH; Makkah, Muharram 187 AH
Reported to have been a highway robber between Abiward and Sarakhs
Studied in Kufa, then lived near the Haram in Makkah
His fear of Allah, his weeping, and his teaching in the Sacred Mosque

t: Adh-Dhahabi, quoting earlier sources, writes that al-Fudayl was “a highway robber between Abiward and Sarakhs.” One night he planned to go to a girl he loved, and he was climbing a wall to reach her. At that moment someone in a nearby house was reciting the verse: “Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humbly submit to the remembrance of Allah?” (57:16).

He stopped on the wall and said: “Yes, my Lord, the time has come.” He came down and left. The account in the biographies says that he spent the night in a ruin. In it was a caravan resting, and he heard some of the travellers saying: “Let us go on.” Others said: “Let us wait until morning, for al-Fudayl is on the road and will rob us.” He said to himself: “I am doing wrong at night and these Muslims are afraid of me. I do not think that Allah has led me here except to make me stop.” He said: “O Allah, I repent to You, and I have made my home in Your Sacred House.”

He went to Kufa and studied hadith with its scholars, among them al-A‘mash, Mansur ibn al-Mu‘tamir and Hisham ibn Hassan. He then moved to Makkah, where he lived near the Haram until his death. He taught there to the people who came for pilgrimage, and among his students were ash-Shafi‘i and ‘Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak. Ibn al-Mubarak wrote to him in verse from the battlefield.

The scholars of hadith accepted him as a trustworthy narrator, and his collection of sayings, mostly on fear of Allah, trust, and avoidance of the world, was widely read. He was known to be someone who cried at the mention of Allah and the Hereafter, and who kept the company of the poor.

The caliph Harun ar-Rashid is reported to have asked to see him. When Fudayl came, the caliph said: “How I wish I had your calm.” In one version, Fudayl reminded him of the weight of the office and told him to fear Allah, and Harun wept. The reports of the details vary, and different versions are told, but they agree on the main point: that Fudayl did not flatter rulers.

It is reported that he said: “If I knew that I had a single accepted supplication, I would make it for the ruler, because if the ruler is sound, the people and the land are sound.” This was a sign that his fear of rulers was not hostility. He wished for good for the whole community.
One of his sayings, often quoted, is: “Leaving a deed for the sake of people is showing off, and doing it for the sake of people is polytheism, and sincerity is when Allah saves you from both.”

He died in Makkah in Muharram 187 AH, after a long illness. The story of how he began, a man who climbed a wall to do wrong and heard a verse, is retold by preachers to people who believe they have gone too far to turn back. They say to such people what the verse said to him: that the time has come.

facts: August 636 CE (Rajab 15 AH), over about six days
The Yarmouk river, near the present borders of Syria, Jordan and Israel
Abu ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, with Khalid ibn al-Walid in the field
The Byzantine army sent by Heraclius

t: When the Byzantines were reported to be gathering a huge army, Abu ‘Ubaydah decided to withdraw from several of the towns the Muslims had taken, such as Hims, and to concentrate his forces. He told the governor to return the taxes that had been collected from the people, and he wrote: “We took these taxes from you for protecting you, and now we cannot. We return them to you.” The people of Hims, according to al-Baladhuri, said: “May Allah bring you back to us, and may He give you victory over them.”

The Muslims gathered at the plain of Yarmouk. The sources differ on the numbers. Some say there were around 25,000 to 40,000 Muslims and 100,000 or more Byzantines; modern historians suggest the real figures were much smaller on both sides, though the Byzantine force was clearly larger. The Muslim leaders wrote to ‘Umar for help, and he sent reinforcements from Iraq.

The command lay with Abu ‘Ubaydah, but, according to the sources, he asked Khalid ibn al-Walid to organise the battle, because Khalid had experience of the Roman and Persian ways of fighting. Khalid divided the army into small regiments, many of them, in place of the usual single block, so that they could support each other and not be broken as one. He kept a mobile force of cavalry under his own command.

The Byzantine army was a mix of Armenians, Slavs, Arabs of the Ghassanid tribes and Byzantine troops. They reportedly marched with chains linking some of their soldiers to prevent them from fleeing, which suggests the way the battle was understood by the Muslims: as an army that could not retreat. The two sides fought for days along the plain, with the Byzantines pressing and the Muslims holding.

The accounts of at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report a moving scene on one of the days. ‘Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, the son of the man who had been one of the Prophet’s worst enemies and who fought at Uhud and the Trench, now stood among the Muslims. He is said to have called out: “I fought the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in many places. Shall I run away from you today?” He called for volunteers to pledge to fight until death. Several hundred are said to have given the pledge, and many of them, including ‘Ikrimah and his son, died of wounds.

The report is part of the traditional account, and it is found in biographical works as well as histories. Even if the details are shaped by retelling, it expresses something that the early Muslims valued: that a man could have been an enemy of the Prophet ﷺ and could later give his life for him, for a cause he had opposed.

On the final day, a dust storm is said to have blown into the faces of the Byzantines. The Muslim cavalry under Khalid cut off their cavalry from the infantry and drove them back. The Byzantine infantry, pushed against the edge of the ravine of the Yarmouk, panicked. Many fell into the gorge. The historians describe it as a rout.

The Byzantine army was destroyed, and Heraclius, who was in Antioch, is said to have left Syria with the words: “Peace be upon you, Syria, a farewell from one who will not return.” The words are reported by later writers and may be legendary. What is certain is that Syria was lost to Byzantium, that Damascus, Jerusalem and Antioch passed into Muslim hands within a few years, and that the people of the region, many of whom were tired of the Byzantine taxes and persecutions of dissenting Christians, mostly accepted the change.

facts: Rajab 92 AH (April 711 CE), landing; battle in Ramadan (July 711)
About 7,000 at the start, reinforced by a further 5,000
Guadalete (Wadi Lakka), in the south of Spain

s.h: A governor, a freedman and a request
t: Musa ibn Nusayr was the governor of Ifriqiya for the Umayyad caliph al-Walid I in Damascus. He had conquered much of North Africa, and was based in Qayrawan. His lieutenant, Tariq ibn Ziyad, was a Berber who governed Tangier. Between them lay a few miles of sea and the far shore of a country ruled by the Visigoths, who were divided by quarrels over the crown.

Some sources tell that a Visigothic noble, called Julian in the Latin and Arabic tradition, who held the area of Ceuta, had a grievance against the king Roderic and encouraged the Muslims to attack. The story of Julian and his daughter is told in several versions and is considered legendary by many modern scholars. What is likely is that factions in Spain made it easier for the Muslims to enter.

In the spring of 711, Tariq crossed with a force of about seven thousand men in ships that had been provided by Julian or by other local help. They landed near the rock that now carries his name. Musa sent reinforcements, bringing his strength up to around twelve thousand. They were mostly Berbers, who had recently accepted Islam and were fighting alongside their Arab commanders.

Roderic, who was fighting a rebellion in the north, hurried south with a large army. The two armies met at the river Guadalete, near the modern city of Jerez, in Ramadan 92 AH (July 711 CE). The Muslims were outnumbered, and the battle lasted several days. Roderic’s forces broke when some of his nobles are said to have left the field. The king himself disappeared and was not seen again.

The speech attributed to Tariq is among the best-known passages in Arabic history writing: “O people, where can you flee? The sea is behind you and the enemy is in front of you. By Allah, you have nothing but your courage and your patience.” It goes on to promise them that the enemy’s towns will be rich prizes. Some versions say that he burned the ships to remove any thought of retreat.

The speech and the burning appear in sources written several centuries after the event, the best known being al-Maqqari’s Nafh at-Tib, in the seventeenth century. The earlier historians do not mention them. Many modern scholars regard them as later embellishment, which reflects how the Muslims of later times wanted to imagine the beginning of their history in Spain. It is a good example of how legend grows around a real event.

The Muslim forces went on to take Cordoba, and Tariq himself marched to Toledo, the capital of the Visigoths. In 712 CE, Musa himself came with another army of about eighteen thousand and took more towns. The speed of the conquest, in which the whole peninsula except for the mountainous north was taken in a few years, is one of the extraordinary episodes in history.

In 714, the caliph called both Musa and Tariq back to Damascus. What happened to Tariq afterwards is unclear, and the sources say little: that he lived on obscurely in the East. The land that he opened, al-Andalus, lasted for nearly eight centuries as a Muslim land, and it produced some of the most celebrated scholars, scientists and poets of the Islamic world.

facts: ‘Ayn Jalut, the Spring of Goliath, near Beisan in the Jezreel valley
A Mamluk victory; Syria returned to Muslim rule

s.h: The fall of Baghdad and what followed
t: The destruction of Baghdad in February 1258 shook the Muslim world. The city had been the seat of the caliphs for five hundred years. Hulagu’s army killed a very large number of its people, burned many of its libraries, and executed the caliph al-Musta‘sim. Many Muslims felt that no power could stand against the Mongols.

In 1260, they crossed into Syria. Aleppo fell in January, and Damascus surrendered in March. The Mongol army was commanded in Syria by Kitbuqa, a Nestorian Christian, as Hulagu had had to withdraw most of his forces to the east because of the death of the Great Khan Mongke, and he left a smaller force behind. It was still formidable. The envoys of the Mongols came to Cairo and told Qutuz to submit or be destroyed.

Qutuz was a Mamluk, a former slave soldier, who had taken power in Egypt in 1259, in the face of the Mongol danger. The accounts say that he called a council of the emirs, and that some of them wanted to wait. He said, according to al-Maqrizi: “O emirs of the Muslims, you have long eaten from the treasury, and you dislike the war. I am going out, and whoever wishes to join me will do so, and whoever does not may go home. Allah sees whoever stays behind, and the sin of the women of the Muslims will be on the necks of those who stay.”

The scholar al-‘Izz ibn ‘Abd as-Salam, the great jurist of Cairo, is reported to have given a legal opinion that allowed the sultan to raise funds for the army from the emirs’ own wealth before asking anything from the people. The reports differ in the details, but they agree that the religious scholars gave their support.

The Mamluk army marched through Gaza, where the Mongols were not expecting it, and Baybars, who led the advance guard, took the lead. The two armies met in the Jezreel valley, by a spring named after Goliath, the giant killed by Dawud. The name is part of the tradition, since the Qur’an mentions Jalut. The Mamluks used a feint: Baybars’s forces fell back, drawing the Mongol army forward into a place where the main Mamluk force was hidden in the hills.

The Mongols charged, as was their way, and the Mamluks held. According to Ibn Taghribirdi, at one point the left flank wavered, and Qutuz threw off his helmet so that the soldiers could see him and cried out: “Wa Islamah!” “O Islam!” and charged. The Mongol army was broken and Kitbuqa was killed or captured and executed. It was the first time a Mongol army of that size had been decisively beaten in battle.

The Mamluks pushed the Mongols out of Syria, and Damascus and Aleppo were retaken within weeks. Qutuz did not live to enjoy the victory. In October, on his way back to Egypt, he was killed by a group of emirs, among them, according to most accounts, Baybars, who became sultan. The two had quarrelled over a promised governorship in Syria.

The battle halted the Mongol advance in the west. Egypt and the Hijaz, with the holy cities, were spared. Within a few decades, the Mongols of Persia became Muslims, and some of the greatest patrons of Islamic culture came from among them. Historians debate how decisive the battle was, since the Mongols were distracted by their own wars, but for the Muslims of the time it was a deliverance, and Ramadan 658 is still remembered.

facts: Mansa Musa I of Mali, who reigned about 1312–1337
In July 1324, where he stayed for several months
Scholars and architects he brought back strengthened Timbuktu and Gao

t: Mali was one of the great states of West Africa, founded in the thirteenth century by Sundiata Keita. Its wealth came from gold, mined in the south, and from the trade across the Sahara, in salt, copper and goods. Its rulers had been Muslims for generations, but Mansa Musa made the faith a central part of the identity of the state. “Mansa” means king.

Musa’s journey was a pilgrimage, and like any pilgrim he went to perform the rites, but his position as the king of a rich land made it a public event. He travelled with a large retinue. The sources do not agree on the numbers. Al-‘Umari, who heard from Egyptians who saw it, says that he had around twelve thousand servants dressed in silk brocade, and that a hundred camels each carried about three hundred pounds of gold. Others say that the caravan numbered sixty thousand people. The figures may be exaggerated, but all agree that it was enormous.

Al-‘Umari relates that when the king reached Cairo, the Mamluk sultan, an-Nasir Muhammad, wanted him to kiss the ground before him, as was the custom. Mansa Musa refused, saying that he prostrated only to Allah. After some persuasion, he bowed in a way that avoided it. The sultan received him with respect.

During his stay in Cairo, Mansa Musa and his men spent and gave gold freely. They bought gifts, paid for whatever they wanted, and handed out money to the poor and to officials. The flood of gold into a small market lowered its value. Al-‘Umari, who visited Cairo in about 1336, said that the price of gold had fallen and had not recovered in twelve years, and that people there still spoke of him with praise. The story shows how much was given, and has been repeated ever since.

On the way back, Mansa Musa persuaded a number of scholars and craftsmen to return with him. Among them, according to Ibn Khaldun, was a poet and architect from Andalusia named Abu Ishaq as-Sahili, who built, in Mali, a number of buildings in a new style, including a palace and, it is said, a mosque. Later tradition links him to the Great Mosque of Timbuktu, the Djinguereber, though the evidence is not clear.

The king also brought back books and scholars of the Maliki school. Under him and his successors, Timbuktu grew into one of the great centres of Islamic learning, with the mosque of Sankore as a school, and a trade in manuscripts. The Timbuktu manuscripts, which survived in family collections, now number hundreds of thousands, and they include works on law, astronomy, medicine and history.

The Catalan Atlas, drawn in Majorca in about 1375, shows a king seated on a throne, wearing a golden crown and holding a gold nugget, with a caption that calls him the lord of the black people of Guinea and the richest and most noble king of his land. It is a portrait of Mansa Musa, made in Europe fifty years after his journey, and it shows how far the news of his wealth had travelled.

It would be wrong to remember him only for gold. He is called by the chronicles a just man and a pious one, who sent gifts to the poor of the holy cities, and who is said to have spent so much on his journey that he had to borrow for the return. It is a picture of a ruler who understood the pilgrimage as an act of devotion that also brought his people into the world of Islamic scholarship.

facts: Basra, about 965 CE; Cairo, about 1040 CE
Kitab al-Manazir (The Book of Optics), in seven books
Alhazen or Alhacen; the Latin Opticae thesaurus was influential on Kepler and others
Controlled experiments to test theories of light and sight

t: Al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham grew up in Basra and worked for a time as an administrator, and studied mathematics, physics and philosophy. He then moved to Egypt, which was under the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim. The old biographies, such as that of Ibn Abi Usaybi‘ah, say that he had boasted that he could regulate the Nile floods, and that the caliph invited him to do it.

When he reached Aswan and examined the river, he realised that the project was not possible with the means available. He returned to Cairo, and, afraid of the caliph’s anger, pretended to be mad until al-Hakim’s death in 1021. During those years he lived in a kind of confinement. The story is reported in later biographies, and historians treat it with caution, but it is the traditional account of how he ended up at leisure to write.

Between 1011 and 1021, in seven books, he wrote Kitab al-Manazir. The first books are about the nature of light and vision. He showed that light travels in straight lines, that it comes from a source, reflects from objects and enters the eye, which acts as a receiver. He described the eye’s parts and tried to explain how an image forms in it. He did not get everything right, since he believed the lens was the place where vision happens. But the central idea, that vision depends on light entering the eye, was a breakthrough.

To support his claims, he used experiments. In one, he made a dark room with a small hole in one wall and observed that the light from outside formed an inverted image on the opposite wall, which showed that light moves in straight lines. This is a camera obscura. He used it to discuss how images form. The second part of the book deals with perception: how we judge distance, size, shape and movement, and how illusions occur. He explained that the moon seems larger near the horizon because of the way the mind judges size with respect to distance.

In another book, Ibn al-Haytham wrote “Doubts Concerning Ptolemy,” in which he pointed out contradictions in Ptolemy’s works on astronomy and optics. His position was that one should respect great authorities but not follow them blindly. In the introduction he wrote that the seeker of the truth is not the one who studies the writings of the ancients and, following his natural disposition, puts his trust in them, but rather the one who suspects his faith in them and questions what he gathers from them.

This approach, of testing everything by reason and experiment, is one of the reasons that historians of science credit him as a founder of the experimental method. He lived in a culture that held the Qur’an’s call to reflect and observe in the highest regard, and he is reported to have said that he found no way of drawing closer to Allah than seeking truth and knowledge.

The Book of Optics was translated into Latin in about 1200, and it was influential on European scientists, such as Roger Bacon, John Pecham and Witelo. In the seventeenth century, Johannes Kepler used it in his studies on the eye and the telescope. The name Alhazen, a Latin version of his first name, was well known to scholars of the Renaissance.

He wrote many other works, on astronomy, mathematics and philosophy, and is credited with some two hundred titles, though only some of them have survived.
