He is said to have supported himself by copying books, such as Euclid’s Elements and the Almagest, and selling them, and he died in Cairo around 1040. A crater on the moon has been named after him, and in 2015, the United Nations marked the International Year of Light, with Ibn al-Haytham remembered as one of its pioneers.

facts: Madinat az-Zahra’ near Cordoba, about 936 CE; died about 1013 CE
Kitab at-Tasrif, an encyclopaedia of medicine in 30 parts
Translated by Gerard of Cremona in the twelfth century as Liber Servitoris, or Chirurgia

t: Al-Zahrawi lived through the high point of Islamic Spain. The caliph ‘Abd ar-Rahman III had built Madinat az-Zahra’ in the hills above Cordoba, and its libraries and workshops drew scholars. Al-Zahrawi served the caliphs, and had a practice among the people of the city. The biographies say that he treated the poor without charge and asked for no fees from them.

He wrote in the preface to his book that he undertook to write down what he had learned from his own practice, so that others could use it. He said that the doctors of his day had neglected surgery, and that knowledge of the craft had been lost. He wanted to revive it and to teach it.

Kitab at-Tasrif li-man ‘ajaza ‘an at-ta’lif, which means “the arrangement of medical knowledge for one who is not able to compile it,” was a thirty-part collection. The first parts dealt with general medicine, drugs, preparations and diet. But the thirtieth, on surgery, was distinct. It is divided into three sections: cautery, operations such as cutting and bleeding, and the treatment of fractures and dislocations.

He described how to use cautery for different conditions, how to treat wounds, how to remove stones from the bladder, how to extract teeth, how to deal with abscesses and hernias, and the delivery of difficult births. He insisted that the surgeon should know anatomy well, and he warned that a physician who does not understand it will do harm. He used catgut for stitching internal wounds, and described the tying of blood vessels to prevent bleeding.

What made the surgical part famous was its illustrations. He drew about two hundred instruments, including scalpels, forceps, probes, hooks, saws, cauteries, specula and dental tools, and described each, along with how to use it. Some were of his own design. This was a new feature in medical writing. A surgeon in Europe, who could read the Latin translation, could see exactly what the Cordoban surgeon used.

The drawings showed a high degree of specialisation. There are instruments for the ear, the throat and the eye, and for the dissection of the bladder. He recommended that the instruments be made of fine steel, and that they be kept clean. He also stressed attention to the patient: that the surgeon should be calm, should explain what he was going to do, and should refuse to operate on cases that he thought hopeless, to avoid false hope and disgrace.

In the twelfth century, Gerard of Cremona translated the thirtieth part into Latin in Toledo, a city that had passed to the Christians in 1085. It became one of the main textbooks of surgery in the medical schools of Europe, and was used into the sixteenth century. Surgeons like Guy de Chauliac in the fourteenth century quote him often, under the name Albucasis.

The man who wrote it was known in his own time for his modesty. A tradition says that he lived to a great age and died around 1013, when the Umayyad caliphate in Cordoba was being torn by civil war. His works survived, and the surgical tools he drew can be seen in modern museums as a record of a mind that combined skill, observation and care for patients.

facts: Khwarazm (in Central Asia), about 780 CE; Baghdad, about 850 CE
The House of Wisdom, under the caliph al-Ma’mun
Algebra (from al-jabr) and algorithm (from his name)

t: Al-Khwarizmi was from Khwarazm, a region south of the Aral Sea. He came to Baghdad in the time of the caliph al-Ma’mun, who supported scholars and had a library and observatory in the city. Greek, Persian and Sanskrit works were being translated into Arabic. Al-Khwarizmi worked in this environment, and his writings show that he learned from all these traditions.

He wrote on astronomy and geography. His astronomical tables, a zij, were based on Indian and Greek methods, and he is credited with a book on the shape of the earth that gave the coordinates of cities and places. But he is best known for two books on mathematics.

In his introduction, he says that the caliph encouraged him to write a short work on calculation by restoring and balancing, containing what is easiest and most useful in arithmetic, “such as men constantly require in cases of inheritance, legacies, partition, lawsuits and trade, and in all their dealings with one another, or where the measuring of lands, the digging of canals, geometrical computations, and other objects of various sorts and kinds are concerned.”

Al-jabr means to restore or complete: moving a subtracted quantity from one side of an equation to the other so that it becomes added. Al-muqabalah means to balance: cancelling equal quantities from both sides. The book gives a systematic treatment of equations, which he sorted into six types, for example “squares equal roots,” “squares plus roots equal numbers.” For each, he gave a method of solution and explained it with a geometrical figure, as in completing the square.

His other great contribution was a book on the use of Indian numerals, with the place value and the zero. The Arabic original is lost, but a Latin translation survives, beginning with the words “Dixit Algorizmi,” “Al-Khwarizmi said.” This book, which spread the decimal system of ten digits to Europe, led to the term “algorism” for calculating by those numerals, and eventually to “algorithm” for any step-by-step procedure.

It is worth noting what he did not do. He did not invent the numbers, which came from India, and the ideas in algebra had precedents in Babylonian and Greek mathematics. His contribution was to make them into a clear, general and teachable method, written in a language that was open to all. As a result, his book became the foundation of a discipline.

In the twelfth century, the book of al-jabr was translated into Latin by Robert of Chester in 1145 and by Gerard of Cremona. It was one of the sources through which European mathematicians learned algebra. It was used in universities for centuries. Words that European languages inherited from the Arabic of this field include algebra and algorithm, and many mathematical terms.

Al-Khwarizmi died around 850 CE. He is remembered with the other scholars of the House of Wisdom as someone who took knowledge from many sources and gave it a new life. It is a story that is a reminder that the learning of the Muslim world was part of a wider human heritage, and that the Qur’an’s call to reflect and to calculate, in matters from inheritance to the stars, found a response in the work of people like him.

facts: Near Bukhara, about 980 CE; Hamadan, June 1037 CE
Al-Qanun fi’t-Tibb (The Canon of Medicine) and Kitab ash-Shifa’ (The Book of Healing)
Gerard of Cremona translated the Canon in the twelfth century

t: Ibn Sina’s father was a tax official from Balkh, and the family had settled near Bukhara, then a great centre of learning under the Samanids. He says in his autobiography, quoted by his student al-Juzjani, that by the age of ten he had learned the Qur’an and much of Arabic literature. His father had him study Indian arithmetic with a greengrocer, geometry and logic with a visiting teacher, and then he continued on his own.

He turned to medicine when he was about sixteen, and found it a lighter subject than others. “Medicine is not one of the hard sciences,” he says, “and I soon surpassed my teachers in it, and physicians began to read medicine with me.” He also treated patients, and learned by seeing. At seventeen he was called to the court to treat Nuh ibn Mansur, the Samanid emir, and cured him. As a reward, he asked for access to the royal library.

s.h: The book he read forty times
t: Ibn Sina studied logic, geometry and physics by himself, but he could not understand Aristotle’s Metaphysics. He says: “I read it forty times until I had memorised it, but I still could not understand what the author meant. I despaired of it and said to myself: this is a book that cannot be understood.”

One afternoon he was in the booksellers’ market, when a dealer offered him a book. He did not want it, and refused. But the man pressed him, saying that it was cheap, only three dirhams, and that the owner needed the money. He bought it. It was a work by al-Farabi on the aims of the Metaphysics. He went home and read it, and, he says, “the purposes of the book became clear to me, for I already had it by heart.” He was so pleased that the next day he gave a sum in charity to the poor in thanks to Allah.

After the fall of the Samanids, he travelled through Persia, serving as a physician and vizier to different rulers. In the middle of this restless life, he wrote his great works. Al-Qanun fi’t-Tibb, the Canon of Medicine, is in five books: general principles, simple drugs, diseases by organ, general diseases such as fevers, and compound medicines. It is clear, organised, and based on the Greek tradition of Galen and Hippocrates, with his own additions and the results of his clinical experience.

Among its features was the idea that diseases can be spread by contact and that some are carried through water and soil. He described the symptoms of many conditions, including meningitis, and he gave rules for testing a new drug: it should be free of impurities, should be used on a disease that it is suited to, and should be tried on different patients. The Canon was used in medical colleges in Europe until the seventeenth century.

In 1037, while travelling with the ruler of Isfahan, Ibn Sina became ill with a severe colic. His servants, according to al-Juzjani, gave him too many treatments, and he reached Hamadan weak. He is said to have told his students that his physician’s regimen had failed. When he realised that he was dying, he gave away his money to the poor, freed his slaves, and listened to the recitation of the Qur’an, finishing it every three days.

He died in Ramadan 428 AH, in Hamadan, where his tomb is still. His works on philosophy and medicine were studied for centuries, and the Latin world knew him as Avicenna, one of the greatest authorities. In the East, he was called ash-Shaykh ar-Ra’is, “the leading master.”

facts: Al-Andalus from 756 CE; the caliphate from 929 CE
Begun by ‘Abd ar-Rahman I in 785 CE and extended several times

t: ‘Abd ar-Rahman I, a survivor of the Umayyad family when the Abbasids took the caliphate in Damascus, came to Spain in 756 and founded an emirate with Cordoba as its capital. He began the Great Mosque in 785 on the site of a church that had been shared by Muslims and Christians. It was enlarged by later rulers, including ‘Abd ar-Rahman II, al-Hakam II and al-Mansur.

The mosque is known for its prayer hall, a forest of columns topped by double arches of red and white stone, and for its mihrab, decorated with gold mosaics. The columns, of which hundreds survive, were largely taken from Roman and Visigothic buildings. The prayer hall reflects the early Muslims’ practice of using the best of existing materials and giving them a new order.

In 929, ‘Abd ar-Rahman III, whose power had grown, took the title of caliph. He built Madinat az-Zahra’, a palace-city a few miles west of Cordoba, which, according to the chroniclers, took twenty-five years to build and employed thousands of workers. It had audience halls, gardens, a mosque and a mint. Foreign ambassadors, from Byzantium, Germany and elsewhere, were received there with great ceremony.

The city of Cordoba itself was famous. The chroniclers describe wide streets, many mosques and baths, and a system of water supply. Population estimates range widely, from a hundred thousand to half a million. Some later writers say that the streets were paved and lit at night, which, if true, would have been very unusual in Europe. The truth lies partly in praise by those who lived there and partly in the reports of visitors.

Al-Hakam II, who ruled from 961 to 976, was a lover of books. He sent agents to buy and copy manuscripts in Baghdad, Cairo and Damascus. His library, in the palace, is said to have held four hundred thousand volumes, with a catalogue of forty-four volumes. The number is probably an overstatement by later writers, but the library was certainly very large.

The city produced or hosted a long line of figures: the physician al-Zahrawi, the poet and jurist Ibn Hazm, the philosopher Ibn Rushd (Averroes), and the Jewish philosopher Maimonides, who was born in Cordoba in 1135, and the musician Ziryab, who introduced fashions in dress and food. Muslims, Jews and Christians took part in its intellectual life, with translations between Arabic, Hebrew and Latin.

The caliphate broke up in a civil war in the early eleventh century, and Madinat az-Zahra’ was sacked in 1010. Cordoba remained an important city under later dynasties, but power moved to Seville and Granada. In 1236, after a siege, King Ferdinand III of Castile took it. The great mosque became a cathedral, a role it still keeps.

The city’s scholars left, as al-Qurtubi did, and took what they had to other lands, from Egypt to Morocco. The memory of Cordoba remained in poetry, in the names of families, and in the buildings that survive. The mosque-cathedral is visited by millions of people each year. It is a reminder of an age when Muslims were the guardians of learning in the west of Europe, and when that learning travelled in both directions.

facts: Julaybib, a man of the Ansar (some say of Banu Thaslabah)
The Prophet ﷺ asked a man of the Ansar for his daughter’s hand on Julaybib’s behalf
He killed seven men before being killed
“He is from me and I am from him”

t: Anas reports in the Musnad of Ahmad that the Prophet ﷺ went to a man of the Ansar and asked for his daughter in marriage. The man said: “Gladly, O Messenger of Allah, and it is a blessing.” The Prophet ﷺ said: “I am not asking her for myself.” “Then for whom?” “For Julaybib.” The man said: “O Messenger of Allah, let me consult her mother.”

He went to his wife and told her, and she said: “Julaybib? By Allah, we will not marry her to Julaybib.” The man was going to go back to the Prophet ﷺ to tell him this when the girl, who had been listening from inside, said: “Who has asked you for me?” Her mother told her. She said: “Do you reject the request of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ? Send me to him, for he will not let me be ruined.”

Her father went to the Prophet ﷺ and said: “If you are pleased with him, then we are pleased.” The Prophet ﷺ said: “I am pleased with him.” The marriage was made. The Prophet ﷺ prayed for the girl: “O Allah, pour good upon her, and do not make her life one of hardship.” The words of this prayer are in the report, and Anas adds that she became one of the most generous spenders among the women of the Ansar.

It is easy to see what the Prophet ﷺ was doing. A man without rank or looks would have been passed over by most families. By asking for him as his own representative, he gave him standing, and by praying for the bride, he gave a blessing to the household. The girl’s faith in his judgement was the thing that made it work.

Some time later, Julaybib went with the Prophet ﷺ on an expedition. Abu Barzah al-Aslami reports in Sahih Muslim that after the battle, the Prophet ﷺ asked his Companions: “Do you miss anyone?” They said: “So-and-so, and so-and-so.” He asked again: “Do you miss anyone?” They named others. He asked once more, and they said: “No.” The Prophet ﷺ said: “But I miss Julaybib. Look for him.”

They searched among the dead and found him next to seven of the enemy whom he had killed, and then he had been killed. The Prophet ﷺ stood over him and said: “He killed seven and then they killed him. He is from me and I am from him. He is from me and I am from him.” He repeated it two or three times.
Then the Prophet ﷺ put him on his own forearms, and there was no bier for him but the Prophet’s arms. A grave was dug, and he put him in it. The report does not mention a washing or a shroud for him.

The story carries one of the clearest signs of the Prophet’s attitude to those on the margins. When he looked for the missing, it was Julaybib he missed, though others had not noticed that he was gone. And the words “from me and I am from him” are among the highest that any Companion received.

facts: In the presence of the Prophet ﷺ
Would you like it for your mother, daughter, sister, aunt?
“O Allah, forgive his sin, purify his heart and guard his chastity”

t: Abu Umamah says: “A young man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: ‘O Messenger of Allah, give me permission to commit fornication.’ The people turned to him and rebuked him, and said: ‘Stop! Stop!’” They were horrified. A man who had said that in front of the Prophet ﷺ seemed to have lost all shame.

But the Prophet ﷺ said: “Bring him near.” The young man came close and sat down. The Prophet ﷺ did not rebuke him or send him away. He had understood something about the question: the young man’s desire was real and he was struggling, but he had also come to the right person to ask. He had not gone away to do it in secret.

The Prophet ﷺ asked: “Would you like it for your mother?” The man said: “No, by Allah. May Allah make me your ransom.” The Prophet ﷺ said: “And people do not like it for their mothers.” Then: “Would you like it for your daughter?” “No, by Allah, O Messenger of Allah.” “And people do not like it for their daughters.” “Would you like it for your sister?” “No.” “And people do not like it for their sisters.” “Would you like it for your paternal aunt?” “No.” “And people do not like it for their paternal aunts.” “Would you like it for your maternal aunt?” “No.” “And people do not like it for their maternal aunts.”

It was not an argument that required a long reply. By the fifth question, the picture was complete. The man had been looking at the act from his own side, and now he was shown it from the side of those who would be harmed. The Prophet ﷺ led him there with his own answers.

Then the Prophet ﷺ placed his hand on the young man’s chest and prayed: “O Allah, forgive his sin, purify his heart, and protect his private parts.” The report ends with a line that tells what it did: “After that, the young man never turned to anything of the kind.”

Scholars have drawn out a number of lessons. First, a person who is tempted should be treated as a patient, not as an enemy. Second, the right way to answer a question that offends is to find what the person actually needs. Third, the Prophet’s dua was as much a part of the cure as the questions. This hadith is often given as an example for parents, teachers and preachers who face the same sort of problem.

facts: A day of festival, in Madinah
In the courtyard of the Prophet’s Mosque
Abyssinians, with spears and small shields

t: ‘A’ishah reports in the two Sahihs: “The Abyssinians were playing with their spears in the mosque on the day of the festival, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called me. I put my head on his shoulder and began to watch their play over his shoulder, until I was the one to tire.”

The Abyssinians, many of whom lived in Madinah, were skilled in the use of spears and shields, and their display was a form of martial dance. They performed on festival days. The mosque in Madinah was a public space, a place for gatherings, delegations and community events, and not only for prayer.

In the narration of Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ was encouraging them. He said: “Carry on, Banu Arfidah,” using the nickname by which the Abyssinians were known. He wanted them to continue. Then ‘Umar entered, and when he saw them, he picked up pebbles to throw at them or struck them. The Prophet ﷺ said: “Leave them, ‘Umar.”

It shows two ways of thinking about a mosque. ‘Umar’s instinct was for the mosque to be quiet. The Prophet ﷺ taught that a permitted entertainment on a festival day, kept within limits, was not a violation. A report in the Musnad of Ahmad, with a weaker chain, adds that he said on the occasion: “So that the Jews know that in our religion there is room for relaxation. I have been sent with a tolerant, easy religion.”

‘A’ishah says: “The Prophet ﷺ was standing for my sake, and I was resting my cheek against his, as he asked: ‘Is that enough, is that enough?’ I kept on saying: ‘Not yet,’ so that I could see how much I meant to him, until I got tired. Then he said: ‘Go.’” In another narration, she adds: “So understand the position of a young girl who wishes to watch for entertainment.”

The sentence is a rare glimpse of the Prophet’s home. He stood in the doorway, on a festival day, and gave his wife time and attention to enjoy something she liked. The Companions who heard it told it for the same reason: a lesson in how to treat a family. The Prophet ﷺ said: “The best of you are the best to their families, and I am the best of you to my family.”

facts: ‘Umar ibn Abi Salamah, the stepson of the Prophet ﷺ, born in Abyssinia
Umm Salamah, wife of the Prophet ﷺ
Say Allah’s name, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is near you
He was a governor of Bahrain under ‘Ali

s.h: A boy in the Prophet’s care
t: ‘Umar was born in Abyssinia, where his parents, Abu Salamah and Umm Salamah, had gone as emigrants. After Abu Salamah died, Umm Salamah married the Prophet ﷺ, and her children lived in his household. ‘Umar was a small boy, and the Prophet ﷺ treated him as a member of the family.

‘Umar says: “I was a boy in the care of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and my hand used to roam about the dish.” He was probably doing what any boy does when eating from a shared bowl, reaching for the bits he liked best. In an Arab household, a common dish was placed in the middle, and everyone ate from it.

The Prophet ﷺ said to him: “O boy, say the name of Allah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is near you.” This is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. ‘Umar adds: “And that remained my way of eating ever after.”

There was no scolding in it, and no mention of his mistake. The Prophet ﷺ taught him what to do, in three short steps that a child could keep in mind. The first gave the meal a spiritual character, since it begins with Allah’s name. The second gave it order and cleanliness. The third gave it consideration for others, since one does not reach across a shared dish.

The scholars have said that this hadith contains the main points of the etiquette of eating. They add other points from other hadith: not to eat from the middle of the dish but from its edge, since the blessing descends in the middle; not to blow on food; to eat what one needs, since a believer fills a third of his stomach with food, a third with drink and leaves a third for breath; and to thank Allah when done.

‘Umar grew up to be a man of reliability, and ‘Ali made him governor of Bahrain and then Persia. He lived to about 83 AH. People remember him less for his offices than for this one detail from the table. It shows how the Prophet ﷺ raised children: not by shaming them, but by giving each moment a small lesson, and by letting it stay.

facts: Banu Sulaym; a recent convert living away from Madinah
Speaking to people breaks the prayer; one says “Alhamdulillah” silently if one sneezes

t: Mu‘awiyah says: “While I was praying with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, a man in the congregation sneezed. I said: ‘Yarhamuka Allah.’ The people looked at me with hard looks. I said: ‘Alas! What is the matter with you, why are you staring at me?’ They began to strike their thighs with their hands. When I saw that they were silencing me, I became angry, but I kept silent.”

It is the way of a person who is new and who has been taught that one says “Yarhamuk Allah” when someone sneezes and praises Allah, which is correct outside the prayer. In the prayer, it is not the right time. The congregation’s reaction was a reasonable one, but it frightened him. He was a man from the desert who had made the effort to come to Madinah, and he felt that he had done something wrong without knowing what.

When the Prophet ﷺ finished the prayer, Mu‘awiyah says: “By my father and mother, I have never seen a teacher before him or after him who taught better than he did. By Allah, he did not rebuke me, he did not hit me, and he did not curse me.”

The Prophet ﷺ said: “In this prayer, nothing from the speech of the people is suitable. It is only tasbih, takbir and the recitation of the Qur’an,” or as he said. The point was complete, and no more was said.

After that, Mu‘awiyah went on to ask about things that had been a burden on him. “O Messenger of Allah, I am a new convert from the age of ignorance, and Allah has brought Islam. Some of us go to soothsayers.” He said: “Do not go to them.” “And some of us practise bird-omens.” He said: “That is something they find in their hearts. Let it not stop you.” “And some of us write in the sand.” He said: “There was a prophet who used to write, so whoever matches his writing, that is fine.” Scholars take this last answer as a way of saying that such practices are not to be followed in any case.

He also told the Prophet ﷺ about a slave girl whom he had struck in anger. He felt bad and wanted to free her. The Prophet ﷺ asked her: “Where is Allah?” She said: “In the heaven.” He asked: “Who am I?” She said: “You are the Messenger of Allah.” He said: “Free her, for she is a believer.” This is in the same chapter of Sahih Muslim. It brings up the manner of the Prophet’s teaching: that a new Muslim could ask him anything, and he would answer.

facts: Abu Hurayrah, in the two Sahihs; also Rifa‘ah ibn Rafi‘ in the Sunan
Take your time in each position, with ease and calm
The hadith of the one who prayed badly (al-musi’ salatah)

t: Abu Hurayrah reports that the Prophet ﷺ entered the mosque, and a man came in and prayed. Then the man came and greeted the Prophet ﷺ, who returned the greeting and said: “Go back and pray, for you have not prayed.” The man went back, prayed as he had before, and came again. The Prophet ﷺ said again: “Go back and pray, for you have not prayed.” This happened three times.

It might seem harsh, and some people wonder why the Prophet ﷺ did not at once explain what was wrong. The scholars say that the first rejection was to make the man pay attention, that the repeated trial was to let him show that he could not do better without teaching, and that a lesson learned after trying is better remembered. He also did not shout or insult the man. He asked him to pray again, and waited.

The man said: “By the One who sent you with the truth, I cannot do better than this. Teach me.” The Prophet ﷺ said: “When you stand for the prayer, say the takbir. Then recite what is easy for you of the Qur’an. Then bow until you are at rest in the bowing. Then rise until you are standing straight. Then prostrate until you are at rest in the prostration. Then rise until you are at rest sitting. Then do that in all of your prayer.”

The key phrase is “until you are at rest”. The Arabic word tuma’ninah means a calm, a stillness in each position, however brief, in which the body settles before moving on. The man had been hurrying from one posture to another so quickly that no position was held. The Prophet ﷺ was not asking for a long prayer. He was asking for a prayer in which one is present.

Elsewhere the Prophet ﷺ called the one who steals from his prayer the worst of thieves. When asked how a person could steal from his prayer, he said that he does not complete its bowing and prostration. In another hadith he said that the prayer of a man who does not straighten his back in bowing and prostration is not sufficient. And Hudhayfah, who saw a man praying like this, said to him in Sahih al-Bukhari: “You have not prayed,” and added that if the man died in that state, he would die on a way other than that of Muhammad.

The hadith is a reminder that the form of prayer carries its meaning. A person who rushes loses the feeling of speaking to Allah. When a Muslim hears “Go back and pray” in his own heart, it is to say that the prayer calls for presence. The Companions who learned this carried it as part of the practice, and scholars have written in detail on what each position involves, all based on this one scene.

facts: ‘A’ishah, in Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah and Ahmad
The Prophet ﷺ won, years later

t: ‘A’ishah says: “I was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a journey, and I was a slim girl. He said to the people: ‘Go on ahead,’ so they went. Then he said to me: ‘Come, let us race.’ I raced him, and I beat him. He said nothing about it.”

The detail that he sent the people ahead is the most important. A man of his position, the Prophet of Allah and the leader of the community, did not hold a race in front of the army. He took his wife aside, away from the others, and played a game with her where nobody would watch. He did not think that it would reduce his standing to race with his wife, and he did not wish to embarrass her in front of the people.

‘A’ishah continues: “Then, when I had put on weight and had forgotten about it, I was with him on another journey. He said to the people: ‘Go on ahead,’ and they went. Then he said to me: ‘Come, let us race.’ I raced him, and he beat me. He began to laugh and said: ‘This for that,’” that is, “this win is for that win.”

It is a sentence of just a few words, and it shows a husband enjoying the memory of an old defeat. He had remembered all those years, through everything that happened in between, the war, the treaties and the delegations, that she had once beaten him on a road. And he had waited for the chance to even the score. ‘A’ishah told it to students of hadith many years afterwards as one of the sweetest memories of her life.

The report is one of a number that describe what the Prophet’s home was like. He used to help with the housework. He mended his own sandals and sewed his clothes. He listened to ‘A’ishah as she told him the long story of Umm Zar‘, and replied that he was to her like Abu Zar‘ to Umm Zar‘. He ate from the same place on a cup that she had drunk from. In the incident of the Abyssinians’ display, he let her watch with her cheek against his.

He said: “The most complete of believers in faith are the best of them in character, and the best of you are the best to their wives.” The race on the road is a sample of what he meant. A man who could be a prophet in the mosque and a playful husband on the road is the example that the Muslims are given.

facts: A Jewish youth who used to serve the Prophet ﷺ
The Prophet ﷺ went to his bedside when he was ill
The boy accepted Islam in front of his father

t: Anas says: “A Jewish boy used to serve the Prophet ﷺ, and he became ill. The Prophet ﷺ went to visit him. He sat by his head and said to him: ‘Become a Muslim.’” The boy’s father was beside him.

The Prophet ﷺ had a rule of visiting the sick, whether friend or neighbour. In another hadith, he listed the rights of a Muslim over another as six: returning a greeting, visiting the sick, following a funeral, accepting an invitation, saying “Yarhamuka Allah” to a sneezer, and giving advice. Here he applied the principle of visiting the sick to a boy of another religion, who had been working in his household.

The boy looked at his father, who was beside him. The father said: “Obey Abu al-Qasim.” “Abu al-Qasim” was the Prophet’s name by which people called him. The boy then said the testimony of faith, that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.

Some of the commentators note that the father’s response shows that the father himself did not stand in the way of his son, and that he had enough respect for the Prophet ﷺ to leave the choice to the boy. The Qur’an teaches that there is no compulsion in religion, and the Prophet ﷺ only invited the boy gently, with his father present. The answer came from within the family.

s.h: What the Prophet ﷺ said as he left
t: The Prophet ﷺ left, saying: “Praise be to Allah who has saved him from the Fire through me.” That is the whole report. He did not boast or claim credit. He thanked Allah, and attributed the thing to Him, though he had been the means.

The scholars derive three rulings from this. First, it is permitted to visit a sick person from another religion, and especially a neighbour or servant, and a good opportunity to speak of faith. Second, a child may enter Islam, especially with the consent of a parent. Third, a believer’s joy is in a person’s guidance, not in an argument won. The Prophet ﷺ had told ‘Ali: “If Allah guides one man through you, it is better for you than red camels.” This scene is an example of the same attitude.

facts: Eleven women of the people of Yemen, in the Age of Ignorance
“I was to you like Abu Zar‘ to Umm Zar‘”
A long story in rhymed, vivid language

t: ‘A’ishah said: “There were eleven women who sat together and pledged and promised that they would not hide anything about their husbands.” The first said: “My husband is the meat of a lean camel on top of a mountain: not an easy road to climb, and not so fat as to be worth carrying.” She was describing a man who was both mean and proud. The second said: “I will not spread the news about my husband. I fear that I could not stop. If I mention him, I will mention all his faults, outer and inner.” The third said: “My husband is the tall one. If I speak, I am divorced, and if I am silent, I am left hanging.”

The fourth said: “My husband is like the night of Tihamah, neither hot nor cold, with neither fear nor weariness.” He was a gentle and easy man. The fifth: “When my husband enters, he is a leopard, and when he goes out he is a lion, and he does not ask about what he knows is in the house.” He was bold outside and easy at home. The sixth said: “My husband, if he eats, he stuffs; if he drinks, he drains; if he lies down, he wraps himself up, and he does not stretch out a hand to know my sorrow.” The seventh: “My husband is the one who cannot get anything right; everything wounds your head or breaks you, or both.”

The eighth said: “My husband: the touch is the touch of a rabbit, and the scent is the scent of the zarnab,” a fragrant plant. The ninth: “My husband is tall of pillar, long of sword-belt, great in ashes, and his house is near the gathering place,” meaning that he is hospitable and noble. The tenth: “My husband is Malik, and what is Malik? Malik is better than anything I can say. He has many camels at home, and few at pasture. When they hear the sound of the lute, they know they are for slaughter,” that is, for entertaining guests.

The eleventh woman was Umm Zar‘. She said: “Abu Zar‘, and what is Abu Zar‘? He hung ornaments on my ears and filled my arms with fat. He pleased me and I became pleased with myself. He found me among a family of sheep-herders in a poor and rocky place, and he took me to a family of horses and camels, who threshed and winnowed. With him, I speak and am not rebuked, I sleep late into the morning, and I drink until I am satisfied.”

She went on to praise his family. “Umm Abu Zar‘, and what is Umm Abu Zar‘? Her storage baskets are full, and her house is spacious. The son of Abu Zar‘, and what is the son of Abu Zar‘? His bed is like a drawn sword, and a lamb’s forearm satisfies him. The daughter of Abu Zar‘, and what is the daughter of Abu Zar‘? She obeys her father and mother, she fills her cloak, and she is the envy of her co-wife. The slave girl of Abu Zar‘, and what is that slave girl? She does not spread our news, she does not waste our food, and she does not fill our house with rubbish.”

Then she told what happened. “One day, when the milk was being churned, Abu Zar‘ went out and met a woman with two sons of hers who were like two leopards, playing with two pomegranates under her waist. He divorced me and married her.” Umm Zar‘ then married a noble man, a rider on a swift horse and carrier of a spear. “He gave me a share of every kind of herd, a pair of each, and said: ‘Eat, Umm Zar‘, and give to your family.’ But if I gathered everything he gave me, it would not fill the smallest vessel of Abu Zar‘.”

‘A’ishah ended: “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: ‘I was to you like Abu Zar‘ to Umm Zar‘.’” In a version found in other collections, with a weaker chain, he added: “Except that he divorced and I do not divorce,” and ‘A’ishah answered that he was better to her than Abu Zar‘ was to Umm Zar‘. In the version of the two Sahihs, the Prophet ﷺ said only the first sentence.

Scholars have written about this hadith for many pages. They ask what the Prophet ﷺ meant. Most say that he meant that he was to her like Abu Zar‘ in his goodness and love, and that he was telling her he valued her as Abu Zar‘ had valued his wife in the early years. Ibn Hajar says it also shows that it is permitted to tell stories and use poetry, for the sake of entertainment, within the household.

It also teaches something about marriages. The women describe the faults and virtues of their husbands with clarity, and the stories show that a woman’s criticisms are often about unkindness and neglect, and her praise is for generosity and good company. The Prophet ﷺ was a listener who took the time to hear a long story from his wife, and answered it with a sentence that she remembered all her life.

guides.title: The pillars of Islam and Iman
guides.blurb: The five pillars of Islam and the six articles of faith, from the hadith of Jibril.

t: To bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. A person enters Islam by saying it with understanding and sincerity.
steps.ar: أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ
steps.tl: Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah, wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulu Allah.

t: Five prayers each day at their times: Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib and Isha. It is the daily link between the servant and Allah.
The obligatory charity paid by those whose savings reach the nisab and have been held for a lunar year, generally 2.5% of the wealth. It purifies wealth and supports those in need (9:60).
Fasting from dawn to sunset in the month of Ramadan, for those who are able, with understanding that the fast is also from wrongdoing in speech and action.
Visiting the Sacred House in Makkah once in a lifetime for those who are able to make the journey (3:97).
Belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the divine decree, its good and its bad. The Prophet ﷺ explained these to Jibril in the well-known hadith (Sahih Muslim).
In the same hadith, ihsan is to worship Allah as though you see Him, for even if you do not see Him, He sees you.

guides.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 8 (the five pillars, Ibn ‘Umar) and Sahih Muslim 8 (the hadith of Jibril, ‘Umar).

guides.title: How to make wudu
guides.blurb: The washing that prepares you for prayer, step by step.

t: Intend in your heart to make wudu for the sake of Allah, and say Bismillah. Use clean water.
Wash both hands up to the wrists, three times, right hand first.
Rinse the mouth and sniff water into the nose and blow it out, three times each.
Wash the whole face from the hairline to the chin and from ear to ear, three times. Run wet fingers through a beard.
Wash the right arm up to and including the elbow, three times, then the left arm.
Wipe over the head once with wet hands, then wipe the ears, inside with the forefingers and outside with the thumbs.
Wash the right foot up to and including the ankle, three times, then the left foot, passing the fingers between the toes.
The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever makes wudu well and then says this, the eight gates of Paradise are opened for him to enter by any he wishes (Sahih Muslim).
steps.ar: أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا عَبْدُهُ وَرَسُولُهُ
steps.tl: Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah wahdahu la sharika lah, wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan ‘abduhu wa rasuluh.

notes: The command is in Surah al-Ma’idah (5:6): wash the face and the arms to the elbows, wipe the head, and wash the feet to the ankles.
Wudu is broken by anything that comes out of the private parts, by deep sleep, and by loss of consciousness. The schools differ on some other matters, such as touching, or eating camel meat.
Do not waste water: the Prophet ﷺ used little water for wudu.
guides.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 159 and Sahih Muslim 226 (the wudu of ‘Uthman, describing the Prophet ﷺ), and Surah al-Ma’idah 5:6.

guides.title: How to pray
guides.blurb: A rak’ah step by step, with the Arabic of what is recited. Small differences between the schools are noted.

t: Be in wudu, wear clean clothes that cover the awrah, and stand facing the qibla, the direction of the Ka’bah. The prayer time must have started.
Intend in your heart which prayer you are praying. Raise your hands to the shoulders or ears and say:
steps.en: Place the right hand over the left on the chest (or below the navel, in the Hanafi view).

t: Many pray this quietly before the recitation:
steps.ar: سُبْحَانَكَ اللَّهُمَّ وَبِحَمْدِكَ وَتَبَارَكَ اسْمُكَ وَتَعَالَى جَدُّكَ وَلَا إِلَٰهَ غَيْرُكَ
steps.tl: Subhanaka Allahumma wa bihamdika wa tabarakasmuka wa ta’ala jadduka wa la ilaha ghayruk.

t: Say “A’udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim”, then Bismillah, then al-Fatihah. Reciting it is a pillar of every rak’ah in most schools.
In the first two rak’ahs of any prayer, recite a surah or some verses after al-Fatihah, for example al-Ikhlas:
Say “Allahu akbar” and bow with your back level and your hands on your knees. Then say three times:
steps.en: Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great.

t: Rise saying “Sami’a Allahu liman hamidah” and, standing, say:
Say “Allahu akbar” and go down so that the forehead and nose, both palms, both knees and the toes touch the ground. Say three times:
steps.en: Glory be to my Lord, the Most High. The Prophet ﷺ said the servant is closest to his Lord in prostration, so make dua there (Sahih Muslim).

t: Sit up saying “Allahu akbar”, and say:
steps.en: My Lord, forgive me. Then prostrate a second time as before.

steps.h: The second rak’ah and the first tashahhud
t: Stand for the second rak’ah and repeat it from al-Fatihah (without the opening supplication). In a prayer of three or four rak’ahs, sit after the second rak’ah and recite the tashahhud:
steps.ar: التَّحِيَّاتُ لِلَّهِ وَالصَّلَوَاتُ وَالطَّيِّبَاتُ، السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكَ أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ وَرَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ وَبَرَكَاتُهُ، السَّلَامُ عَلَيْنَا وَعَلَى عِبَادِ اللَّهِ الصَّالِحِينَ، أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا عَبْدُهُ وَرَسُولُهُ

steps.h: The final sitting: blessings on the Prophet
t: In the last rak’ah, after the tashahhud, send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ:
steps.ar: اللَّهُمَّ صَلِّ عَلَى مُحَمَّدٍ وَعَلَى آلِ مُحَمَّدٍ كَمَا صَلَّيْتَ عَلَى إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَعَلَى آلِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ إِنَّكَ حَمِيدٌ مَجِيدٌ، اللَّهُمَّ بَارِكْ عَلَى مُحَمَّدٍ وَعَلَى آلِ مُحَمَّدٍ كَمَا بَارَكْتَ عَلَى إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَعَلَى آلِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ إِنَّكَ حَمِيدٌ مَجِيدٌ
steps.en: You may then make any dua you wish before ending the prayer.

t: Turn your face to the right, then to the left, saying each time:

notes: Obligatory rak’ahs: Fajr 2, Dhuhr 4, Asr 4, Maghrib 3, Isha 4. Maghrib and Isha’s first two rak’ahs, and Fajr, are recited aloud; Dhuhr and Asr quietly.

The regular sunnah prayers are two before Fajr, four before and two after Dhuhr, two after Maghrib and two after Isha. The Prophet ﷺ said whoever prays twelve rak’ahs in a day, Allah builds him a house in Paradise (Sahih Muslim).
If you are learning, it is fine to start with the shortest recitations. It is better to pray imperfectly than not to pray; ask a teacher to correct you.
guides.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 757 (the hadith of the man who prayed badly), 6251 and Sahih Muslim (tashahhud, sujud, rak’ahs).

guides.title: Friday (Jumu’ah)
guides.blurb: How to make the most of the best day of the week.

t: Take a bath, wear your best clean clothes and perfume (for men), and go early to the mosque. The Prophet ﷺ described the reward as increasing for whoever comes earlier (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
It is recommended to read Surah al-Kahf on Friday. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever does so will have a light between the two Fridays (reported by al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi).

steps.h: Send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ
t: “The best of your days is Friday; so send many blessings upon me on it” (Sunan Abi Dawud, graded sound).

steps.h: Listen to the sermon and pray
t: Two sermons are given before the prayer. Listen in silence; the prayer is two rak’ahs behind the imam. The call to it is described in Surah al-Jumu’ah:

There is an hour on Friday in which a dua is answered (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). Scholars suggest it is after ‘Asr, or while the imam sits between the sermons. Be generous with dua throughout the day.

guides.src: Sahih al-Bukhari 881, 929 and Sahih Muslim 852; Sunan Abi Dawud 1047.

guides.title: Fasting in Ramadan
guides.blurb: What the fast is, who must fast, and how to make the most of the month.

t: Fasting Ramadan is prescribed for the believers in the verse:
Intend the next day’s fast before Fajr, in the night. Eat the pre-dawn meal (suhoor), since the Prophet ﷺ said there is blessing in it (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).

Refrain from eating, drinking and marital relations from the start of Fajr until Maghrib. Guard the tongue and the eyes: the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever does not give up false speech and acting upon it, Allah has no need of his leaving food and drink (Sahih al-Bukhari).
Break the fast as soon as the sun sets, preferably with fresh dates, or else dates or water (Sunan Abi Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, hasan). A dua reported from the Prophet ﷺ when breaking the fast:
steps.ar: ذَهَبَ الظَّمَأُ وَابْتَلَّتِ الْعُرُوقُ وَثَبَتَ الْأَجْرُ إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ
steps.tl: Dhahaba az-zama’u wabtallat il-‘uruqu wa thabata al-ajru in sha’ Allah.
steps.en: The thirst has gone, the veins are moist, and the reward is confirmed, if Allah wills (Sunan Abi Dawud, hasan).

t: The sick, the traveller, women who are menstruating or with postnatal bleeding, and those for whom fasting is a serious hardship (the elderly, some pregnant or nursing women) may be excused. Those who can recover or travel make up the days later; those who cannot give a fidyah of feeding a poor person for each day (2:184). Ask a scholar for your case.
Seek Laylat al-Qadr in the odd nights of the last ten. ‘A’ishah asked the Prophet ﷺ what to say if she found it, and he told her:
steps.ar: اللَّهُمَّ إِنَّكَ عَفُوٌّ تُحِبُّ الْعَفْوَ فَاعْفُ عَنِّي
steps.en: O Allah, You are forgiving and love forgiveness, so forgive me (Sunan at-Tirmidhi, sound).

t: At the end of Ramadan, give zakat al-fitr on behalf of yourself and your dependents before the Eid prayer: a measure of staple food for each person (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). The Prophet ﷺ encouraged fasting six days of Shawwal afterwards (Sahih Muslim).

guides.src: Surah al-Baqarah 2:183–187; Sahih al-Bukhari 1903, 1923; Sunan Abi Dawud 2357; Sunan at-Tirmidhi 3513.

guides.title: The Eid prayer and its sunnahs
guides.blurb: What to do on Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha.

t: Take a bath, wear your best clothes and perfume. On Eid al-Fitr, eat some dates before going out; on Eid al-Adha, it is preferred to eat after the prayer (Sahih al-Bukhari, Sunan at-Tirmidhi).
Say the takbir on the way and until the prayer. A form reported from the Companions:
steps.ar: اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَاللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ وَلِلَّهِ الْحَمْدُ
steps.tl: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, la ilaha illa Allah, wallahu akbar, Allahu akbar, wa lillahil-hamd.

t: Two rak’ahs in congregation, without an adhan or iqamah, with extra takbirs in each rak’ah (the schools differ on their number), followed by a sermon. Everyone is encouraged to attend, including women and children (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).

Greet each other. A form reported from the Companions is “Taqabbala Allahu minna wa minkum” (may Allah accept it from us and from you). The Prophet ﷺ used to return by a different road from the one he took (Sahih al-Bukhari).

Those who are able offer an animal (udhiyah) after the prayer on the 10th of Dhul Hijjah or the three days after it, and share the meat with family and the needy. Fasting on Eid days is not permitted (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).

guides.title: How to perform Umrah
guides.blurb: The lesser pilgrimage, which can be made at any time of the year.

t: Before the miqat (the boundary point) take a bath, put on ihram clothes (two plain white sheets for men; ordinary modest clothes for women), and make the intention for Umrah, saying “Labbayka Allahumma ‘umrah”. From now on avoid the things forbidden in ihram: perfume, cutting hair or nails, covering the head (men), marital relations and hunting.
Repeat the talbiyah as you travel, men aloud:
steps.ar: لَبَّيْكَ اللَّهُمَّ لَبَّيْكَ، لَبَّيْكَ لَا شَرِيكَ لَكَ لَبَّيْكَ، إِنَّ الْحَمْدَ وَالنِّعْمَةَ لَكَ وَالْمُلْكَ، لَا شَرِيكَ لَكَ
steps.tl: Labbayka Allahumma labbayk, labbayka la sharika laka labbayk, innal-hamda wan-ni’mata laka wal-mulk, la sharika lak.

t: Enter al-Masjid al-Haram and begin at the Black Stone, with the Ka’bah on your left, circling seven times. Men uncover the right shoulder (idtiba’) and walk briskly in the first three circuits of the arrival tawaf. Between the Yemeni corner and the Black Stone the Prophet ﷺ used to say:
steps.en: He also said it as his dua between those two corners (Sunan Abi Dawud, hasan).

t: After tawaf, pray two rak’ahs near the Maqam Ibrahim if you can, otherwise anywhere in the mosque. The Prophet ﷺ recited al-Kafirun and al-Ikhlas in them (Sahih Muslim). Then drink Zamzam.
Go to Mount Safa. As you approach it, recite:
steps.en: Face the Ka’bah, praise Allah and make dua, then walk to Marwa. That is one lap. Complete seven laps, ending at Marwa. Men jog between the green markers.

t: Men shave the head or trim the hair; shaving is better. Women trim a fingertip’s length from the ends of their hair. Then the Umrah is complete and the restrictions of ihram end.

notes: Tawaf and sa’i can be tiring. Allow time, drink water, and be gentle with others in the crowds.
Details such as the exact placement of the miqat or what is done if a mistake is made differ in fiqh. Follow your group leader or a scholar.
guides.src: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, chapters on Hajj and Umrah; Surah al-Baqarah 2:158.

guides.title: The days of Hajj
guides.blurb: An outline of the rites, day by day. The Hajj is once in a lifetime for those who can.

t: Tamattu’: perform Umrah first, leave ihram, then enter ihram for Hajj on the 8th. Qiran: Umrah and Hajj together in one ihram. Ifrad: Hajj only. Tamattu’ and qiran require a sacrificial animal.
Enter ihram for Hajj (if in tamattu’) and go to Mina. Pray Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, Isha and Fajr there, shortening the four-rak’ah prayers without combining them.
After sunrise go to Arafah and stay until sunset. This is the essence of the Hajj: “Hajj is Arafah” (Sunan at-Tirmidhi). Make dua at length. The best dua on this day is:
steps.ar: لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ، لَهُ الْمُلْكُ وَلَهُ الْحَمْدُ وَهُوَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ
steps.en: The Prophet ﷺ said the best dua is the dua of the Day of Arafah (Sunan at-Tirmidhi, hasan). Pray Dhuhr and Asr together, shortened, at Arafah.

t: After sunset, go to Muzdalifah without praying Maghrib on the way, then pray Maghrib and Isha together there. Spend the night, pray Fajr, make dua until it is bright, and collect pebbles for stoning.

Go to Mina and do four rites: stone Jamrat al-‘Aqabah with seven pebbles, offer the sacrifice, shave or trim the hair, and then perform Tawaf al-Ifadah at the Ka’bah (with sa’i if you are in tamattu’ or have not yet done it).
Stay at Mina and stone the three jamarat each day after noon, seven pebbles each, beginning with the smallest. You may leave on the 12th after stoning, or stay until the 13th, which is better.
Before leaving Makkah, make a final tawaf, so that the last thing you do is at the House (Sahih Muslim).

notes: Hajj is a big topic with many details. Learn from a qualified guide before you go, and rely on your group’s scholar for rulings during the journey.
The Prophet ﷺ said whoever performs Hajj and does not commit obscenity or transgression returns as on the day his mother bore him (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim).
guides.src: Sahih Muslim 1218 (the hadith of Jabir on the Prophet’s Hajj), and Sahih al-Bukhari, chapters on Hajj.

guides.title: The funeral prayer
guides.blurb: What to do when a Muslim dies: a community duty.

t: When news of a death reaches you, say:
steps.tl: Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji’un.
steps.en: We belong to Allah and to Him we return (2:156).

t: The body is washed by Muslims of the same sex (many scholars allow a husband and wife to wash each other), then wrapped in plain white cloth. This is a community duty (fard kifayah).

It is prayed standing, with four takbirs and no bowing or prostration. After the first takbir, recite al-Fatihah; after the second, send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ as in the tashahhud; after the third, make dua for the deceased; after the fourth, pause briefly and give the salam. A dua reported from the Prophet ﷺ:
steps.ar: اللَّهُمَّ اغْفِرْ لَهُ وَارْحَمْهُ وَعَافِهِ وَاعْفُ عَنْهُ
steps.tl: Allahumma ighfir lahu warhamhu wa ‘afihi wa’fu ‘anhu.
steps.en: O Allah, forgive him, have mercy on him, give him well-being and pardon him (Sahih Muslim).

t: The deceased is buried quickly in the grave, laid on the right side facing the qibla. Those present may throw some earth into the grave and then make dua that he is kept steadfast (Sunan Abi Dawud, sound).
Bring food for the family of the deceased and visit them. Mourning is limited to three days, except for a widow, who observes four months and ten days (2:234; Sahih al-Bukhari 1280).

guides.src: Sahih Muslim 963 and Sahih al-Bukhari, chapters on funerals; Surah al-Baqarah 2:156 and 2:234.

surahIntros.1: The opening of the Book, recited in every rak’ah of the prayer. It praises Allah, affirms that He alone is worshipped and asked for help, and asks for guidance on the straight path.
surahIntros.2: The longest surah, mostly from the first years in Madinah. It lays out guidance for the believers, the story of Adam, Bani Isra’il, Ibrahim and the Ka’bah, the change of the qibla, fasting, Hajj, spending and debts, and ends with Ayat al-Kursi (255) and the last two verses.
surahIntros.3: The family of ‘Imran: the births of Maryam and ‘Isa, the oneness of Allah, and lessons from the Battle of Uhud about patience and obedience.
surahIntros.4: Rights and duties in family and community: women, orphans, inheritance, justice, and how to treat each other with fairness.
surahIntros.5: Among the last surahs revealed. It speaks of keeping covenants, lawful and unlawful food, justice, the table sent down for the disciples of ‘Isa, and the completion of the religion (5:3).
surahIntros.6: The oneness of Allah argued from His creation: the livestock, the stars of Ibrahim’s reflection, and the rejection of idol worship and false prohibitions.
surahIntros.7: The stories of Adam and Iblis and of the prophets Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut, Shu’ayb and Musa, and the “heights” between Paradise and the Fire.
surahIntros.8: Revealed around the Battle of Badr: how to deal with spoils, the value of unity and steadfastness, and trust in Allah in battle.
surahIntros.9: The only surah without the Bismillah. It deals with treaties, the expedition of Tabuk, the hypocrites, and the acceptance of repentance.
surahIntros.10: Allah’s oneness and the truth of the message, the people of Yunus who believed in time, and Musa with Fir’awn.
surahIntros.11: Prophets and their peoples, with the command to stay on the right course: “So remain on a right course as you have been commanded” (11:112).
surahIntros.12: The whole surah tells the story of Yusuf, which the Qur’an calls the best of stories: jealousy, patience, temptation, prison, and forgiveness.
surahIntros.13: Thunder and the signs of Allah in nature, and the verse: “Unquestionably, by the remembrance of Allah hearts find rest” (13:28).
surahIntros.14: Ibrahim’s prayer for Makkah and his offspring, and the promise: “If you are grateful, I will surely increase you” (14:7).
surahIntros.15: The protection of the Qur’an (15:9), the people of al-Hijr, and the story of Adam and Iblis.
surahIntros.16: The bee and the many blessings of Allah, a call to gratitude, and the verse of justice and kindness recited at the end of Friday sermons (16:90).
surahIntros.17: The Night Journey, and a set of commands: kindness to parents, honesty, humility and the avoidance of waste and arrogance (17:23–39).
surahIntros.18: Four stories of trial: the people of the cave, the owner of two gardens, Musa and al-Khidr, and Dhul-Qarnayn. It is recommended to read it on Fridays.
surahIntros.19: Zakariyya and Yahya, Maryam and the birth of ‘Isa, and short accounts of Ibrahim, Musa, Isma’il and Idris.
surahIntros.20: Musa from the burning bush to the confrontation with Fir’awn, the story of Adam, and a consolation for the Prophet ﷺ.
surahIntros.21: The prophets as one community with one message: Musa, Ibrahim, Lut, Nuh, Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Yunus, Zakariyya and Maryam.
surahIntros.22: The call to Hajj raised by Ibrahim, the rites and their meaning, and the first permission to defend against oppression (22:39).
surahIntros.23: The qualities of the successful believers, the stages of human creation, and the messengers who came before.
surahIntros.24: The Verse of Light (35), the manners of the home and community, lowering the gaze, and the false accusation against ‘A’ishah.
surahIntros.25: The Qur’an as the criterion between right and wrong, and the portrait of the servants of the Most Merciful (25:63–76).
surahIntros.26: Prophets and their peoples told with a repeated refrain: Musa, Ibrahim, Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut and Shu’ayb.
surahIntros.27: The ant, Sulayman and the Queen of Sheba, and the stories of Salih, Lut and Musa.
surahIntros.28: The story of Musa from his birth to Madyan and back to Egypt, and the arrogant wealth of Qarun.
surahIntros.29: The spider’s house as an image of weak refuge, and the reminder that faith is tested through trials.
surahIntros.30: The Romans, signs of Allah in creation and love between spouses (30:21), and the call to turn to the upright religion.
surahIntros.31: Luqman’s advice to his son: no partner with Allah, kindness to parents, prayer, patience and humility.
surahIntros.32: The creation of the heavens, earth and humankind, the Day of Resurrection, and the rewards of those who rise at night to pray.
surahIntros.33: The Battle of the Trench, the household of the Prophet ﷺ, the rules of modesty, and the statement that he is the Seal of the Prophets (33:40).
surahIntros.34: Dawud and Sulayman, the people of Saba and their ungrateful end, and the certainty of resurrection.
surahIntros.35: Allah as the Originator of the heavens and earth, and the verse: “Only those fear Allah, from among His servants, who have knowledge” (35:28).
surahIntros.36: The Qur’an’s call to the Hereafter, the messengers sent to a town, and the signs of Allah’s power over death and life.
surahIntros.37: The ranks of angels, and the stories of Nuh, Ibrahim and the sacrifice of his son, Musa and Harun, Ilyas, Lut and Yunus.
surahIntros.38: Dawud, Sulayman and Ayyub, the story of Adam and Iblis, and the contrast between the pious and the transgressors.
surahIntros.39: Sincere worship of Allah alone, the groups led to Paradise and the Fire, and the verse of hope: “Do not despair of the mercy of Allah” (39:53).
surahIntros.40: Allah as the Forgiver of sin, and the believing man of Fir’awn’s household who defended Musa.
surahIntros.41: The Qur’an explained in Arabic, the signs in creation, and the advice to repel evil with what is better (41:34).
surahIntros.42: Consultation as a trait of the believers, the nature of revelation, and the verse: “There is nothing like Him” (42:11).
surahIntros.43: Ornaments and worldly show, Ibrahim’s declaration of faith, Musa and ‘Isa, and the Hereafter’s friendships.
surahIntros.44: The Qur’an revealed in a blessed night, the warning of a day of smoke, and the fate of Fir’awn.
surahIntros.45: The signs in the heavens and earth, the people who kneel on the Day of Judgment, and the record of deeds.
surahIntros.46: The people of ‘Ad and their sand dunes, the jinn who listened to the Qur’an, and the dua of one who reaches forty (46:15).
surahIntros.47: Fighting in defence, steadfastness, the hypocrites, and reflecting on the Qur’an. It names the Prophet ﷺ directly.
surahIntros.48: The victory and peace after Hudaybiyyah, the pledge under the tree, and the calm sent down on the believers’ hearts.
surahIntros.49: The manners of a community: respect for the Prophet ﷺ, checking news, avoiding mockery and backbiting, and the verse: “The most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous” (49:13).
surahIntros.50: Resurrection and the two angels who record, and the reminder that Allah is nearer than the jugular vein (50:16).
surahIntros.51: The winds, the guests of Ibrahim, and the statement that humans and jinn were created to worship Allah (51:56).
surahIntros.52: Mount Tur, the Day of Judgment, and the reward of the believers and their families.
surahIntros.53: The Prophet’s vision of Jibril and his ascent, and the call to bow and prostrate at the end.
surahIntros.54: The splitting of the moon, the destruction of earlier peoples, and the refrain: “We have made the Qur’an easy for remembrance.”
surahIntros.55: Allah’s blessings in creation and the Hereafter, with the refrain: “So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?”
surahIntros.56: The Event of the Day of Judgment and the three groups of people: the foremost, the companions of the right and the left.
surahIntros.57: Iron as a symbol of strength, the call to spend in Allah’s cause, and the true value of this worldly life (57:20).
surahIntros.58: The woman (Khawlah) who pleaded with the Prophet ﷺ about her husband, and the manners of gatherings and private counsel.
surahIntros.59: The exile of Banu Nadir, and the closing verses that list many of the Names of Allah.
surahIntros.60: The woman who is tested, the example of Ibrahim, and how to treat those who did not fight the believers.
surahIntros.61: The ranks: believers should act on what they say, and ‘Isa gave glad tidings of a messenger named Ahmad (61:6).
surahIntros.62: The Friday prayer: respond to the call and leave trade, then spread through the land and remember Allah much.
surahIntros.63: The traits of the hypocrites, and the warning that wealth and children should not distract from remembering Allah.
surahIntros.64: The Day of Mutual Loss and Gain, and the reminder that spouses and children can be a trial.
surahIntros.65: The rules of divorce and the waiting period, with repeated calls to taqwa: “Whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out” (65:2).
surahIntros.66: A matter in the Prophet’s household, repentance, and Maryam and Asiya as examples for believers.
surahIntros.67: The sovereignty of Allah, the creation of death and life as a test, and reflection on the heavens. The Prophet ﷺ said it intercedes for its reader (Sunan at-Tirmidhi).
surahIntros.68: The pen, the Prophet’s great character (68:4), and the lesson of the owners of the garden.
surahIntros.69: The Inevitable Reality, the fate of ‘Ad, Thamud and Fir’awn, and the truth of the Qur’an.
surahIntros.70: The stairways of ascent, patience, and the qualities of those who are saved: prayer, charity and trustworthiness.
surahIntros.71: Nuh’s long call to his people, his dua, and its outcome.
surahIntros.72: The jinn who heard the Qur’an and believed, and the Prophet’s duty to convey.
surahIntros.73: The wrapped one: the command to rise at night, recite the Qur’an in measured tones, and bear a weighty word.
surahIntros.74: The cloaked one: an early command to rise and warn, to glorify his Lord, purify his clothes and be patient.
surahIntros.75: Resurrection, the fingertips Allah can restore, and the moment of death.
surahIntros.76: The human being, and the righteous who give food to the needy, orphan and captive for Allah’s sake alone (76:8).
surahIntros.77: The winds sent forth, with the repeated warning: “Woe that Day to the deniers.”
surahIntros.78: The Great News of resurrection, the Day of Decision, and the signs of Allah’s power.
surahIntros.79: Those who pull out souls, the confrontation of Musa and Fir’awn, and the coming of the Hour.
surahIntros.80: He frowned: a gentle correction when the blind man ‘Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum came to the Prophet ﷺ, and a reminder that the Qur’an is for all who fear Allah.
surahIntros.81: The folding up of the sun and the signs of the Last Day, and the truth of the Qur’an as the word of a noble messenger.
surahIntros.82: The cleaving of the heavens, and the angels who record every deed.
surahIntros.83: A warning against cheating in weights and measures, and the picture of the sinners and the righteous in the Hereafter.
surahIntros.84: The splitting of the sky, and the book of deeds taken in the right hand or from behind. It has a verse of prostration.
surahIntros.85: The oath by the constellations and the story of the People of the Ditch who were persecuted for their belief.
surahIntros.86: The night comer, the creation of humankind, and the Qur’an as a decisive word.
surahIntros.87: Glorify your Lord, the Most High. The Prophet ﷺ used to recite it in the Friday and Eid prayers and in Witr (Sahih Muslim, Sunan Abi Dawud).
surahIntros.88: The overwhelming Day, Paradise and the Fire, and a call to look at the camel, the sky, the mountains and the earth.
surahIntros.89: The dawn, the fates of ‘Ad, Thamud and Fir’awn, and the call to the tranquil soul to return to its Lord.
surahIntros.90: The city of Makkah, and the steep path: freeing a slave, feeding in a time of hunger, being among those who believe and enjoin patience.
surahIntros.91: The sun and the soul: whoever purifies it has succeeded, and whoever corrupts it has failed.
surahIntros.92: The night, and two paths: one who gives and fears Allah, and one who is stingy and thinks himself self-sufficient.
surahIntros.93: The morning brightness: Allah’s reassurance to the Prophet ﷺ, and His command to care for the orphan and the beggar.
surahIntros.94: The opening of the chest and the promise: “So, surely with hardship comes ease” (94:5–6).
surahIntros.95: The fig and the olive, and the creation of the human being in the best of forms.
surahIntros.96: The first five verses revealed to the Prophet ﷺ in the cave of Hira: “Read in the name of your Lord who created.”
surahIntros.97: The Night of Power, which is better than a thousand months.
surahIntros.98: The clear evidence, and the call to sincere worship of Allah, prayer and zakat.
surahIntros.99: The earthquake of the Last Day, and the accounting of even an atom’s weight of good or evil.
surahIntros.100: The charging horses, and a reproach to the human who is ungrateful to his Lord.
surahIntros.101: The Striking Calamity, the weighing of deeds, and the heavy and light scales.
surahIntros.102: The competition in wealth and numbers that keeps people from the Hereafter until the grave.
surahIntros.103: Time: all of humankind is in loss, except those who believe, do good, and advise each other to truth and patience.
surahIntros.104: A warning against the one who slanders and hoards wealth.
surahIntros.105: The story of Abraha’s army with its elephant, which was destroyed in the year the Prophet ﷺ was born.
surahIntros.106: The security Allah gave Quraysh in their trade journeys, and the call to worship the Lord of this House.
surahIntros.107: The one who denies the Judgment, harshly pushes away the orphan and does not encourage feeding the poor, and the heedless in prayer.
surahIntros.108: The shortest surah: the abundance Allah gave to the Prophet ﷺ, and the command to pray and sacrifice for Him.
surahIntros.109: A clear declaration of worship: “For you is your religion, and for me is my religion.”
surahIntros.110: The help of Allah and the conquest, and the command to glorify and seek forgiveness. It was among the last revealed.
surahIntros.111: The fate of Abu Lahab, an uncle of the Prophet ﷺ who opposed him.
surahIntros.112: The oneness of Allah in four verses. The Prophet ﷺ said it equals a third of the Qur’an (Sahih al-Bukhari).
surahIntros.113: Seeking refuge with the Lord of daybreak from evil. The Prophet ﷺ recited it with the next surah before sleeping (Sahih al-Bukhari).
surahIntros.114: Seeking refuge with the Lord of mankind from the whisperer who withdraws when Allah is remembered.
